Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Namakkārapāḷi

The Text on Veneration

1.

1.

Sugataṃ [M 0.0001] sugataṃ seṭṭhaṃ, kusalaṃkusalaṃ jahaṃ;

Amataṃ amataṃ santaṃ, asamaṃ asamaṃ dadaṃ.

To the Well-Gone One, the supreme good destiny; to the Wholesome One, who abandons the unwholesome; to the Deathless One, the tranquil Deathless; to the Unequaled One, who gives the unequaled.

Saraṇaṃ saraṇaṃ lokaṃ, araṇaṃ araṇaṃ karaṃ;

Abhayaṃ abhayaṃ ṭhānaṃ, nāyakaṃ nāyakaṃ name.

The refuge for the world, the ultimate refuge; the peacemaker, who brings non-conflict; the fearless one, the state of fearlessness; to the leader, the true leader, I pay homage.

2.

2.

Nayanasubhagakāyaṅgaṃ,

Madhuravarasaropetaṃ;

Amitaguṇagaṇādhāraṃ,

Dasabalamatulaṃ vande.

I venerate the one whose body and limbs are beautiful to the eyes, endowed with a sweet and excellent voice, the repository of a host of immeasurable virtues, the incomparable one possessing the ten powers.

3.

3.

Yo buddho dhitimāññadhārako,

Saṃsāre anubhosi kāyikaṃ;

Dukkhaṃ cetasikañca lokato,

Taṃ vande naradevamaṅgalaṃ.

That Buddha, resolute, a bearer of final knowledge, who in saṃsāra experienced bodily and mental suffering for the sake of the world—him, the blessing for humans and gods, I venerate.

4.

4.

Bāttiṃsatilakkhaṇacitradehaṃ,

Dehajjutiniggatapajjalantaṃ;

Paññādhitisīlaguṇoghavindaṃ,

Vande munimantimajātiyuttaṃ.

I venerate the sage whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks, blazing with the radiance issuing from his body, possessor of the flood of virtues such as wisdom, energy, and morality, the sage endowed with his final birth.

5.

5.

Pātodayaṃ bāladivākaraṃva,

Majjhe yatīnaṃ lalitaṃ sirīhi;

Puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhaṃ anejaṃ,

Vandāmi sabbaññumahaṃ munindaṃ.

Like the newly risen morning sun, graceful with splendors amidst the ascetics, whose face is like the full moon, unperturbed—that all-knowing lord of sages I venerate.

6.

6.

Upetapuñño [M 0.0002] varabodhimūle,

Sasenamāraṃ sugato jinitvā;

Abojjhi bodhiṃ aruṇodayamhi,

Namāmi taṃ mārajinaṃ abhaṅgaṃ.

Endowed with merit, at the foot of the excellent Bodhi tree, the Well-Gone One, having conquered Māra with his army, awakened to enlightenment at the break of dawn. I bow to that unbreakable conqueror of Māra.

7.

7.

Rāgādichedāmalañāṇakhaggaṃ,

Satīsamaññāphalakābhigāhaṃ;

Sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ taṃ,

Namāmibhiññāvaramiddhupetaṃ.

To him who wields the sword of stainless wisdom that severs lust and other defilements, who has grasped the shield of mindfulness and clear comprehension, who is adorned with the ornament of the flood of virtue, endowed with supreme supernormal knowledge and psychic power—to him I bow.

8.

8.

Dayālayaṃ sabbadhi dukkaraṃ karaṃ,

Bhavaṇṇavātikkamamaggataṃ gataṃ;

Tilokanāthaṃ susamāhitaṃ hitaṃ,

Samantacakkhuṃ paṇamāmi taṃmitaṃ.

The abode of compassion, who everywhere performs what is difficult to do; who has gone by the path that transcends the ocean of existence; the Lord of the Three Worlds, well-composed and beneficent; the one with all-around vision—to him, the immeasurable one, I pay homage.

9.

9.

Tahiṃ tahiṃ pāramisañcayaṃ cayaṃ,

Gataṃ gataṃ sabbhi sukhappadaṃ padaṃ;

Narānarānaṃ sukhasambhavaṃ bhavaṃ,

Namānamānaṃ jinapuṅgavaṃ gavaṃ.

He who here and there accumulated the collection of perfections; who has gone to the state that gives happiness to the good; whose existence is the source of happiness for humans and non-humans—to that bull among victors, the eminent one, I repeatedly bow.

10.

10.

Maggaṅganāvaṃ munidakkhanāviko,

Īhāphiyaṃ ñāṇakarena gāhako;

Āruyha yo tāya bahū bhavaṇṇavā,

Tāresi taṃ buddhamaghappahaṃ name.

The sage is the skilled ferryman of the ship of the path factors; effort is the oar and wisdom the rudder. He who, having boarded it, ferried many across the ocean of existence—to that Buddha, the dispeller of evil, I bow.

11.

11.

Samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇaṃ,

Varabodhidume catusaccadasaṃ;

Varamiddhigataṃ naradevahitaṃ,

Tibhavūpasamaṃ paṇamāmi jinaṃ.

I bow to the Victor, who fulfilled the thirty perfections, who saw the Four Truths under the excellent Bodhi tree, who attained excellent psychic powers, the benefactor of humans and gods, the pacifier of the three realms of existence.

12.

12.

Satapuññajalakkhaṇikaṃ virajaṃ,

Gaganūpamadhiṃ dhitimerusamaṃ;

Jalajūpamasītalasīlayutaṃ,

Pathavīsahanaṃ paṇamāmi jinaṃ.

I bow to the Victor, stainless, marked by the hundred signs born of merit, whose wisdom is like the sky, whose resolution is like Mount Meru, endowed with virtue as cool as a lotus, and as patient as the earth.

13.

13.

Yo [M 0.0003] buddho sumati dive divākarova,

Sobhanto ratijanane silāsanamhi;

Āsīno sivasukhadaṃ adesi dhammaṃ,

Devānaṃ tamasadisaṃ namāmi niccaṃ.

That Buddha of good wisdom, who, like the sun in the sky, sat shining on the delightful stone seat and taught the Dhamma that gives blissful happiness to the gods—to him, the unequaled one, I always bow.

14.

14.

Yo pādapaṅkajamuduttalarājikehi,

Lokehi tīhivikalehi nirākulehi;

Sampāpuṇe nirupameyyatameva nātho,

Taṃ sabbalokamahitaṃ asamaṃ namāmi.

The Lord whose lotus feet are worshipped by the flawless and untroubled three worlds headed by their supreme kings, who has attained a truly incomparable state—to him, honored by all the world, the unequaled one, I bow.

15.

15.

Buddhaṃ narānarasamosaraṇaṃ dhitattaṃ,

Paññāpadīpajutiyā vihatandhakāraṃ;

Atthābhikāmanaradevahitāvahaṃ taṃ,

Vandāmi kāruṇikamaggamanantañāṇaṃ.

I venerate the Buddha, the refuge for humans and gods, of resolute mind, who has dispelled the darkness with the radiance of the lamp of wisdom, who brings the welfare desired by humans and gods—the compassionate one, the supreme, of infinite wisdom.

16.

16.

Akhilaguṇanidhāno yo munindopagantvā,

Vanamisipatanavhaṃ saññatānaṃ niketaṃ;

Tahimakusalachedaṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavatto,

Tamatulamabhikantaṃ vandaneyyaṃ namāmi.

He who is the Lord of Sages, a treasury of all virtues, having gone to the wood named Isipatana, the abode of the self-restrained, there set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, which severs the unwholesome—to him, the incomparable, the excellent, the venerable, I bow.

17.

17.

Suciparivāritaṃ surucirappabhāhi rattaṃ,

Sirivisarālayaṃ gupitamindriyehupetaṃ;

Ravisasimaṇḍalappabhutilakkhaṇopacittaṃ,

Suranarapūjitaṃ sugatamādaraṃ namāmi.

I respectfully bow to the Well-Gone One, who is surrounded by the pure, glowing with exceedingly beautiful radiance, an abode of widespread glory, endowed with guarded sense faculties, adorned with marks having the splendor of the orbs of the sun and moon, and worshipped by gods and humans.

18.

18.

Maggoḷumpena muhapaṭighāsādiullolavīciṃ,

Saṃsāroghaṃ tari tamabhayaṃ pārapattaṃ pajānaṃ;

Tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ asamasaraṇaṃ ekatitthaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ,

Puññakkhettaṃ paramasukhadaṃ dhammarājaṃ namāmi.

He who crossed the flood of saṃsāra—with its tossing waves of delusion, aversion, and craving—by means of the raft of the path, and reached the further shore, the fearless state for all beings; who is a protection, a shelter, an unequaled refuge, a unique ford, and a firm support—to that King of Dhamma, the field of merit, the giver of supreme happiness, I bow.

19.

19.

Kaṇḍambaṃmūle parahitakaro yo munindo nisinno,

Accheraṃ sīghaṃ nayanasubhagaṃ ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ;

Dujjāladdhaṃsaṃ munibhijahitaṃ pāṭiheraṃ akāsi,

Vande taṃ seṭṭhaṃ paramaratijaṃ iddhidhammehupetaṃ.

The Lord of Sages, benefactor of others, who sat at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree and performed the Twin Miracle—a wonder, swift, beautiful to the eyes, a net of fire and water that destroys the evil snares of heretics—I venerate that supreme one, born of supreme delight, endowed with psychic power and the Dhamma.

20.

20.

Munindakko [M 0.0004] yveko dayudayaruṇo ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo,

Vineyyappāṇoghaṃ kamalakathitaṃ dhammaraṃsīvarehi;

Subodhesī suddhe tibhavakuhare byāpitakkittinañca,

Tilokekaccakkhuṃ dukhamasahanaṃ taṃ mahesiṃ namāmi.

The one Lord of Sages, the rising sun of compassion, whose orb of wisdom is vast; who with the excellent rays of the Dhamma fully awakened the flood of trainable beings, spoken of as lotuses; whose fame pervades the pure cavern of the three realms of existence; the one eye for the three worlds, unshaken by suffering—to that great seer, I bow.

21.

21.

Yo jino anekajātiyaṃ saputtadāramaṅgajīvitampi,

Bodhipemato alaggamānaso adāsiyeva atthikassa;

Dānapāramiṃ tato paraṃ apūri sīlapāramādikampi,

Tāsamiddhiyopayātamaggataṃ tamekadīpakaṃ namāmi.

That Victor who, in many births, out of love for enlightenment and with unattached mind, gave his children, wife, limbs, and even his life to those in need; who thereby fulfilled the perfection of giving and then also the perfections of morality and so on; who reached the supreme state through the success of these perfections—to him, the one beacon, I bow.

22.

22.

Devādevātidevaṃ nidhanavapudharaṃ mārabhaṅgaṃ abhaṅgaṃ,

Dīpaṃ dīpaṃ pajānaṃ jayavarasayane bodhipattaṃdhipattaṃ;

Brahmābrahmāgatānaṃ varagirakathikaṃ pāpahīnaṃ pahīnaṃ,

Lokālokābhirāmaṃ satatamabhiname taṃ munindaṃ munindaṃ.

The God beyond gods, bearer of the final body, the breaker of Māra, the unbreakable; the lamp and island for beings, who attained supreme enlightenment on the excellent seat of victory; whose excellent speech is praised by Brahmās, who has utterly abandoned all evil; the delight of all worlds—to him, the lord of sages, the foremost sage, I always bow.

23.

23.

Buddho nigrodhabimbo mudukaracaraṇo brahmaghoseṇijaṅgho,

Kosacchādaṅgajāto punarapi sugato suppatiṭṭhitapādo;

Mūdodātuṇṇalomo athamapi sugato brahmujuggattabhāvo,

Nīlakkhī dīghapaṇhī sukhumamalachavī thomyarasaggasaggī.

The Buddha has the proportions of a banyan tree, soft hands and feet, a voice like Brahmā, and legs like an antelope; his private parts are concealed in a sheath, his feet are well-placed, his body hairs grow upwards, his body is divinely straight, he has deep blue eyes, long heels, fine and smooth skin, and a supreme sense of taste.

24.

24.

Cattālīsaggadanto samakalapanajo antaraṃsappapīno,

Cakkenaṅkitapādo aviraḷadasano mārajussaṅkhapādo.

He has forty teeth, which are even and without gaps; the flesh between his shoulders is full; his feet are marked with wheels and his ankles are well-set.

Tiṭṭhanto [M 0.0005] nonamantobhayakaramudunā jaṇṇukānāmasanto,

Vaṭṭakkhandho jino gotaruṇapakhumako sīhapubbaḍḍhakāyo.

The Victor, when standing upright without bending, can touch his knees with both hands; he has a rounded torso, a chest like a lion, and eyelashes like a heifer.

25.

25.

Sattappīno ca dīghaṅguli matha sugato lomakūpekalomo,

Sampannodātadāṭho kanakasamataco nīlamuddhaggalomo.

He has seven convex surfaces and long fingers and toes; the Well-Gone One has one hair per pore, very white canine teeth, skin with a golden sheen, and deep blue-black hair on the crown of his head.

Sambuddho thūlajivho atha sīhahanuko jālikappādahattho,

Nātho uṇhīsasīso itiguṇasahitaṃ taṃ mahesiṃ namāmi.

The Perfectly Enlightened One has a long and broad tongue and a jaw like a lion; the Protector's hands and feet are webbed, and his head has a cranial protuberance. I bow to that Great Sage endowed with these virtues.

26.

26.

Buddhobuddhotighoso atidulabhataro kā kathā buddhabhāvo,

Loke tasmā vibhāvī vividhahitasukhaṃ sādhavo patthayantā.

The very sound 'Buddha, Buddha' is exceedingly rare; what then is to be said of the state of Buddhahood? Therefore, the good in the world, aspiring for it, should bring about diverse welfare and happiness.

Iṭṭhaṃ atthaṃ vahantaṃ suranaramahitaṃ nibbhayaṃ dakkhiṇeyyaṃ,

Lokānaṃ nandivaḍḍhaṃ dasabalamasamaṃ taṃ namassantu niccaṃ.

May they always pay homage to him, who brings what is wished for and beneficial, who is honored by gods and humans, fearless, worthy of offerings, who increases the joy of the worlds, the unequaled one possessing the ten powers.

27.

27.

Puññenetena sohaṃ nipuṇamati sato samparāye ca titto,

Dakkho diṭṭhujjupañño avikalavīriyo bhogavā saṃvibhāgī.

By this merit, may I be of skillful intellect and mindful, content in the future life, skillful, of upright view and wisdom, of unimpaired energy, wealthy, and one who shares.

Tikkho sūro dhitatto saparahitacaro dīghajīvī arogo,

Dhañño vaṇṇo yasassī atibalavadharo kittimā khantupeto.

May I be sharp, heroic, resolute, acting for my own and others' welfare, long-lived and free from illness, fortunate, of good appearance, famous, possessing great strength, renowned, and endowed with patience.

28.

28.

Saddho [M 0.0006] dātaṅgupeto paramasiridharo diṭṭhadhamme viratto,

Lajjī kalyāṇamitto abhiratakusalo pañcasīlādirakkho.

May I be faithful, endowed with the qualities of a donor, a bearer of supreme glory, dispassionate towards the present life, conscientious, a good friend, delighting in what is wholesome, and a guardian of the five precepts and so on.

Appiccho appakodho ativujuhadayo iddhimā appameyyo,

Pāsaṃso pemavāco sujanaguṇavidū māmako so bhaveyyaṃ.

May I be of few wishes, with little anger, with an exceedingly straight heart, possessing psychic power, immeasurable, praiseworthy, of loving speech, and a knower of the virtues of good people; may I become such a one.

29.

29.

Itthaṃ asaṅkhaye nātha, guṇe lakkhaṇadīpite;

Gāthāsu sūcakāsveka, gāthampi sarate budho.

If a wise person remembers even a single stanza from among these verses that indicate the innumerable virtues and illuminating marks of the Protector,

30.

30.

Caturāpāyamutto so, sādhakatthadvayassa ca;

Hatūpaddavajālo ca, lābhī hitasukhassa ca.

he is freed from the four woeful states, accomplishes the twofold benefit, destroys the net of calamities, and gains welfare and happiness.

31.

31.

Adhipo naradevānaṃ, catudīpissaropi vā;

Bhaveyya antime dehe, tamaññaṃ setachattakaṃ.

He becomes a lord of human kings or even the ruler of the four continents. In his final body, he would be an unequaled one under the white parasol.

32.

32.

Bhāvanāyānamāruyha, samamessati subbato;

Imasmiṃ attabhāvepi, arogo dīghajīviko.

Having mounted the vehicle of mental development, the virtuous one will attain peace. Even in this very life, he will be free from illness and long-lived.

33.

33.

Pūjito sabbalokehi, bhāvanābhiratīmano;

Janappiyo manāpo ca, kā kathākhiladhāraṇe.

He is worshipped by all worlds, his mind delights in mental development, and he is dear and beloved to people—what then is to be said of his complete retention of these teachings?

Namakkārapāḷi niṭṭhitā.

The Text on Homage is concluded.

Namakkāraṭīkā

The Subcommentary on the Homage

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

1.

1.

Sugatantyādivaṇṇehi[M 0.0007], pasatthañca sukhaddadaṃ;

Vandantānaṃ jinaṃ natvā, dhammaṃ suddhaṃ gaṇuttamaṃ.

Having bowed to the Victor—praised with qualities beginning with 'Sugata' and the giver of happiness to those who pay homage—and to the pure Dhamma and the most excellent Sangha.

2.

2.

Namakkāraṃ hitatthīhi, porāṇācariyehi ca;

Likhitvā ṭhapitaṃ puñña, buddhiyā tena vandinaṃ.

This Homage was written and established by the ancient teachers, who sought the welfare of others, for the sake of merit and for the wisdom of those who pay homage.

3.

3.

Tassatthavaṇṇanaṃ kassaṃ, gambhīratthasubodhanaṃ;

Movipunāmena santena, sīlupetena yācito.

I will compose an explanation of its meaning—profound in meaning and easy to understand—having been requested to do so by the peaceful Movipu, who is endowed with virtue.

4.

4.

Vaṇṇantopi ca tassatthaṃ, taṃ taṃ aṭṭhakathādisu;

Vuttañāyena kassāmi, saddhā suṇātha sādhavo.

And in explaining its meaning, I will do so according to the method stated in the various commentaries and other works. O good people, listen with faith.

5.

5.

Namanaṃ namatītī vā, namatī tena vā namo;

Tassa kāronti tāhīti, namakkāroti vuccati.

It is the act of bowing (namanaṃ); or, because one bows (namati), or because one bows by means of it, it is 'namo.' It is called 'namakkāro' (homage) because it is the making (kāro) of that (tassa).

6.

6.

Tañca buddhaghosācari, yena pubbasutaṃ kataṃ;

Buddhaghosuppattiyañca, taṃ taṃ pana kathādisu.

[It is said that] this was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa, as has been heard before, and is found in the Buddhaghosuppatti and in various other stories.

7.

7.

Na diṭṭhaṃ katakāraṇaṃ, tasmā hitatthikehi ca;

Porāṇācariyehī ca, ṭhapitanti mayā vuttaṃ;

Taṃ kāraṇaṃ viññūhī ca, vicāretvā vijānitanti.

The reason for its composition is not seen. Therefore, I have said that it was established by those who seek the welfare of others and by the ancient teachers. That reason should be investigated and understood by the wise.

1.

1.

Sugataṃ sugataṃ seṭṭhaṃ, kusalaṃkusalaṃ jahaṃ;

Amataṃ amataṃ santaṃ, asamaṃ asamaṃ dadaṃ.

To the Well-Gone One (sugataṃ), who has gone well (sugataṃ), the best; to the Skillful One (kusalaṃ), who abandons the unskillful (akusalaṃ); to the Deathless One (amataṃ), who has attained the deathless (amataṃ), the peaceful; to the Incomparable One (asamaṃ), who gives the incomparable (asamaṃ).

Saraṇaṃ saraṇaṃ lokaṃ, araṇaṃ araṇaṃ karaṃ;

Abhayaṃ abhayaṃ ṭhānaṃ, nāyakaṃ nāyakaṃ name.

To the Refuge of the world, who makes a refuge; to the one without conflict, who brings an end to conflict; to the Fearless One, the fearless state; to the Leader, the true leader, I pay homage.

1. [Ka] idāni [M 0.0008] paṭhamaṃ tāva sugatantyādīhi aṭṭhārasahi guṇehi thometvā buddhassa vanditukāmena sugatantiādi gāthādvayaṃ āraddhaṃ. Ayaṃ pana sabbapādādiyamakapathyā vattagāthāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃ pana yamakaṃ subodhālaṅkāre kiliṭṭhadosanti vuttaṃ.

1. Now, in the first place, one who wished to pay homage to the Buddha composed the pair of verses beginning with "Sugata," having praised him with the eighteen qualities beginning with "Sugata." This, however, should be understood as a vattagāthā of the pathyā type with yamaka at the beginning of every foot. But in the Subodhālaṅkāra, that kind of yamaka is said to be the "fault of obscurity."

Vuttañhi tattha –

For it was said there:

“Yaṃ kiliṭṭhapadaṃ mandā, bhidheyyaṃ yamakādikaṃ;

Kiliṭṭhapadadoseva, tampi anto karīyatī”ti.

"Whatever has obscure and dull phrasing, and yamaka and the like that are difficult to analyze, that too is included within the fault of obscure phrasing."

Ayaṃ panettha patītasaddaracitattāyeva pasādaguṇa saṅkhātena saddālaṅkārena saṃyuttā hoti. Tasmā taṃ yamakaṃ suvuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ parāsu yamakagāthāsu. Tena vuttaṃ punā laṅkāre –

Here, however, precisely because it is composed of pleasing sounds, this verse is endowed with the sound-ornament known as the quality of lucidity. Therefore, that yamaka should be understood as well-spoken. The same applies to other yamaka verses. Thus it is said again in the Alaṅkāra:

“Patītasaddaracitaṃ, siliṭṭhapadasandhikaṃ;

Pasādaguṇasaṃyuttaṃ, yamakaṃ matamedisa”nti.

"Composed of pleasing sounds, with smooth conjunctions of words, and endowed with the quality of lucidity—such a yamaka is considered acceptable."

Tattha sugatanti sobhanagamanattā sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā sammā gatattā ca sugato, so hi sobhanaṃ ariyamaggena gacchatīti sugatoti vuccati, supubbo gamudhātu ta. Susaddo sobhanattho. Ariyamaggagamanena parisuddhaṃ anavajjaṃ khemaṃ disaṃ asajjamāno gatoti attho. Tañca gamanaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti kāyagamanaṃ, ñāṇagamanañcāti. Tattha bhagavato veneyyajanupasaṅkamanaṃ ekantena tesaṃ hitasukhassa nipphāda nato sobhanaṃ kāyena gamanaṃ kāyagamanaṃ nāma. Sayambhū ñāṇena pana sakalampi lokaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena parijānanato ñāṇena gamanaṃ ñāṇagamanaṃ nāma. Idha pana ñāṇagamanaṃ adhippetaṃ. Aṅguttaraṭīkāyaṃ pana “sobhanaṃ gataṃ gamanaṃ etassāti sugato”ti vuttaṃ. Sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchatīti sugatoti ca vuccati, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena amataṃ nibbānaṃ gatoti [M 0.0009] attho. Sammā aviparītaṃ cesa gacchatīti sugatoti vuccati. Susaddo sammāsaddattho. Tena tena maggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti attho. Atha vā sammā āgacchatīti sugatoti ca vuccati, dīpaṅkarapādamūlato pabhuti yāva bodhimaṇḍā tāva samatiṃsapāramipūrikāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sabbalokassa hitasukhameva karonto sassataṃ ucchedaṃ kāmasukhaṃ attakilamathañcāti ime cante anupagacchanto āgatoti attho. Taṃ sugataṃ buddhaṃ name namāmīti sambandho.

Therein, "Sugata" means one who has gone well, one who has gone to a beautiful place, and one who has gone rightly. He is called "Sugata" because he goes well by way of the noble path. The root is gam with the prefix su and the suffix ta. The word su means "beautiful." The meaning is that he has gone by way of the noble path to a destination that is purified, blameless, and secure, without getting stuck. That going is twofold: bodily going and going by knowledge. Here, the Blessed One's approaching those who can be trained is entirely for the purpose of effecting their welfare and happiness; this beautiful going with the body is called "bodily going." Then, by means of his self-originated knowledge, he fully understands the entire world through the aspects of full understanding and realization; this going by knowledge is called "going by knowledge." Here, however, it is the going by knowledge that is intended. But in the Subcommentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya it is said: "His going (gataṃ gamanaṃ) is beautiful (sobhanaṃ), thus he is a Sugata." He is also called "Sugata" because he goes to a beautiful place; the meaning is that he has gone to the deathless Nibbāna, having made it his object. He is also called "Sugata" because he goes rightly, without deviation. Here the word su has the meaning of "rightly." The meaning is that he does not return to, come back to, or revert to those defilements that have been abandoned by this or that path. Or, he is called "Sugata" because he has come rightly. The meaning is that from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara up to the Bodhi seat, by fulfilling the thirty perfections through right practice, working only for the welfare and happiness of the entire world, he came without approaching these two extremes: eternalism and annihilationism, and sensual indulgence and self-mortification. "To that Sugata, the Buddha, I pay homage"—this is the connection.

Puna sugatanti sammā gadattā sugato. So hi sammā gadati bhāsatīti sugatoti vuccati. Supubbagadadhātu bhāsāyaṃ viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ vā, ta, dassa to. Chasu vācāsu yuttaṭṭhāne yuttameva dvivācaṃ bhāsatīti attho. Vuttañhi majjhimapaṇṇāsapāḷiyaṃ abhayarājakumārasutte –

Again, "Sugata" means one who speaks rightly. Because he speaks rightly, he is called Sugata. The root is gad with the prefix su, used in the sense of speaking, articulating, or speech; the d [of gad] becomes t before the suffix ta. The meaning is that in a situation involving six kinds of speech, he speaks only the two kinds of speech that are appropriate. For it is said in the Abhayarājakumāra Sutta in the Middle Fifty of the Pāli Canon:

1

1

. “Rājakumāra yaṃ tathāgato taṃ vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsati. 2. Yampi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā. Tampi tathāgato vācaṃ na bhāsati. 3. Yañca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, tatrakālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya. 4. Yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsati. 5. Yampi tathāgato jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, tampi tathāgato vācaṃ na bhāsati. 6. Yañca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā[M 0.0010]. Tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāyā”ti.

“Prince, the speech that the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and which is also disagreeable and unendearing to others: such speech the Tathāgata does not speak. The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct but unbeneficial, and which is also disagreeable and unendearing to others: such speech the Tathāgata does not speak. The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, but which is disagreeable and unendearing to others: therein the Tathāgata is a knower of the time for declaring that speech. The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, but which is agreeable and endearing to others: such speech the Tathāgata does not speak. The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct but unbeneficial, and which is also agreeable and endearing to others: such speech the Tathāgata does not speak. The speech that the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, and which is also agreeable and endearing to others: therein the Tathāgata is a knower of the time for declaring that speech.”

Ettha pāḷiyaṃ panesā sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ saṅkhepena veditabbā. Kathaṃ hesā abhūtā anatthasaṃhitā appiyā vācā ca, bhūtā anatthasaṃhitā appiyā vācā ca, bhūtā attha saṃhitā appiyā vācā ca, abhūtā anatthasaṃhitā piyā vācā ca, bhūtā anatthasaṃhitā piyā vācā ca, bhūtā atthasaṃhitā piyā vācā cāti chabbidhā hotīti. Tattha acoraṃyeva coro ayantiādivasena vattabbavācā paṭhamavācā nāma. Coraṃyeva coro ayantiādivasena vattabbavācā dutiyavācā nāma. Akatapuññatāya duggato dubbaṇṇo appesakkho, idha pana ṭhatvāpi puna puññaṃ na karoti, dutiyacittavāre kathaṃ catūhi apāyehi muccissatīti evaṃ mahājanassa atthapurekkhārena dhammapurekkhārena anusāsanīpurekkhārena vattabbavācā tatiyavācā nāma. Eko dhutto āha-mayhaṃ bho mātu mayi kucchigate kapiṭṭhaphaladohaḷo ahosi. Sā aññaṃ kapiṭṭhahārakaṃ alabhamānā maṃyeva pesesi. Ahaṃ gantvā rukkhaṃ abhiruhituṃ asakkonto attanāva attānaṃ pāde gahetvā muggaraṃ viya rukkhassa upari khipiṃ. Atha sākhato sākhaṃ vicaranto phalāni gahetvā otarituṃ asakkonto gharaṃ gantvā nisseṇiṃ āharitvā oruyha mātu santike gantvā phalāni mātuyā adāsiṃ. Tāni pana mahantāni honti cāṭippa māṇāni. Tato me mātarā ekāsane nisinnāya samasaṭṭhiphalāni khāditānīti. Evamādivasena vattabbavācā catutthavācā nāma. Āmisahetu cāṭukamyatādivasena nānappakārakaṃ paresaṃ thomanā vācā ceva rājakathaṃ corakathantiādinayappavattā tiracchānakathā ca pañcamavācā nāma. Ariyasaccasannissitā dhammakathā chaṭṭhamavācā nāma. Taṃ pana vassasatampi suṇantā paṇḍitā neva tittiṃ gacchanti[M 0.0011]. Tāsu pana bhagavā tatiyachaṭṭhamā dvivācāeva bhāsati. Tasmā sappurisehi sāyeva dvivācā vattabbāti. Ayaṃ tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgato saṅkhepanayo. Visuddhimagga mahāṭīkāyaṃ pana sāratthadīpanīṭīkāyañca tadaññākārena vaṇṇito. Tāsu pana taṃ oloketvā gahetabbanti. Ayaṃ panettha saṅgahagāthā –

Here, this Pāli passage should be understood in brief for the sake of easy comprehension. How so? Speech is sixfold: (1) speech that is untrue, unbeneficial, and disagreeable; (2) speech that is true, unbeneficial, and disagreeable; (3) speech that is true, beneficial, and disagreeable; (4) speech that is untrue, unbeneficial, and agreeable; (5) speech that is true, unbeneficial, and agreeable; and (6) speech that is true, beneficial, and agreeable. Among these, the first kind of speech is, for example, saying to one who is not a thief, “You are a thief.” The second kind of speech is, for example, saying to one who is a thief, “You are a thief.” The third kind of speech is that spoken with a focus on the welfare of the multitude, with a focus on the Dhamma, with a focus on instruction, such as saying: “Due to not having made merit, you are unfortunate, of poor appearance, and of little influence. If you do not make merit again while you are here, how will you be freed from the four planes of misery at the time of the second thought-moment?” The fourth kind of speech is, for example, when a certain rogue said: “Friends, when I was in my mother’s womb, she had a craving for wood-apples. Unable to find anyone else to fetch them, she sent me. Unable to climb the tree, I grabbed myself by the feet and threw myself up into the tree like a club. Then, moving from branch to branch, I gathered the fruits. Unable to get down, I went home, brought a ladder, descended, went to my mother, and gave her the fruits. They were huge, the size of large pots. Then my mother, sitting on a single seat, ate sixty of them.” The fifth kind of speech consists of various kinds of praise of others out of a desire for material gain, such as flattery, and worldly talk such as talk about kings, talk about thieves, and so on. The sixth kind of speech is Dhamma talk connected with the Noble Truths. Even if the wise were to listen to it for a hundred years, they would not become tired of it. Among these, the Blessed One speaks only the third and sixth kinds of speech. Therefore, good people should speak only these two kinds of speech. This is the concise method that comes in its commentary. However, in the Great Subcommentary to the Visuddhimagga and in the Sāratthadīpanī Subcommentary, it is explained in a different way. One should look into them and grasp the meaning from there. Here is the summary verse:

“Yo bhūtamatthasaṃhītaṃ, paresamappiyā vācaṃ;

Bhūtamatthasahītañca, paresaṃ piyavācanti;

Dvivācaṃ yuttaṭṭhāneva, vadatīti sugatoti;

Vuccatī ca dakārassa, katvā takāraviññunā”ti.

“He who speaks speech that is true and beneficial but disagreeable to others, and speech that is true and beneficial and agreeable to others—since he speaks only these two kinds of speech in the appropriate situation, he is called ‘Sugata.’ And he is so called by the wise, who understand the change of the letter ‘d’ to ‘t’.”

Seṭṭhanti guṇamahantattā pasatthataraṃ. So hi pasatthānaṃ visesena pasatthoti seṭṭhoti vuccati. Pasatthapadaṃ, visesataddhite iṭṭhapaccayo. Pasatthasaddassa so, pasatthānaṃ paccekabuddhāriyasāvakādīnaṃ sīlasamādhipaññādi guṇehi visesena pasatthoti attho. Atha vā sundare satipaṭṭhānādibhede dhamme esati gavesati esiṃ gavesinti vā seṭṭho, buddho. Supubboesa gavesane ta. Tassa raṭṭho. Susaddo sundarattho. Santehi sappurisehi esitabbo gavesitabboti vā seṭṭho. Santasaddūpapado isa gavesane ta, santasaddassa so, ikārasse, tassa ṭṭho. Santehi sappurisehi icchiyati kantiya tīti vā seṭṭho. Santasaddūpapado isu icchākantīsu ta. Atha vā santānaṃ sappurisānaṃ hitasukhaṃ icchatīti seṭṭho, buddho. Kattusādhanoyaṃ. Sundare satipaṭṭhānā dibhede dhamme eseti buddhetīti vā seṭṭho. Hetu kattusādhanoyaṃ. Supubbaesadhātu buddhiyaṃ ta. Taṃ seṭṭhaṃ.

Seṭṭha means ‘more praiseworthy’ due to the greatness of his qualities. For he is called ‘seṭṭha’ because he is especially praiseworthy among the praiseworthy. The superlative suffix ‘-iṭṭha’ is applied to the word ‘pasattha’ (praiseworthy), and the ‘sa’ of ‘pasattha’ is dropped. The meaning is that he is especially praiseworthy among praiseworthy beings—such as Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples—by qualities like virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Alternatively, seṭṭha refers to the Buddha, who seeks and investigates the good Dhamma with its divisions like the foundations of mindfulness. It is formed from the root ‘is’ (to seek) with the prefix ‘su-’ (good) and the suffix ‘-ta’. Or, seṭṭha is the one who is to be sought or investigated by good people. It is formed with the word ‘santa’ (good) as a prefix to the root ‘is’ (to seek) with the suffix ‘-ta’; the ‘sa’ of ‘santa’ is dropped, the ‘i’ becomes ‘e’, and the ‘t’ becomes ‘ṭṭha’. Or, seṭṭha is he who is desired and liked by good people. It is formed with the word ‘santa’ as a prefix to the root ‘is’ indicating desire and liking, with the suffix ‘-ta’. Alternatively, seṭṭha is the Buddha, who desires the welfare and happiness of good people; this is a derivation in the agentive sense. Or, seṭṭha is the one who causes others to understand the good Dhamma with its divisions like the foundations of mindfulness; this is a derivation in the causal agentive sense. It is from the root ‘is’ in the sense of understanding, with the prefix ‘su-’ and the suffix ‘-ta’. That is seṭṭha.

Kusalaṃkusalaṃ jahanti ettha kusalaṃ akusalaṃ jahanti padavibhāgo kātabbo. Kucchitaṃ pāpadhammaṃ salayati calayati [M 0.0012] kampeti viddhaṃsetīti kusalaṃ, catubhūmikakusalaṃ labbhati. Kupubbo saladhātu a. Tattha kāmāvacarakusalaṃ tadaṅgappahānena pāpadhammaṃ salayati calayati, mahaggata kusalaṃ vikkhambhanappahānena salayati kampeti, lokuttara kusalaṃ samucchedappahānena salayati viddhaṃsetīti attho.

In kusalaṃkusalaṃ jahanti, a word division should be made: kusalaṃ akusalaṃ jahanti (they abandon the wholesome and the unwholesome). That which shakes, stirs, agitates, and destroys contemptible, evil states is called kusala (wholesome); the wholesome of the four planes is meant. It is formed from the root ‘sal’ with the prefix ‘ku-’ and the suffix ‘-a’. Therein, sense-sphere wholesome shakes and stirs evil states by means of abandonment by substitution; sublime wholesome shakes and agitates them by means of abandonment by suppression; and supramundane wholesome shakes and destroys them by means of abandonment by eradication. This is the meaning.

Atha vā kucchitaṃ apāyadvāraṃ salanti saṃvaranti pidahanti sādhavo etenāti kusalaṃ, karaṇasādhanoyaṃ. Idha pana jahanti vuttattā tebhūmakakusalamevādhippetaṃ. Taṃ pana anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ, akusalaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, vodāna paccupaṭṭhānaṃ, iṭṭhavipākapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā, yonisomanasikāra padaṭṭhānaṃ. Na kusalaṃ akusalaṃ, mittapaṭipakkho amitto viya pahāyakapahātabbabhāvena kusalapaṭipakkhanti attho. Taṃ pana sāvajjadukkhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ, sāvajjāniṭṭhavipāka lakkhaṇaṃ vā, anatthajananarasaṃ, aniṭṭhavipākapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Puññābhisaṅkhāraāneñjā bhisaṅkhārasaṅkhātaṃ kusalaṃ apuññābhisaṅkhārasaṅkhātaṃ akusalañca kusalaṃkusalaṃ. Taṃ pana padaṃ jahantipade kammaṃ.

Alternatively, because good people cut off, restrain, and close the contemptible door to the plane of misery by means of it, it is called ‘wholesome’; this is a derivation in the instrumental sense. Here, however, since ‘they abandon’ is stated, only the wholesome of the three planes is intended. It has the characteristic of having blameless and pleasant results, the function of destroying the unwholesome, the manifestation of purification or of desirable results, and the proximate cause of wise attention. The unwholesome is ‘not wholesome’; like an enemy is the opposite of a friend, it is the opposite of the wholesome by way of being that which is to be abandoned by that which abandons. It has the characteristic of having blameworthy and painful results, or blameworthy and undesirable results; the function of generating what is not beneficial; the manifestation of undesirable results; and the proximate cause of unwise attention. The wholesome, designated as meritorious formations and imperturbable formations, and the unwholesome, designated as demeritorious formations, are ‘the wholesome and the unwholesome.’ That term, however, is the object of the verb ‘they abandon’.

Jahanti maggakkhaṇe samucchedappahānena phalakkhaṇe paṭippassambhanappahānena pajahantaṃ viddhaṃsentanti attho. Tañhi arahattamaggañāṇena jahati pajahati, phalañāṇena jahiṃ pajahiṃ paṭippassambhinti vā jaho, buddho. Hādhātu cāge a. Kiñcāpi panettha kusalaṃ maggena pahātabbadhamme na vuttaṃ, vaṭṭamūlabhūte avijjātaṇhādikilese pana arahattamagga ñāṇena jahite lokiyakusaluppattiyā mūlabhūtāya avijjātaṇhāya abhāvā puññābhisaṅkhāro saṃsāre puna paṭisandhiyā nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti, tasmā vaṭṭamūlabhūte kilese jahite phalūpacārena kusalampi jahitaṃ nāma hoti. Rūpaṃ bhikkhave na tumhākaṃ taṃ pajahathātiādīsu viya[M 0.0013]. Arahantena hi abhisamācārikavattaṃ katampi kusalanti na vuttaṃ, kriyāti pana vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

They abandon means they relinquish and destroy it at the moment of the path by means of abandonment by eradication, and at the moment of fruition by means of abandonment by tranquilization. For he abandons and relinquishes it with the knowledge of the path of arahantship; or, because he has abandoned, relinquished, and tranquilized it with the knowledge of fruition, he is jaho, the Buddha. The root is 'hā' in the sense of abandoning, with the suffix '-a'. Although it is not stated here that wholesome states are to be abandoned by the path, when the defilements such as ignorance and craving, which are the root of the round of existence, are abandoned by the knowledge of the path of arahantship, the meritorious formations cannot produce a new rebirth in saṃsāra because of the absence of ignorance and craving, which are the root for the arising of worldly wholesome states. Therefore, when the defilements that are the root of the round are abandoned, by extension from the result the wholesome is also said to be abandoned. This is like the passage: 'Bhikkhus, form is not yours. Abandon it.' For it should be understood that even the proper conduct undertaken by an arahant is not called 'wholesome' but is called 'functional'.

Vuttañhi nidānavaggasaṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “khīṇāsavena hi kataṃ kammaṃ neva kusalaṃ hoti nākusalaṃ, avipākaṃ hutvā kriyamatte tiṭṭhatī”ti.

For it is said in the Commentary to the Nidānavagga Saṃyutta: 'An action done by one whose taints are destroyed is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; being without result, it remains as a mere functional deed.'

Aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyañca “arahattamaggo ca kusalākusala kammakkhayāya saṃvattatīti evaṃ tena taṃ bhijjatī”ti vuttaṃ.

And in the Commentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya it is said: 'The path of arahantship leads to the destruction of wholesome and unwholesome kamma; thus that is broken by it.'

Tena vuttaṃ cūḷaniddesapāḷiyaṃ “arahattamaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena ye uppajjeyyuṃ nāmañca rūpañca, etthete nirujjhanti vūpasamanti atthaṃ gacchanti paṭippassambhantī”ti.

Therefore it is said in the Cūḷaniddesa: 'Through the knowledge of the path of arahantship, with the cessation of formational consciousness, whatever name-and-form might arise, right there they cease, are pacified, come to an end, and are tranquilized.'

Amatanti maraṇavirahitaṃ. So jino hi na mato amato, maraṇadhammassa nibbattakānaṃ kilesānaṃ arahatta maggena samucchinditattā puna maraṇato virahitoti vā amato. Atha vā nibbāne ārammaṇakaraṇavasena adhigate natthi mataṃ maraṇaṃ yassa jinassāti amatoti vuccati. Jinena hi khandhamaccumāraṃ ajitopi kilesamāraṃ jayitvā tesaṃ avassaṃ jiyamānattā phalūpacārena amatoti vuccatīti veditabbaṃ.

Amata means 'devoid of death.' That Victor is indeed not subject to death, he is deathless. Or, he is deathless because, having eradicated with the path of arahantship the defilements that produce the state of mortality, he is again devoid of death. Alternatively, because Nibbāna has been attained by way of making it an object, he is called 'deathless' because for that Victor there is no death. For although the Victor has not conquered Māra as death-and-the-aggregates, since he has conquered Māra as the defilements, he is called 'deathless' by extension from the result, as the former will inevitably be conquered. This should be understood.

Puna amatanti amatanibbānasamannāgataṃ. Natthi mataṃ maraṇaṃ etthāti amataṃ, nibbānaṃ. Taṃ pana santilakkhaṇaṃ, accutarasaṃ, animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, nissaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā, nibbānassa pana padaṭṭhānaṃ na labbhati.

Again, amata means endowed with the deathless Nibbāna. Because there is no death or dying in it, it is amata, the deathless, that is, Nibbāna. It has the characteristic of peace, the function of being imperishable, the manifestation of the signless, or the manifestation of escape. But a proximate cause for Nibbāna is not found.

Vuttañhi milindapañhe nāgasenattherena “na kenaci kāraṇena nibbānaṃ uppajjatī”ti.

For it was said in the Milindapañha by the Elder Nāgasena: 'Nibbāna does not arise from any cause.'

Taṃ assa atthīti amato, jino. Saddhādito ṇāti suttena assathyatthe ṇapaccayo. Saddho paññotiādīsu viya[M 0.0014]. Assa jinassa catumaggañāṇena sacchikataṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ atthīti attho, taṃ amataṃ.

Because that (deathless) exists for him, he is amato, the Victor. By the grammatical rule 'saddhādito ṇa,' the suffix '-a' is used in the possessive sense of 'it is his.' This is seen in words like 'saddho' (one with faith), 'pañño' (one with wisdom), etc. The meaning is: for this Victor there exists the deathless Nibbāna, realized by the knowledge of the four paths. Such is the deathless.

Santanti sabbakilesadarathehi ca vaṭṭadukkhehi ca suvūpasantaṃ. So hi buddho sabbakilesadarathavaṭṭadukkhehi samittha vūpasamitthāti santoti vuccati. Samudhātu upasame ta. Dhātvantassa lopaṃ tapaccayassantoādesaṃ katvā padasiddhi veditabbā. Saṃsāravaṭṭe darathakārakānaṃ kilesānaṃ bodhimaṇḍe arahattamaggañāṇena samucchinditattā sītibhūto santakāyacittoti vuttaṃ hoti, taṃ santaṃ.

Santa (peaceful) means thoroughly pacified from all defilements, torments, and the suffering of the round. For that Buddha is called 'santa' because he is thoroughly pacified from all defilements, torments, and the suffering of the round. The root 'sam' is in the sense of pacification, with the suffix '-ta'. The formation of the word should be understood as involving the elision of the final of the root and the substitution of '-anta' for the suffix '-ta'. Because the defilements that cause torment in the round of saṃsāra have been eradicated by the knowledge of the path of arahantship at the seat of awakening, he has become cool, with peaceful body and mind. Such is santa.

Asamanti sīlādiguṇehi kenaci puggalena asadisaṃ, so hi buddho natthi sīlādiguṇehi samo sadiso etassāti asamoti vuccati. Imasmiṃ sattaloke sīla samādhipaññādiguṇehi buddhena sadiso koci manusso vā devo vā brahmā vā natthīti attho. Bhagavato hi asīti anubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍita bāttiṃsa mahāpurisalakkhaṇehi vicitrarūpakāyo ca sabbākārehi parisuddhasīlakkhandhādiguṇa ratanasamiddho dhammakāyo ca puññamahattathāmamahatta iddhimahattayasamahattapaññāmahattādiguṇehi ca paramukkaṃsagato ca atthi, tasmā bhagavā sīlādiguṇehi kenaci asamo asadisoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Asama (incomparable) means unequal to any person in qualities such as virtue. For that Buddha is called 'asama' because there is no one equal or similar to him in qualities such as virtue. The meaning is that in this world of beings, there is no human, deva, or brahmā who is similar to the Buddha in qualities such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom. For the Blessed One possesses a beautiful physical body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and ornamented with the eighty minor characteristics, and a Dhamma-body endowed with the jewels of such qualities as the perfectly pure aggregate of virtue; and he has reached the supreme excellence in qualities such as greatness of merit, greatness of strength, greatness of psychic power, greatness of fame, and greatness of wisdom. Therefore, it is said that the Blessed One is unequal and dissimilar to anyone in qualities such as virtue.

Asamaṃ dadanti lokiyadhammena asadisaṃ maggaphalanibbāna dhammaṃ veneyyānaṃ sattānaṃ desanāñāṇena dāyakaṃ. Ettha ca asamanti natthi ettha etesaṃ vā samo sadiso lokiyadhammoti asamo, maggaphalanibbānaṃ labbhati. Atha vā asamanti aññesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggabhāvato catubbidhena ariya maggena sacchikātabbaṃ nibbānaṃ vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “yāvatā bhikkhave dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti. Tassa pana padassa dadantipadena [M 0.0015] kammabhāvena sambandho. Dadātīti dado, buddho. Dādhātu a, so kenaci lokiyadhammena asamaṃ asadisaṃ maggaphalanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ mahākaruṇāppadhānena amatādhigamapaṭipattidassanena desanāñāṇena veneyyānaṃ sattānaṃ dātāti attho. Taṃ asamaṃ dadaṃ.

Giver of the Incomparable means the giver, by means of the knowledge of teaching, of the Dhamma of path, fruition, and Nibbāna—which is dissimilar to any worldly state—to trainable beings. Herein, incomparable means that there is no worldly state equal or similar to it; the path, fruition, and Nibbāna are meant. Alternatively, incomparable refers to Nibbāna, which is to be realized by the fourfold noble path, because it is the highest of all other states. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, whatever states there are, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the chief among them.' The connection of that word ('incomparable') with the word 'giver' is as its object. Giver (dado) means 'he gives'; this is the Buddha. It is from the root 'dā' with the suffix '-a'. The meaning is that he is the giver to trainable beings of the supramundane Dhamma—designated as path, fruition, and Nibbāna, which is unequal and dissimilar to any worldly state—with great compassion as the principal factor, by showing the practice for attaining the deathless through the knowledge of teaching. Such is the Giver of the Incomparable.

(Kha) dutiyagāthāyaṃ pana saraṇanti sabbasattalokassa paṭisaraṇabhūto parāyaṇo leṇo tāṇoti vuttaṃ hoti. So hi buddho saranti paṭisaranti ettha sattalokāti saraṇoti vuccati. Saradhātu yu. Atha vā saranti osaranti samosaranti ettha sattalokāti saraṇoti vuccati. Saranti cintenti ettha saddhā pasannā devamanussā saraṇamidanti saraṇoti ca. Saranti paṭivijjhanti etthupagatā devamanussā saddhammanti saraṇoti ca vuccati. Sara cintāyaṃ yu. Saraṇagamanaṭṭhāne pana sarati hiṃsati bhayaṃ santāpaṃ dukkhaṃ kilesañcāti saraṇaṃ. Ratanatta yanti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Taṃ saraṇaṃ.

(b) In the second verse, however, saraṇa (refuge) is said to mean the resort, the final destination, the shelter, and the protection for the entire world of beings. For the Buddha is called saraṇa because the world of beings goes to him for refuge and relies on him. [The derivation is from] the root sar with the suffix yu. Or alternatively, it is called saraṇa because the world of beings resorts to it, converges on it, and assembles at it. And it is called saraṇa because faithful and devoted devas and humans reflect on it, thinking, 'This is a refuge.' And it is also called saraṇa because devas and humans who have approached it penetrate the good Dhamma. [Here the derivation is from] the root sar in the sense of reflecting, with the suffix yu. However, in the context of going for refuge, saraṇa is that which crushes and destroys fear, torment, suffering, and defilements. It is said in the commentaries that the Triple Gem is meant. That is the refuge.

Puna saraṇaṃ lokanti sattasaṅkhārokāsasaṅkhataṃ lokaṃ sarantaṃ jānantaṃ. Ettha hi lokayati patiṭṭhayati ettha puññāpuññañca tabbipāko cāti loko, satta loko labbhati. Lokadhātu patiṭṭhāyaṃ ṇa. Lujjati palujjatīti loko, saṅkhāraloko. Lujadhātuṇa. Lokiyati vicittākārena dissatīti loko, lokiyanti patiṭṭhiyanti ettha vā jaṅgamā ca thāvarā cāti loko, cakkavāḷasaṅkhato okāsaloko labbhati. Lokadhātuṇa. Ettha ca sassato lokoti vā asassato lokoti vāti āgataṭṭhāne indriyabaddhānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ khandhānaṃ samūho santāno ca sattoyeva loko sattalokoti vacanatthena sattalokoti veditabbo. Eko loko sabbe sattā āhā raṭṭhitikāti [M 0.0016] āgataṭṭhāne indriyabaddhānaṃ vā anindriyabaddhānaṃ vā khandhānaṃ samūho santāno ca paccayehi saṅkhariyantīti saṅkhārā, saṅkhārāeva loko saṅkhāralokoti vacanatthena saṅkhāralokoti.

Again, `lokaṃ saraṇaṃ` means remembering and knowing the world, which is designated as the world of beings, the world of formations, and the world of space. Here, 'world' (loko) is so called because merit and demerit and their results are established in it (lokayati); this is the world of beings. The derivation is from the root `lok` in the sense of being a foundation, with the suffix `ṇa`. 'It crumbles and disintegrates' (lujjati palujjati), thus it is the 'world' (loko); this is the world of formations. The derivation is from the root `luj` with the suffix `ṇa`. 'It is seen' (lokiyati), it appears in diverse forms, thus it is the 'world' (loko); or, 'moving and stationary beings are established in it' (lokiyanti), thus it is the 'world' (loko); this is the world of space, designated as the world-sphere. The derivation is from the root `lok` with the suffix `ṇa`. Here, in the context where it is said, 'Is the world eternal or is the world not eternal?' the collection and continuity of the aggregates of form, etc., bound to the sense faculties, is the being itself, so 'world' should be understood as the 'world of beings' by the meaning of the expression 'world of beings.' In the context where it is said, 'There is one world: all beings are sustained by nutriment,' the collection and continuity of the aggregates, whether bound to the sense faculties or not, are conditioned by causes, thus they are formations. The formations themselves are the world, so 'world' should be understood as the 'world of formations' by the meaning of the expression 'world of formations.'

“Yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharanti,

Disā bhanti virocamānā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko,

Ettha te vattati vaso”ti.

“So long as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the quarters, shining brightly, so far extends the thousand-fold world; within it your sovereignty prevails.”

Āgataṭṭhāne anindriyabaddhānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ samūho santāno ca avakasanti patiṭṭhahanti etthāti okāso, soyeva loko okāsalokoti vacanatthena okāsa lokoti veditabbo, taṃ lokaṃ. Sarati jānāti ajānīti vā saraṇo, buddho. Sara cintāyaṃ yu. Lokaṃ saraṇanti sambandho. Buddho pana sattalokaṃ, saṅkhāralokaṃ, okāsalokaṃ, kilesalokaṃ, bhavalokaṃ, indriya lokaṃ, khandhalokaṃ, āyatanalokaṃ dhātulokañcātiādimanekalokaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇena paṭivijjhatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the context where the collection and continuity of form, etc., not bound to the sense faculties, find space and are established, that is 'space' (okāso). That itself is the world, so it should be understood as the 'world of space' (okāsaloka) by the meaning of the expression 'world of space.' That world (he knows). He who remembers (sarati), knows (jānāti), or has understood (ajānī) is 'one who remembers' (saraṇo), that is, the Buddha. The derivation is from the root `sar` in the sense of reflecting, with the suffix `yu`. The connection is `lokaṃ saraṇaṃ`. It is said that the Buddha, for his part, penetrates with unobstructed knowledge the many kinds of worlds, such as the world of beings, the world of formations, the world of space, the world of defilements, the world of existence, the world of the sense faculties, the world of the aggregates, the world of the sense bases, and the world of the elements.

Araṇanti nikkilesaṃ, kilesasaṅkhātaraṇavirahitaṃ vā. Raṇasaddo ca kilesesu ca yuddhe cuṇṇavicuṇṇakaraṇe ca dissati. Tathā hi saraṇā dhammā araṇā dhammātiādīsu kilesesu dissati. Te hi raṇanti kandanti sattā etehīti raṇāti vuccanti.

`Araṇaṃ` means 'without defilements,' or 'devoid of the conflict (raṇa) designated as defilements.' The word `raṇa` is seen in the sense of defilements, battle, and crushing to powder. Thus, it is seen in the sense of defilements in such passages as 'states with conflict, states without conflict,' and so on. For they are called 'conflicts' (raṇā) because beings make a noise (raṇanti) and cry out on account of them.

“Dhanuggaho asadiso, rājaputto mahabbalo;

Sabbāmitte raṇaṃ katvā, saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamī”ti.

“The archer without an equal, the prince of great strength, having made war on all his foes, undertook the life of restraint.”

Asadisajātake yuddhe dissati. Raṇaṃ katvāti hi yuddhaṃ katvā, saṃyamanti saṃyataṃ isipabbajjaṃ ajjhupāgamīti attho. Tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca raṇaṃ karonto, dhāviṃsu te aṭṭhadisā [M 0.0017] samantatoti chaddantajātake cuṇṇavicuṇṇakaraṇe dissati. Raṇaṃ karontoti hi cuṇṇaṃ vicuṇṇaṃ karonto. Teti sabbe aṭṭhasahassanāgāti attho. Idha pana kilese daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho. Raṇanti satte rāgādayo cuṇṇenti pīḷentīti raṇā, raṇanti sattā etehi kandanti paridevantīti vā raṇā, kilesā. Raṇadhātu sadde a. Natthi raṇā kilesā etassāti araṇoti vuccati. Jinassa kilesamārassa bodhimūle jiyamānattā raṇā kilesā na santīti attho. Taṃ araṇaṃ.

In the Asadisa Jātaka, it is seen in the sense of battle. For 'having made war' (raṇaṃ katvā) means having made battle. 'Undertook restraint' (saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamī) means he undertook the restrained life of a seer's going forth; this is the meaning. In the Chaddanta Jātaka, it is seen in the sense of crushing to powder: 'Making `raṇa` of grass and wood, they rushed around in the eight directions.' 'Making `raṇa`' means making into powder, crushing to powder. 'They' means all the eight thousand elephants; this is the meaning. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of defilements. This is the verbal meaning here: 'Conflicts' (raṇā) are so called because they crush and oppress beings—these are lust and so on; or they are called 'conflicts' because beings make a noise (raṇanti), cry out, and lament on account of them—these are the defilements. The root is `raṇ` in the sense of sound, with the suffix `a`. He is called 'without conflict' (araṇo) because for him there are no conflicts, no defilements. The meaning is that because the defilements, which are Māra, were conquered by the Victor at the root of the Bodhi tree, for him there are no conflicts, no defilements. That is `araṇaṃ`.

Araṇaṃ karanti veneyyasantāne raṇasaṅkhatakilesassa abhāvakaraṇaṃ. Ettha ca raṇanti etaṃ yehi abhibhūtā sattā kandanti paridavanti etesaṃ rāgādīnaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tesaṃ abhāvaṃ veneyyasantāne desanāñāṇena karoti attho. Atha vā karotīti karo, buddho. Taṃ karaṃ.

`Araṇaṃ karanti` means causing the absence, in the mental continuities of those to be trained, of the defilements designated as conflict. Here, 'conflict' (raṇa) is a designation for lust and so on, on account of which beings, when overwhelmed, cry out and lament. The meaning is that he brings about their absence in the mental continuities of those to be trained by means of his knowledge of teaching. Or alternatively, 'he makes' (karoti), thus he is the 'maker' (karo), the Buddha. That maker (`karaṃ`).

Abhayanti jātibhayādīnaṃ abhāvato nibbhayaṃ. Ettha hi bhayaṃ cittutrāsabhayaṃ, ñāṇabhayaṃ, ārammaṇabhayaṃ, ottappa bhayañcāti catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha bhāyati cittenāti bhayaṃ, cittutrāsabhayaṃ. Ñāṇena tīretvā bhāyatīti bhayaṃ, ñāṇaṃ. Bhāyati etasmāti bhayaṃ, ārammaṇabhayaṃ. Bhāyati etena pāpatoti bhayaṃ, ottappabhayaṃ. Bhīdhātu bhaye ṇa.

`Abhayaṃ` means 'fearless' because of the absence of the fears of birth and so on. Here, fear is fourfold: fear as mental terror, fear as knowledge, fear as an object, and fear as moral dread. Therein, 'one fears with the mind' (bhāyati cittena), thus it is 'fear' (bhayaṃ); this is fear as mental terror. 'One fears after judging with knowledge,' thus it is 'fear'; this is knowledge. 'One fears on account of this,' thus it is 'fear'; this is fear as an object. 'One fears this as evil,' thus it is 'fear'; this is fear as moral dread. The root is `bhī` in the sense of fear, with the suffix `ṇa`.

Mahāniddesapāḷiyaṃ pana āgatāni jātibhayaṃ, jarābhayaṃ, byādhibhayaṃ, maraṇabhayaṃ, rājabhayaṃ, corabhayaṃ, aggibhayaṃ, udakabhayaṃ, attānuvādabhayaṃ, parānuvādabhayaṃ, daṇḍabhayaṃ, duggatibhayaṃ, ūmibhayaṃ, kumbhīḷabhayaṃ, āvaṭṭabhayaṃ, susukabhayaṃ, ājīvikabhayaṃ, asilokabhayaṃ, parisayasārajjabhayaṃ, madana bhayaṃ, duggatibhayantiādīni gahitāni. Natthi bhayāni etassāti abhayo, buddho. Tassa bhayānaṃ kāraṇa bhūtānaṃ [M 0.0018] sabbakilesānaṃ arahattamaggena samucchinditattā sabbabhayaṃ natthīti attho.

In the Pāli of the Mahāniddesa, however, the fears mentioned are taken, such as: the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of sickness, the fear of death, the fear of kings, the fear of thieves, the fear of fire, the fear of water, the fear of self-reproach, the fear of others' reproach, the fear of punishment, the fear of a bad destination, the fear of waves, the fear of crocodiles, the fear of whirlpools, the fear of sharks, the fear of livelihood, the fear of disrepute, the fear of diffidence in assemblies, the fear of intoxication, and the fear of a bad destination. 'For him there are no fears,' thus he is 'fearless' (abhayo), the Buddha. The meaning is that because all defilements, which are the cause of fears, have been extirpated by the path of arahatship, he is without any fear.

Puna abhayaṃ ṭhānaṃ nāyakanti ettha abhayantipadaṃ ṭhānantipade visesanaṃ. Ṭhānantipadaṃ nāyakantipade kammaṃ. Bhayasaddassa attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Natthi sabbabhayaṃ ettha nibbāneti abhayaṃ, nibbānaṃ. Buddhapaccekabuddha arahantā ṭhanti uppajjanti etthāti ṭhānaṃ, nibbānaṃ. Veneyyasatte netīti nāyako, buddho. Nīdhātu nayane ṇvu. So buddho bhabbe kulaputte maggādhi gamappattiyā dhammadesanāya maggaphalañāṇaṃ adhigamento nibbānaṭṭhānaṃ netīti attho, taṃ nāyakaṃ.

Again, in the phrase `abhayaṃ ṭhānaṃ nāyakaṃ`, the word 'fearless' (abhayaṃ) is an adjective for the word 'state' (ṭhānaṃ). The word 'state' is the object of the word 'leader' (nāyakaṃ). The meaning of the word 'fear' has already been stated above. 'In it there is no fear at all,' thus it is 'fearless' (abhayaṃ); this is Nibbāna. 'Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants stand and arise in it,' thus it is a 'state' (ṭhānaṃ); this is Nibbāna. 'He leads those to be trained,' thus he is the 'leader' (nāyako), the Buddha. The root is `nī` in the sense of leading, with the suffix `ṇvu`. The meaning is that the Buddha, by teaching the Dhamma for the attainment of the path, leads suitable sons of good family who are attaining the knowledge of the path and fruit to the state of Nibbāna. That leader (`nāyakaṃ`).

Puna nāyakaṃ nameti nāyakaṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ name namāmīti sambandho. Tattha nāyakanti veneyyasatte saṃsāraṇṇavato nibbānapāraṃ netīti nāyako, buddho. So hi yathā nāviko jane nāvāya orimatīrato pārimatīraṃ neti, evaṃ satte maggaṅganāvāya saṃsāraṇṇavato nibbāna pāraṃ neti pāpuṇetīti attho. Atha vā nāyakanti tiṇṇaṃ lokānaṃ jeṭṭhabhāvagamanattā nāyako jeṭṭha seṭṭhavuḍḍhataro. So hi jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ neti gacchati pāpuṇātīti nāyakoti vuccati. Nīdhātu gatimhi ṇvu. So pana idha loke avijjaṇḍagatānaṃ sabbapajānaṃ paṭhamataraṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ arahattamaggena padāletvā ariyāya jātiyā jātattā sabbasattānaṃ seṭṭhajeṭṭhavuḍḍhatarabhāvaṃ gatoti attho. Taṃ nāyakaṃ. Nameti ahaṃ tīhi dvārehi sakkaccaṃ namāmīti attho. Ettha hi vattamānamivibhattiyā kvacidhātutyādisuttena eādeso hoti. Ayaṃ panettha vāccatthādinayo. Nametipadassa ākhyātapadattā vacanattho na kātabbo. Vuttañhi saddavidūhi –

Again, `nāyakaṃ name` is connected thus: 'I revere (name, i.e., namāmi) the leader (nāyakaṃ), the Buddha.' Here, 'leader' (nāyako) is one who leads those to be trained from the ocean of saṃsāra to the further shore of Nibbāna; this is the Buddha. For just as a sailor takes people in a boat from the near shore to the far shore, so he leads beings with the boat of the path factors from the ocean of saṃsāra to the further shore of Nibbāna, causing them to arrive there; this is the meaning. Or alternatively, 'leader' (nāyako) means the eldest, the best, the most senior, because he has gone to the state of being the chief of the three worlds. He is called 'leader' (nāyako) because he leads to, goes to, and attains the state of being chief. The root is `nī` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ṇvu`. He, in this world, having been the very first to break open the eggshell of ignorance with the path of arahatship for all creatures caught in the egg of ignorance, and having been born with the noble birth, has gone to the state of being the best, the eldest, and the most senior of all beings; this is the meaning. That leader (`nāyakaṃ`). `Name` means: 'I revere (namāmi) respectfully with the three doors'; this is the meaning. Here, the `e` is a substitute for the present tense `mi` ending according to the grammatical rule `kvaci dhātu`, etc. This here is the method of direct meaning, etc. Since the word `name` is a verb, a verbal analysis should not be done. For it has been said by the experts in grammar:

“Ruḷhīkhyātaṃ nipātañcu, pasaggālapanaṃ tathā;

Sabbanāmantimetesu, na kato viggaho chasū”ti.

“In a conventional term, a verb, a particle, a prefix, and a vocative, and likewise in a pronoun—in these six no analysis is made.”

Taṃ [M 0.0019] pana padaṃ namudhātuvattamānaamhayogaparassapadamivibhatyantaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ. Namudhātuyā vāccattho namanakriyā saṅkhāto kusalacittuppādo padhānavasena labbhati. Mivibhattiyā vāccattho tena cittuppādena upalakkhito uppāda vanto tadākāro puggalo appadhānavasena labbhati. Padasamudāyassa pana vāccattho kattukammabhāvesu kattubhūto atītādikālesu paccuppannakālabhūto dhātvattha kiriyāvisesova labbhati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo.

That word, however, is a verb ending in the mi personal ending of the active voice, present tense, first person, from the root namu. The expressed meaning of the root namu is the act of homage, reckoned as the arising of a wholesome consciousness, which is obtained as the primary sense. The expressed meaning of the mi ending is the person who possesses that arising, who is characterized by that arising of consciousness, who has that form; this is obtained as the secondary sense. However, the expressed meaning of the entire word is the specific action of the root, occurring in the present tense and having the agent as its subject. This is the summary here.

Vitthāro panevaṃ veditabbo. Namudhātuyā vaccaṃ sugatādi buddhaguṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vandanākārappavatto kāyavacī viññattisamuṭṭhāpako saddhācetanāpaññāpadhāno kusala cittuppādo ca dve viññattiyo asamuṭṭhāpetvā manodvāre vandanākārappavatto kusalacittuppādo ca mukhyena labbhati. Buddhaguṇānussaraṇavasena pavatto yonisomanasikā rādipurecarānucarakusalacittuppādo phalūpacārena. Diṭṭhadhammi kasamparāyikasaṅkhātaṃ pacchimapacchimaphalaṃ rogādiantarāyānaṃ abhāvañca vā saggamokkhasampattisukhañca kāraṇūpacārena, pure pure vandanā sadisyūpacārena, vandanassa nāmapaññatti ṭhānūpacārena, vatthudvārārammaṇaṃ ṭhānūpacārena, vandana guṇena lakkhitaṃ puggaladabbaṃ guṇūpacārena. Ukkaṭṭhamajjha muduttamattabhāvo guṇyūpacārena, avayavabhūtā vandanā ekadesūpacārena. Samūhabhūtā vandanā ekadesyūpacārena, pubbapubbakusalacittuppādo samīpūpacārena, pacchimapacchima kusalacittuppādo samīpyūpacārena, paṇāmakusalacittuppādabhūtānaṃ paramatthadhammānaṃ nibyāpārabhāvo taddhammūpacārena. Tesaṃ evaṃ dhammatābhāvo ataddhammūpacārena, vandanākāro abhedabhedūpacārena. Vandanasatti bhedaabhedūpacārena labbhati. Mivibhattiyā vāccaṃ taṃmukhyādīhi lakkhito kattu kriyāvisesena ca vattamānavibhattisaṅkhātena vibhattivise sena [M 0.0020] ca parassapadasaṅkhātena padavisesena ca uttamapurisa visesena ca amhayogavisesena ca sabbadhātuvisesena ca ekavacanavisesena ca paccuppannakālavisesena ca dhātvatthakriyāvisesena ca aliṅga visesena ca bhūvādigaṇa visesena ca novikaraṇavisesena ca bhāvakammakattūsukattuvisesena ca lakkhito ahaṃsaṅkhāto khandhasaṅkhato santāno appadhānena labbhati. Kriyāpadassa kriyāya padhānena vācakattā dhātvatthova padhānena labbhati. Apaccayassa vāccaṃ bhūvādigaṇajotakā rūpasiddhimattā pada siliṭṭhatā labbhati.

The detailed explanation should be understood thus. What is meant by the root nam is primarily: (1) the wholesome arising of consciousness—predominant in faith, volition, and wisdom, and producing bodily and verbal intimation—that proceeds by way of veneration, having taken as its object the Buddha’s virtues such as ‘Well-Gone’; and (2) the wholesome arising of consciousness that proceeds by way of veneration at the mind-door without producing the two intimations. The wholesome arising of consciousness that proceeds by way of recollection of the Buddha’s virtues, with wise attention, etc., as its forerunner and attendant, is obtained by transference of fruit. The subsequent fruit, described as visible in this very life and in a future life—that is, the absence of dangers such as disease, or the happiness of attainment in heaven and liberation—is obtained by transference of cause. Past acts of veneration are obtained by transference of similarity. The nominal concept of veneration is obtained by transference of place. The object-base and door are obtained by transference of place. The person or substance characterized by the quality of veneration is obtained by transference of quality. The state of being superior, middling, or inferior is obtained by transference of the possessor of the quality. Veneration that is a component is obtained by transference of a part. Veneration that is a collection is obtained by transference of the whole. The wholesome arising of consciousness that occurred previously is obtained by transference of proximity. The wholesome arising of consciousness that occurs subsequently is obtained by transference of the thing in proximity. The non-active nature of the ultimate realities that constitute the wholesome arising of consciousness in bowing is obtained by transference of the nature of that. The nature of things being so for them is obtained by transference of the absence of that nature. The mode of veneration is obtained by transference of non-difference and difference. The power of veneration is obtained by transference of difference and non-difference. What is meant by the suffix mi is the continuum designated as the aggregates, called ‘I,’ which is obtained non-preeminently. It is characterized by being foremost, etc.; by the specific action of the agent; by the specific verbal inflection called the present tense; by the specific term called parassapada; by the specific first person; by the specific usage of ‘we/I’; by the specific verbal root; by the specific singular number; by the specific present time; by the specific meaning and action of the root; by the specific genderless nature; by the specific verbal class such as bhū; by the specific a-suffix; and by the specific active voice among the impersonal, passive, and active voices. Since the verbal noun is primary in expressing the action, the meaning of the root is obtained preeminently. What is meant by the a-suffix is merely the accomplishment of the form indicating the bhū-class and the elegance of the word.

Atha vā yo ahaṃ namāmīti so name. Sāmaññattha viggahoyaṃ. Vāccattho pana vuttanayena veditabbo. Namanañcettha buddhassa sīlādianantaguṇesu ninnapabbhāratāvasena paṇāmakriyābhinipphādikā kusalacetanā. Sā ca vandaneyya vandanakānaṃ khettajjhāsayasampadāhi diṭṭhadhammavedanīyabhūtā yathāladdhasampattinimittakassa purimakammassa anubalappadāna vasena tannibbattitavipākasantatiyā antarāyakarāni upapīḷakaupacchedakakammāni paṭibāhitvā pavattikāle rogādiantarāyānamappavattiṃ sādheti. Samparāye ca upapajjavedanīyabhūtā saggamokkhasampattisukhaṃ nibbattetīti.

Alternatively: ‘I who pay homage’—that is `name`. This is the analysis for the general meaning. The expressed meaning, however, should be understood according to the method stated. Herein, veneration is the wholesome volition that accomplishes the act of bowing, characterized by an inclination and gravitation towards the boundless virtues of the Buddha, such as his morality. Through the excellence of the field (the one venerated) and the disposition (of the venerator), that volition, having become experienceable in this very life, gives supporting strength to a previous kamma that is the sign for whatever attainment has been gained. By warding off obstructive, oppressive, and destructive kammas that are dangerous to the continuity of the result produced by that previous kamma, it brings about the non-occurrence of dangers such as disease during one's lifetime. And in the future, having become experienceable in a subsequent life, it produces the happiness of attainment in heaven and liberation.

Ayaṃ panettha dassanatthanayo. Nametiiminā buddhassa sugatādiguṇaṃ ārabbha pavattā tividhā paṇāmakusala cetanā mukhyena dasseti. Taṃ dassanena tassā kāraṇabhūtā yonisomanasikārādayo ca catucakkasampattiñca buddhuppādanavamakhettañca pubbabhāge pavattaṃ saddhāpaññāpadhānaṃ kusalacittuppādañca phalūpacārena dīpeti. Taddīpanena tassā phalabhūtaṃ diṭṭhadhammarogādiantarāyavisosanañca saggamokkha sukhañca paṭhamakāraṇūpacārena pakāseti. Tappakāsanena buddhassa paṇāmārahabhāvaṃ dutiyakāraṇūpacārena vibhāveti[M 0.0021]. Taṃvibhāvanena vandakassa me khettaṅgatabhāvañca paṇāme tabbabhāvañca tatiyakāraṇūpacārena anubhāveti.

Herein, this is the method of exposition. By this word `name`, it primarily shows the threefold wholesome volition of bowing that proceeds in relation to the Buddha’s virtues, such as ‘Well-Gone.’ By showing that, it illuminates by transference of fruit its causes, such as wise attention; the fourfold cycle of accomplishment; the supreme field of the Buddha’s arising; and the arising of wholesome consciousness predominant in faith and wisdom that occurred in the preliminary stage. By that illumination, it discloses by the first transference of cause its fruit: the purification from dangers such as disease in this very life and the happiness of heaven and liberation. By that disclosure, it clarifies by the second transference of cause the Buddha’s state of being worthy of bowing. By that clarification, it makes one experience by the third transference of cause my state as a venerator of having arrived at the field and my suitability for bowing.

Ayaṃ panettha alaṅkāranayo. Nametivācakapadassa vāccabhūtā tividhā buddhapaṇāmakusalacetanā samaṭṭhāyī bhāvo nāma. Kasmā, sarīrattā. Atha vā tividhāya buddhapaṇā makusalacetanāya sampayutto samādhippadhāno mahā kusalacittuppādo samaṭṭhāyībhāvo nāma. Kasmā, buddhassa sugatādiguṇārammaṇe ekaggattā samāhitacittattā vā. Soyeva pana santaraso nāma. Kasmā, buddhapaṇāmacetanā kusalaṅgena akusalaṅgassa pahīnattā. Buddhantipāṭhasesa padassa vāccabhūto buddhadabbo ārammaṇavibhāvo nāma. Kasmā, tassa paṇāmakusalacittuppādassa ārammaṇapaccayena upakārattā. Buddhassa sugatantyādiguṇo uddīpanavibhāvo nāma. Kasmā, paṇāmassa kāraṇattā. Kāraṇabhūtaṃ taṃ samaṭṭhāyībhāvaṃ upādāya jānitabbo diṭṭhadhammarogā diantarāyābhāvo ca samparāye saggamokkhasukhasampatti ca ānubhāvo nāma. Kasmā, ānisaṃsaphalattā.

Herein, this is the method of embellishment. The threefold wholesome volition of bowing to the Buddha, which is the expressed meaning of the word `name`, is the permanent mood (thāyibhāva). Why? Because it is the essence. Alternatively, the great arising of wholesome consciousness, predominant in concentration and associated with the threefold wholesome volition of bowing to the Buddha, is the permanent mood. Why? Because of one-pointedness on the object of the Buddha’s virtues, such as ‘Well-Gone,’ or because the mind is concentrated. This itself is the sentiment of tranquility (santarasa). Why? Because, through the wholesome factor of the volition to bow to the Buddha, the unwholesome factor is abandoned. The substance ‘Buddha,’ which is the expressed meaning of the remaining word ‘Buddhaṃ,’ is the objective determinant (ārammaṇavibhāva). Why? Because it is helpful to the arising of the wholesome consciousness of bowing by way of the object condition. The Buddha’s virtues, such as ‘Well-Gone,’ are the excitant determinant (uddīpanavibhāva). Why? Because they are the cause of bowing. It should be known that, based on that permanent mood which is the cause, the absence of dangers such as disease in this very life and the attainment of the happiness of heaven and liberation in a future life is the ensuant state (anubhāva). Why? Because it is the fruit of the benefit.

Tattha hi kiñcāpi ānubhāvadīpakaṃ padaṃ natthi. Kāraṇassa pana phalena vinābhāvato kāraṇassa phalaṃ viññeyyanti. Atha vā nametipadassa sāmatthiyato ānubhāvo dassitoyevāti daṭṭhabbo. Āvibhūto ussuko ca buddhapaṇāmassa ānisaṃsapajānanā mati ca alasābhāvo ca cittappasādo ca samādhityādi ca byabhicārībhāvo nāma. Lomahaṃsādibhāvo satvaṃkābhāvo nāmāti alaṅkāra nayo veditabbo. Evaṃ pacchimapacchimagāthāsūti.

Herein, although there is no word that illuminates the ensuant state (anubhāva), the fruit of the cause is to be understood from the fact that a cause cannot exist without its fruit. Alternatively, it should be seen that the ensuant state is indeed shown by the capacity of the word `name`. Manifest eagerness and zeal, understanding the benefits of bowing to the Buddha, absence of laziness, confidence of mind, concentration, etc., constitute the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva). The state of having goosebumps, etc., constitutes the involuntary states (sāttvikabhāva). Thus the method of embellishment should be understood. So it is in the subsequent verses.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Sugataṃ sobhanagataṃ sundaranibbānaṭṭhānaṃ gataṃ vā sammā gataṃ vā, sugataṃ sammā vacanaṃ gadaṃ bhāsanaṃ, seṭṭhaṃ pasatthataraṃ satipaṭṭhānādibhede dhamme [M 0.0022] gavesantaṃ vā santehi gavesitabbaṃ vā sattānaṃ hitasukhaṃ icchitaṃ vā, kusalaṃkusalaṃ kusalaṃakusalaṃ, jahaṃ jahitaṃ, amataṃ maraṇavirahitaṃ amataṃ amatanibbānasamannā gataṃ, santaṃ kilesadarathavūpasamaṃ, asamaṃ lokiyadhammena asadisaṃ maggaphalanibbānadhammaṃ. Dadaṃ dātaṃ dāyakaṃ vā, saraṇaṃ sabbasattalokassa paṭisaraṇabhūtaṃ. Lokaṃ sattasaṅkha rokāsasaṅkhataṃ tilokaṃ, saraṇaṃ jānantaṃ, araṇaṃ nikkilesaṃ, kilesasaṅkhātaraṇavirahitaṃ vā. Araṇaṃ sattesu kilesarajassābhāvaṃ, karaṃ desanāñāṇena kataṃ, abhayaṃ nibbhayaṃ, abhayaṃ nibbhayaṭṭhānaṃ nibbānadisaṃ, nāyakaṃ satte nibbānapāraṃ nentaṃ, nāyakaṃ tilokānaṃ jeṭṭhaṃ pāmokkhaṃ buddhaṃ sakkaccaṃ tīhi dvārehi ahaṃ name namāmīti.

Herein, this is the concise construction: To the Buddha—who is Sugata (Well-Gone), because he has gone to a beautiful place, the state of Nibbāna, or has gone rightly; who is Sugada (Well-Spoken), because he speaks rightly; who is Seṭṭha (Best), because he seeks the Dhamma divided into such things as the foundations of mindfulness, or is to be sought by the good, or desires the welfare and happiness of beings; who is Akusalajaha (Abandoner of the Unwholesome), because he has abandoned what is unwholesome; who is Amata (Deathless), because he is without death, endowed with deathless Nibbāna; who is Santa (Peaceful), because he has pacified the affliction of the defilements; who is Asama (Incomparable), because the Dhamma of the path, fruition, and Nibbāna is dissimilar to worldly phenomena; who is Dada (Giver), because he is a donor; who is Saraṇa (Refuge), because he is a shelter for the entire world of beings; who knows the world (lokaṃ jānantaṃ), the three worlds designated as the world of beings and the world as receptacle; who is Araṇa (Conflict-Free), because he is without defilements, or devoid of the conflict called defilements; who is a maker of non-defilement (araṇaṃ karaṃ), because he creates an absence of the dust of defilements in beings through the knowledge of teaching; who is Abhaya (Fearless) and a giver of fearlessness, the direction of Nibbāna; who is Nāyaka (Leader), because he leads beings to the far shore of Nibbāna, the chief and foremost leader of the three worlds—to that Buddha, I (ahaṃ) reverently (sakkaccaṃ) with the three doors (tīhi dvārehi) pay homage (name).

Paṭhamavandanagāthādvayavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the first pair of veneration verses is complete.

2.

2.

Nayanasubhagakāyaṅgaṃ,

Madhuravarasaropetaṃ;

Amitaguṇagaṇādhāraṃ,

Dasabalamatulaṃ vande.

I venerate him whose body and limbs are lovely to the eye,

Endowed with a sweet, excellent voice,

The repository of a collection of limitless virtues,

The incomparable one possessing the ten powers.

2. Evaṃ paṭhamaṃ gāthādvayena buddhassa namassitvā idāni nayanasubhagakāyaṅgantyādīhi pañcahi guṇehi thomitvā buddhaṃ vandituṃ nayanasubhagakāyaṅgantiādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana na na magaṇayuttattā navakkharehi lakkhitā bhujagasu sugāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “bhujagasusumatā nāmo”ti.

2. Thus, having first paid homage to the Buddha with a pair of verses, and now having praised him with the five qualities beginning with ‘lovely bodily limbs and eyes,’ the author utters the verse beginning ‘lovely bodily limbs and eyes’ in order to venerate the Buddha. This verse, however, should be understood as the Bhujagasusugatā gāthā. It is characterized by nine syllables because it is composed of the feet na, na, and ma. For it is said in the Vuttodaya: ‘It is named Bhujagasusumatā.’

Ayaṃ panettha yojanā. Yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ nā ca dve nagaṇāmo ca magaṇo ca yadi siyā. Sā bhujagasusu gāthāti matā ñātabbāti. Tattha pana nayanasubhagakāyaṅganti sabbasattānaṃ cakkhussa sobhanaṃ gatena kāyaṅgenasamannāgataṃ. Ettha [M 0.0023] hi nayananti samavisamaṃ dassentaṃ attabhāvaṃ netīti nayanaṃ, cakkhu labbhati. Nīdhātu yu. Subhaṃ sobhanaṃ gacchatīti subhagaṃ, kāyaṅgaṃ labbhati. Subhasaddūpapado gamudhātu kvi. Kāyassa aṅgaṃ avayavaṃ kāyaṅgaṃ. Bhagavato kāyaṅgaṃ labbhati. Chaṭṭhītappurisasamāsoyaṃ. Nayanassa subhagaṃ nayanasubhagaṃ, taṃ kāyaṅgaṃ yassa buddhassāti nayanasubhaga kāyaṅgo, buddho. So hi rūpakāyassa dassanā nuttariyaguṇayogato sabbasattānaṃ pasādacakkhussa sobhanaṃ gatena dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi ca asītyā nubyañjanalakkhaṇehi ca lakkhitena kāyaṅgena samannāgatoti attho.

Herein, this is the application. A verse line in which there are two na-feet and a ma-foot, should it be so, is to be known as a bhujagasusugatā verse. Therein, 'one with bodily limbs pleasing to the eye' means one endowed with bodily limbs that are beautiful to the eyes of all beings. Herein, 'nayana' is so called because it leads one's personal existence, showing what is even and uneven; thus 'eye' is obtained, from the root nī with the suffix yu. 'Subhaga' is one who goes beautifully; 'kāyaṅga' is obtained. It is formed with the prefix subha, the root gam, and the suffix kvi. 'Kāyaṅga' is a limb or part of the body. The Blessed One's bodily limb is obtained. This is a genitive determinative compound. 'Pleasing to the eye' is nayanasubhagaṃ; he whose bodily limb is such is nayanasubhagakāyaṅgo, the Buddha. For he, on account of the quality of the excellence of his visible form, is endowed with a bodily form—marked with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics—that is beautiful to the confident eye of all beings. This is the meaning.

Madhuravarasaropetanti piyapemanīyauttamasaddena samannāgataṃ, so hi bhagavā madhiyati piyati pemiyati vāti madhuro. Madhadhātu uro. Vuttañhi majjhimapaṇṇāsaṭīkāyaṃ “madhuroti piyo pemanīyo apalibuddho”ti. Atha vā madhiyati assādiyatīti madhuro, madhati sabbasattānaṃ pītiṃ undeti vaḍḍhetīti madhuro, madhadhātu unde uro. Tena vuttaṃ saddanītiyaṃ “madha unde”ti. Varitabbo icchitabbo patthitabbo vāti varo, saro. Varadhātu icchāyaṃ a. Sarati gacchati sotaviññāṇārammaṇabhāvanti saro, saddo. Saradhātu gatiyaṃ a. Sarati gacchati suyyamānatanti vā saro, sariyati suṇiyatīti vā saro, bhagavato aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato saddo labbhati. Upasampajjatīti upeto, upapubbaidhātu ta. Madhuro ca varo ca so saro cāti madhuravarasaro, tena upeto sampanno samannāgatoti madhuravarasaropetoti vuccati. Bhagavato pana hadaya vatthuno suvisuddhattā pittasemhādīhi apalibuddhattā deva manussehi madhurena piyena manāpiyena varena icchitapatthi tena aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatena sarena saddena upeto sampanno samannāgatoti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Endowed with a sweet, excellent voice' means endowed with a voice that is dear, beloved, and supreme. For the Blessed One is delighted in, loved, and held dear, thus he is madhura (sweet). From the root madh with the suffix ura. It is said in the subcommentary to the Majjhima Nikāya: '“Madhura” means dear, beloved, unhindered.' Alternatively, he is delighted in and savored, thus he is madhura; or he makes the joy of all beings well up and increase, thus he is madhura. From the root madh in the sense of 'to well up' with the suffix ura. Thus it is said in the Saddanīti: 'madh in the sense of 'to well up'.' 'It is to be chosen, desired, or wished for,' thus it is vara (excellent). From the root var in the sense of 'to desire' with the suffix a. 'It proceeds, it goes to the state of being an object for ear-consciousness,' thus it is sara, a sound. From the root sar in the sense of 'to go' with the suffix a.
