Or, 'it proceeds, being heard,' thus it is sara; or 'it is heard,' thus it is sara. The Blessed One's voice, endowed with eight factors, is obtained. 'One is endowed with it,' thus upeta. From the root i preceded by upa, with the suffix ta. 'Sweet' and 'excellent' and 'that voice,' thus madhuravarasara; 'endowed with,' 'possessed of,' 'furnished with' that, thus he is called madhuravarasaropeta. Because the Blessed One’s heart-basis is utterly pure and unobstructed by bile, phlegm, and the like, it is said that he is endowed with a voice, a sound, that is sweet, dear, delightful to the mind, excellent, wished for, and longed for by gods and humans, and which possesses eight factors.

Ettha [M 0.0024] ca kiñcāpi saropetanti sāmaññavasena vuttaṃ, bhagavato saro pana visaṭṭho ca, viññeyyo, mañju, savanīyo, bindu, avisārī, gambhīro, ninnādi cāti visesena aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatoti attho daṭṭhabbo. Vuttañhi majjhima paṇṇāse brahmāyusutte “aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato kho panassa gotamassa mukhato ghoso niccharati visaṭṭho ca, viññeyyo ca, mañju ca, savanīyo ca, bindu ca, avisārī ca, gambhīro ca, ninnādi ca. Yathāparisaṃ kho pana so bhavaṃ gotamo sarena viññāpeti, na cassa bahiddhā parisāya ghoso na niccharatī”ti.

Here, although it is said in a general way 'endowed with a voice,' it should be understood that the Blessed One's voice, in particular, is endowed with eight special qualities: it is distinct, intelligible, lovely, audible, rounded, not diffuse, deep, and resonant. For it is said in the Brahmāyu Sutta in the Middle Fifty: 'Indeed, the sound that issues from the mouth of the recluse Gotama is endowed with eight factors: it is distinct, intelligible, lovely, audible, rounded, not diffuse, deep, and resonant. The venerable Gotama makes himself understood to the assembly with his voice, yet his voice does not go outside the assembly.'

Tassāṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana visaṭṭhoti siniddho apalibuddho. Viññeyyoti viññāpanīyo pākaṭo. Visaṭṭhattāyeva cesa viññeyyo hoti. Mañjūti madhuro. Savanīyoti sotasukho, madhurattāyeva cesa savanīyo hoti. Bindūti sampiṇḍito. Avisārīti avisaṭo. Binduttāyeva cesa avisārī hoti. Gambhīroti gambhīrasamuṭṭhito. Ninnādīti ninnadavā. Gambhīrattāyeva cesa ninnādi hoti. Yathāparisanti cakkavāḷapariyantāpi ekabaddhaṃ parisaṃ viññāpeti. Bahiddhāti aṅgulimattampi parisato bahiddhā na gacchati. Kasmā. So evarūpo madhurasaro akāraṇā mā nassīti. Iti bhagavato ghoso parisāya mattakeneva caratīti vaṇṇitoti. Abhidhānappadīpikāyañca vuttā saṅgahagāthā –

In its commentary, however: visaṭṭha means smooth, unhindered. Viññeyya means easy to understand, manifest. It is intelligible precisely because it is distinct. Mañju means sweet. Savanīya means pleasant to the ear; it is pleasant to the ear precisely because it is sweet. Bindu means compact. Avisārī means not scattered. It is not scattered precisely because it is compact. Gambhīra means deep in origin. Ninnādī means resonant. It is resonant precisely because it is deep. 'According to the assembly' means it makes an assembly, even one bound together and extending to the limits of a world-system, understand. 'Outside' means it does not go outside the assembly even by a finger's breadth. Why? So that such a sweet voice might not be lost without reason. Thus it is praised that the Blessed One's voice travels only as far as the assembly. And in the Abhidhānappadīpikā, a summary verse is stated:

“Visaṭṭhamañjuviññeyyā, savanīyāvisārino;

Bindugambhīraninnādi, tyevamaṭṭhaṅgiko saro”ti.

"Distinct, lovely, and intelligible, audible and not diffuse; rounded, deep, and resonant—thus the voice has eight factors."

Yathā hi brahmuno saro pittasemhehi apalibuddhattā visuddho madhuro hoti. Yathā ca sīhabyagghādīhi vāḷamigehi anubandhā dhāvantā khuddakamigā karavīkasakuṇassa vikūjamānaṃ saddaṃ sutvā sarassa madhurattā maraṇabhayaṃ hitvā adhāvitvā ukkhittapādaṃ [M 0.0025] anikkhipitvā tiṭṭhantā suṇanti, evaṃ karavīkassa saddo dhammatābhāvena madhuro piyo manāpo hoti. Evaṃ bhagavatā kataṃ kammaṃ vatthuṃ sodheti, vatthussa suddhattā pittasemhehi ca apalibuddhattā bhagavato nābhito samuṭṭhahanto saropi aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato suvisuddho atimadhuro atipiyo atimanāpo hoti. Sā panesā hīnūpamā hoti, bhagavato hi saro tehi saddehi satabhāgena sahassabhāgena atimadhuro atipiyo atimanāpo hoti, tathā hi dhammāso karañño asandhimittā devī karavīkasakuṇassa madhurasaddaṃ sutvā cintesi “imassa tiracchānassa madhuro saddo, ko nāma sabbaññutañāṇasiriṃ pattassa bhagavato atimadhuro saddo”ti, pītiṃ uppādetvā taṃ pītiṃ avijahitvā sattahi jaṅghasatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāti, tasmā bhagavato madhuravarasaropetanti thometīti.

For just as the voice of a Brahmā is pure and sweet because it is unobstructed by bile and phlegm, and just as small deer, pursued by fierce beasts such as lions and tigers, upon hearing the warbling of the karavīka bird, abandon their fear of death because of the sweetness of its sound and, ceasing to run, stand listening with a foot raised and not yet set down—so too, by its very nature, the sound of the karavīka is sweet, dear, and delightful. In the same way, the kamma performed by the Blessed One purifies the physical basis of his speech. Because that basis is pure and unobstructed by bile and phlegm, the voice arising from the Blessed One’s navel is endowed with eight factors, being utterly pure, exceedingly sweet, most dear, and most delightful. But this is an inferior comparison, for the Blessed One’s voice is a hundred times, a thousand times more sweet, dear, and delightful than those sounds. Thus, when Queen Asandhimittā, wife of King Dhammāsoka, heard the sweet sound of the karavīka bird, she thought: 'If the voice of this animal is so sweet, what must the exceedingly sweet voice of the Blessed One be like, who has attained the splendor of omniscient knowledge!' Arousing rapture, and not abandoning that rapture, she, together with seven hundred attendants, became established in the fruit of stream-entry. Therefore, he is praised as 'endowed with a sweet, excellent voice'.

Amitaguṇagaṇādhāranti aparimiṇitabbasīlādiguṇasamūhānaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Ettha ca samitoti parimiṇitabboti mito, mādhātu parimāṇe ta, na mito amito. Guṇoti sīlādayo dhammā. Te hi guṇenti taṃsamaṅgīpuggalaṃ pakāsentīti guṇāti vuccanti. Guṇadhātu pakāsane a. Maṇisāramañjūsāṭīkāyaṃ pana “guṇanti attano ādhāraṃ pākaṭaṃ karontīti guṇā”ti vuttaṃ.

'A receptacle for a host of limitless virtues' means one who is the ground for collections of virtues, such as moral discipline, that cannot be measured. Herein, 'that which is to be measured' is mita; from the root mā in the sense of 'to measure,' with the suffix ta. Not mita is amita (limitless). 'Virtue' (guṇa) refers to qualities such as moral discipline. They are called guṇā because they enhance, that is, they make manifest, the person endowed with them. The root guṇa is in the sense of 'to make manifest,' with the suffix a. In the Maṇisāramañjūsā-ṭīkā, however, it is said: 'Guṇā are so called because they make their own receptacle manifest.'

Saddanītidhātumālāyañca “guṇa āmantane, guṇoti sīlādayo dhammā, kenaṭṭhena te guṇā, goṇāpiyati āmantāpiyati attani patiṭṭhito puggalo daṭṭhuṃ sotuṃ pūjituñca icchantehi janehīti guṇo. Ettha kiñcāpi sīlādi dhammānaṃ āmantāpanaṃ natthi, tathāpi taṃhetu āmantanaṃ nimantanañca teyeva karonti nāmāti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Aññe pana guñjante abyayante iti guṇāti atthaṃ vadanti. Tadanurūpaṃ pana dhātusaddaṃna passāma[M 0.0026]. Guṇa āmantane icceva passāma. Vicāretvā gahetabba”nti vuttaṃ. Amito guṇo amitaguṇo, tesaṃ gaṇo samūho amitaguṇagaṇo, tesaṃ. Ādhārati tiṭṭhati etthāti amitaguṇagaṇādhāro, jino labbhati. So pana samuddodakaṃ nāḷipattena aparimitaṃ viya kenaci aparimitānaṃ sīlādiguṇasamūhānaṃ ādhāro patiṭṭhānabhūtoti attho.

And in the Dhātumālā of the Saddanīti it is said: 'Guṇa is in the sense of 'to call.' Guṇa refers to qualities such as moral discipline. In what sense are they guṇā? A person established in them is called or invited by people who wish to see, hear, and honor him; thus guṇa. Here, although qualities such as moral discipline do not themselves do the calling, they are still the cause of calling and invitation; thus it is said. Others, however, state the meaning is 'they hum' or 'they sound,' hence they are called guṇā. But we do not see a root word corresponding to this. We see only 'guṇa in the sense of 'to call.' This should be accepted after investigation.' 'Limitless virtue' is amitaguṇa; a host or collection of these is amitaguṇagaṇa. 'They are held, they stand in this,' thus it is an ādhāra (receptacle); amitaguṇagaṇādhāra is 'a receptacle for a host of limitless virtues'; the Victor is obtained. Just as the water of the ocean is immeasurable by anyone with the tip of a blade of grass, so too he is the receptacle, the ground, for a host of limitless virtues such as moral discipline. This is the meaning.

Dasabalanti aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ tathāgatadasabalasampannaṃ. Ettha hi balanti kehici viruddhehi kāraṇe hi balanti na kampenti thirantīti balaṃ, dasa balāni yassa soti dasabalo, buddho. Taṃ pana duvidhaṃ hoti tathā gatassa dasabalaṃ kāyadasabalañca, ñāṇadasabalañcāti. Tesu hi kāyabalaṃ hatthikulānusārena veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

'One with the ten powers' means one endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, which are unshared by others. Herein, 'power' (bala) is so called because powers are strong (balanti), are not shaken by any opposing causes, and are firm; thus it is balaṃ. He who has ten powers is dasabalo, the Buddha. These ten powers of a Tathāgata are twofold: the ten powers of the body and the ten powers of knowledge. Among these, the bodily power should be understood in terms of the elephant clans. For it was said by the ancients:

“Kāḷā vakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ tambapiṅgalaṃ;

Gandha maṅgalahemañca, uposathaṃ chaddantime dasā”ti.

"Kāḷāvaka and Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, Piṅgala; Gandha, Maṅgala, and Hema, Uposatha, Chaddanta—these are the ten."

Imāni hi dasa hatthikulāni. Tattha kāḷāvakanti pakatihatthikulaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ dasannaṃ purisānaṃ kāyabalaṃ, taṃ ekassa kāḷāvakahatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ kāḷāvakānaṃ balaṃ, taṃ ekassa gaṅgeyyassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gaṅgeyyānaṃ, taṃ ekassa paṇḍarassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ paṇḍarānaṃ, taṃ ekassa tambassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ tambānaṃ, taṃ ekassa piṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ piṅgalānaṃ, taṃ ekassa gandhahatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gandhahatthīnaṃ, taṃ ekassa maṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ maṅgalānaṃ, taṃ ekassa hemavatassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ hemavatānaṃ, taṃ uposathassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ uposathānaṃ, taṃ ekassa chaddantassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ chaddantānaṃ, taṃ ekassa tathāgatassa, nārāyanasaṅghātabalantipi idameva vuccati. Tadetaṃ pakatihatthīnaṃ gaṇanāya hatthikoṭisahassānaṃ[M 0.0027]. Purisagaṇanāya dasannaṃ purisakoṭisahassānaṃ balaṃ hoti. Idaṃ tathāgatassa kāyabalaṃ hoti. Idaṃ pana tāsu tāsu pāḷīsu na āgataṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsuyeva āgataṃ. Tena vuttaṃ dasaka nipāta aṅguttaraṭīkāyaṃ “dasa balañāṇaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva. Na kāyabalaṃ viya aṭṭha kathārūḷhamevāti adhippāyo”ti. Ettha ca nārāyana saṅghāta balanti ettha nārā vuccanti rasmiyo, tā bahū nānāvidhā ito uppajjantīti nārāyanaṃ, vajiraṃ. Tasmā nārāyanasaṅghāta balanti vajirasaṅghātabalanti atthoti.

These are the ten families of elephants. Among them, the Kāḷāvaka should be understood as the ordinary family of elephants. The strength of ten men is that of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The strength of ten Kāḷāvaka elephants is that of one Gaṅgeyya. The strength of ten Gaṅgeyya elephants is that of one Paṇḍara. The strength of ten Paṇḍara elephants is that of one Tamba. The strength of ten Tamba elephants is that of one Piṅgala. The strength of ten Piṅgala elephants is that of one Gandha elephant. The strength of ten Gandha elephants is that of one Maṅgala. The strength of ten Maṅgala elephants is that of one Hemavata. The strength of ten Hemavata elephants is that of one Uposatha. The strength of ten Uposatha elephants is that of one Chaddanta. The strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is that of one Tathāgata; this is also called the strength of Nārāyana's solid mass. By calculation in terms of ordinary elephants, this amounts to a thousand crores of elephants. By calculation in terms of men, the strength is that of ten thousand crores of men. This is the bodily strength of the Tathāgata. This, however, is not found in the Pāḷi texts themselves but has come down only in the commentaries. Therefore it is said in the subcommentary on the Book of Tens of the Aṅguttara Nikāya: 'The ten powers of knowledge, however, have come down in the Pāḷi itself. The meaning is that it is not, like the bodily strength, established only in the commentaries.' And here, regarding 'the strength of Nārāyana's solid mass': `nārā` are said to be rays; because many diverse kinds arise from this, it is `nārāyana`, a thunderbolt. Therefore, 'the strength of Nārāyana's solid mass' means the strength of a solid thunderbolt.

Ñāṇadasabalaṃ pana vibhaṅgapāḷiyañca mūlapaṇṇāse mahā sīhanādasutte dasakanipātaaṅguttarapāḷiyañca vitthārena āgatameva. Sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ pana saṅkhepena dassayissāmi. Seyyathidaṃ. Ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇañca, kammasamādānānaṃ vipākañāṇaṃ, sabbatthagāminipaṭipadāñāṇaṃ, anekadhātu nānādhātu loka ñāṇaṃ, sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikataṃ ñāṇaṃ, parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattiñāṇaṃ, jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesaṃ vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇaṃ, pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ, sattānaṃ cutūpapātaṃ ñāṇaṃ, āsavānaṃ khayañāṇañcāti. Ayaṃ pana kamo abhidhammavibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ āgatakkamo.

The ten powers of knowledge, however, have come down in detail in the Vibhaṅga-pāḷi, in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta in the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, and in the Dasakanipāta-aṅguttarapāḷi. However, for the sake of easy comprehension, I will show them in brief. They are as follows: (1) the knowledge of what is possible and impossible; (2) the knowledge of the results of actions undertaken; (3) the knowledge of the path leading to all destinations; (4) the knowledge of the world with its many and diverse elements; (5) the knowledge of the diverse inclinations of beings; (6) the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other beings and other persons; (7) the knowledge of the defilement, cleansing, and emergence in regard to the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; (8) the knowledge of recollecting past lives; (9) the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; and (10) the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. This, however, is the sequence that has come down in the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga-pāḷi.

Cutūpapātañāṇaṭṭhāne pana mūlapaṇṇāsapāḷiyaṃ mahāsīhanādasutte ca dasakanipātaaṅguttarapāḷiyaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ āgataṃ. Atthato pana dibbacakkhuñāṇena cutūpapātassa passitattā sadisamevāti. Tattha hi ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇanti kāraṇākāraṇaṃ yathābhūtaṃ jānanañāṇaṃ. Kāraṇañhi yasmā tattha phalaṃ tiṭṭhati tadāyattavuttitāya uppajjati ceva pavattati ca, tasmā ṭhānanti vuccati. Kammasamādānānaṃ vipākañāṇanti samādiyitvā katānaṃ atītānāgata paccuppannānaṃ kusalākusalakammānaṃ sugatiduggatipaṭisandhisaṅkhātaṃ vipākaṃ nibbānaphalañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānanañāṇaṃ. Sabbattha gāminipaṭipadaṃ [M 0.0028] ñāṇanti sabbagatigāminiñca paṭipadaṃ maggaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānanañāṇaṃ. Tattha ca paṭipadanti paṭipajjati pāpuṇāti etenāti paṭipadaṃ, maggaṃ. Gatigāmininti nirayādipañcagatigāminiṃ. Agatigāmininti nibbānagāminiṃ. Vuttañhi “nibbānañcāhaṃ sāriputta pajānāmi nibbānagāminiñca paṭipada”nti.

However, in place of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, the knowledge of the divine eye is found in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa-pāḷi and in the Dasakanipāta-aṅguttarapāḷi. In meaning, however, it is the same, because one sees the passing away and rebirth of beings with the knowledge of the divine eye. Therein, 'the knowledge of what is possible and impossible' is the knowledge of knowing cause and non-cause as they really are. For a cause is called a 'possibility' (ṭhāna) because the fruit stands (tiṭṭhati) on it; dependent on it, it arises and continues. 'The knowledge of the results of actions undertaken' is the knowledge of knowing as it really is the result—designated as relinking in a good or bad destination—of wholesome and unwholesome kamma undertaken in the past, future, and present, and also the fruit of Nibbāna. 'The knowledge of the path leading to all destinations' is the knowledge of knowing as it really is the path, the way leading to all destinations. And therein, a 'path' (paṭipadā) is so called because one proceeds (paṭipajjati) and arrives (pāpuṇāti) by means of it; it is the way (magga). 'Leading to a destination' (gatigāminiṃ) means leading to the five destinations beginning with hell. 'Leading to no destination' (agatigāminiṃ) means leading to Nibbāna. For it is said: 'Sāriputta, I understand Nibbāna and the path leading to Nibbāna.'

Anekadhātunānādhātulokaṃ ñāṇanti ettha aneka dhātūti cakkhudhātuādīhi kāmadhātūhi vā bahudhātuṃ. Nānādhātūti tāsaṃyeva dhātūnaṃ vilakkhaṇattā visadisa sabhāvattā nānāppakāradhātuṃ. Lokanti khandhāyatana dhātulokaṃ. Ñāṇanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanañāṇaṃ. Sattānaṃ adhimuttikataṃ ñāṇanti sattānaṃ hīnādīhi adhimuttīhi nānādhimuttikabhāvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānanañāṇaṃ. Parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattiñāṇanti ettha parasattānanti padhānasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti tato paresaṃ hīnasattānaṃ. Ekatthameva vā etaṃ padadvayaṃ veneyyavasena dvedhā vuttaṃ. Indriyaparopariyattiñāṇanti saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ parabhāvaṃ vaḍḍhañca aparabhāvaṃ hāniñca yathābhūtaṃ pajānanañāṇaṃ.

'The knowledge of the world with its many and diverse elements': here, 'many elements' means the numerous elements such as the eye-element, etc., or the elements of the sense sphere. 'Diverse elements' means elements of various kinds, because those very elements are distinct and have dissimilar natures. 'The world' means the world of aggregates, sense bases, and elements. 'Knowledge' means the knowledge of knowing as it really is. 'The knowledge of the diverse inclinations of beings' is the knowledge of knowing as it really is the state of diverse inclinations of beings, due to their inferior, etc., inclinations. 'The knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other beings and other persons': here, 'other beings' means principal beings. 'Other persons' means other inferior beings. Or, this pair of terms is stated in two ways for the sake of those to be trained, but has a single meaning. 'Knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties' is the knowledge of knowing as it really is the superiority, or growth, and the inferiority, or decline, of the faculties such as faith.

Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesaṃ vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇanti ettha jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnanti paṭhamādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ, rūpī rūpāni passatītiādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ, savitakkasavicārādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samādhīnaṃ, paṭhamajjhāna samāpattiādīnañca navannaṃ anupubbasamāpattīnaṃ. Saṃkilesanti hānabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vodānanti visesabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vuṭṭhānanti yena kāraṇena jhānādīhi vuṭṭhahanti, taṃ kāraṇaṃ. Ñāṇanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānanañāṇaṃ. Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇanti pubbe nivutthakkhandhānussaraṇasaṅkhātaṃ pajānanañāṇaṃ. Sattānaṃ cutūpapātaṃ ñāṇanti sattānaṃ cutiñca upapātañca pajānanaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇanti kāmāsavādīnaṃ khayasaṅkhātaṃ āsavanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānana ñāṇanti[M 0.0029]. Imāni pana ñāṇāni aññehi asādhāraṇāni tathāgatassa dasabalañāṇānīti daṭṭhabbāni.

'The knowledge of the defilement, cleansing, and emergence in regard to the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments': here, 'jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments' refers to the four jhānas beginning with the first; the eight liberations beginning with 'Possessed of form, one sees forms'; the three concentrations beginning with that accompanied by initial and sustained thought; and the nine successive attainments beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna. 'Defilement' means a state conducive to decline. 'Cleansing' means a state conducive to distinction. 'Emergence' means the cause by which one emerges from the jhānas and so on. 'Knowledge' means the knowledge of knowing as it really is. 'The knowledge of recollecting past lives' is the knowledge of knowing designated as the recollection of formerly inhabited aggregates. 'The knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings' is the knowledge of the divine eye, which knows the passing away and rebirth of beings. 'The knowledge of the destruction of the taints' is the knowledge of knowing as it really is Nibbāna, the cessation of the taints, designated as the destruction of the taints such as the taint of sensual desire. These knowledges, however, are unshared by others and should be understood as the ten powers of knowledge of the Tathāgata.

Honti cettha –

And here there are these verses:

“Ṭhānāṭṭhānaṃ vipākañca, ñāṇaṃ paṭipadaṃ ñāṇaṃ;

Anekadhātulokañca, sattānaṃ adhimuttikaṃ. [sā panesā setavavipulāgāthāti daṭṭhabbā;]

Knowledge of the possible and impossible, and of results, knowledge of the path; knowledge of the world with its many elements, and of the inclinations of beings. [This should be understood as the extensive verse of Setavā.]

Indriyaparāparañca, jhānādinaṃ saṃkilesaṃ;

Vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇaṃ, pubbenivāsānussatiṃ;

Sattānaṃ cutūpapātaṃ, āsavakkhayaṃ ñāṇanti;

Dasimāni buddhassa cā, sādhāraṇāni ñāṇānī”ti. [sā panesā sāmaññagāthāti daṭṭhabbā;]

The superior and inferior faculties; the defilement, cleansing, and emergence of the jhānas, etc.; knowledge of recollecting past lives, of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and knowledge of the destruction of the taints—these ten are the knowledges common to the Buddha. [This should be understood as the general verse.]

Nanu dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ natthi, sabbaññutañāṇameva hoti, atha kasmā taṃ ñāṇaṃ dasabhedena vuttanti. Vuccate. Aññameva hi dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutañāṇaṃ, dasabalañhi sakasakakiccameva jānāti. Sabbaññutañāṇaṃ pana tampi tato avasesampi pajānāti. Dasabalañāṇesu hi paṭhamaṃ kāraṇākāraṇameva jānāti. Dutiyaṃ kammantara vipākantarameva. Tatiyaṃ kammaparicchedameva. Catutthaṃ dhātu nānattakāraṇameva. Pañcamaṃ sattānaṃ ajjhāsayādhimuttimeva. Chaṭṭhaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvameva. Sattamaṃ jhānādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ saṃkilesādimeva. Aṭṭhamaṃ pubbe nivutthakhandhasantatimeva. Navamaṃ sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhimeva. Dasamaṃ saccaparicchedameva. Sabbaññutañāṇaṃ pana etehi jānitabbañca tato uttariñca pajānāti. Etesaṃ pana kiccaṃ na sabbaṃ karoti. Tañhi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ na sakkoti. Iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ na sakkoti. Maggo hutvā kilese khepetuṃ na sakkoti. Evaṃ tesaṃ ñāṇadvayānaṃ visesoti. Taṃ pana idha ñāṇadvayaṃ adhippetanti.

But is not the knowledge of the ten powers without an individual essence, being simply the knowledge of omniscience? So why is that knowledge spoken of with ten divisions? It is said: The knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another. For the knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective function. But the knowledge of omniscience knows that and what remains beyond it. Among the powers of knowledge: the first knows only cause and non-cause; the second, only the diversity of kamma and the diversity of its results; the third, only the delimitation of kamma; the fourth, only the cause of the diversity of elements; the fifth, only the dispositions and inclinations of beings; the sixth, only the keenness and dullness of the faculties; the seventh, only their defilement and so on, along with the jhānas, etc.; the eighth, only the continuity of aggregates formerly inhabited; the ninth, only the passing away and relinking of beings; the tenth, only the determination of the truths. But the knowledge of omniscience knows what is to be known by these and what is beyond them. However, it does not perform their entire function. For it cannot, having become a jhāna, attain absorption; having become a spiritual power, perform transformations; having become the path, destroy the defilements. Such is the distinction between these two kinds of knowledge. But here, both kinds of knowledge are intended.

Atulanti [M 0.0030] sīlādīhi guṇehi kenaci puggalena asadisaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho. Tulanaṃ ummānaṃ tulā, tula sadisyaṃ. Saddanītiyañhi “tula ummāne”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā tuliyati pamiyati etāyāti tulā, pakatitulā. Tulā viyāti tulā, ñāṇaṃ. Tāya sammito tulo. Sammita taddhite apaccayo. Tulasadisañāṇena sammito puggalo. Na tulo atulo. Kammadhārayamissakatappurisa samāsoyaṃ. Sīlādiguṇehi kenaci puggalena asadiso bhagavā labbhati. Atha vā natthi tulo sadiso puggalo etassāti atulo, bhagavā. Atagguṇasaṃviññāṇoyaṃ bahubbīhi. Sīlādiguṇehi kenaci asadiso aggapuggaloti attho. Sadevake loke aggapuggalabhāvato. Yathāha “yāvatā bhikkhave sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā catuppadā vā, tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati, virāgo seṭṭho dhammānaṃ dvipadānañca cakkhumā”ti. Taṃ atulaṃ buddhanti sambandho. Vandeti buddhassa nayanasubhagakāyaṅgādiguṇaṃ anussaritvā tīhi dvārehi sakkaccaṃ ahaṃ vandāmīti attho. Ettha ca mivibhattiyā mahāvisayasuttena ekārā desoti daṭṭhabbo. Vandanā pana tividhā hoti kāyavacīmanovandanāvasenāti. Yathāha “tisso imā bhikkhave vandanā. Katamā tisso. Kāyena vandati, vācāya vandati, manasā vandatī”ti.

Incomparable means unequalled by any individual in virtues such as moral discipline. This is the verbal meaning here. Measuring is estimation, a balance; `tula` means similarity. For in the Saddanīti it is said: '`tula` in the sense of estimation.' Or, that by which one is weighed or measured is a `tulā`, a standard balance. Like a balance is knowledge. Measured by that is `tulo`. The suffix `a` is applied in the taddhita formation of `sammita`. A person measured by knowledge similar to a balance. Not `tulo` is `atulo`, incomparable. This is a compound that is a `kammadhāraya` mixed with a `tappurisa`. The Blessed One is obtained as one unequalled by any individual in virtues such as moral discipline. Or, 'there is no individual equal or similar to him,' thus he is `atulo`, the Blessed One. This is a `bahubbīhi` compound indicating the possession of that quality. The meaning is: the supreme individual, unequalled by anyone in virtues such as moral discipline, because of being the foremost individual in the world with its devas. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings—whether footless or two-footed or four-footed—the Tathāgata is declared the chief among them... dispassion is the best of states, and the one with vision is the best of two-footed beings.' 'That incomparable Buddha'—this is the connection. 'I pay homage' means: 'Recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, such as the beauty of his eyes and limbs, I respectfully pay homage with the three doors.' Here, it should be understood that the substitution of `e` for the `mi` ending occurs according to the Mahāvisayasutta. Veneration, indeed, is threefold: by way of bodily, verbal, and mental veneration. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of veneration. What three? One venerates with the body, one venerates with speech, and one venerates with the mind.'

Tattha yoniso manasikāracittaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā jāṇudvayakapparadvayanalāṭasaṅkhātāni pañca aṅgāni bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā vandaneyyānaṃ abhimukhaṃ nipatanto kāyena vandati nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya “pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā”ti aṭṭha kathādīsu vuttaṃ. Buddhaguṇapadāni vācāya pavattento vācāya vandati nāma. Vipassissa namatthu, sikhissāpi namatthu, vessa bhussa namatthu, kakusandhassa namatthu, koṇāgamanassa namatthu[M 0.0031], kassapassa namatthu, aṅgīrassassa namatthu tyādīsupi vācāvandanāyeva. Buddhādi guṇāni anussaranto manasā vandati nāmāti.

Herein, having established the mind with wise attention, one places the five points—the two knees, the two elbows, and the forehead—on the ground and prostrates towards those worthy of veneration: this is called veneration with the body. In reference to this, it is said in the commentaries and other works: 'Having venerated with the five-point prostration.' Causing words about the Buddha’s qualities to be uttered is called veneration with speech. For example: 'Homage to Vipassī, homage to Sikhī, homage to Vessabhū, homage to Kakusandha, homage to Koṇāgamana, homage to Kassapa, homage to Aṅgīrasa'—these too are instances of verbal veneration. Recollecting the qualities of the Buddha and others is called veneration with the mind.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Nayanasubhagakāyaṅgaṃ sabbasattānaṃ cakkhussa sobhanaṃ gatena kāyaṅgena samannāgataṃ, madhuravarasaropetaṃ piyapemanīyena assādi yena uttamasaddena samannāgataṃ, amitaguṇagaṇādhāraṃ aparimiṇitabbasīlādiguṇasamūhānaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ, dasabalaṃ anaññasādhāraṇena tathāgatassa kāyañāṇadasa balena samannāgataṃ, atulaṃ sīlādiguṇehi kenaci asadisaṃ buddhaṃ tīhi dvārehi sakkaccaṃ ahaṃ vande vandāmīti.

This is the concise construal here: 'Him whose physical form is beautiful to the eye' means endowed with a physical form beautiful to the eyes of all beings; 'him who is endowed with a sweet and excellent voice' means endowed with a supreme voice that is dear, endearing, and delightful; 'him who is the support for a collection of immeasurable qualities' means who has become the basis for a collection of immeasurable qualities such as moral discipline; 'him who has the ten powers' means endowed with the ten powers of the Tathāgata's physical strength and knowledge, which are not shared by others; 'him who is incomparable' means unequalled by anyone in virtues such as moral discipline—'that Buddha I respectfully pay homage to with the three doors.'

Dutiyavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the second verse of veneration is concluded.

3.

3.

Yo buddho dhitimāññadhārako,

Saṃsāre anubhosi kāyikaṃ;

Dukkhaṃ cetasikañca lokato,

Taṃ vande naradeva maṅgalaṃ.

That Buddha, resolute, upholder of final knowledge,

Who in saṃsāra experienced bodily

And mental suffering arising from the world,

To him, the auspicious god among men, I pay homage.

3. Evaṃ tatiyagāthāya buddhassa vanditvā idāni samādhi ādīhi catūhi guṇehi thomitvā vanditukāmo yo buddho dhitimāññadhārako tiādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana masajagaṇa garuyuttattā dasakkharehi lakkhitā suddhavirā jitagāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye-msā jgā suddhavirā jitaṃ matanti. Tassattho. Yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ msā masagaṇā ca jgā jagaṇagarukā ca ce siyyuṃ, taṃ vuttaṃ suddhavirājitanti mataṃ ñātabbanti. Dhitimā aññadhārako yo buddho lokato saṃsāre kāyikaṃ dukkhañca cetasikaṃ dukkhañca anubhosi naradevamaṅgalaṃ, taṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ vandeti sambandho.

3. Having thus venerated the Buddha with the third verse, now, desiring to praise and venerate him for the four qualities beginning with concentration, he utters the verse starting, 'Yo buddho dhitimāññadhārako.' This verse, being composed of an `m-gaṇa`, an `s-gaṇa`, a `j-gaṇa`, and a heavy syllable, and thus having ten syllables, should be understood as a Suddhavirājitagāthā. For it is said in the Vuttodaya: 'An `m-gaṇa`, `s-gaṇa`, `j-gaṇa`, and a heavy syllable make a Suddhavirājita.' Its meaning is: When each line has an `m-gaṇa`, an `s-gaṇa`, a `j-gaṇa`, and a heavy syllable, that verse is to be known as Suddhavirājita. The connection is: 'That Buddha who is resolute, an upholder of final knowledge, who in saṃsāra experienced, on account of the world, bodily suffering and mental suffering—to him, that auspicious god among men, I pay homage.'

Tattha [M 0.0032] hi yoti aniyamaniddeso. Yo yādisoti attho. Tassa ca aniyamavācaka sabbanāmapadattā vacanattho na kātabbo. Tassa pana ya oti padavibhāgo kātabbo. Tesu ca yasaddassa vāccaṃ aniyamo buddhadabbo appadhānena labbhati, tassa yādisayuttajaccanāmagottasīlavihārī gocarasaṅkhātaṃ aniyamasāmaññākārattaguṇameva padhānena labbhati. Paṭhamāsivibhattiyā kāriyabhūtassa okārassa vāccaṃ pakatūpanissayasaṅkhātaṃ kattukārakekavacanasaṅkhyaṃ labbhati. Atha vā sabbanāmabhāvaṃ yāti gacchatīti yo, aniyamavācakabhāvaṃ yāti gacchatīti vā yo, sabbanāma bhāvena yāti pavattatīti vā yo, sabbanāmabhāvena yātabbo ñātabboti vā yo, yātabbo ñātabbo etena vā aniyamatthoti yo.

Herein, `yo` is an indefinite designation. The meaning is 'whoever' or 'of whatever kind.' And because it is a pronoun signifying indefiniteness, a verbal analysis should not be made. However, a division of the word into `ya` and `o` should be made. Of these, the meaning of the word `ya`, indefiniteness, is obtained secondarily with reference to the substance 'Buddha'; its primary meaning is obtained as the quality of being a general, indefinite form—designated as its 'domain'—connected with such things of an indefinite kind as birth, name, clan, virtue, and abiding. The meaning of the `o`, which is the result of the first case ending, is obtained as the agent in the singular number, designated as having its own nature as support. Alternatively, `yo` is so called because it 'goes' (`yāti`) to the state of being a pronoun; or because it 'goes' to the state of expressing indefiniteness; or because it 'proceeds' (`yāti`) by way of being a pronoun; or because it is to be 'known' (`yātabbo`) by way of being a pronoun; or because the indefinite meaning is to be 'known' (`yātabbo`) by means of it.

Tenāhu porāṇā –

Thus the ancients have said:

“Nānākāraṇaṃ paṭicca, dhātupaccayaviggahaṃ;

Cintakānaṃ pabhāvova, padhānaṃ hoti cintane”ti.

"Relying on various reasons and the analysis of roots and suffixes, the power of thinkers becomes the primary factor in their thought."

Buddhoti paṭividdhacatusaccadhammo. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho. Bujjhati cattāri saccānīti buddho, bhagavā. Suddhakattusādhanoyaṃ. Budhadhātu ta. Bodhetā pajāyāti vā buddho, hetu kattusādhanoyaṃ. Aññesaṃ cattāri saccāni bodhetīti attho. Atha vā anaññabodhito hutvā savāsanāya sammohaniddāya bujjhati jāgarotīti buddho, dinakarakiraṇa samāgamena paramarucirasirīsobhaggappattiyā vikasitamiva padumaṃ aggamaggañāṇasamāgamena aparimitaguṇagaṇālaṅkata sabbaññutañāṇappattiyā bujjhati vikasatīti vā buddho, nibbāna saṅkhātaṃ ekāyanamaggaṃ bujjhati gacchatīti vā buddho. Budhasaddo hi ñāṇādīsu catūsvatthesu vattati.

'Buddha' means one who has penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Truths. This is the verbal meaning here. 'He awakens to the Four Truths,' thus he is a Buddha, the Blessed One. This is a derivation in the simple agentive sense, from the root `budh` with the suffix `ta`. Or, 'He awakens the generation of beings,' thus he is a Buddha; this is a derivation in the causal agentive sense. The meaning is that he causes others to awaken to the Four Truths. Alternatively, he is a Buddha because, not being awakened by another, he awakens from the sleep of delusion with its latent tendencies and is vigilant—just as a lotus, having attained supreme and delightful beauty and splendor through the convergence of the sun's rays, blossoms, so too he awakens and blossoms upon attaining omniscient knowledge, adorned with a collection of immeasurable qualities, through the convergence with the knowledge of the noble path. Or, he is a Buddha because he 'awakens to,' that is, 'goes to,' the one-way path called Nibbāna. For the word `budha` is used in four meanings, such as knowledge.

Tena [M 0.0033] vuttaṃ –

Thus it is said:

“Ñāṇe vikasane ceva, gamane cāpi jāgare;

Catūsvetesu atthesu, budhasaddo pavattatī”ti.

"In the sense of knowledge and of blossoming,

and also of going and of being awake:

in these four meanings

the word `budha` is used."

Atha vā sabbañeyyadhamme bujjhati jānātīti buddho, pārami bhāvitāya paññāya sabbe saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhamme bujjhati abujjhi bujjhissatīti vā buddho, sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavāti adhigatañāṇaguṇavisesehi bujjhitabboti vā buddho, bhagavatā bujjhitabbaṃ ñātabbanti buddhaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ, sabbaññuta ñāṇaṃ, tadassatthīti buddho, bhagavā. Atthato pana pāramitā bhāvito sayambhūñāṇena saha vāsanāya vihataviddhasta niravasesakleso mahākaruṇāsabbaññutañāṇādiapari meyyaguṇagaṇādhāro khandhasantāno buddho. Yathāha “buddhoti yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto, balesu ca vasībhāva”nti.

Or, 'he awakens to, he knows, all knowable things,' thus he is a Buddha. Or, 'with the wisdom developed by the perfections, he awakens to, has awakened to, and will awaken to all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena,' thus he is a Buddha. Or, he is a Buddha because he is to be awakened to through the special qualities of knowledge he has attained, as in 'Indeed, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One.' Or, that which is to be awakened to and known by the Blessed One is `buddhaṃ`. What is that? Omniscient knowledge. He possesses this, therefore he is a Buddha, the Blessed One. In terms of meaning, however, a Buddha is that continuity of aggregates which, through self-arisen knowledge developed from the perfections, has utterly destroyed the defilements with their latent tendencies without remainder, and is the basis for a collection of immeasurable qualities such as great compassion and omniscient knowledge. As it is said: 'A Buddha is that Blessed One who is self-arisen, without a teacher, who by himself fully awakened to the truths concerning things unheard before, and therein attained omniscience and gained mastery over the powers.'

Ettha ca buddho nāma sabbaññubuddha, paccekabuddha, catusaccabuddha, suta buddhavasena catubbidho hoti. Tattha kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni samatiṃsapāramiyo pūretvā sambodhippatto sabbaññubuddho nāma. Kappasatasahassādhikāni dve asaṅkhyeyyāni pāramiyo pūretvā sayambhūpatto paccekabuddho nāma. Avasesā khīṇāsavā catusaccabuddho nāma. Bahussuto sutabuddho nāma. Idha pana sabbaññubuddho adhippeto.

Herein, the term 'Buddha' is fourfold: the Omniscient Buddha, the Private Buddha, the Four-Truths Buddha, and the Buddha-by-learning. Among these, the Omniscient Buddha is one who has attained full enlightenment after fulfilling the thirty perfections over four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more. The Private Buddha is one who has attained self-enlightenment after fulfilling the perfections over two incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more. The remaining taint-destroyers are called Four-Truths Buddhas. One of great learning is called a Buddha-by-learning. Here, however, it is the Omniscient Buddha that is meant.

Dhitimāññadhārakoti ettha dhitimā aññadhārakoti padacchedo kātabbo. Dhitimāti samādhivanto, sampayutta dhamme ekārammaṇe dhāretīti dhiti, samādhi. Dhādhātuti. Ākārassa ikārādeso. Dhiyati ṭhapeti ekārammaṇe sampayuttadhammeti dhiti, cittena yogeneveso ekā rammaṇe [M 0.0034] patiṭṭhāpanavasena cittassa ārammaṇe niccalabhāvena patiṭṭhāpetīti attho. Dhiti assa atthīti dhitimā, buddho. So hi yathā mahāmeru catūhi disāhi bhusaṃ āgatehi vātehi na samiñjati, evaṃ paṭipakkhehi micchāvāda vātehi ca iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇehi ca lābhālābha yasāyasa nindā pasaṃsa sukhadukkhasaṅkhātehi lokadhammehi ca na samiñjati, samādhivantoyeva hotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, in the phrase `Dhitimāññadhārako`, the word-division should be made as `dhitimā aññadhārako` (resolute, upholder of final knowledge). `Dhitimā` means endowed with concentration. 'It holds associated states on a single object,' thus it is `dhiti`, concentration. It is from the root `dhā`; the `ā` is replaced by `i`. It is called `dhiti` because it places, it establishes, associated states on a single object; that is, by the application of the mind, it establishes the mind on an object with an unwavering nature. 'He has `dhiti`,' thus he is `dhitimā`, the Buddha. For just as the great Mount Meru does not tremble when struck by fierce winds coming from the four directions, so too he does not tremble when struck by the opposing winds of wrong views, by desirable and undesirable objects, and by the worldly conditions of gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, and pleasure and pain. He is, it is said, endowed with concentration.

Aññadhārakoti arahattaphalahārako. Vimuttisaṅkhātaṃ arahattaphalasetacchattaṃ dhārento vā. Jānāti paṭhama maggena diṭṭhasaccassa āmariyādaṃ anatikkamitvā vāti aññaṃ, arahattaphalaṃ. Āpubbañādhātu kvi. Āsaddo mariyādattho. Saṃyogaparattā ākārassa rasso, taṃ dhāretīti aññadhārako. Aññasaddūpapadadharadhātu ṇvu. Saṃsāreti khandhadhātuāyatanānaṃ abbocchinnaṃ pavattamāne saṃsāravaṭṭe.

'Bearer of final knowledge' means one who partakes of the fruit of arahantship. Or, one who bears the white parasol of the fruit of arahantship, which is designated as liberation. He knows final knowledge—the fruit of arahantship—by not transgressing the limit of the truth seen by means of the first path. The word 'aññā' is derived from the prefix 'ā' and the root 'ñā' with the suffix 'kvi'; the particle 'ā' has the meaning of 'limit,' and the long 'ā' is shortened because a conjunct consonant follows. 'He bears that' (taṃ dhāreti), thus he is a 'bearer of final knowledge' (aññadhārako). Alternatively, the word is formed from 'aññā' as a prefix, the root 'dhar,' and the suffix 'ṇvu.' One wanders on in the round of rebirths, where the aggregates, elements, and sense bases proceed without interruption.

Vuttañhi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

For it is said in the commentary:

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti.

“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense bases, proceeding without interruption, is called ‘wandering on.’”

Khandhadhātuāyatanānaṃ aññamaññasambandhena saṃpunappunaṃ sarati gacchati pavattatīti saṃsāro. Saṃpubbasaradhātu gatimhi ṇa. Atha vā khandhāyatanadhātuyo saṃ abbocchinnaṃ saranti gacchanti pavattanti etthāti saṃsāroti vacanattho kātabbo, tasmiṃ. Anubhosīti anupunappunaṃ abhuñji, avedayīti attho. Kāyikanti kāye sarīre pavattaṃ kāyikaṃ. Cetasikanti cetasi pavattaṃ cetasikaṃ. Taṃ pana padadvayaṃ dukkhantipade visesanaṃ. Dukkhanti vaṭṭadukkhaṃ. Dukkhanaṃ dukkhaṃ, atha vā dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ, dukkhadhātu a. Idaṃ pana nibbacanaṃ kāritavasena vuttaṃ. Yassa uppajjati, taṃ dukkhitaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Lokatoti sattalokahetu. Lokiyanti [M 0.0035] pavattanti ettha puññāpuññāni tabbipāko cāti loko. Lokadhātu ṇa. Atha vā kusalādīni lāti gaṇhātīti loko. Lādhātu okapaccayo. Satta lokova labbhati. Dhitimā aññadhārako yo buddho saṃsāravaṭṭe nimuggānaṃ sattānamanudayāya saṃsāravaṭṭadukkhato pamocetukāmo kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni atidukkarāni samatiṃsapāramiyo pañca mahā pariccāge ca karonto sattalokahetu kāyikaṃ cetasikaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭadukkhaṃ anubhavasīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tanti tādisaṃ buddhaṃ. Vandeti vandāmi.

It is called saṃsāra because the aggregates, elements, and sense bases repeatedly fare on, go, and proceed in relation to one another. The word is formed from the prefix 'saṃ' and the root 'sar' in the sense of 'going,' with the suffix 'ṇa.' Alternatively, the meaning of 'saṃsāra' should be understood as that wherein the aggregates, sense bases, and elements fare on, go, and proceed uninterruptedly. 'He experienced' (anubhosi) means he repeatedly partook of, that is, he felt. 'Bodily' (kāyikaṃ) refers to what occurs in the body. 'Mental' (cetasikaṃ) refers to what occurs in the mind. These two terms are adjectives qualifying the word 'suffering' (dukkhaṃ). 'Suffering' here means the suffering of the round of existence. It is suffering because it torments, or because it causes torment; the word is from the root 'dukkh' with the suffix 'a.' This explanation is given in a causative sense: it means that what arises makes one who experiences it suffer. 'For the world's sake' (lokatoti) means for the sake of the world of beings. The 'world' (loko) is that wherein merit, demerit, and their results proceed; the word is from the root 'lok' with the suffix 'ṇa.' Alternatively, 'loko' is so called because it takes up (lāti), that is, receives (gaṇhāti), wholesome states and so on; the word is from the root 'lā' with the suffix 'oka.' The world of beings is thus obtained. The meaning is: The steadfast one, the bearer of final knowledge, that Buddha, desiring to liberate beings submerged in the round of rebirths from its suffering, for the sake of the world of beings, endured bodily and mental suffering belonging to the round of rebirths while fulfilling the thirty perfections, which are extremely difficult, and the five great relinquishments over four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand kappas. 'Him' (taṃ) refers to such a Buddha. 'I venerate' (vande) means 'I pay homage' (vandāmi).

Naradevamaṅgalanti naradevānaṃ maṅgalabhūtaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha vacanatto. Nirayaṃ neti pāpuṇātīti naro, manusso. Nidhātu pāpunane aro. Ariyamanusso pana bhūtapubbagatika nayena naro nāmāti. Atha vā seṭṭhabhāvaṃ netīti naro, uttamaṃ pabbajjaṃ netīti attho. Vimānavatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ netīti naro. Puttabhātubhūtopi hi puggalo mātujeṭṭhabhaginīnaṃ pituṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, pageva bhattubhūto itarāsanti vuttaṃ. Visuddhimaggamahāṭīkāyaṃ pana naratīti naro, puriso. Yathā hi paṭhamapakatibhūto satto itarāya pakatiyā seṭṭhaṭṭhena puriucce ṭhāne seti pavattatīti purisoti vuccati, evaṃ nayanaṭṭhena naroti vuccati. Puttabhātu bhūtopi hi puggalo mātujeṭṭhabhaginīnaṃ pituṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Pageva itarā itarāsanti vuttaṃ. Tasmā idha pana naranti sāmaññena vuttampi visesena purisanaranti viññāyati padhānanayena gahaṇassa yuttattā. Dibbanti kāmaguṇa jhānābhiññācittissariyādīhi kīḷantīti devā. Divudhātu ṇa. Atha vā sarīrālaṅkārajutiyā dibbantīti devā. Devā ca nāma tividhā honti sammutidevā, upapattidevā, visuddhidevā cāti. Tattha mahāsammatakālato paṭṭhāya lokena [M 0.0036] devāti sammatattā rājāno deviyo rājakumārā ca sammutidevā nāma. Devaloke upapannā upapattidevā nāma. Buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavā visuddhidevā nāma. Idha pana upapattidevā adhippetā.

'The auspicious one for humans and devas' means one who is a blessing for humans and devas. Herein is the explanation of the words. One who leads to hell (nirayaṃ neti) is a 'nara,' a human. The word is from the root 'nī' in the sense of 'making reach,' with the suffix 'aro.' A noble person, however, is called a 'nara' by way of a previous state of existence. Alternatively, one who leads to the state of excellence is a 'nara'; the meaning is, one who leads to the supreme homeless life. In the commentary on the Vimānavatthu, however, it is said that a 'nara' is one who leads to the state of being the eldest. For even a person who becomes a son or brother stands in the position of a father to his mother's elder sisters; how much more so one who becomes a husband to other women. In the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā, however, it is said: 'He leads (nayati), thus he is a 'nara,' a man (purisa).' Just as a being of a primary nature is called a 'purisa' because he lies (seti) or proceeds in a high (ucca) place in the front (puri) by reason of his excellence over other natures, so too 'nara' is said in the sense of 'leading.' For even a person who becomes a son or brother stands in the position of a father to his mother's elder sisters; how much more so to other women. Therefore, here, though 'nara' is spoken of generally, it is specifically understood as a male human (purisanara), since it is appropriate to take it in its primary sense. 'Devas' are so called because they sport (dibbanti) with sensual pleasures, jhānas, supernormal powers, sovereignty over the mind, etc. The word is from the root 'div' with the suffix 'ṇa.' Alternatively, 'devas' are so called because they shine (dibbanti) with the radiance of their bodily ornaments. Devas are of three kinds: conventional devas, devas by rebirth, and devas by purification. Among these, from the time of Mahāsammata onwards, kings, queens, and princes are called 'conventional devas' because they are designated as 'devas' by the world. Those reborn in a deva world are called 'devas by rebirth.' The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants are called 'devas by purification.' Here, however, devas by rebirth are intended.

Maṅgalanti maṅgalabhūtaṃ. Tantipade visesanaṃ. Maṅganti vaḍḍhenti sabbasampattīhi sattānaṃ etenāti maṅgalo, buddho. Maṅgala dhātu vaḍḍhane alo. Atha vā maṅgaṃ vuccati pāpaṃ, taṃ veneyyānaṃ desanāya lunāti chindatīti maṅgalo, buddho. Maṅgasaddūpapadaludhātu kvi. Narā ca devā ca naradevā, tesaṃ maṅgalo naradevamaṅgalo, buddho. So pana manussadevabrahmānaṃ pūjanīyattā ca saṅkhe, cakkaṃ, puṇṇakumbho, garā, sirī, setacchattaṃ, aṅkuso, dhajaṃ, sovattikañcāti aṭṭhahi lokiyamaṅgalehi seṭṭhattā uttamattā ca maṅgalo nāmāti vuccati, tasmā buddhassa naradevamaṅgalanti thometīti adhippāyoti.

'Auspicious' (maṅgalaṃ) means being a blessing. It is an adjective for the word 'him' (taṃ). By this, they augment or increase the good fortune of beings, thus he is 'auspicious' (maṅgalo), the Buddha. The root 'maṅgala' is in the sense of 'increasing,' with the suffix 'alo.' Alternatively, 'maṅga' is said to be evil; he cuts or severs that for those to be trained by means of his teaching, thus he is 'auspicious' (maṅgalo), the Buddha. The word is formed from the word 'maṅga' as a prefix, the root 'lū,' and the suffix 'kvi.' Humans and devas are 'naradevā'; their auspicious one is the 'naradevamaṅgalo,' the Buddha. He is called 'auspicious' because he is worthy of veneration by humans, devas, and brahmās, and because he is the highest and most excellent, superior to the eight worldly auspicious symbols—the conch, the wheel, the full pot, the garā, the śrīvatsa, the white parasol, the goad, the banner, and the svastika. Therefore, the meaning is that he praises the Buddha as 'the auspicious one for humans and devas'.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Dhitimā samādhivanto aññadhārako arahattaphaladhārako arahattaphalase tacchattaṃ dhārento vā, yo yādiso buddho, saṃsāre saṃsāravaṭṭe, kāyikaṃ kāye pavattaṃ dukkhañca vaṭṭadukkhañca cetasi pavattaṃ dukkhañca vaṭṭadukkhañca, lokato lokahetu, anubhosi punappunaṃ abhavasi avedayi, naradevamaṅgalaṃ naradevānaṃ maṅgalabhūtaṃ, taṃ tādisaṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ vande vandāmīti.

Herein is the concise construal: I (ahaṃ) venerate (vande) that (taṃ) Buddha (buddhaṃ) of such a kind (yādiso), who is steadfast (dhitimā), possessing concentration (samādhivanto), the bearer of final knowledge (aññadhārako)—that is, the bearer of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphaladhārako) or one who bears the white parasol of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphalasetacchattaṃ dhārento vā)—and who is the auspicious one for humans and devas (naradevamaṅgalaṃ), a blessing for humans and devas (naradevānaṃ maṅgalabhūtaṃ); who for the sake of the world (lokato), that is, on account of the world (lokahetu), experienced (anubhosi)—that is, repeatedly became subject to (punappunaṃ abhavasi), felt (avedayi)—bodily suffering (kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ), that is, suffering occurring in the body (kāye pavattaṃ) and suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkhañca), and mental suffering, that is, suffering occurring in the mind (cetasi pavattaṃ) and suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkhañca), in saṃsāra (saṃsāre), that is, in the round of rebirths (saṃsāravaṭṭe).

Tatiyavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

Here ends the explanation of the third verse of veneration.

4.

4.

Bāttiṃsatilakkhaṇacitradehaṃ,

Dehajjutiniggatapajjalantaṃ;

Paññādhitisīlaguṇoghavindaṃ,

Him whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks, who is ablaze with the light issuing from his body's radiance, who has found the flood of the qualities of wisdom, resolution, and virtue,

Vande munimantimajātiyuttaṃ.

I venerate that sage, endowed with his final birth.

4. Evaṃ [M 0.0037] tatiyagāthāya buddhassa natvā idāni bāttiṃsatilakkhaṇacitradehantyādīhi chahi guṇehi thomitvā munino vanditukāmo bāttiṃsati lakkhaṇa citra deha ntyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana ta ja ja gaṇa garudvaya yuttattā ekādasakkharehi lakkhitā upaṭṭhitā gāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye tjā jgā garunāyamupaṭṭhitā sā”ti. Tassattho. Yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ tjā tajagaṇā ca jgājagaṇagarū ca garunā pādantagarunā ce yuttā, sā ayaṃ gāthā upaṭṭhitā nāmāti. Ettha ca eka garuke satipi dvigarukepi lakkhaṇasamānattā upaṭṭhitā gāthā nāmāti daṭṭhabbā. Tattha bāttiṃsati lakkhaṇa citra dehanti dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi vicitraṃ sarīravantaṃ. Ettha ca dvīhi adhikaṃ tiṃsaṃ bāttiṃsati. Dvisaddassa bādeso. Lakkhiyati lakkhitabbaṃ buddhasarīraṃ etenāti lakkhaṇaṃ. Dihati upacayati vaḍḍhati vā ettha kusalā kusalanti dehaṃ, sarīraṃ. Dihadhātu upacaye vaḍḍhane vā ṇa. Bāttiṃsati mahāpurisalakkhaṇehi citraṃ vicitraṃ dehaṃ sarīraṃ yassa soti bāttiṃsatilakkhaṇacitradeho, muni labbhati.

4. Having thus venerated the Buddha with the third verse, now, desiring to venerate the sage by extolling him with the six qualities beginning with 'Him whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks,' he recites the verse starting 'Him whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks.' This verse should be understood as being an Upaṭṭhitā stanza, characterized by eleven syllables, as it contains a ta-gaṇa, a ja-gaṇa, a ja-gaṇa, and two heavy syllables. For it is said in the Vuttodaya: 'That with t, j, j, g, g is the Upaṭṭhitā.' Its meaning is: That verse in each line of which there are a ta-gaṇa, a ja-gaṇa, a ja-gaṇa, and two heavy syllables is called Upaṭṭhitā. And here, although there is only one heavy syllable at the end, because of the similarity of the characteristic, it should be understood as an Upaṭṭhitā verse. Therein, 'Him whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks' means one having a body beautified by the thirty-two marks of a great man. Here, 'thirty-two' (bāttiṃsati) is thirty plus two; 'bā' is a modification of 'dvi.' 'Mark' (lakkhaṇaṃ) is that by which the Buddha's body is marked or recognized. 'Body' (dehaṃ) is that wherein wholesome and unwholesome states accumulate (dihati), are heaped up (upacayati), or increase (vaḍḍhati); the word is from the root 'dih' in the sense of 'heaping up' or 'increasing,' with the suffix 'ṇa.' He whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man is 'one whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks'; this refers to the sage.

Idaṃ panettha dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasarūpassa saṅkhepa dassanaṃ. Suppatiṭṭhitapādo ca, āyatapaṇhi, dīghaṅguli, muduta luṇahatthapādo, jālahatthapādo, ussaṅkhapādo, eṇijaṅgho, ṭhitakova anonamanto ubhohi pāṇitalehi jāṇu kāni parimasati parimajjati, kosohitavatthaguyho, suvaṇṇa vaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco, sukhumacchavī, ekekalomo, uddhaggalomo, brahmujugatto, sattussado, sīhapubbaddha kāyo, citantaraṃso, nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo, samavaṭṭakkhandho, rasaggarasī, sīhahanu, cattālīsadanto, samadanto, aviraḷadanto, susukkadāṭho, pahūtajivho, brahmassaro karavīkabhāṇi, atinīlanetto, gopakhumo, uṇṇā bhamu kantare [M 0.0038] jāto, uṇhīsasīso cāti dvattiṃsavidhāni honti mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni.

Herein is a brief presentation of the thirty-two marks of a great man: he has well-set feet, long heels, long fingers and toes, soft and tender hands and feet, net-like hands and feet, high-raised ankles, antelope-like calves, and standing and without bending he can touch and rub his knees with both hands; his male organ is enclosed in a sheath, his complexion is golden-hued like burnished gold, his skin is so delicate that no dust clings to it, he has one hair per pore, his body hairs grow upwards, he has a divinely straight body, he has seven convex surfaces, he has a lion-like upper body, the furrow between his shoulders is filled in, he has the proportions of a banyan tree, he has an evenly rounded torso, he has a supreme sense of taste, he has a jaw like a lion's, he has forty teeth, his teeth are even, his teeth are without gaps, his canine teeth are very white, he has a long and broad tongue, he has a voice like Brahmā's, like the call of the karavīka bird, his eyes are deep blue, he has eyelashes like a cow's, a white tuft of hair grows between his eyebrows, and his head has a cranial protuberance. These are the thirty-two marks of a great man.

Tena vuttaṃ pātheyyavagge lakkhaṇasutte “katamāni tāni bhikkhave dvattiṃsamahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dve gatiyo bhavanti, anaññā. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati rājā hoti cakkavatti…pe… sace khopana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammā sambuddho loke vivaṭacchado 1. idha bhikkhave mahā puriso suppatiṭṭhitapādo hoti. Yampi bhikkhave mahā puriso suppatiṭṭhitapādo hoti. Idampi bhikkhave mahā purisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati 2. puna caparaṃ bhikkhave mahāpurisassa heṭṭhāpādatalesu cakkāni jātāni honti sahassārāni sanemikāni sanābhikāni sabbā kāraparipūrāni. Idampi bhikkhave mahāpurisassa mahāpurisa lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati 3. puna caparaṃ bhikkhave mahāpuriso āyatapaṇhī hoti 4. dīghaṅgulī hoti 5. mudutaluṇa hatthapādo hoti 6. jālahatthapādo hoti 7. ussaṅkhapādo hoti 8. eṇijaṅgho hoti 9. ṭhitakova anonamanto ubhohi pāṇitalehi jāṇukāni parimasati parimajjati 10. kosohitavatthaguyho hoti 11. suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco 12. sukhumacchavī hoti sukhumattā chaviyā rajojallaṃ kāye na upalimpati 13. ekekalomo hoti, ekekāni lomāni lomakūpesu jātāni 14. uddhaggalomo hoti. Uddhaggāni lomāni jātāni nīlāni añjanavaṇṇāni kuṇḍalā vattāni padakkhiṇāvattakajātāni 15. brahmujugatto hoti 16. sattussado hoti 17. sīhapubbaddha kāyo hoti 18. citantaraṃso hoti 19. nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo hoti, yāvatakvassa byāmo, tāva takvassa [M 0.0039] kāyo 20. samavaṭṭakkhandho hoti 21. rasagga saggī hoti 22. sīhahanu hoti 23. cattālīsadanto hoti 24. samadanto hoti 25. aviraḷadanto hoti 26. susukkadāṭho hoti 27. pahūtajivho hoti 28. brahmassaro hoti karavīkabhāṇi 29. atinīlanetto hoti 30. gopakhumo hoti 31. uṇṇā bhamukantare jātā hoti odātā mudutūla sannibhā. Yampi bhikkhave mahāpurisassa uṇṇā bhamukantare jātā hoti odātā mudutūlasannibhā. Idampi bhikkhave mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati 32. puna caparaṃ bhikkhave mahāpuriso uṇhīsasīso hoti. Yampi bhikkhave mahāpuriso uṇhīsasīso hoti. Idampi bhikkhave mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati. Imāni kho tāni bhikkhave dvattiṃsamahāpurisassa mahāpurisa lakkhaṇānī”ti. Etesaṃ pana dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇānaṃ attho pacchā āvibhavissatīti.

Thus it is said in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta in the Pāthika Vagga: "What, bhikkhus, are the thirty-two marks of a great man, possessed of which a great man has only two destinies, and no other? If he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch... but if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, one who has rolled back the veil in the world. 1. Here, bhikkhus, the great man has well-set feet. That the great man has well-set feet, bhikkhus, this too is a mark of a great man. 2. Furthermore, bhikkhus, on the soles of the great man’s feet, wheels appear, with a thousand spokes, with their rims and hubs, complete in all aspects. This too, bhikkhus, is a mark of a great man. 3. Furthermore, bhikkhus, the great man has projecting heels. 4. He has long fingers and toes. 5. His hands and feet are soft and tender. 6. His hands and feet are net-like. 7. He has high-raised ankles. 8. His shanks are like an antelope’s. 9. Standing and without bending over, he can touch and rub his knees with both hands. 10. His male organ is enclosed in a sheath. 11. His complexion is golden; his skin has a golden sheen. 12. His skin is so fine that no dust or dirt adheres to his body. 13. His body-hairs grow one to a pore; single hairs grow in single pores. 14. The hairs on his body grow straight up; they are blue-black, the color of collyrium, and curl to the right in rings. 15. He has a frame as straight as Brahmā’s. 16. He has seven convexities. 17. The front half of his body is like a lion’s. 18. The furrow between his shoulders is filled in. 19. He has the proportions of a banyan tree: the span of his arms is the same as his height. 20. His shoulders are evenly rounded. 21. He has a supreme sensitivity of taste. 22. His jaw is like a lion’s. 23. He has forty teeth. 24. His teeth are even. 25. His teeth are without gaps. 26. His canines are very white. 27. He has a long tongue. 28. He has a Brahmā-like voice, like the call of the karavīka bird. 29. His eyes are deep blue. 30. His eyelashes are like an ox’s. 31. Between his eyebrows there is a tuft of hair, white and soft like cotton wool. That the great man has a tuft of hair between his eyebrows, white and soft like cotton wool, bhikkhus, this too is a mark of a great man. 32. Furthermore, bhikkhus, the great man has a cranial protuberance. That the great man has a cranial protuberance, bhikkhus, this too is a mark of a great man. These, bhikkhus, are the thirty-two marks of a great man." The meaning of these thirty-two marks of a great man will become clear later.

Dehajjutiniggatapajjalantanti bhagavato rūpakāyato nikkhantehi chabbaṇṇaraṃsīsaṅkhātehi obhāsehi parisamantato vijjotavantaṃ. Javati dibbatīti juti. Judhātuti. Nigacchati niccharatīti niggatā, rasmi. Nipubbagamudhātu ta. Pakārena jalate dibbate pajjalantaṃ. Ettha ca dehaniggatajutīti vattabbe chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ padavipariyāyena dehajjutiniggatanti vuttaṃ. Tasmā dehato niggatā jutīti samāso daṭṭhabbo. Dehato rūpakāyato niggatehi niccharehi jutīhi raṃsīhi pajjalantaṃ yassa soti dehajjuti niggatapajjalanto, muni labbhati. Munino hi puratthimakāyato chabbaṇṇarasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ agga hesi. Pacchimakāyato dakkhiṇahatthato vāmahatthato chabbaṇṇā rasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesi. Upari kesantato paṭṭhāya sabbakesavattehi moragīvavaṇṇā rasmi [M 0.0040] uṭṭhahitvā gaganatale asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesi. Heṭṭhāpādatalehi pavāḷavaṇṇā rasmi uṭṭhahitvā ghanapathaviyaṃ asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesi, evaṃ samantā asītihatthamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo vijjotamānā vipphandamānā kañcanadaṇḍadīpikāhi niccharitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandajālā viya catuddīpika mahāmeghato nikkhantavijjulatā viya vidhāviṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā dehajjutiniggatapajjalantanti thometīti.

'Blazing with light emitted from the body' means shining all around with the radiances, known as the six-colored rays, that issued from the Blessed One's physical body. Juti (radiance) is so called because 'it shines, it gleams' (javati dibbatīti), from the root ju. Niggatā (emitted) is so called because 'it goes forth, it issues' (nigacchati niccharatīti); it is from the root gam preceded by ni, with the suffix ta. Pajjalantaṃ (blazing) means 'it shines, it gleams in a special way' (pakārena jalate dibbate). Here, although one should say dehaniggatajutī (light emitted from the body), for the sake of preserving the meter, the words are inverted and it is said dehajjutiniggata. Therefore, the compound should be understood as 'the light emitted from the body' (dehato niggatā juti). 'One who is blazing with the light emitted from the body' (dehajjutiniggatapajjalanto) is one who is blazing with the radiances, the rays, that issue from the physical body; this refers to the Muni. For from the front of the Muni's body, six-colored rays arose and extended for a distance of eighty cubits. From the back of his body, from his right hand, and from his left hand, six-colored rays arose and extended for a distance of eighty cubits. From the top of his head, from the tip of every hair, rays the color of a peacock's neck arose and extended for a distance of eighty cubits into the sky. From the soles of his feet, coral-colored rays arose and extended for a distance of eighty cubits into the solid earth. Thus, it is said that in all directions, for a distance of eighty cubits, the six-colored Buddha-rays shone and vibrated, spreading out like flames leaping into the sky from golden torches, like streaks of lightning flashing from a great cloud covering the four continents. Therefore, he is praised with the words 'blazing with light emitted from the body'.

Paññādhiti sīla guṇoghavindanti ettha paññāti sabbaññuta ñāṇaṃ. Dhitīti jhānamaggaphalasampayuttasamādhi. Sīlanti pacceka buddhāriyasāvakehi asādhāraṇaṃ suvisuddhaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Oghanti samūhaṃ. Vindanti laddhaṃ. Pakārena yathāsabhāvaṃ sabbañeyyadhammaṃ vā jānāti paṭivijjhatīti paññā. Sabbaññuta ñāṇaṃ. Papubbañādhātu a. Sā panesā pajānanalakkhaṇā paṭivedhalakkhaṇā obhāsanalakkhaṇā ca, visayobhāsa rasā, asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā, samādhipadaṭṭhānā. Dhitisaddassa vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Sīlatīti sīlaṃ. Kāyavacīkammāni sammā dahati sammā ṭhapetīti attho. Atha vā sīlati samādhiyati kāyakammādīnaṃ susilya bhāvena na vippakiratīti sīlaṃ, sīlanti samādahanti cittaṃ etenāti vā sīlaṃ, catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Sīladhātu a. Idaṃ pana patiṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇaṃ, dussilyaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ anavajjarasaṃ vā, soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, hiriottappapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Guṇasaddassa vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Uhanati samūhaṃ karoti ettha avayavanti ogho, samūho. Upubbahanadhātu ṇa. Ussa o. Hanassa gho. Abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkāyaṃ pana “avayavaṃ byapiyati gacchatīti ogho”ti vuttaṃ. Vindanaṃlabhanaṃ vindaṃ, vindiyittha labbhitthāti vā vindaṃ, paññā ca dhiti ca sīlañca taṃ guṇañcāti paññādhitisīlaguṇā, tesaṃ ogho samūhoti tathā, taṃ vindaṃ labhanaṃ yassāti paññādhitisīlaguṇoghavindo, muni[M 0.0041]. Atha vā vindaṃ labhitabbaṃ paññādhitisīlaguṇoghaṃ yenāti paññādhitisīlaguṇoghavindo. Tatiyābahubbīhi samāsoyaṃ. Vindānaṃ labhitabbānaṃ paññādhitisīla saṅkhātānaṃ guṇānaṃ samūho atthīti attho. Taṃ.

Regarding 'one who has found the mass of qualities: wisdom, steadfastness, and virtue': Herein, paññā (wisdom) is the knowledge of omniscience. Dhiti (steadfastness) is the concentration associated with the jhānas, paths, and fruits. Sīla (virtue) is the perfectly pure fourfold purification virtue, which is not shared by Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples. Ogha (mass) means a collection. Vinda (found) means obtained. Paññā is so called because it knows (jānāti) or penetrates (paṭivijjhati) all knowable things in their particular nature and as they really are; it is the knowledge of omniscience. It is formed from the root ñā with the prefix pa and the suffix a. It has the characteristic of understanding, penetration, and illumination; the function of illuminating its object; the manifestation of non-delusion; and the proximate cause of concentration. The etymology of the word dhiti has been explained above. Sīla is so called because it composes (sīlati); the meaning is that it properly settles and establishes bodily and verbal actions. Or, sīla is so called because it concentrates (sīlati samādhiyati), not allowing bodily actions and so on to be scattered, through their being well-behaved. Or, sīla is that by which they compose (sīlanti samādahanti) the mind; it is the fourfold purification virtue. It is from the root sīl with the suffix a. It has the characteristic of establishing; the function of destroying misconduct or of being blameless; the manifestation of purity; and the proximate cause of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing. The etymology of the word guṇa has been explained above. Ogha (mass, collection) is that wherein parts are gathered (uhanati) or collected (samūhaṃ karoti). It is from the root han with the prefix u and the suffix ṇa; the u becomes o, and han becomes gho. But in the subcommentary to the Abhidhānappadīpikā it is said: 'Ogha is so called because it pervades (byāpiyati) or goes to (gacchati) the parts.' Vindaṃ means 'finding' or 'obtaining'; or it means 'what was found' or 'what was obtained'. 'Wisdom, steadfastness, and virtue are the qualities' (paññādhitisīlaguṇā); their 'mass' (ogha) or collection is such. He for whom there is the 'finding' (vindaṃ) of that is paññādhitisīlaguṇoghavindo, the Muni. Alternatively, he by whom the mass of qualities to be found (vindaṃ)—wisdom, steadfastness, and virtue—was found is paññādhitisīlaguṇoghavindo. This is an instrumental bahubbīhi compound. The meaning is that he possesses the collection of qualities to be found, called wisdom, steadfastness, and virtue. Him.

Vandeti ahaṃ vandāmi. Muninti buddhaṃ. Munāti jānāti paricchindati vā hitāhitanti muni, buddho. Munadhātu ñāṇe i. Atha vā munāti jānāti ubho attheti muni, khandhādi loke tulaṃ āropetvā minanto viya ime ajjhattikā khandhā ime bāhirātiādinā nayena idhalokatthañca paralokatthañca bhagavā jānātīti attho. So panesa agāriyamuni, anāgāriyamuni, sekhamuni, asekhamuni, paccekamuni, munimuni cāti anekavidho. Tattha agāriyamunīti gihipi āgataphalo viññātasāsano. Anāgāriyamunīti tathārūpova pabbajito. Sekhamunīti satta sekkhā. Asekhamunīti khīṇāsavo. Paccekamunīti paccekabuddho. Munimunīti sammāsambuddho. Tesu pana idha munimuni adhippeto, taṃ muniṃ. Antimajātiyuttanti antimena carimabhavena yuttaṃ. Avasānaṃ amati gacchatīti antaṃ. Amadhātu ta. Massa no. Ante bhavo antimo, carimabhavo. Jānanaṃ nibbattanaṃ jāti, khandhānaṃ pavatti. Kammena janiyati nibbattiyatīti vā jāti. Upapattibhavo labbhati. Jānidhātuti. Dhātvanta lopo. Antimajātiyā yuttoti antimajātiyutto, muni. Āyatiñhi tīsu bhavesu paṭisandhijanakānaṃ sabba kilesānaṃ bodhipallaṅkeyeva aggamaggena samucchinditattā bhagavato anāgate punabbhavo natthi, tasmā ayaṃ ariyajāti pacchimattabhāvayuttoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Vande means 'I pay homage.' Muniṃ means the Buddha. A muni (sage) is one who knows (munāti), understands (jānāti), or discerns (paricchindati) the beneficial and the harmful; this is the Buddha. The root mun is used in the sense of knowing; the suffix is i. Alternatively, a muni is one who knows (munāti) both benefits, that is, the benefit of this world and the benefit of the next world. The meaning is that the Blessed One knows these by, as it were, placing the aggregates and so on upon a scale and weighing them, in the manner of 'these are the internal aggregates, these are the external aggregates,' and so on. This sage is of many kinds: the householder sage, the homeless sage, the trainee sage, the adept sage, the solitary sage, and the Sage of Sages. Therein, a householder sage is a layperson who has attained a fruit and understood the teaching. A homeless sage is one who has gone forth and is of the same kind. A trainee sage refers to the seven trainees. An adept sage is one whose taints are destroyed. A solitary sage is a Paccekabuddha. The Sage of Sages is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Among these, the Sage of Sages is intended here. 'That sage' (taṃ muniṃ). 'Endowed with the final birth' means endowed with the last existence. Anta (end) is so called because one goes (amati) to the cessation (avasānaṃ). It is from the root am with the suffix ta; the m becomes n. Antimo means 'that which is at the end'; the final existence. Jāti (birth) is the arising, the production, the continuity of the aggregates. Or, jāti is that which is born or produced by kamma; the plane of rebirth is meant. It is from the root jan with the suffix ti; the final of the root is elided. 'Endowed with the final birth' is antimajātiyutto; this refers to the Muni. For in the future, there is no further rebirth for the Blessed One, since all the defilements that generate rebirth in the three planes of existence were utterly eradicated by the supreme path right at the seat of awakening. Therefore, it is said that this noble birth is endowed with the final state of existence.

Tena vuttaṃ dhammacakkapavattanasutte –

Therefore it was said in the Dhammacakkapavattana Sutta:

“Ñāṇañca medassanaṃ udapādi, akuppāme vimutti, ayamantimā jāti, natthidāni punabbhavo”ti.

“Knowledge and vision arose in me; unshakeable is my liberation; this is my last birth; there is now no more renewed existence.”

Ayaṃ [M 0.0042] panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Bāttiṃsatilakkhaṇacitraṃ dehaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi vicitraṃ rūpakāyavantaṃ, dehajjutiniggata pajjalantaṃ rūpakāyato niggatehi chabbaṇṇaraṃ sīhi parisamantato vijjotavantaṃ, paññādhitisīlaguṇo ghavindaṃ paññādhitisīlasaṅkhatānaṃ guṇānaṃ samūhaṃ labhanavantaṃ, vinditabbānaṃ paññādhitisīlasaṅkhātānaṃ guṇānaṃ samūhavantaṃ vā, antimajātiyuttaṃ carimabhavena carimattabhāvena vā yuttaṃ muniṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ tīhi dvārehi sakkaccaṃ vande vandāmīti.

Here is the concise explanation of this: I reverently pay homage with the three doors (of body, speech, and mind) to the Sage, the Buddha, whose physical body is adorned with the thirty-two characteristics and variegated with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; who shines forth with the radiance of his body, illuminating all around with six-colored rays emanating from his physical body; who possesses a wealth of qualities, namely wisdom, steadfastness, and virtue, or a collection of qualities known as wisdom, steadfastness, and virtue; and who is endowed with his final birth, or ultimate existence.

Catutthavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the fourth verse of homage is concluded.

5.

5.

Pātodayaṃ bāladivākaraṃva,

Majjhe yatīnaṃ lalitaṃ sirīhi;

Puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhaṃ anejaṃ,

Vandāmi sabbaññumahaṃ munindaṃ.

I pay homage to the Omniscient One, the Lord of Sages, whose face is like the full moon, unstirring, graced with splendor amidst the monks, like the newly risen sun at dawn.

5. Evaṃ catutthagāthāya buddhaṃ vanditvā idāni sirīhi lalitantyādīhi catūhi guṇehi thomitvā vanditukāmo pātodayantyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana ta ta ja gaṇadvigarūhi yuttattā ekādasakkharehi lakkhitā indavajirā gāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “indādikā tā vajirā jagāgo”ti. Tassattho, yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ tā dveta gaṇā ca jagā jagaṇa garu ca go garu ca ce bhavanti, sā indā dikā indasaddaādikā vajirā vajirāgāthā nāmāti.

5. Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the fourth verse, now wishing to praise him with the four qualities beginning with 'graced with splendor,' he speaks the verse beginning with 'Pātodayaṃ'. This verse, marked by eleven syllables due to its composition with two `ta` gaṇas, a `ja` gaṇa, and two long syllables, should be understood as the Indavajirā verse. For it is said in the Vuttodaya: 'Indādikā tā vajirā jagāgo.' Its meaning is: that in which each foot has two `ta` gaṇas, a `ja` gaṇa, and two `garu` syllables, is called the Indavajirā verse, named after the initial word 'inda'.

Tattha pātodayanti ettha pāto udayanti padacchedo kātabbo. Page pubbaṇhasamaye pācīnalokadhātuto uggatanti attho. Pāto page pācīnalokadhātuto udeti uggacchatīti pātodayo, sūriyo. Pātopubba udadhātu uggamane ayo, taṃ pātodayaṃ. Bāladivā karaṃ [M 0.0043] vāti bāladivākaraṃ ivātipadacchedo. Bāladivākaraṃ vāti niggatābhinavasūriyaṃ viya. Ettha ca bāloti sampati jāto taruṇadārako potako vā. So hi balati assasitapassasitamattena jīvati na seṭṭhena paññājīvitenāti bālo, taruṇadārako. Baladhātu pāṇane jīvāyaṃ vā. Sūriyaraṃsinā divati dibbatīti divā. Divudhātu a. Atha vā dīyati khīyati andhakāro etenāti divā. Dīdhātu khaye a, vāgamo. Taṃ karotīti divākaro, divā divase vā karo ābhā yassāti divākaro, sūriyo. Bālasadiso divākaro bāladivākaro. Atha vā bālo iva divākaroti bāladivākaro, navuggatasūriyo. So pana ākāse nakkhattatārānaṃ majjhe sahassaraṃsīhi lalati vilāsati viyāti attho.

Here, in `pātodayanti`, the word division should be made as `pāto udayanti`. The meaning is: it rises from the eastern world-sphere in the early morning. `Pāto` means 'in the early morning'; `udeti` or `uggacchati` means 'rises' from the eastern world-sphere. Thus, `pātodayo` is the sun. The word `pātodayaṃ` is formed from `pāto` and the root `uda` (to rise) with the suffix `ayo`. `Bāladivākaraṃ vā` should be divided as `bāladivākaraṃ iva`. `Bāladivākaraṃ` means 'like a newly risen sun'. Here, `bālo` refers to a newly born young child or offspring. For such a one lives merely by breathing in and out, not by the superior life of wisdom; hence, `bālo` means a young child. The root `bala` is in the sense of 'breathing' or 'living'. `Divā` is derived from `divati` or `dibbatī`, meaning 'it shines with the sun's rays'. The root is `divu` with the suffix `a`. Alternatively, `divā` comes from `dīyati` or `khīyati`, meaning 'darkness is dispelled by it'. The root is `dī` in the sense of 'destruction', with the suffix `a` and the augment `va`. `Divākaro` means 'that which makes it' (the day), or 'that which makes light during the day'—the sun. `Bālasadiso divākaro` means 'a sun like a young one', or `bālo iva divākaroti` means 'a sun like a young one', a newly risen sun. It shines and sports amidst the stars and constellations in the sky with a thousand rays—this is the meaning.

Yatīnanti bhikkhūnaṃ. Te hi yatanti uṭṭhahanti ghaṭanti vāyamanti kusale dhammeti yatīti vuccanti. Yata dhātu patiyatane vāyāme vā i. Atha vā yamanti uparamanti akusale dhammeti yatīti vuccanti. Yamudhātu uparame i. Dhātvantalopo. Tesaṃ yatīnaṃ. Lalitanti vilāsitaṃ. Lalati vilāsetīti lalito, muni. Laladhātu vilāse ta. Taṃ. Sirīhīti bhagavato kāyaṅgasobhaggapattehi sirīhi, bāttiṃsalakkhaṇāsītyā nubyañjanachabbaṇṇaraṃsīsaṅkhatehi sampattisirīhi vā. Katapuññe nissayatīti sirī. Sidhātu sevāyaṃ rapaccayo itthi liṅgajotakaīpaccayo ca. Katapuññehi seviyatīti vā sirī, sampatti. Mūlaṭīkāyaṃ pana “sirīti paññāpuññāna metaṃ adhivacana”nti vuttaṃ. Yatīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ majjhe sirīhi lalitaṃ vilāsitanti sambandho. Ettha ca idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, yathā pāto udito uggato sūriyo ākāse nakkhattatārānaṃ [M 0.0044] majjhe sahassaraṃsīhi lalati vilāsati, evaṃ muni loke yatīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ majjhe bāttiṃsalakkhaṇā sītyānubyañjanachabbaṇṇaraṃsīhi alaṅkatehi sarīrasobhagga pattīhi sampattisirīhi lalati vilāsatīti.

`Yatīnaṃ` means 'of the monks'. For they strive, exert, and endeavor in wholesome qualities; thus, they are called `yatī`. The root `yata` is in the sense of 'striving' or 'exertion', with the suffix `i`. Alternatively, they restrain themselves from unwholesome qualities; hence, they are called `yatī`. The root `yamu` is in the sense of 'restraint', with the suffix `i` and the elision of the root-ending. Thus, `yatīnaṃ` (of the monks). `Lalitaṃ` means 'graced'. `Lalati` means 'to grace'; thus, `lalito` (graced), the Muni. The root `lala` is in the sense of 'grace', with the suffix `ta`. That is, `taṃ`. `Sirīhi` refers to the splendor of the Blessed One’s bodily beauty, or to the splendor of attainment consisting of the thirty-two major characteristics, eighty minor characteristics, and the six-colored rays. `Sirī` is that which is resorted to by those who have done merit. The root `sidh` is in the sense of 'service', with the affix `ra` and the feminine marker `ī`. Alternatively, `sirī` means 'prosperity', as it is served by those with merit. However, in the Mūlaṭīkā it is said: '`Sirī` is a term for wisdom and merit'. The connection is: 'graced with splendor amidst the monks'. Here, this is said: Just as the sun, having risen at dawn, shines and sports amidst the stars and constellations in the sky with a thousand rays, so too the Muni, in the world, shines and sports amidst the monks with the thirty-two major characteristics, eighty minor characteristics, six-colored rays, and the splendor of his bodily beauty and attainment of prosperity.

Puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhanti puṇṇacandena sadisaṃ ānanasampannaṃ. Yathā hi cando kāḷapakkhe pāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāya dine dine ūno hoti, evaṃ na munino mukhaṃ ānanaṃ ūnaṃ. Bhagavato pana mukhaṃ niccaṃ paripuṇṇacandamaṇḍalaṃ viya anūnaṃ hutvā sobhati, tasmā puṇṇasaddena visesetvā puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhanti thometi. Soḷasakalehi pūretīti puṇṇaṃ. Pūradhātu ta, tassa ṇṇo. Idati nakkhattatārānaṃ issariyaṃ karotīti indu, ididhātu issariyaṃ u. Puṇṇaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ indu puṇṇindu, cando. Saṅkāsanti sadisaṃ. Saṅkāsasaddo hi upamāvācako nipāto. Vuttañhi

`Puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhaṃ` means 'endowed with a countenance resembling the full moon'. For just as the moon wanes day by day from the first day of the dark fortnight, so the face of the Muni does not wane. However, the Blessed One's face always shines without waning, like the complete orb of the full moon; therefore, it is praised as `puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhaṃ`, distinguishing it with the word `puṇṇa` (full). `Puṇṇaṃ` (full) means 'it fills with sixteen parts'. The root is `pūra` with the suffix `ta`, which becomes `ṇṇa`. `Indu` means 'it exercises lordship over the constellations of stars'; the root is `idi` in the sense of 'lordship', with the suffix `u`. `Puṇṇaṃ` (full) and `indu` (moon) together make `puṇṇindu`, meaning the full moon. `Saṅkāsaṃ` means 'similar'.
