For the word `saṅkāsa` is a particle indicating comparison. For it is said:

Subodhālaṅkāre –

In the Subodhālaṅkāra:

“Ivādi iva vā tulya, samānanibhasannibhā;

Yathā saṅkāsa tulita, ppakāsa patirūpakā”tyādi.

“`Iva`, `ādi`, `iva`, `vā`, `tulya`, `samāna`, `nibha`, `sannibhā`; `yathā`, `saṅkāsa`, `tulita`, `pakāsa`, `patirūpakā`,” and so on.

Puṇṇacandaṃ viya mukhati sobhatīti mukhaṃ, ānanaṃ. Mukhadhātu a. Puṇṇindunā saṅkāsaṃ sadisaṃ mukhaṃ ānanaṃ yassa soti puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukho, munindo. Taṃ. Munindassa pana puṇṇa candassa sahassaraṃsīhi sassiriko viya bhikkhūnaṃ majjhe bāttiṃsa mahāpurisa lakkhaṇāsītyānubyañjana paṭimaṇḍitehi sirīhi ca byāmappabhāparikkhittehi āveḷāveḷā yamakāyamakā gumbāgumbā hutvā viniccharantīhi ghanabuddharasmisaṅkhātehi alaṅkito sassirikamukho hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhanti thometi.

`Mukhaṃ` (face) or `ānanaṃ` (countenance) means 'it shines like the full moon'; the root is `mukha` with the suffix `a`. One whose face or countenance is similar to or resembles the full moon is `puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukho`, the Lord of Sages. Him. Furthermore, it is said that the Lord of Sages has a radiant face, just as the full moon is radiant with its thousand rays. His face is adorned with the splendors of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics, and also with what are known as the dense Buddha-rays, which are enveloped by a fathom-wide aura and stream forth in waves upon waves, in pairs upon pairs, and in clusters upon clusters. Therefore, he is praised as `puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhaṃ`.

Anejanti nittaṇhaṃ. Lābhālābhādiṃ paṭicca ejati kampatīti ejā, taṇhā. Ejadhātu kampane a, natthi ejā yassāti [M 0.0045] anejo, munindo. Vuttañhi mahāniddesapāḷiyaṃ “lābhālābha yasāyasa nindāninda sukhadukkhehi na iñjatīti anejo, bhagavā labbhatī”ti.

`Anejaṃ` means 'free from craving'. That which stirs and trembles on account of gain and loss and so on is `ejā`, craving. The root `eja` is in the sense of 'trembling', with the suffix `a`. One who has no `ejā` is `anejo`, the Lord of Sages. For it is said in the Mahāniddesa: 'The Blessed One is called `anejo` because he does not stir at gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain'.

Sabbaññunti paṭividdha sabbañeyyadhammaṃ. Saṅkharavikāralakkhaṇanibbāna paññattivasena pañcavidhaṃ sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ jānāti paṭivijjhati sīlenāti sabbaññū, munindo. Sabbasaddūpapada ñādhātu rū. Ettha ca sabbe saṅkhatadhammā saṅkharā nāma sakasakapaccayehi saṅkhariyantīti katvā. Viññattidvayaṃ lahutādittayañca vikāro nāma catūhi mahābhūtehi virūpaṃ kariyatīti katvā. Viññattidvayassa yathākkamaṃ cittajavāyodhātu cittajapathavī dhātūnaṃ visesaguṇattā, lahutādittayassa ca citto tvāhārajanipphannarūpānaṃ visesaguṇattā. Phassādidhammānaṃ phusanādilakkhaṇañca pathavīdhātvādīnaṃ kakkhaḷādilakkhaṇañca, cittassa ārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇañca, nibbānassa santilakkhaṇañca, rūpassa ruppanalakkhaṇañca, nāmassa namanalakkhaṇañca, aniccatādittayāni ca upacayādicattāri lakkhaṇarūpāni ca lakkhaṇāni nāma lakkhiyanti etena lakkhitabbā dhammāti katvā. Asaṅkhatadhātunibbānaṃ nāma vānaṃ vuccati taṇhā, tato nikkhantanti katvā. Paricchedarūpaṃ itthipurisādighaṭapaṭādayo sabba vohāratthā ca paññatti nāma paññāpiyati pakārena ñāpiyatīti katvā. Ettha ca saṅkhāranibbānāni paramatthadhammā honti. Vikārādīsu pana vikāralakkhaṇāni paññattivisesattā visuṃ vuttāni. Imehi dvīhi vinimuttā pana paricchedarūpā sabbavohāratthā paññattīti vuttāti veditabbā. Apadāna aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sabbaṃ atītādibhedaṃ hatthāmalakaṃ viya jānātīti sabbaññū”ti vuttaṃ.

`Sabbaññu` (Omniscient) means 'one who has penetrated all knowable phenomena'. The Lord of Sages is called `sabbaññu` because he knows and penetrates by his inherent nature all five kinds of knowable phenomena—namely, formations, alterations, marks, Nibbāna, and designations. The word `sabbaññu` is formed from the word `sabba` (all) as a pre-verb with the root `ñā` (to know) and the suffix `rū`. Here, all conditioned phenomena are called `saṅkhārā` (formations) because they are formed by their respective conditions. The two kinds of intimation and the threefold lightness are called `vikāra` (alterations) because they are made to be different by the four great elements. This is because the two kinds of intimation are, in order, the distinctive qualities of the mind-born air element and the mind-born earth element, and the threefold lightness is the distinctive quality of mind-born, temperature-born, and nutriment-produced materiality. The characteristic of contact and other phenomena is touching; that of the earth element and others is hardness; that of consciousness is the cognition of objects; that of Nibbāna is peace; that of materiality is being afflicted; that of mentality is bending. Also, the three characteristics (impermanence, etc.) and the four characteristic material qualities (production, etc.) are called `lakkhaṇa` (marks) because phenomena are marked by them and should be marked by them. The unconditioned element, Nibbāna, is so called because `vāna` means craving, and it is that from which one has departed. Limiting form, such as male, female, pots, and cloth, and all conventional realities are called `paññatti` (designations) because they are designated or made known in a particular way. Here, formations and Nibbāna are ultimate realities. However, among alterations and so on, alterations and marks are mentioned separately because they are specific kinds of designations. It should be understood that limiting form and all conventional realities, which are distinct from these two, are called `paññatti`. However, in the Apadāna commentary it is said: '`Sabbaññu` (Omniscient) means 'one who knows all divisions, such as past, etc., as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the hand'.'

Sabbaññūti ca kamasabbaññū, sakiṃ sabbaññū, satatasabbaññū, satti sabbaññū, ñātasabbaññū cāti pañcavidhā hoti sabbaññū. Tattha yathākkamaṃ sabbaṃ jānanadhammo kamasabbaññū nāma. Ekāvajjanena javanavārena [M 0.0046] jānitabbaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ jānanadhammo sakiṃsabbaññū nāma. Cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ niyatārammaṇattaṃ jānanadhammo satatasabbaññū nāma. Ekappahārena sabbadhammaṃ jānanasamattho dhammo sattisabbaññū nāma. Āvajjanābhedena jānitabbaṃ sabbadhammaṃ jānanadhammo ñātasabbaññū nāma. Tesu ca sakiṃ sabbaññū sattisabbaññūvasena dve dhammā maggañāṇāniyeva. Tadavasesā sabbaññutañāṇāni honti. Taṃ sabbaññuṃ.

Omniscience is fivefold: sequential omniscience, simultaneous omniscience, continuous omniscience, potential omniscience, and omniscience of the known. Herein, the quality of knowing all things successively is called sequential omniscience. The quality of knowing the Dhamma of the Four Truths in a single cognitive process of adverting and impulsion is called simultaneous omniscience. The quality of knowing the fixed nature of the objects of eye-consciousness and so on is called continuous omniscience. The quality of being capable of knowing all phenomena in a single stroke is called potential omniscience. The quality of knowing all phenomena through distinctions of adverting is called omniscience of the known. Among these, simultaneous omniscience and potential omniscience are solely the path knowledges. The remainder are the knowledges of omniscience. That Omniscient One.

Munindanti ettha munisaddassa attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Munīnaṃ indo issaro munindo, taṃ munindaṃ ahaṃ vandāmīti sambandhoti.

Herein, the meaning of the word 'muni' has already been stated above. Muninda is the lord and master of sages; 'I pay homage to that Muninda'—this is the connection.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Pātodayaṃ pageva udayaṃ uggataṃ, bāladivākaraṃva navuggatasūriyamāṇavoiva, yatīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ majjhe sirīhi bāttiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇā sītyānubyañjanasampattisaṅkhātehi sirīhi lalitaṃ vilāsitaṃ, puṇṇindusaṅkāsamukhaṃ puṇṇacandena sadisaṃ ānanavantaṃ, anejaṃ nittaṇhaṃ, lokadhammehi aniñjanaṃ vā, sabbaññuṃ sabbadhamma vijānantaṃ, munindaṃ buddhaṃ sakkaccaṃ tīhi dvārehi ahaṃ vandāmīti.

This is the concise application here: I reverently pay homage with the three doors to the Lord of Sages, the Buddha—who is risen at the break of dawn like the morning sun, like a youth who is the newly risen sun; who, amidst ascetics, that is, bhikkhus, is graceful and resplendent with the glories consisting of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics; whose face is like the full moon; who is unperturbed, that is, without craving, or unshaken by worldly conditions; the Omniscient One, who knows all phenomena.

Pañcamavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the fifth verse of homage is concluded.

6.

6.

Upetapuñño varabodhimūle,

Sasenamāraṃ sugato jinitvā;

Abojjhi bodhiṃ aruṇodayamhi,

Namāmi taṃ mārajinaṃ abhaṅgaṃ.

Endowed with merit, the Sugata, at the foot of the excellent Bodhi tree, having conquered Māra with his army, awakened to enlightenment at the rise of dawn. I bow to him, the unbreakable Conqueror of Māra.

6. Evaṃ pañcamagāthāya munindaṃ vanditvā idāni mārajinaguṇena thomitvā vanditukāmo upetapuñño tyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana ja ta ja gaṇa dvigaruyuttattā ekādasakkharehi lakkhitā upendavajirāgāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “upādikā [M 0.0047] sāva jatā jagā go”ti. Tassattho, yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ jatā jagaṇa tagaṇā ca jagā jagaṇagarū ca go garu ca ce siyā, sāva sāgāthāeva upādikā upasaddādikā indavajirāgāthā nāmāti.

6. Having thus paid homage to the Lord of Sages with the fifth verse, now, desiring to pay homage by extolling his quality as Conqueror of Māra, he uttered the verse beginning 'Upetapuñño.' This verse, however, should be understood as an Upendavajirā verse, marked by eleven syllables, as it is composed of the feet ja, ta, ja, and two long syllables. For it is stated in the Vuttodaya: 'upādikā sāva jatā jagā go.' Its meaning is: that verse in each of whose lines there are the feet ja and ta, the foot ja and a long syllable, and a long syllable, that very verse, beginning with the prefix 'upa', is called an Indavajirā-type verse.

Upetapuñño yo sugato varabodhimūle sasena māraṃ jinitvā aruṇodayamhi bodhiṃ abojjhi mārajinaṃ abhaṅgaṃ, taṃ sugataṃ ahaṃ namāmīti sambandho. Tattha upetapuññoti sampannadānasīlādipāramīpuññavā. Dānasīlādi pāramīpuññena samannāgato vā. Dānasīlādipāramīpuññena upeto samupeto upagato samupagato sampanno samannāgatoti attho. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho, upanno sampanno hutvā eti gacchati pavattatīti upetaṃ, puññaṃ. Upapubbaidhātu gatiyaṃ ta. Punāti attano kārakanti puññaṃ, pāramīpuññaṃ labbhati. Pudhātu pīṇane sodhane vā ṇyo. Tassa ño. Tattha attano kārakanti punappunaṃ pavattiyā sacittasantatiñca saṃjanitapaṇītarūpavisaṭena sanissaya rūpasantatiñca punāti pīṇeti sodheti vāti attho. Ayaṃ paṭisambhidāmaggagaṇṭhipade vutto. Pūreti ajjhāsayanti vā puññaṃ. Pūradhātu ṇya. Yo puggalo puññaṃ karoti tassa ajjhāsayaṃ pūretīti attho.

'The Sugata who, endowed with merit, at the foot of the excellent Bodhi tree, having conquered Māra with his army, awakened to enlightenment at the rise of dawn—to that unshakeable Conqueror of Māra, to that Sugata, I bow.' This is the connection. Herein, 'endowed with merit' (upetapuñño) means one who possesses the merit of the perfections such as giving and virtue, or one endowed with the merit of the perfections such as giving and virtue. The meaning is: approached, fully approached, attained, fully attained, accomplished, or possessed. This is the verbal analysis herein: having arisen and become accomplished, it comes, goes, and proceeds; thus it is 'approached' (upetaṃ). (From the root 'i' preceded by 'upa' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'ta'). 'Merit' (puñña) is so called because it purifies (punāti) its doer; the merit of the perfections is meant. (From the root 'pū' in the sense of gratifying or purifying, with the suffix 'ṇya'). Here, 'it purifies its doer' means that through its repeated occurrence, it gratifies and purifies the continuity of one's own mind and the refined material continuity produced in dependence on it. This is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga-gaṇṭhipada. Or, 'merit' (puñña) is so called because it fulfills (pūreti) one's disposition (ajjhāsaya). (From the root 'pūr' with the suffix 'ṇya'). The meaning is that when a person performs a meritorious act, it fulfills their disposition.

Atha vā pujjañca bhavaṃ nibbattetīti puññaṃ. Nibbattitaddhitāyaṃ. Pūja padaṃ ṇyapaccayo. Yo puññaṃ karoti, tassa pūjitabbaṃ bhavaṃ pavattetīti attho. Tena vuttaṃ sammohavinodanī aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “punāti attano kārakaṃ pūreti cassa ajjhāsayaṃ pujjañca bhavaṃ nibbattetīti puñño”ti. Mūlaṭīkāyañca “punātīti sodheti apuññaphalato dukkhasaṃkilesato ca hitajjhāsayena puññaṃ karotīti taṃ nipphādanena kārakassajjhāsayaṃ pūretīti puñño. Pūrako pujjanibbattako ca niruttilakkhaṇena puññoti veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ[M 0.0048]. Visuddhimaggamahāṭīkāyañca- “punāti attano santānaṃ apuññaphalato dukkhasaṃkilesato ca visodhetīti puññaṃ. Hitasukhajjhāsayena puññaṃ karotīti taṃnipphādanena kārakassa ajjhāsayaṃ pūreti, pujjabhavaṃ nibbattetīti vā puññaṃ. Iti pūrako pujjanibbattako ca niruttinayena puññanti veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Upetaṃ sampannaṃ puññaṃ pāramīpuññaṃ yassa soti upetapuñño, sugato labbhati.

Alternatively, it generates a worshipful existence (pujjaṃ bhavaṃ), thus it is 'merit' (puñña). (This is a taddhita derivative in the sense of 'produced'; the word is 'pūja' with the suffix 'ṇya'). The meaning is that for one who performs a meritorious act, it generates an existence worthy of worship. Therefore, it is said in the Sammohavinodanī commentary: 'It purifies its doer, fulfills their disposition, and generates a worshipful existence—thus it is merit.' And in the Mūlaṭīkā it is said: '“It purifies” means it cleanses from the fruit of demerit and from the defilements of suffering. Because one performs merit with a beneficial disposition, by producing it one fulfills the doer’s disposition; thus it is merit. By its etymological characteristic, it should be understood as a fulfiller and a generator of what is worshipful.' And in the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā it is said: 'It purifies one’s own continuum from the fruit of demerit and from the defilements of suffering, thus it is merit. Because one performs merit with a disposition for welfare and happiness, by producing it one fulfills the doer’s disposition, or it generates a worshipful existence, thus it is merit. Thus, by way of etymology, it should be understood as a fulfiller and a generator of what is worshipful.' He for whom there is approached, accomplished merit—the merit of the perfections—is 'upetapuñño.' This refers to the Sugata.

Varabodhimūleti uttamassa bodhirukkhassa samīpe. Tattha varoti varitabbo patthitabbo icchitabboti vā varo. Bodhimūleti ettha bodhīti vuccati rukkhopi, maggopi, sabbaññutañāṇampi, nibbānampi. Tattha hi bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhi sambuddhoti ca, antarā ca bodhiṃ antarā ca gayanti ca āgataṭṭhāne rukkho. Bodhīti vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇanti āgataṭṭhāne maggo. Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūri medhasoti āgataṭṭhāne sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Patvāna bodhiṃ amataṃ asaṅkhatanti āgataṭṭhāne nibbānaṃ bodhīti vuccati. Idha pana bodhirukkhoti adhippeto. Ayaṃ pana tesaṃ vacanattho. Bujjhati abujjhi bujjhissati cattāri ariyasaccāni sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammampi etthāti bodhi, bodhirukkho. Budhadhātu ṇi. Bujjhati cattāri saccānīti bodhi, maggo. Bujjhati sabbañeyyadhammanti bodhi, sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Ariyena bujjhitabbanti bodhi, nibbānaṃ labbhati. Varo uttamo bodhirukkhoti varabodhi, tassa mūlaṃ samīpaṃ varabodhimūlaṃ, tasmiṃ.

'At the foot of the excellent Bodhi tree' means near the supreme Bodhi tree. Herein, 'excellent' (vara) means that which should be chosen, sought after, or desired. In the phrase 'at the foot of the Bodhi tree,' 'bodhi' can refer to the tree, the path, the knowledge of omniscience, and Nibbāna. For in the passage 'at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he became the first fully enlightened one' and in 'between Bodhi and Gayā,' the tree is meant. In the passage 'Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths,' the path is meant. In the passage 'He of excellent and vast wisdom attains Bodhi,' the knowledge of omniscience is meant. In the passage 'Having attained Bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned,' Nibbāna is meant. Here, however, the Bodhi tree is intended. This is the verbal analysis of these terms: 'One awakens (bujjhati), has awakened (abujjhi), or will awaken (bujjhissati) to the Four Noble Truths and all knowable phenomena thereat (ettha)'; thus it is 'bodhi,' the Bodhi tree. (From the root 'budh' with the suffix 'ṇi'). 'One awakens to the four truths'; thus it is 'bodhi,' the path. 'One awakens to all knowable phenomena'; thus it is 'bodhi,' the knowledge of omniscience. 'It is to be awakened to by the noble ones'; thus it is 'bodhi,' Nibbāna is meant. 'Excellent' (vara) means supreme; the Bodhi tree; thus 'excellent Bodhi' (varabodhi). Its foot (mūlaṃ), its vicinity, is 'varabodhimūlaṃ.' 'At it' (tasmiṃ).

Sasenamāranti saha senāya pavattaṃ mārarājaṃ. Tattha siyati bandhiyatīti senā. Sidhātu bandhaneyu. Tāya saha pavattatīti saseno, mārarājā. Anatthe niyojento guṇamāraṇena satte māretīti māro. Maradhātu ṇa. Sattānaṃ kusalaṃ māreti vināsetīti vā māro. Saseno ca so māro cāti sasenamāro, mārarājā. Taṃ[M 0.0049]. Jinitvāti pade kammaṃ. Upetapuñño yo sugatoti sambandho. Sugatasaddassa attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

'Māra with his army' means the Māra-king who proceeds together with his army. Herein, it is an 'army' (senā) because it binds (siyati/bandhiyati). (From the root 'si' in the sense of binding). He who proceeds with that army is 'one with an army' (saseno), the Māra-king. He is 'Māra' because, engaging beings in what is harmful, he kills (māreti) them by slaying their virtues. (From the root 'mar' with the suffix 'ṇa'). Or he is 'Māra' because he kills, he destroys, the wholesome states of beings. He is with his army and he is Māra, thus 'Māra with his army' (sasenamāro), the Māra-king. 'Him' (taṃ) is the object of the word 'having conquered' (jinitvā). The connection is with 'The Sugata who is endowed with merit...'. The meaning of the word 'Sugata' has already been stated above.

Jinitvāti visākhapuṇṇamiyaṃ buddhadine anatthaṅgateyeva sūriye pāramīpuññatejena vijayitvāti attho. Abojjhīti paṭivijjhi adhigami vā. Bodhinti anuttaraṃ sammā sambodhiṃ, arahattamaggasabbaññutañāṇanti attho. Sabbaññuta ñāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca sabbaññutañāṇaṃ bodhīti vuccati. Taṃ bodhiṃ.

'Having conquered' means that he gained victory by the power of the merit of his perfections on the Visākha full-moon day, the day of the Buddha, while the sun had not yet set. 'He awakened' (abojjhi) means he penetrated or attained. 'Enlightenment' (bodhiṃ) means unsurpassed perfect full enlightenment, that is, the knowledge of the Arahant path and the knowledge of omniscience. For path knowledge is the proximate cause of the knowledge of omniscience, and the knowledge of omniscience is the proximate cause of path knowledge; this is called 'bodhi.' 'That enlightenment'.

Aruṇodayamhīti aruṇaudayamhīti padacchedo. Aruṇuggamanavelāyanti attho. Tattha āsamantato ālokaṃ karonto unati gacchatīti aruṇo. Āpubbaunadhātu gatimhi ṇa. Ākārassa rasso. Rakārāgamo. Nassa ṇo. Sūriyassa udayato pubbe uggataraṃsi aruṇo nāmāti attho. Vuttañhi dasakanipāta aṅguttarapāḷiyaṃ “sūriyassa bhikkhave udayato etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ yadidaṃ aruṇuggaṃ, evameva kho bhikkhave kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ yadidaṃ sammādiṭṭhī”ti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ abhidhānappadīpikāyaṃ “sūrassodayato pubbu, ṭṭhitaraṃsi siyāruṇo”ti. Abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkāyaṃ pana “aruṇavaṇṇatāya arati gacchatīti aruṇo”ti vuttaṃ. Udeti uggacchatīti udayo, sūriyo. Udidhātu a. Udayassa sūriyassa aruṇo uggataraṃsīti aruṇodayo. Tassaṃ aruṇuggamanavelāyaṃ. Bodhiṃ abojjhīti sambandho.

'At the rise of dawn' (aruṇodayamhi): the word division is 'aruṇa-udayamhi.' The meaning is 'at the time of the appearance of the dawn.' Herein, it is 'aruṇa' because, making light all around, it rises (unati) or goes (gacchati). (From the root 'una' preceded by 'ā' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'ṇa'; the 'ā' is shortened, 'r' is inserted, and 'n' becomes 'ṇ'). The meaning is that 'aruṇa' is the ray that has risen before the rising of the sun. As it is said in the Dasakanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya: 'Bhikkhus, just as the appearance of the dawn is the forerunner and precursor of the sunrise, so too, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner and precursor of wholesome states.' And it is said in the Abhidhānappadīpikā: 'The ray standing before the rising of the sun would be aruṇa.' But in the subcommentary to the Abhidhānappadīpikā it is said: 'Because of its reddish color, it goes, thus it is aruṇa.' 'It rises' (udeti), 'it goes up' (uggacchati), thus it is 'udaya,' the sun. (From the root 'ud-i' with the suffix 'a'). The 'aruṇa,' the risen ray of the rising sun (udaya), is 'aruṇodaya.' At that time of the appearance of the dawn. The connection is 'he awakened to enlightenment'.

Bhagavā hi visākhapuṇṇamiyaṃ anatthaṅgateyeva sūriye mārabalaṃ vidhametvā cīvarūpari patamānehi bodhirukkhaṅkarehi rattapavāḷapallavehi viya pūjayamāno rattiyā paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussaritvā majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhetvā pacchimayāme paṭiccasamuppādaṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ manasikaritvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva pādakaṃ katvā mahāvajirañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ [M 0.0050] vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā adhigatena catutthamaggañāṇena sabbakilese khepetvā yadā aruṇo uggamissati, tadā sabbaññutañāṇādisabba buddhaguṇe paṭivijjhi adhigamīti vuttaṃ hoti.

For on the full-moon day of Visākha, while the sun had not yet set, the Blessed One dispelled the forces of Māra. Being honored by Bodhi tree buds falling upon his robe like red coral shoots, in the first watch of the night he recollected his past lives; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye; and in the last watch, having contemplated dependent origination forwards and backwards, he produced the fourth jhāna based on mindfulness of breathing. Using that as a foundation, he developed the insight known as the Great Diamond Knowledge and, by means of the fourth path-knowledge attained in due course, he destroyed all defilements. It is said that as dawn was arising, he then penetrated and attained all the qualities of a Buddha, beginning with omniscient knowledge.

Mārajinanti pañcamārānaṃ vijitāviṃ. Devaputta kilesābhi saṅkhārakhandhamaccusaṅkhāte pañcamāre jināti ajini jinissatīti mārajino, sugato. Devaputtakilesābhisaṅkharasaṅkhataṃ mārattayaṃ jināti ajini, khandhamaccusaṅkhataṃ māradvayaṃ avassaṃ jinissatīti attho. Yadi evaṃ kasmā vijitāvinti vuttanti. Aviraddhaṃ ekantena jiyamānattāti. Abhaṅganti sasenamārassa bhañjituṃ viddhaṃsituṃ asamatthaṃ. Yassa kassaci bhañjituṃ viddhaṃsituṃ asamatthaṃ vā. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho. Mārena yena kenaci bhañjituṃ na sakkotīti abhaṅgo, tena vā na bhañjiyati na viddhaṃsiyatīti abhaṅgo, sugato. Napubba bhanjadhātu ta. Tassa dhātvantena gakārādeso. Atha vā bhanjati viddhaṃsatīti bhaṅgo, māro. Yo koci vā. Natthi bhaṅgo māro yo koci vā yassāti abhaṅgo, sugato. Taṃ abhaṅgaṃ. Tanti sugataṃ. Mārajinaṃ abhaṅgaṃ taṃ sugataṃ ahaṃ namāmīti sambandho.

`Mārajina` (Conqueror of Māra) means one who has vanquished the five Māras. Because the Sugata conquers, has conquered, and will conquer the five Māras—namely, the Māra of the godling, the Māra of defilements, the Māra of formations, the Māra of the aggregates, and the Māra of death—he is called Mārajina. The meaning is: he has conquered the threefold Māra consisting of the godling, defilements, and formations; and he will certainly conquer the twofold Māra consisting of the aggregates and death. If so, why is it said `vijitāvi` (one who has conquered)? Because they are invariably conquered without opposition. `Abhaṅga` (Unbreakable) means unable to be broken or destroyed by Māra with his army, or unable to be broken or destroyed by anyone whatsoever. The word-meaning here is this: he is `abhaṅga` because he cannot be broken by Māra or anyone; or, he is `abhaṅga` because he is not broken or destroyed by him (Māra). He is the Sugata. Or, `bhaṅga` is one who breaks or destroys—that is, Māra or anyone else. He for whom there is no `bhaṅga` (breaker)—no Māra or anyone else—is `abhaṅga`, the Sugata. That Unbreakable One. That is, the Sugata. 'To him, the Mārajina, the Unbreakable One, the Sugata, I pay homage'—this is the connection.

Imissaṃ pana gāthāyaṃ ekanipātajātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ, apadānaṭṭhakathāyañca āgatanayena buddhassa māravijayādiṃ sotujanānaṃ bahussutatthaṃ saṅkhepena veditabbaṃ. Bodhi satto hi mahāsampattiṃ anubhavitvā hatthagataṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya anapekkho chaṭṭetvā ekūnatiṃsavasse āsaḷhipuṇṇamāya uttarasaḷhanakkhattena yutte mahābhinikkhamaṃ nikkhamitvā anomanadītīre ghaṭīkārabrahmunā dinnaṃ arahatta dhajabhūtaṃ aṭṭhaparikkhāraṃ paṭiggahetvā nivāsetvā samaṇapabbajjaṃ katvā chabbassāni dukkarakārikaṃ caritvā nigrodharukkhamūle senanigame senakuṭumbikassa dhītarāya sujātāya saha satasahassagghiyā [M 0.0051] suvaṇṇapātiyā dinnaṃ sabbaṃ appodakaṃ madhupāyāsaṃ ekaṭṭhitālapakkappamāṇaṃ ekūnapaññāsālopaṃ paribhuñjitvā sāyanhasamaye devatāhi alaṅkatena maggena bodhirukkhābhimukho gacchante antaramagge sotthiyena nāma tiṇahārakena dinnaṃ aṭṭhamuṭṭhikatiṇaṃ gahetvā bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha idaṃ ṭhānaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitaṃ acalaṭṭhānaṃ kilesabhañjanaṭṭhānanti ñatvā tāni tiṇāni agge gahetvā cālesi. Tāvadeva cuddasahattho pallaṅko ahosi. Tānipi tiṇāni tathārūpena saṇṭhānena santhariṃsu saṇṭhahiṃsu vā. Yathārūpaṃ sukusalopi vicittakāro vā potthatāro vā ālikhitumpi samattho natthi. Bodhi satto bodhikhandhaṃ piṭṭhito katvā puratthābhimukho daḷhamānaso hutvā –

Now, in connection with this verse, the brief account of the Buddha’s victory over Māra and other events should be understood as it is found in the commentary on the Ekanipāta Jātaka and in the Apadāna commentary, for the sake of the erudition of the audience. The Bodhisatta, having enjoyed great prosperity, renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch that was within his grasp as though it were a lump of spittle. At the age of twenty-nine, on the full-moon day of Āsaḷhi, under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha, he went forth in the great renunciation. On the bank of the Anomā River, he accepted the eight requisites—the banner of arahantship—given by the Brahmā Ghaṭīkāra. Having put them on, he undertook the ascetic life and for six years practiced austerities. At the foot of the banyan tree in the village of Senā, he received from Sujātā, the daughter of the householder Senāni, milk-rice with honey containing little water, in a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand. He consumed it in forty-nine mouthfuls, each the size of a ripe single-stoned palmyra fruit. In the evening, as he was proceeding towards the Bodhi tree along a path adorned by deities, he accepted eight handfuls of grass from a grass-cutter named Sotthiya. Ascending the Bodhi terrace, he recognized, 'This is the unabandoned, unshaken spot of all Buddhas, the place for crushing the defilements.' Taking the blades of grass by their tips, he shook them out. Instantly, a seat of fourteen cubits appeared. And that grass spread out and settled in such a pattern that not even a very skilled artist or painter could draw it. The Bodhisatta, placing his back against the trunk of the Bodhi tree, faced east and, with a resolute mind, made this vow:

“Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasussatu;

Upasussatu nisesaṃ, sarīre maṃsalohita”nti.

“Willingly, let skin, sinews, and bones wither away; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up completely.”

Na tveva sammāsambodhiṃ apatvā imaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bhindissāmīti asanisatasannipātenapi abhejjarūpaṃ taṃ pallaṅkaṃ abhañjitvā nisīdi. Tasmiṃ samaye māro devaputto siddhatthakumāro “mayhaṃ vasaṃ atikkamitukāmo, na dāni assa atikkamituṃ dassāmī”ti mārabalassa santikaṃ gantvā etamatthaṃ ārocetvā māraghosanaṃ nāma ghosāpetvā mārabalaṃ ādāya nikkhami. Sā mārasenā mārassa purato dvādasa yojanā honti. Dakkhiṇato ca vāmato ca dvādasa yojanā. Pacchato cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā ṭhitā, uddhaṃ navayojanubbedhā. Yassā unnādantiyā unnādasaddo yojanasahassato paṭṭhāya pathavīundriyasaddo viya suyyati. Atha māro devaputto diyaḍḍhayojanasatikaṃ girimekhalaṃ nāma hatthiṃ abhirūhitvā bāhusahassaṃ māpetvā nānāvudhāni aggahesi. Avasesāyapi māraparisāya dve janā ekasadisaṃ [M 0.0052] āvudhaṃ na gaṇhiṃsu. Nānappakāravaṇṇā nānappakāra mukhā hutvā mahāsattaṃ ajjhottharamānā āgamaṃsu.

Having resolved, 'I will certainly not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained perfect self-enlightenment,' he sat down without breaking that posture on the seat that was unbreakable even by the impact of a hundred thunderbolts. At that time, Māra the godling thought: 'Prince Siddhattha wants to escape from my domain. I will not let him escape now.' He went to his forces, announced the matter, had the 'Māra-summons' proclaimed, and set out with his army. That army of Māra extended twelve yojanas in front of him, twelve yojanas to his right and to his left, and behind him it filled the space up to the rim of the world-sphere. It was nine yojanas high. The roar of the advancing army was heard from a thousand yojanas away, like the sound of the earth splitting asunder. Then Māra the godling, mounting the elephant named Girimekhala, who was one hundred and fifty yojanas tall, created a thousand arms for himself and grasped various weapons. Among the rest of Māra’s retinue, no two people took up a similar weapon. With varied complexions and varied faces, they advanced, intent on overwhelming the Great Being.

Dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā pana mahāsattassa thuti yo vadamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Sakko devarājā vijayuttarasaṅkhaṃ dhamamāno aṭṭhāsi. So kira saṅkho vīsahatthasatiko hoti. Sakiṃ vātaṃ gāhāpetvā dhamanto cattāro māse saddaṃ karitvā nissaddo hoti. Mahākāḷanāga rājā atirekapadasatena vaṇṇaṃ vadanto aṭṭhāsi. Mahābrahmā setacchattaṃ dhārayamāno aṭṭhāsi. Māra bale pana bodhimaṇḍalaṃ upasaṅkamante tesaṃ ekopi ṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi. Sammukha sammukhaṭṭhāneneva palāyiṃsu. Kāḷo nāma nāgarājā pathaviṃ nimujjitvā pañcayojanasatikaṃ mantirakanāgabhavanaṃ gantvā ubhohi hatthehi mukhaṃ pidahitvā nipanno. Sakko vijayuttarasaṅkhaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ katvā cakkavāḷamukha vaṭṭiyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Mahābrahmā setacchattaṃ koṭiyaṃ gahetvā brahmalokameva agamāsi. Ekadevatāpi ṭhātuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi. Mahāpuriso ekakova nisīdi. Māropi attano parisaṃ āha “tāta suddhodanaputtena siddhatthena sadiso añño puriso nāma natthi, mayaṃ sammukhā yuddhaṃ dātuṃ na sakkhissāma, pacchā bhāgena dassāmā”ti. Mahāpurisopi tīṇi passāni oloketvā sabbadevatānaṃ palāyitattā suññāni addasa. Puna uttarapassena mārabalaṃ ajjhottharamānaṃ disvā “ayaṃ ettako jano maṃ ekakaṃ sandhāya mahantaṃ vāyāmaṃ karoti, imasmiṃ ṭhāne mayhaṃ mātā vā pitā vā bhātā vā añño koci ñātako vā natthi, imā pana dasa pāramiyova mayhaṃ dīgharattaṃ puttaparijanasadisā, tasmā mayā pāramiyova phalakaṃ katvā pāramisattheneva paharitvā ayaṃ balakāyo mayā viddhaṃsetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti dasa pāramiyo āvajjamāno nisīdi.

The deities of the ten-thousand world-systems stood uttering praises of the Great Being. Sakka, king of the gods, stood blowing the conch Vijayuttara. That conch, it is said, is one hundred and twenty cubits long; when filled with a single breath and blown, it resounds for four months before falling silent. The great nāga-king Mahākāla stood reciting praises with over a hundred stanzas. Mahābrahmā stood holding a white parasol. But when Māra's army approached the Bodhi-terrace, not a single one of those deities was able to stand their ground; they fled from wherever they stood. The nāga-king named Kāḷa plunged into the earth and went to his nāga-abode Mañjerika, five hundred yojanas in extent, where he lay down covering his face with both hands. Sakka slung the conch Vijayuttara over his back and stood at the rim of the world-sphere. Mahābrahmā, holding the white parasol by its edge, returned to the Brahmā world. Not a single deity was able to remain. The Great Being sat alone. Then Māra said to his retinue: 'Sirs, there is no other man like Siddhattha, son of Suddhodana. We will not be able to give him battle from the front; we must attack from the rear.' The Great Being looked in the three directions and saw that they were empty, for all the deities had fled. Then, seeing Māra's army overwhelming the northern quarter, he reflected: 'This great host is making such a huge effort directed at me alone. In this place I have no mother or father, no brother or other relative. But these ten perfections have for a long time been like my children and retinue. Therefore, making the perfections my shield and striking with the weapon of the perfections, it is right that I should scatter this army.' Reflecting thus on the ten perfections, he remained seated.

Atha [M 0.0053] māro devaputto eteneva siddhatthaṃ palāpessāmīti vātamaṇḍalaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Taṅkhaṇaññeyeva puratthimā dibhedā vātā samuṭṭhahitvā aḍḍhayojanaekayojana dviyojanatiyojanappamāṇāni pabbatakūṭāni padāletvā vanagaccharukkhādīni uddhaṃ mūlāni katvā sāmantā gāmanigame cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kātuṃ samatthāpi mahāpurisassa puññatejena mahānubhāvena bodhisattaṃ patvā cīvarakaṇṇamattampi cāletuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tato udakena ajjhottharitvā māressāmāti mahāvassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Tassānubhāvena uparūpari satapaṭalasahassapaṭalādibhedā vaḷāhakā uṭṭhahitvā vassiṃsu. Vuṭṭhidhārāvegena pathavī bhinnā ahosi. Vanarukkhādīnaṃ uparibhāgena mahāmegho āgantvā mahā sattassa cīvare ussāvabinduggahaṇamattampi temetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tato pāsāṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Mahantāni pabbatakūṭāni dhūmāyantāni pajjalantāni ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibbamālāguḷabhāvaṃ āpajjiṃsu. Tato paharavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Ekatodhārā ubhatodhārā asisattikhurappādayo dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattaṃ patvā dibbapupphāni ahesuṃ. Tato aṅgāravassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Kiṃsukavaṇṇā aṅgārā ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibba pupphāni hutvā vikiriṃsu. Tato kukkuḷavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Accuṇho aggivaṇṇo kukkuḷo ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibbacandanacuṇṇaṃ hutvā nipatati. Tato vāḷukavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Atisukhumavāḷikā dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā nipatiṃsu. Tato kalalavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ kalalavassaṃ dhūmāyantaṃ pajjalantaṃ ākāse nāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibbavilepanaṃ hutvā patati. Tato iminā bhiṃsetvā siddhatthaṃ palāpessāmīti andhakāraṃ [M 0.0054] samuṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ andhakāraṃ viya mahātamaṃ hutvā bodhisattaṃ patvā sūriyappabhā vihataṃ viya antaradhāyati.

Then Māra, the son of a god, thinking, 'I will drive away Siddhattha with this,' raised a whirlwind. At that very moment, winds arose from the eastern direction, shattering mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas, uprooting forest trees, and though capable of reducing nearby villages and towns to dust, due to the power of the Great Being’s merit and his great might, upon reaching the Bodhisatta they could not stir even the corner of his robe. Then, thinking, 'I will kill him by overwhelming him with water,' he caused a great rainstorm. By his power, clouds arose in layers—hundreds and thousands of layers—and poured down rain. The force of the rain split the earth, yet the great raincloud, passing over the trees, could not wet even so much as a dewdrop on the Great Being's robe. Then he raised a shower of stones. Great mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, came through the sky and turned into divine garlands of flowers at the Bodhisatta’s feet. Then he raised a shower of weapons. Single-edged and double-edged swords, spears, and razors, smoking and blazing, came through the sky and turned into divine flowers upon reaching the Bodhisatta. Then he raised a shower of embers. Embers the color of the kiṃsuka flower came through the sky and scattered as divine flowers at the Bodhisatta’s feet. Then he raised a shower of hot ashes. Extremely hot ashes, the color of fire, came through the sky and fell as divine sandalwood powder at the Bodhisatta’s feet. Then he raised a shower of sand. Very fine sand, smoking and blazing, came through the sky and fell as divine flowers at the Bodhisatta’s feet. Then he raised a shower of mud. That rain of mud, smoking and blazing, came through the sky and fell as divine ointment at the Bodhisatta’s feet. Then, thinking, 'I will terrify and drive away Siddhattha with this,' he raised a darkness. That darkness, like a fourfold deep gloom, upon reaching the Bodhisatta, vanished as if dispelled by the light of the sun.

Evaṃ māro imāhi navahi vātavassapāsāṇapaharaaṅgāra kukkuḷavāḷuka kalalaandhakāravuṭṭhīhi bodhisattaṃ palāpetuṃ asakkonto “kiṃ bhaṇe tiṭṭhatha imaṃ siddhatthakumāraṃ gaṇhatha hanatha palāpethā”ti parisaṃ āṇāpetvā sayampi girimekhalassa hatthino khandhe nisinno cakkāvudhaṃ ādāya bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “siddhattha uṭṭhāhi etasmā pallaṅkā, nāyaṃ tumhākaṃ pāpuṇāti, mayhaṃeva pāpuṇātī”ti āha. Mahāsatto tassa vacanaṃ sutvā avoca “māra neva tayā dasapāramiyo pūritā, na upapāramiyo na paramattha pāramiyo nāpi pañcamahāpariccāgā pariccattā na ñātatthacariyā na lokatthacariyā na buddhatthacariyā pūritā, sabbā tā mayāyeva pūritā, tasmā nāyaṃ pallaṅko tuyhaṃ pāpuṇāti, mayhameva pāpuṇātī”ti. Māro kuddho kodhavegaṃ asahanto mahāpurisassa cakkāvudhaṃ vissajjesi. Taṃ tassa dasapāramiyo āvajjantassa uparibhāge mālāvitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ kira khuracakkāvudhaṃ aññadā tena kuddhena vissaṭṭhaṃ ekaghanapāsāṇa thambhe vaṃsakaḷīre viya chindantaṃ gacchati. Idāni pana tasmiṃ mālāvitānaṃ hutvā ṭhite avasesā māraparisā idāni pallaṅkato vuṭṭhāya palāyissatīti mahantamahantāni selakūṭāni vissajjesuṃ. Tānipi mahāpurisassa pāramiyo āvajjantassa mālāguḷabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā bhūmiyaṃ patiṃsu.

Thus Māra, unable to drive away the Bodhisatta with these nine rains of wind, rain, rocks, weapons, embers, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness, commanded his assembly, saying, 'Why do you stand there? Seize this Prince Siddhattha, kill him, drive him away!' Then, mounting the elephant Girimekhala himself, he took up his discus weapon and approached the Bodhisatta, saying: 'Siddhattha, arise from this seat! It does not belong to you; it belongs only to me.' Hearing his words, the Great Being replied: 'Māra, you have not fulfilled the ten perfections, nor the secondary perfections, nor the ultimate perfections. Nor have you made the five great sacrifices, nor fulfilled the practices for the benefit of kinsmen, for the benefit of the world, or for Buddhahood. All these have been fulfilled by me alone. Therefore, this seat does not belong to you; it belongs only to me.' Enraged and unable to contain his fury, Māra hurled his discus weapon at the Great Being. But as the Bodhisatta reflected on his ten perfections, it transformed into a canopy of flowers and remained suspended above him. It is said that this razor-sharp discus, when thrown by him in anger at other times, would slice through solid stone pillars as if they were bamboo shoots. But now, as it had become a floral canopy and stayed there, the rest of Māra’s assembly, thinking, 'Now he will rise from his seat and flee,' hurled huge mountain peaks. These too, as the Great Being reflected on his perfections, turned into garlands of flowers and fell to the ground.

Devatā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhitā gīvaṃ pasāretvā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā “naṭṭho vata bho siddhatthakumārassa rūpaggappatto attabhāvo, kiṃ nu kho karissatī”ti olokenti. Tato [M 0.0055] mahāpuriso pūritapāramīnaṃ bodhisattānaṃ abhi sambujjhanadivase pattapallaṅko mayhaṃva pāpuṇātīti vatvā ṭhitaṃ māraṃ āha “māra tuyhaṃ dānassa dinnabhāve ko sakkhī”ti. Māro “ettakā janā sakkhino”ti māra balābhimukhaṃ hatthaṃ pasāreti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe māraparisāya “ahaṃ sakkhī ahaṃ sakkhī”ti pavattasaddo pathavīundriyasaddasadiso ahosi. Atha kho māro mahāpurisaṃ āha “siddhattha tuyhaṃ dānassa dinnabhāve ko sakkhī”ti. Mahāpuriso “tuyhaṃ tāva dānassa dinnabhāve sacetanā sakkhino. Mayhaṃ pana imasmiṃ ṭhāne sacetano koci sakkhī nāma natthi. Tiṭṭhatu tāva me avasesattabhāvesu dinnadānaṃ, vessantarattabhāve pana ṭhatvā mayhaṃ sattasattaka mahādānassa dinnabhāve acetanāpi ghanamahāpathavī sakkhī”ti cīvaragabbhantarato dakkhiṇahatthaṃ nīharitvā vessantarattabhāve mayhaṃ sattasattakamahādānassa dinnabhāve tvaṃ sakkhi na sakkhīti mahāpathaviyābhimukhaṃ hatthaṃ pasāresi. Mahā pathavī “ahaṃ te dānassa sakkhī”ti viravasahassena viravasatasahassena mārabalaṃ avattharamānā viya unnadi.

The devas standing at the rim of the world-system stretched out their necks and raised their heads, gazing and saying: 'Alas, the supremely beautiful form of Prince Siddhattha is lost! What will he do now?' Then the Great Being, after first declaring to Māra who stood there, 'This seat, attained on the day of supreme enlightenment by Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections, belongs to me,' then asked him: 'Māra, who is witness to your having given gifts?' Māra replied, 'All these people are my witnesses,' and he stretched out his hand toward his army. At that moment, the shout from Māra’s host, 'I am a witness! I am a witness!' arose, like the sound of the earth splitting asunder. Then Māra said to the Great Being: 'Siddhattha, who is witness to your having given gifts?' The Great Being replied: 'For your gifts, there are sentient witnesses. But in this place, there is no sentient witness for me. Let alone the gifts given in my other existences, for the great gift of seven-hundreds that I gave when I was Vessantara, this insentient, solid great earth is my witness.' Drawing his right hand from within his robe, he stretched it out towards the great earth, asking: 'For the great gift of seven-hundreds that I gave in my existence as Vessantara, are you my witness or not?' The great earth, as if to overwhelm Māra’s army, thundered forth with thousands, with hundreds of thousands of roars: 'I am witness to your gift!'

Tato mahāpurise dinnaṃ te siddhattha mahādānaṃ uttama dānanti vessantaradānaṃ sammasante diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko girimekhalo hatthī jāṇukehi patiṭṭhāsi. Māraparisā disāvidisā palāyiṃsu. Dve ekamaggena gatā nāma natthi. Sīsābharaṇāni ceva vatthābharaṇāni ca pahāya sammukha sammukhaṭṭhāne disāvidisāhiyeva palāyiṃsu. Tato devasaṅgho palāyamānaṃ mārabalaṃ disvā mārassa parājayo jāto. Siddhatthakumārassa jayo. Jayapūjaṃ karissāmāti nāgā nāgānaṃ, supaṇṇā supaṇṇānaṃ, devatā devatānaṃ, brahmāno brahmānaṃ pesetvā gandhamālādi hatthā mahāpurisassa santikaṃ bodhipallaṅkaṃ āgamaṃsu. Evaṃ gatesu ca panetesu –

Then, while the Great Being was contemplating the Vessantara-gift—'The great gift, the supreme gift, was given by you, Siddhattha!'—the elephant Girimekhala, one hundred and fifty yojanas tall, fell to its knees. Māra’s host fled to the cardinal and intermediate directions. No two went by the same path. Abandoning their headdresses and garments, they fled in every which way from wherever they stood. Then the assembly of devas, seeing Māra’s army in flight, declared: 'Māra is defeated! Prince Siddhattha is victorious! Let us pay homage to his victory!' The nāgas sent word to the nāgas, the supaṇṇas to the supaṇṇas, the devas to the devas, and the brahmās to the brahmās, and holding perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they approached the Great Being at the seat of Awakening. And as they came, they sang:

“Jayo [M 0.0056] hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ,

Mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosisuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā,

Jayaṃ tadā nāgagaṇā mahesino.

This is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha, and the defeat of Māra, the evil one. Delighted at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, the hosts of Nāgas then proclaimed the victory of the great sage.

Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ,

Mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosisuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā,

Jayaṃ tadā supaṇṇasaṅghā mahesino.

This is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha, and the defeat of Māra, the evil one. Delighted at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, the hosts of Supaṇṇas then proclaimed the victory of the great sage.

Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ,

Mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosisuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā,

Jayaṃ tadā devagaṇā mahesino.

This is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha, and the defeat of Māra, the evil one. Delighted at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, the hosts of devas then proclaimed the victory of the great sage.

Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ,

Mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosisuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā,

Jayaṃ tadā brahmagaṇāpi tādino”ti.

This is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha, and the defeat of Māra, the evil one. Delighted at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, the hosts of Brahmās too then proclaimed the victory of the Steadfast One.

Avasesesu dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu devatā mālāgandhavilepanehi ca pūjayamānā nānappakāra thutiyo ca vadamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Evaṃ anatthaṅgateyeva sūriye mahāpuriso mārabalaṃ vidhametvā cīvarūpari pata mānehi bodhirukkhaṅkurehi rattapavāḷapallavehi viya pūjayamāno paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ anussaritvā majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhetvā pacchimayāme paṭicca samuppāde ñāṇaṃ otāresi. Athassa dvādasapadikaṃ paccayā kāraṃ vaṭṭavivaṭṭavasena anulomato paṭilomato sammasantassa dasasahassilokadhātu udakapariyantaṃ katvā dvādasakkhattuṃ sampakampi. Mahāpurisena pana dasasahassi lokadhātuṃ unnādetvā aruṇuggamanavelāyaṃ sabbaññuta ñāṇaṃ [M 0.0057] paṭivijjhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Idha pana vuttāvasesaṃ tāsu ca oloketvā gahetabbanti.

In the remaining ten thousand world-systems, devas stood honoring him with garlands, perfumes, and ointments, and uttering various praises. Thus, while the sun had not yet set, the Great Being, having vanquished Māra’s army and being honored by the shoots of the Bodhi tree that fell upon his robe like tender red coral sprouts, in the first watch of the night recollected his former lives; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye; and in the last watch, he applied his mind to dependent origination. Then, as he contemplated the twelve-factored structure of conditionality in forward and reverse order, in terms of cycling on and cycling off, the ten-thousandfold world-system, to its very water-boundary, quaked twelve times. It is said that the Great Being, having caused the ten-thousandfold world-system to resound, penetrated to omniscient knowledge at the time of sunrise. The remainder of the account should be understood by consulting the relevant texts.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Upetapuñño sampanna dānādipāramīpuññavā dānādipāramīpuññena sampanno vā, yo sugato varabodhimūle uttamassa bodhirukkhassa samīpe, sasenamāraṃ senāya saha pavattaṃ mārarājaṃ, jinitvā pāramīpuññatejena vijayitvā, aruṇodayamhi visākhapuṇṇamiyaṃ aruṇuggamanavelāyaṃ, bodhiṃ arahattamaggañāṇa sabbaññutañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ bodhiṃ, abojjhi paṭivijjhi adhigami vā, mārajinaṃ pañcamārānaṃ vijitāviṃ, abhaṅgaṃ sasenamāro yo koci vā bhindituṃ asamatthaṃ taṃ sugataṃ ahaṃ namāmīti.

This is a concise explanation here. The Sugata, endowed with merit, accomplished in the perfections such as giving, or rather, perfected through the merit of the perfections, at the foot of the supreme Bodhi tree, having conquered Māra, the king who wields an army, along with his host, vanquishing him by the power of the merit of his perfections, at the rising of the dawn on the Visākha full moon day, awakened to Bodhi—Bodhi, reckoned as the knowledge of the Arahantship path and omniscient knowledge—penetrated and attained it. That Sugata, the Conqueror of Māra, victorious over the five Māras, unassailable, whom neither Māra with his host nor anyone else is able to break—that Sugata I worship.

Chaṭṭhamavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the sixth verse of salutation is complete.

7.

7.

Rāgādi chedāmalañāṇakhaggaṃ,

Satīsamaññāphalakābhigāhaṃ;

Sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ taṃ,

Namāmibhiññāvaramiddhupetaṃ.

I bow to him who wields the sword of stainless knowledge that cuts off lust and so forth, who firmly grasps the shield called mindfulness, who is adorned with the ornament of the flood of virtue, and who is endowed with the supreme psychic power of higher knowledge.

7. Evaṃ chaṭṭhamagāthāya sugataṃ vanditvā idāni arahatta maggañāṇādīhi catūhi guṇehi thomitvā vanditukāmo rāgādityādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana indavajira upendavajira gāthādvayassa lakkhaṇassa missakattā ekādasakkharehi lakkhitā upajātigāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “anantarodīritalakkhaṇā ce, pādāvimissā upajātiyo tā”ti. Tassattho. Yassā vuttiyā anantaro dīritalakkhaṇā anantare udīritaṃ vuttaṃ indavajiropenda vajiragāthānaṃ lakkhaṇavantā pādā vimissā saṃsaṭṭhā ce bhavanti, tā vuttiyo upajātiyo nāmāti.

7. Having thus paid homage to the Sugata with the sixth verse, now desiring to praise and worship him with the four qualities beginning with the knowledge of the Arahantship path, he speaks the verse beginning with 'rāgādi.' This, however, should be understood as an Upajāti verse marked by eleven syllables, due to the blending of the characteristics of the two verses, Indavajirā and Upendavajirā. For it is said in the Vuttodaya: 'If the lines have characteristics proclaimed immediately after, and are intermixed, they are Upajāti.' Its meaning is this: If, in a meter, the lines possess the characteristics proclaimed immediately after—that is, the characteristics of the Indavajirā and Upendavajirā verses are stated right after—and whose lines are intermixed and interwoven, such meters are called Upajāti.

Tattha [M 0.0058] rāgādichedāmala ñāṇakhagganti ettha rāgaādicheda amalañāṇakhaggantipadacchedo. Rāgādikilesaṃ chindantaṃ malavira hitaṃ arahattamaggañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ asivantanti attho. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho. Rūpādīsu rañjatīti rāgo. Ranjadhātu rāge ṇa. Rāgo ādi yesanteti rāgādayo, kilesā. Te chindatīti rāgādichedaṃ, arahattamaggañāṇaṃ. Apāyaṃ malati dhāretīti malaṃ, rāgādi. Atha vā malati saṃkilissati etenāti malaṃ. Maladhātu saṃkilesane a. Malato virahitaṃ amalaṃ, ñāṇaṃ. Cattāri saccāni jānāti paṭivijjhatīti ñāṇaṃ, arahattamaggañāṇaṃ. Rāgādichedañca amalañca taṃ ñāṇañcāti rāgādichedāmalañāṇaṃ. Rukkhādiṃ khaggati chindati etenāti vā khaggaṃ, pakatiasi. Khaggaṃ viyāti khaggaṃ, ñāṇaṃ. Rāgādichedāmalañāṇasaṅkhataṃ khaggaṃ yassa soti rāgādichedāmalañāṇakhaggo, buddho. Rāgādikilesaṃ chindantena malavira hitena aggamaggañāṇasaṅkhatena asinā samannāgatoti attho. Taṃ.

Here, the phrase 'rāgādichedāmalañāṇakhaggaṃ' is to be divided as 'rāga-ādi-cheda amala ñāṇa khaggaṃ.' The meaning is: that which cuts off defilements beginning with lust, free from impurity, called the knowledge of the Arahantship path, is called a sword. Herein, this is the explanation of the words: That which delights in forms, etc., is called lust (rāgo). The root 'rañj' with the suffix 'ṇa' denotes lust. Lust and the like are called 'rāgādayo,' the defilements (kilesā). That which cuts them off is called 'rāgādicheda,' which is the knowledge of the Arahantship path. That which stains or holds one in misery is called 'mala' (stain), such as lust, etc. Alternatively, that by which one is defiled is called 'mala.' The root 'mal' denotes defilement, with the suffix 'a.' Free from impurity is 'amala' (stainless), which is knowledge. Knowing and penetrating the four truths is called 'ñāṇa' (knowledge), the knowledge of the Arahantship path. The cutter of lust, etc., and stainless, and that knowledge—thus, 'rāgādichedāmalañāṇa' (the stainless knowledge that cuts off lust, etc.). That which cuts trees, etc., is called 'khagga' (sword), like a common sword. Resembling a sword is 'khagga,' which here refers to knowledge. The one who possesses the sword of stainless knowledge that cuts off lust, etc., is called 'rāgādichedāmalañāṇakhaggo' (the one with the sword of stainless knowledge that cuts off lust), the Buddha. The meaning is: endowed with the sword called the knowledge of the supreme path, which cuts off defilements like lust and is stainless. That.

Satīsamaññā phalakābhigāhanti ettha satisamaññāphalaka abhigāhantipadacchedo. Sammāsatināmikaṃ phalakaṃ daḷhagāha kanti attho. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho. Saraṇaṃ sati, sarati sampayuttadhammā etāyāti, saratīti vā sati. Saradhātuti. Atha vā pamādaṃ sarati hiṃsatīti sati, sammāsati. Saradhātu hiṃsāyaṃti. Sammā ājānāti etāyāti samaññā, satiiti samaññā satisamaññā, asiādisatthaṃ phalati nivāretīti phalakaṃ, kheṭakaṃ. Phaladhātu nivāraṇe ṇvu. Satisamaññaṃ phalakaṃ abhidaḷhaṃ gaṇhatīti satisamaññāphala kābhigāho, buddho labbhati. Yathā hi senāya phalakaṃ asiādisatthaṃ rakkhati, evaṃ satisaṃvaro cakkhādi dvāresu rūpādiārammaṇaṃ pavisituṃ adatvā rakkhati. Tasmā bhagavā satidhammo sabbākusalānaṃ rakkhakattā sabbakusala dhammānaṃ upakārattā sabbatthānaṃ sādhakattā ca satiphalakaṃ daḷhaṃ [M 0.0059] gaṇhatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttañhi “ye keci kusalā dhammā, sabbe te appamādamūlakā appamādasamosaraṇā, appamādo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti ca. “Satiṃ khvāhaṃ bhikkhave sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti ca.

Here, the phrase 'Satīsamaññāphalakābhigāhaṃ' is to be divided as 'sati-samaññā-phalaka-abhigāhaṃ.' The meaning is that the shield designated as right mindfulness is firmly grasped. Herein, this is the explanation of the words: Remembering is mindfulness; it is called mindfulness because associated states are remembered by it, or because it remembers. It is derived from the root 'sara.' Alternatively, it is called mindfulness, right mindfulness, because it remembers and destroys heedlessness. The root 'sara' is also used in the sense of harming. That by which one rightly knows is designation (samaññā); mindfulness is a designation—thus, mindfulness-designation. A shield (phalakaṃ) wards off weapons such as swords; it is a protector. The root 'phala' has the meaning of warding off, with the suffix 'ṇvu.' The one who firmly grasps the shield designated as mindfulness is the 'satisamaññāphalakābhigāho'; the Buddha is to be understood. For just as a shield protects an army from swords and other weapons, so does the restraint of mindfulness protect by not allowing forms and other sense-objects to enter through the doors of the eye and so forth. Therefore, it is said that the Blessed One, whose nature is mindfulness, firmly grasps the shield of mindfulness, as he is the guardian of all unwholesome states, the supporter of all wholesome states, and the accomplisher of all purposes. For it has been said: 'Whatever wholesome states there are, all are rooted in heedfulness, converge upon heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared the foremost among them.' And also: 'Monks, I declare mindfulness to be useful in all circumstances.'

Sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsitanti sīlaoghaalaṅkāra vibhū sitanti padacchedo. Visuddhasīlānaṃ samūhasaṅkhātena alaṅkārena vibhūsitanti attho. Tattha sīlanti lokuttara sīlaṃ. Tassa attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Taṃ pana cetanā sīlaṃ, cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīlañcāti catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha cetanā sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātā dīhi vā viramantassa vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanā. Cetasikasīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi viramantassa virati. Saṃvaro sīlanti ettha saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro, sati saṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaro cāti pañcavidho hoti, sabbametaṃ saṃvaro sīlaṃ nāma. Avītikkamo sīlaṃ nāma samādinnasīlassa kāyikavācasiko anatikkamoti. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “kiṃsīlanticetanā sīlaṃ, cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīla”nti. Idha pana avītikkamo sīlaṃ nādhippetaṃ. Kasmā. Bhagavato samādinnasikkhāpadassa abhāvato. Buddhānañhi sikkhāpadaṃ nāma natthīti. Oghoti samūho. Oghasaddo hi samūhavācako. Tena vuttaṃ abhidhānappadīpikāyaṃ –

Here, the phrase 'Sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ' is to be divided as 'sīla-ogha-alaṅkāra-vibhūsitaṃ.' The meaning is: adorned with the ornament that is the multitude of purified virtues. Herein, 'sīla' (virtue) refers to supramundane virtue. Its meaning has already been stated above. That virtue is fourfold: virtue as volition (cetanā sīlaṃ), virtue as a mental factor (cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ), virtue as restraint (saṃvaro sīlaṃ), and virtue as non-transgression (avītikkamo sīlaṃ). Herein, virtue as volition is the volition of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who fulfills a course of conduct. Virtue as a mental factor is the abstinence of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth. As for virtue as restraint, here restraint is fivefold: restraint by the monastic code (pātimokkhasaṃvaro), restraint by mindfulness (sati saṃvaro), restraint by knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvaro), restraint by patience (khantisaṃvaro), and restraint by energy (vīriyasaṃvaro). All this is called virtue as restraint. Virtue as non-transgression is the bodily and verbal non-transgression of one who has undertaken a precept. As it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'What is virtue? Virtue as volition, virtue as a mental factor, virtue as restraint, and virtue as non-transgression.' Here, however, virtue as non-transgression is not intended. Why? Because the Blessed One has no undertaken training precepts. For Buddhas have no training precepts. 'Ogha' means multitude. The word 'ogha' indeed denotes a multitude. Therefore, it is said in the Abhidhānappadīpikā—

“Samūho gaṇasaṅghātā, samudāyo ca sañcayo;

Sandoho nivaho ogho, visaro nikaro cayo”tyādi.

"A multitude, a group, an assembly, a collection, and an accumulation; a stream, a mass, a flood, a host, a heap, a pile," and so on.

Avahanati gacchati pavattati avayavaṃ etthāti ogho, samūho. Avapubbahanadhātu gatimhi ṇo. Avassa o, hanassa gho. Abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkāyaṃ pana “avayavaṃ katvā [M 0.0060] byāpiyati gacchatīti ogho”ti vuttaṃ. Sīlānaṃ ogho samūho sīlogho. Alaṅkāroti piḷandhano. Alaṃ vibhusaṃ taṃ samaṅgīpuggalaṃ karoti anenāti alaṅkāro, sīlaṃ. Alaṃsaddūpapadakaradhātu ṇo. Sīlogho eva alaṅkāro sīloghālaṅkāro, tena vibhū siyatīti sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsito, buddho. Tena pana aññehi asādhāraṇena lokuttarasīlālaṅkārena vibhūsito. Na cīvarādinālaṅkārenāti attho. Sīlālaṅkārena hi sadiso alaṅkāro nāma natthi. Taṃ sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ.

'Ogho', a multitude, is so called because a component part is carried down, goes, or proceeds within it. It is derived from the root 'han' preceded by 'ava,' in the sense of 'to go,' with the suffix 'ṇo.' 'Ava' becomes 'o,' and 'han' becomes 'gho.' In the subcommentary to the Abhidhānappadīpikā, however, it is said: 'That which pervades and moves by forming parts is ogha.' The multitude (ogho) of virtues is 'sīlogho.' 'Alaṅkāro' means an ornament. 'Alaṅkāro' is that by which one makes a person sufficiently adorned and complete; it signifies virtue. It is derived from the root 'kar' with the prefix 'alaṃ,' with the suffix 'ṇo.' The multitude of virtues itself is the adornment, 'sīloghālaṅkāro.' Adorned by that, one is 'sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsito'; this refers to the Buddha. He is adorned with that supramundane adornment of virtue, which is uncommon to others; the meaning is that he is not adorned with robes or other such ornaments. Indeed, there is no adornment like the adornment of virtue. Thus, he is 'sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ' (adorned with the ornament of the multitude of virtues).

Namāmibhiññāvaramiddhupetanti ettha namāmi abhiññāvaraṃ iddhi upetanti padacchedo. Tattha namāmīti vandāmi. Abhiññāvaramiddhupetanti abhiññāsaṅkhātāya uttamāya iddhiyā samannāgatanti attho. Abhivisesena jānātīti abhiññā, chabbidhaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Tañhi iddhividhadibbasota paracitta vijānana pubbenivāsānussati cutūpapāta āsavakkhaya ñāṇavasena chabbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha iddhividhañāṇanti ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotītiādinayappavatte iddhividhe jānana ñāṇaṃ. Dibbasotañāṇanti dūrasantikādibhedasaddārammaṇāya dibbasotadhātuyā jānanañāṇaṃ. Paracittavijānanañāṇanti parasattānaṃ cittaparicchedassa vijānanañāṇaṃ. Pubbenivāsā nussatiñāṇanti attasantāne vutthavasena ceva gocara nivāsavasena ca pubbe atītabhavesu khandhādīnaṃ anussaraṇa satiyā sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Cutūpapātañāṇanti sattānaṃ cutiyañca upapāte ca jānanañāṇaṃ. Ettha ca aṭṭhakathāsu cutūpapātañāṇaṭṭhāne tassa sādhakattā dibbacakkhuñāṇanti vuttaṃ. Āsavakkhayañāṇanti saccaparicchedassa jānanaṃ arahatta maggañāṇanti. Varanti uttamaṃ. Iddhīti ijjhanaṃ samijjhanaṃ. Ijjhati samijjhatīti vā iddhi. Idhadhātuti. Abhiññāsaṅkhātāya varāya [M 0.0061] iddhiyā upeto samupeto samannāgatoti abhiññāvaramiddhupeto, buddho. Taṃ abhiññāvaramiddhupetaṃ. Taṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ namāmīti sambandho.

Here, the phrase 'Namāmibhiññāvaramiddhupetaṃ' is to be divided as 'namāmi abhiññā-vara-iddhi-upetaṃ.' Herein, 'namāmi' means 'I pay homage.' 'Abhiññāvaramiddhupetaṃ' means 'endowed with the supreme power known as higher knowledge.' 'Abhiññā' is so called because one knows in a special or higher way; it is the sixfold knowledge. It is sixfold as: knowledge of the kinds of psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings, and knowledge of the destruction of the taints. Among these, 'knowledge of the kinds of psychic power' is the knowledge that understands the various psychic powers, which proceed in the manner of 'being one, he becomes many,' and so on. 'Knowledge of the divine ear' is the knowledge of the divine ear element, which has as its object sounds that are distant, near, and so forth. 'Knowledge of others' minds' is the knowledge that discerns and understands the minds of other beings. 'Knowledge of the recollection of past lives' is the knowledge, associated with mindfulness, of recollecting the aggregates and so on in past lives, both in terms of having dwelt in one's own continuity and in terms of the sphere of dwelling. 'Knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings' is the knowledge that understands the passing away and reappearance of beings. Here, in the commentaries, 'knowledge of the divine eye' (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) is mentioned in place of 'knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings,' because it is the means for it. 'Knowledge of the destruction of the taints' is the knowledge that discerns the truths—the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. 'Vara' means supreme. 'Iddhi' means success or accomplishment. It is called 'iddhi' because one succeeds (ijjhati) or accomplishes (samijjhati). It is from the root 'idh.' 'Abhiññāvaramiddhupeto' means one who is endowed, possessed, or furnished with the supreme power known as higher knowledge; this refers to the Buddha. Thus, 'taṃ abhiññāvaramiddhupetaṃ' (to him who is endowed with the supreme power of higher knowledge). The connection is: 'I pay homage to that Buddha.'

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Rāgādichedāmalañāṇa khaggaṃ rāgādikilesaṃ chindantaṃ malavirahitaṃ arahattamaggañāṇa saṅkhātaṃ asivantaṃ, satīsamaññāphalakābhigāhaṃ sammā satināmikaṃ phalakaṃ daḷhagahaṇaṃ, sīloghalaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ sīlānaṃ samūhasaṅkhātena alaṅkārena vibhūsitaṃ, abhiññā varamiddhupetaṃ abhiññāsaṅkhātāya varāya uttamāya iddhiyā upetaṃ samupetaṃ samannāgataṃ taṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ namāmīti.

Here is the concise connection of the words. To him who possesses the sword of immaculate knowledge that severs lust and so on—that is, possessing the sword known as the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, which is free from impurity and severs the defilements of lust and so on; to him who firmly grasps the shield designated as mindfulness—that is, the firm grasping of the shield named right mindfulness; to him who is adorned with the ornament of the multitude of virtues—that is, adorned with the ornament known as the collection of virtues; to him who is endowed with the supreme power of higher knowledge—that is, endowed, possessed, and furnished with the supreme, highest power known as higher knowledge; to that Buddha, I pay homage.

Sattamavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the seventh homage verse is complete.

8.

8.

Dayālayaṃ sabbadhi dukkaraṃ karaṃ,

Bhavaṇṇavātikkamamaggataṃ gataṃ;

Tilokanāthaṃ susamāhitaṃ hitaṃ,

Samantacakkhuṃ paṇamāmi taṃmitaṃ.

I bow to that immeasurable one: the abode of compassion, who performed what is difficult to do everywhere; who has reached the state of having transcended the ocean of existence; the Lord of the three worlds, well-composed and beneficent; the All-Seeing One.

8. Evaṃ sattamagāthāya buddhaṃ vanditvā idāni mahākaruṇā dīhi navahi guṇehi thomitvā vanditukāmo dayālayantyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana ja ta ja ragaṇehi yuttattā dvādasakkharehi lakkhitā catupādantayamakā vaṃsaṭṭhagāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “vadanti vaṃsaṭṭhamidaṃ jatā jarā”ti. Tassattho, yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ jatā jatagaṇā ca jarā jaragaṇā ca ce bhavanti, idaṃ vuttaṃ vaṃsaṭṭhaṃ vaṃsaṭṭhagāthā nāmāti munayo isayo vadantīti.

8. Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the seventh verse, the author, now desiring to praise and pay homage to him with the nine qualities beginning with great compassion, speaks the verse beginning with 'Dayālayaṃ.' This, however, should be understood as a vaṃsaṭṭha verse, having four feet, marked by twelve syllables, endowed with ja, ta, ja, and ra gaṇas, and featuring end-rhyme (antayamaka). For it is said in the Vuttodaya: 'They call this vaṃsaṭṭha, which has ja, ta, ja, ra.' Its meaning is: that in which, in each foot, there are a ja-gaṇa, a ta-gaṇa, a ja-gaṇa, and a ra-gaṇa, this verse is called vaṃsaṭṭha, a vaṃsaṭṭha verse—so declare the sages and seers.

Tattha dayālayanti mahākaruṇāya ca, mettāya ca ādhāraṃ. Dayāsaddo hi karuṇāya ca, mettāya ca vattati. Adayāpannoti ettha hi karuṇāya vattati. Nikkaruṇikataṃ [M 0.0062] āpannoti attho. Dayāpannoti ettha mettāya mettacittataṃ āpannoti attho. Idha pana tadubhayampi vaṭṭati. Tasmā dayā ca dayā ca dayāti saddasarūpekaseso kātabbo. Vacanattho panettha evaṃ veditabbo. Dayati hiṃsati kāruṇikanti dayā, mahākaruṇā. Dayadhātu hiṃsāyaṃ a. Yā karuṇā yāva yathādhippetaṃ parassa hitanipphattiṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva kāruṇikaṃ hiṃsatīti attho. Dayati hiṃsati apaneti paradukkhanti vā dayā. Atha vā dayati attano sukhampi pahāya khedaṃ gaṇhāti sajjano etāyāti dayā, dayati anuggaṇhāti pāpajanampi etāyāti vā dayā, dayanti gaṇhanti bodhisattā sammāsambodhiṃ etāyāti vā dayā, bodhisattā buddhabhāvāya abhinīhārakaraṇa kāle hatthagatampi aggaphalaṃ chaṭṭetvā mahākaruṇāya saṃsārasāgarato satte samuddharitukāmā anassāsa karaṃ mahantaṃ saṃsāradukkhañca pacchimabhave saha amata dhātupaṭilābhena anekaguṇasamalaṅkataṃ sabbaññutañāṇañca gaṇhantīti attho. Dayati dadāti sattānaṃ abhayaṃ etāyāti dayā, mettā. Dayadhātu dāne a. Dayati gacchati vibhāgaṃ akatvā sattesu samaṃ pavattatīti dayā. Yathā udakaṃ sabbasattesu sītena samaṃ pharati rajomalañca pavāheti, evaṃ mettā pāpakalyāṇajanesu vibhāgaṃ akatvā samaṃ pavattatīti attho.

Here, 'dayālayaṃ' means the foundation of great compassion and loving-kindness. Indeed, the word 'dayā' is used for both compassion and loving-kindness. In 'adayāpanno,' it is used for compassion, meaning one has attained mercilessness. In 'dayāpanno,' it is used for loving-kindness, meaning one has attained a state of loving-heartedness. Here, however, both apply. Therefore, 'dayā ca dayā ca' should be treated as 'dayā,' a single form with one remainder. The meaning of the word here should be understood thus: 'Dayati hiṃsati kāruṇikanti dayā,' great compassion. The root 'day' is in the sense of harming. It means that compassion, as long as it does not achieve the intended benefit for others as desired, harms the compassionate one. Or 'dayā' harms, that is, removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, 'dayā' is that by which the virtuous, even abandoning their own happiness, take on distress; or 'dayā' is that by which even the wicked are favored; or 'dayā' is that by which bodhisattvas grasp perfect enlightenment—meaning that bodhisattvas, at the time of making the aspiration for Buddhahood, relinquish even the highest fruit within their grasp and, out of great compassion, wishing to rescue beings from the ocean of saṃsāra, take upon themselves the immense, relentless suffering of saṃsāra, and in their final existence, along with the attainment of the deathless element, grasp the all-knowing wisdom adorned with countless virtues. 'Dayati dadāti,' it gives beings fearlessness—this is 'dayā,' loving-kindness. The root 'day' is in the sense of giving. 'Dayati gacchati,' it moves without discrimination among beings, acting equally—this is 'dayā.' Just as water spreads equally among all beings, cooling them and washing away dust and impurities, so too does loving-kindness act without discrimination between the wicked and the virtuous, moving equally—this is the meaning.

Aparo nayo. Dayanti anurakkhanti satte etāya, sayaṃ vā anuddayati anuddayamattameva vā etanti dayā, karuṇāmettā labbhanti. Tāya ālayati patiṭṭhati etthāti dayālayo, buddho. Bhagavā hi devadattādīsu virodhi sattesu ca avirodhisattesu orase rāhule ca samaṃ niccaṃ hitajjhāsayatāya mahākaruṇāya mettāya ca ṭhito[M 0.0063], tasmā dayālayanti thometīti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ apadānapāḷiyaṃ –

Another explanation. Because they protect and guard beings with this, or because one is compassionate oneself, or because this is simply the state of being inclined to compassion, therefore 'dayā' is obtained as compassion and loving-kindness. Because one dwells and is established in this, therefore, the Buddha is 'dayālaya,' the abode of compassion. Indeed, the Blessed One stands equally with constant intention for their welfare, with great compassion and loving-kindness, whether toward hostile beings like Devadatta, or toward non-hostile beings, or toward his own son Rāhula. Therefore, it is said that he is praised as 'dayālaya,' the abode of compassion. For this is stated in the Apadāna Pāḷi:

“Vadhake devadatte ca, core aṅgulimālake;

Dhanapāle rāhule ca, samacitto mahāmunī”ti.

“Towards the murderer Devadatta, the thief Aṅgulimāla, Dhanapāla, and Rāhula, the great sage is of equal mind.”

Sabbadhīti sabbasmiṃ attabhāve. Buddhabhāvāya abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya sabbattabhāvesūti attho. Dukkaranti dukkhena karitabbaṃ pañcamahāpariccāgādikammaṃ dukkhena karitabbanti dukkaraṃ, pañcamahāpariccāgādikammaṃ labbhati. Ettha ca pañcamahā pariccāgoti dhanapariccāgo, aṅgapariccāgo, puttapariccāgo, bhariyapariccāgo, jīvitapariccāgo cāti pañcavidho hoti. Tattha hatthiassa dāsidāsādi saviññāṇakassa dhanassa vā muttāmaṇirajatādi aviññāṇakassa dhanassa vā pariccāgo dhanapariccāgo nāma. Hatthapādacakkhukaṇṇanāsādisarīrāva yavassa pariccāgo aṅgapariccāgo nāma. Puttassa ca dhītuyā ca pariccāgo puttapariccāgo nāma. Bhariyāya pariccāgo bhariyapariccāgo nāma. Jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhassa sarīrassa pariccāgo jīvitapariccāgo nāma. Kiñcāpi pana dhanapariccāgā dayo dānapāramiyaṃyeva antogadhā, tathāpi pariccāga visesabhāvadassanatthañceva sudukkarabhāvadassanatthañca mahāpariccāgavasena visuṃ katanti adhippāyo. Mahāpadānasuttaṭīkāyaṃ pana “aṅgapariccāgo, nayanapariccāgo, attapariccāgo, rajjapariccāgo, puttadārapariccāgoti ime pañca mahāpariccāgā. Tatthapi kāmaṃ aṅgapariccāgādayopi dānapāramīyeva. Tathāpi pariccāgavisesabhāvadassanatthañceva sudukkarabhāvadassanatthañca mahāpariccāgānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tatoyeva ca aṅgapariccāgatopi visuṃ nayanapariccāgaggahaṇaṃ. Pariccāgabhāvasāmaññepi rajjapariccāga puttadārapariccāgaggahaṇaṃ kata”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ dukkaraṃ. Idaṃ pana karanti etassa kammapadaṃ. Karanti karontaṃ, karotīti karo, buddho. Taṃ.

'Sabbadhi' means in every existence. The meaning is: in all existences from the time of aspiring to Buddhahood. 'Dukkaraṃ' means that which must be done with difficulty; actions such as the five great relinquishments are obtained as 'dukkara,' meaning they must be performed with difficulty. Here, the five great relinquishments are fivefold: the relinquishment of wealth, the relinquishment of limbs, the relinquishment of children, the relinquishment of a wife, and the relinquishment of life. Among these, the relinquishment of wealth is the giving up of animate wealth such as elephants, horses, male and female slaves, or inanimate wealth such as pearls, gems, and silver. The relinquishment of limbs is the giving up of body parts such as hands, feet, eyes, ears, and nose. The relinquishment of children is the giving up of sons and daughters. The relinquishment of a wife is the giving up of one's spouse. The relinquishment of life is the giving up of the body connected to the life faculty. Although the relinquishment of wealth and the others are indeed included within the perfection of giving, the intention is that they are separately mentioned as great relinquishments to show both the special nature of relinquishment and their extreme difficulty. In the commentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta, it is said: 'These are the five great relinquishments: the relinquishment of limbs, the relinquishment of eyes, the relinquishment of self, the relinquishment of kingship, and the relinquishment of children and a wife. Even though the relinquishment of limbs and the others are part of the perfection of giving, they are separately listed as great relinquishments to show both the special nature of relinquishment and their extreme difficulty. Therefore, the relinquishment of eyes is distinguished from the relinquishment of limbs, and the relinquishment of kingship and the relinquishment of children and a wife are separately mentioned despite their common nature as relinquishments.' That is `dukkaraṃ`, the difficult deed. The word `karaṃ` (the one who does) takes this as its object. `Karaṃ` means 'the one who does,' the doer—the Buddha. `Taṃ` refers to him.

Bhavaṇṇavātikkamamaggatanti [M 0.0064] ettha bhavaaṇṇavaatikkamaṃ aggatanti padacchedo. Bhavaṇṇavātikkamanti kāmarūpaarūpabhavasaṅkhatā aṇṇavā samuddato atikkantaṃ. Bhavanti sattā etthāti bhavo. Aṇṇo vuccati udakaṃ. Taṃ etasmiṃ atthīti aṇṇavā, samuddo. Bhavasaṅkhāto aṇṇavoti bhavaṇṇavā, mahāsamuddo. Bahūhi ūmivegādīhi bhayehi okiṇṇo viya tividhopi bhavo bahūhi jātijarāmaraṇādīhi dukkhabhayehi okiṇṇo hoti, tasmā bhavaṇṇavāti vuccati. Taṃ atikkamittha uttaritthāti bhavaṇṇavātikkamo, buddho. Tassa hi gambhīre mahāudakakkhandhe mahāsamudde udakaṃ abbocchinnaṃ pavattati sandatiiva tibhavasaṅkhate saṃsāre paṭisandhicutiyo abbocchinnaṃ nibbattakānaṃ diyaḍḍhasahassakilesānaṃ bodhimaṇḍe arahattamaggañāṇena asesaṃ viddhaṃsitattā tīsu bhavesu punabbhavo natthi. Tasmā buddhaṃ bhavaṇṇavātikkamanti abhitthavituṃ arahatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ bhavaṇṇavātikkamaṃ.

Here, the phrase 'bhavaṇṇavātikkamamaggataṃ' should be divided as 'bhavaṇṇavātikkamaṃ aggataṃ'. 'Bhavaṇṇavātikkamaṃ' means having transcended the ocean of existence, which is designated as the realms of sensuality, form, and formlessness. 'Bhava' is that in which beings exist. 'Aṇṇa' is said to be water. That in which it exists is 'aṇṇavā,' the ocean. The ocean designated as existence is 'bhavaṇṇavā,' the great ocean. Just as the great ocean is filled with many dangers like waves, so too is the threefold existence filled with many dangers of suffering like birth, aging, and death; therefore, it is called 'bhavaṇṇavā.' Having crossed that, having gone beyond it, is 'bhavaṇṇavātikkamo,' the Buddha. For him, there is no further becoming in the three realms of existence. This is because, at the seat of enlightenment, through the knowledge of the path to Arahantship, he completely destroyed the one thousand five hundred defilements which produce the unbroken succession of rebirth and death in saṃsāra—which is designated as the three realms of existence and is likened to the great ocean, a deep and vast mass of water where the water flows and streams without interruption. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha deserves to be praised as `bhavaṇṇavātikkamaṃ`, 'the one who has transcended the ocean of existence'. `Taṃ bhavaṇṇavātikkamaṃ` refers to him.

Aggatanti sabbasattānaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha aggasaddo ādikoṭikoṭṭhāsaseṭṭhesu dissati. Tathā hesa ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gatantiādīsu ādimhi dissati. Teneva aṅgulaggena taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ parāmaseyyātiādīsu koṭiyaṃ. Anujānāmi bhikkhave vihāraggena vā pariveṇaggena vā bhājetuntiādīsu koṭṭhāse. Aggo hamasmi lokassātiādīsu seṭṭhe. Svāyamidhapi soyeva daṭṭhabbo. Devamanussānaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ ajati gacchatīti aggo, buddho. Asadisaṭṭhena guṇavisiṭṭhaṭṭhena asamasamaṭṭhena ca aggo seṭṭho nāmāti attho. Atha vā dullabhapātu bhāvato acchariyamanussabhāvato bahujanahitasukhāvahato adutiyaasahāyādibhāvato ca bhagavā loke aggo seṭṭho nāmāti attho. Vuttañhi aṅguttarapāḷiyaṃ “yāvatā bhikkhave sattā apadā vā dvipadā [M 0.0065] vā catuppadā vā bahuppadā vā, tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti. Aggassa bhāvo aggataṃ. Taṃ pana gatantietassa kammapadaṃ. Gatanti pattaṃ, pāpuṇantanti attho.

'Aggataṃ' means the state of being supreme among all beings. Here, the word 'agga' is seen in the senses of beginning, tip, portion, and supreme. Thus, it appears in the sense of beginning in phrases like 'from this day forward, I have gone for refuge for life.' Similarly, it denotes tip in phrases like 'he should touch that tip of the finger with the tip of his finger.' In the sense of portion, in phrases like 'I allow, monks, to divide by the chief part of the monastery or the chief part of the dwelling.' In the sense of supreme, in phrases like 'I am the foremost in the world.' Here too, the same meaning should be understood. The Buddha is called 'agga' because he attains the supreme state among gods and humans. The meaning is that 'agga' or 'seṭṭha' denotes being incomparable, distinguished in virtues, and unmatched. Alternatively, the Blessed One is called 'agga' or 'seṭṭha' in the world because of his rare appearance, his marvelous human nature, his bringing welfare and happiness to many, his being without equal or companion, and other such qualities. As stated in the Aṅguttara Pāḷi: 'Monks, as far as beings are concerned—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—the Tathāgata is declared their foremost.' The state of being foremost is 'aggataṃ.' This is the object of 'gataṃ.' 'Gataṃ' means attained, reached—that is the meaning.

Tilokanāthanti kāmarūpaarūpasaṅkhatānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ lokānaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ. Ettha ca lokasaddassa attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Tayo lokā tilokā. Nāthasaddo pana nipphannānipphannavasena duvidho hoti. Tattha anipphannanāthasaddo paṭisaraṇattho hoti saṅketavasena. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇa”nti. Tilokānaṃ nātho paṭisaraṇoti tilokanātho, buddho. Sabbānatthaparihāra pubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāyaniratisayāya payogasampattiyā ca sadevamanussāya pajāya accantupakāritāya aparimitanirupamappabhāvaguṇavisesasamaṅgitāya ca sabbasattuttamo bhagavā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ ekapaṭisaraṇo nāmāti attho.

The Lord of the Three Worlds (Tilokanātha) means the refuge of the three worlds, namely, the worlds of sensuality, form, and the formless. Here, the meaning of the word 'world' has been explained previously. The three worlds are the 'tiloka'. The word 'nātha' (lord), however, is twofold: derived and underived. In this context, the underived word 'nātha' signifies refuge by convention. As it is stated in the commentary: 'A conventional expression is true, being a cause of worldly consensus.' The Lord of the Three Worlds is the refuge of the three worlds—that is, the Buddha. The Blessed One, the supreme of all beings, is named the sole refuge for immeasurable beings across immeasurable world-systems, due to his unsurpassed perfection of practice dedicated to providing complete welfare and happiness preceded by the removal of all harm, his supreme beneficence to gods and humans, and his endowment with the special qualities of immeasurable, incomparable, and great power. This is the meaning.

Nipphannanāthasaddo pana yācane, upatāpe, issariye, āsīse cāti catūsvatthesu vattati. Tattha yācane nāthati yācatīti nātho, buddho. Nāthadhātu a. So pana veneyyasatte attano hitakaraṇe yācitvāpi niyojetīti attho. Atha vā bhagavā sādhu bhikkhave bhikkhu kālena kālaṃ attasampattiṃ paccavekkheyyātiādinā sattānaṃ taṃ taṃ hitapaṭipattiṃ yācitvāpi karuṇāya samussāhito te tattha niyojeti. Tasmā nātho nāmāti attho.
