Upatāpe nāthati veneyyagate kilese upatāpetīti nātho, buddho. Dhammadesanāya veneyyasantāne kilese viddhaṃsāpetīti attho. Issariye nāthati issariyati satteti nātho. Paramena pana [M 0.0066] cittissariyena samannāgato bhagavā sabbasatte dhammena isati abhibhavatīti attho. Āsīse pana nāthati āsīsatīti nātho. Veneyyānaṃ hitasukhaṃ mettāya navasena patthetīti attho. Tilokānaṃ nātho tilokanātho, buddho. Taṃ tilokanāthaṃ.

The derived word 'nātha', however, is used in four senses: in requesting, in tormenting, in sovereignty, and in blessing. In requesting, 'nātha' means one who requests—thus, the Buddha. The root 'nāth' is used in the sense of requesting. For he, indeed, after requesting teachable beings, employs them in doing what is beneficial to themselves. Alternatively, the Blessed One, saying, 'Monks, a monk should from time to time reflect on his own attainment,' and so forth, urged by compassion, engages beings in that beneficial practice after having requested it of them. Therefore, he is called 'nātha.' In tormenting, 'nātha' means one who torments the defilements in teachable beings—thus, the Buddha. Through teaching the Dhamma, he destroys the defilements in the mental continuum of the teachable. In sovereignty, 'nātha' means one who rules. The Blessed One, endowed with supreme mastery of mind, rules over and surpasses all beings through the Dhamma. In blessing, 'nātha' means one who blesses. With loving-kindness, he constantly desires the welfare and happiness of teachable beings. The Lord of the Three Worlds is the Buddha. To him, the Lord of the Three Worlds.

Susamāhitanti lābhālābhādilokadhammehi acala mānattā sundarasamādhivantaṃ. Saṃsamaṃ ādhiyati ekārammaṇe sampayuttadhamme ṭhapeti etenāti samādhi. Saṃpubba dhā dhātu i. Sundaro pasattho vā samādhi susamādhi. Taṃ assa atthīti susamāhito, buddho. Assathyatthe to. Pabbatotiādīsu viya. Dhassa ho. Catūhi disāhi āgatehi vātehi acalamāno mahāmerupabbato viya bhagavā lābhālābhādilokadhammehi ca micchāvāda vātehi ca acalamānena samādhinā samannāgatoti attho. Taṃ susamāhitaṃ.

Susamāhita (well-composed) means possessing beautiful concentration, being unshaken by the worldly conditions of gain and loss, and so forth. Concentration (samādhi) is so called because by it, associated mental states are well placed and established on a single object. It is derived from the root 'dhā' (to place) preceded by 'saṃ' and 'ā'. Beautiful or praiseworthy concentration is 'susamādhi'. He possesses that concentration—hence, 'susamāhita', the Buddha. The suffix 'to' is added in the sense of 'possessing,' as in words like 'pabbato' (mountain). The 'dh' becomes 'h'. Like the great Mount Meru, unshaken by winds coming from the four directions, so too is the Blessed One endowed with concentration that is unshaken by worldly conditions such as gain and loss or by the winds of wrong views—this is the meaning. To him, the well-composed.

Hitanti manussadevabrahmasaṅkhātānaṃ sabbasattānaṃ payojana dhārentaṃ. Kāraṇānurūpaṃ hinoti pavattatīti hitaṃ, payojanaṃ. Hidhātu gatiyaṃ ta. Taṃ dhāretīti hito, buddho. Kitanta samāsoyaṃ. Hitadharanti vattabbe chandānurakkhaṇatthāya uttara padalopena hitanti vattabbaṃ. Yathā samajjanī padīpoti. Atha vā dukkhaṃ hiṃsatīti hitaṃ. Hiṃsadhātu hiṃsāyaṃ tapaccayo. Yathā ca byādhiyā osamaṃ rogīnaṃ hitanti vuccati, evaṃ dukkhahananato hitaṃ nāma hoti. Sukhaṃ vidadhātīti vā hitaṃ. Dhādhātu dhāraṇe ta. Yathā ca rudhiramaṃsādi dhātu vaḍḍhanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ kissānaṃ hitanti vuccati, evaṃ sukhavahanato hitanti vuccati. Payojanaṃ taṃ dhāretīti hito, buddho. So pana dhammadesanāya veneyyajanānaṃ dukkhāpanayanampi ñāṇaparipācanampi katvā lokiyalokuttarahitasukhaṃ dhāretīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ hitaṃ.

'Hita' means bearing the benefit for all beings, enumerated as humans, devas, and brahmas. It is called 'hita' (benefit) because it proceeds ('hinoti') in accordance with the cause. The root 'hi' is in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix 'ta'. Because he bears that benefit, the Buddha is called 'hito'. This is a compound ending in a primary suffix. Though it should be 'hitadhara' (bearer of benefit), for the sake of preserving the meter, it is said as 'hita' by elision of the final member, just as 'samajjanī padīpo' becomes 'padīpo'. Alternatively, it is called 'hita' because it injures ('hiṃsati') suffering. The root 'hiṃs' is in the sense of 'to injure', with the suffix 'ta'. Just as medicine that alleviates illness is called 'hita' (beneficial) for the sick, so too is the destruction of suffering called 'hita'. Or, it is called 'hita' because it bestows ('vidadhāti') happiness. The root 'dhā' is in the sense of 'to bear', with the suffix 'ta'. Just as an elixir that increases bodily elements like blood and flesh is called 'hita' for the weak, so too is the bringing of happiness called 'hita'. The Buddha is called 'hito' because he bears this benefit. Through his teaching, he removes the suffering of those ready to be trained and brings their knowledge to maturity, thus bearing worldly and transcendent benefit and happiness—this is what is said. To him, the beneficial one.

Samantacakkhunti [M 0.0067] ettha cakkhu nāma buddhacakkhu, dhammacakkhu, ñāṇa cakkhu, samantacakkhu, dibbacakkhūti pañcavidhaṃ hoti. Tattha addasaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhave buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokentoti idaṃ buddhacakkhu nāma. Virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhunti idaṃ heṭṭhimamaggatta yasaṅkhātaṃ dhammacakkhu nāma. Cakkhuṃ udapādīti idaṃ ñāṇacakkhu nāma. Samantacakkhu vuccati sabbaññutañāṇanti idaṃ samantacakkhu nāma. Addasaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhave dibbena cakkhunā visuddhenāti idaṃ dibbacakkhu nāma. Idha pana samantacakkhu adhippetaṃ. Parisamantato sabbañeyyadhammaṃ passantaṃ sabbaññutañāṇavantanti attho. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho. Samantato sabbañeyyadhammaṃ cakkhati passatīti samantacakkhu, sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Cakkhadhātu u. Tena vuttaṃ mahāniddesapāḷiyaṃ “samantacakkhu vuccati sabbaññutañāṇa”nti. Samantacakkhu assa atthīti samantacakkhu, buddho. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāmagge –

Here, the eye (cakkhu) is of five kinds: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the wisdom-eye, the all-around eye, and the divine eye. Among these, 'I, monks, surveying the world, saw with the Buddha-eye'—this is called the Buddha-eye. 'The dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye'—this refers to the Dhamma-eye, designated as the three lower paths. 'The eye arose'—this is called the wisdom-eye. 'The all-around eye is called the knowledge of omniscience'—this is the all-around eye. 'I, monks, saw with the divine eye, purified'—this is called the divine eye. Here, however, the all-around eye is intended. It means one who sees all knowable phenomena from all around, possessing the knowledge of omniscience. This is the meaning of the word here: 'It sees (cakkhati) all knowable phenomena from all around'—thus, the all-around eye is the knowledge of omniscience. The root is 'cakkh', with the suffix 'u'. Therefore, it is said in the Mahāniddesa: 'The all-around eye is called the knowledge of omniscience.' He possesses the all-around eye—thus, he is the All-Around-Eyed One, the Buddha. For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga—

“Na tassa addiṭṭhamidhatthi kiñci,

Atho aviññātamajānitabbaṃ;

Sabbaṃ abhiññāsi yadatthi neyyaṃ,

Tathāgato tena samantacakkhū”ti.

For him, there is nothing here unseen, nor anything uncognized or unknowable; he has directly known all that is to be known, therefore the Tathāgata is the All-Seeing One.

Tassattho. Tassa tathāgatassa addiṭṭhaṃ apassantaṃ kiñci dhammajātaṃ idhaloke na atthi. Atho aviññātaṃ aviditaṃ apākaṭaṃ vā ajānitabbaṃ dhammajātaṃ na atthi. Neyyaṃ ñātabbaṃ yaṃ dhammajātaṃ atthi. Sabbaṃ taṃ dhammajātaṃ tathāgato abhiññāsi paṭivijjhi. Tena tasmā tathāgato samantacakkhu nāmāti. Taṃ samantacakkhuṃ.

This is its meaning: For that Tathāgata, there is no class of phenomena in this world that is unseen or unperceived. Furthermore, there is no class of phenomena that is uncognized, unknown, unmanifest, or unknowable. Whatever class of phenomena there is to be known, all that the Tathāgata has directly known and penetrated. For that reason, the Tathāgata is called the All-Seeing One. To him, the All-Seeing One.

Paṇamāmi taṃmitanti ettha paṇamāmi taṃ amitanti padacchedo. Amitaṃ taṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ paṇamāmīti sambandho. Tattha amitanti aparimeyyaṃ ñāṇena aparicchinnaṃ vā, sīlasamādhi paññādiguṇavantaṃ. Amitabbaṃ ñāṇena aparicchinditabbanti vā amitaṃ, sīlādiguṇaṃ. Napubba mādhātu parimāṇe ta. Taṃ assa atthīti [M 0.0068] amito, buddho. Yathā hi mahāsamudde na sukaraṃ udakassa pamāṇaṃ gaṇetuṃ ettakāni udakāḷhakānīti vā, ettakāni udakāḷhakasatānīti vā, ettakāni udakāḷhakasahassānīti vā, ettakāni udakāḷhakasatasahassānīti vāti. Atha kho asaṅkhyeyyo appameyyo mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati, evameva buddhassa na sukaraṃ sīlādiguṇassa pamāṇaṃ gaṇetuṃ ettakaṃ sīlaguṇaṃ, ettako samādhiguṇo, ettakā paññāguṇātiādināti. Atha kho asaṅkhyeyyo appameyyo mahāguṇakkhandhotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tenavuttaṃ apadānapāḷiyaṃ –

Here, in 'paṇamāmi taṃmitaṃ', the word division is 'paṇamāmi taṃ amitaṃ.' The connection is: 'I bow to that immeasurable Buddha.' Therein, 'amita' (immeasurable) means boundless or not delimited by knowledge, endowed with virtues such as morality, concentration, and wisdom. Or, 'amita' means that which is not to be measured, not to be delimited by knowledge—the virtues of morality and so on. It is derived from the root 'mā' (to measure), preceded by 'na' (not), with the suffix 'ta'. He who possesses this is 'amita', the Buddha. Just as in the great ocean, it is not easy to measure the quantity of water, saying, 'This many measures of water,' or 'This many hundreds of measures of water,' or 'This many thousands of measures of water,' or 'This many hundreds of thousands of measures of water.' Instead, it is reckoned as an innumerable, immeasurable, great mass of water. In the same way, it is not easy to measure the virtues of the Buddha, saying, 'This much is the virtue of morality,' 'This much is the virtue of concentration,' 'This much is the virtue of wisdom,' and so on. Instead, it is reckoned as an innumerable, immeasurable, great mass of virtues. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatāna”nti ca.

Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon, speaking of nothing else, that eon, in its long duration, might be exhausted, but the praise of the Tathāgatas would not be exhausted.

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāmasahassato”ti ca.

Countless are the names of the Great Sage, according to his virtues; a name should be designated by a virtue, even more so than a thousand names.

Tena buddhaṃ amitanti thometīti.

Thus he praises the Buddha as 'immeasurable'.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Dayālayaṃ mahākaruṇāya mettāya ādhāraṃ. Sabbadhi sabbasmiṃ attabhāve, dukkaraṃ dukkhena karitabbaṃ pañcamahāpariccāgādikammaṃ karaṃ karontaṃ, bhavaṇṇavātikkamaṃ tibhavasaṅkhātasamuddato atikkantaṃ, aggataṃ sabbasattānaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ, gataṃ pattaṃ, tilokanāthaṃ kāmarūpa arūpasaṅkhātassa tilokassa paṭisaraṇaṃ, susamāhitaṃ sundara samādhivantaṃ, hitaṃ sabbasattānaṃ lokiyalokuttarasaṅkhātaṃ atthadhāraṇaṃ, samantacakkhuṃ parisamantato sabbañeyyadhammaṃ passantaṃ sabbaññutañāṇavantaṃ, amitaṃ aparimeyyaṃ sīlādiguṇavantaṃ, taṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ paṇamāmi vandāmīti.

Herein is the concise explanation. `Dayālayaṃ`: the foundation of great compassion and loving-kindness. `Sabbadhi`: in every existence. `Dukkaraṃ karaṃ`: performing a deed difficult to do, such as the five great renunciations. `Bhavaṇṇavātikkamaṃ`: having crossed over from the ocean known as the triple existence. `Aggataṃ gataṃ`: having attained the foremost state among all beings. `Tilokanāthaṃ`: a refuge for the three worlds, designated as the world of desire, the world of form, and the formless world. `Susamāhitaṃ`: well-composed, endowed with beautiful concentration. `Hitaṃ`: bearing the welfare for all beings, designated as worldly and supramundane. `Samantacakkhuṃ`: seeing all knowable phenomena all around, endowed with the knowledge of omniscience. `Amitaṃ`: immeasurable, endowed with boundless virtues such as morality. To that Buddha I bow down, I pay homage.

Aṭṭhamavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the eighth verse of veneration is completed.

9.

9.

Tahiṃ [M 0.0069] tahiṃ pāramisañcayaṃ cayaṃ,

Gataṃ gataṃ sabbhi sukhappadaṃ padaṃ;

Narānarānaṃ sukhasambhavaṃ bhavaṃ,

Namānamānaṃ jinapuṅgavaṃ gavaṃ.

Him who, here and there, accumulated the collection of perfections; who attained the blissful state, a state attained by the good; who is the source of happiness for humans and non-humans, the very being; that Bull among Conquerors, that Bull, who is constantly venerated.

9. Evaṃ aṭṭhamagāthāya buddhaṃ vanditvā idāni pāramisañcayaṃ cayantyādīhi pañcahi guṇehi thomitvā vanditukāmo tahiṃ tahiṃ pāramisañcayaṃcayantyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana jatajara gaṇehi yuttattā dvādasakkharehi lakkhitā sabbapādādyantayamakā vaṃsaṭṭhagāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “vadanti vaṃsaṭṭhamidaṃ jatā jarā”ti. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

9. Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the eighth verse, now wishing to praise and pay homage by extolling him with five qualities beginning with 'accumulating the collection of perfections,' he speaks the verse beginning with 'tahiṃ tahiṃ pāramisañcayaṃ cayant...'. This should be understood as a Vaṃsaṭṭha verse, marked by twelve syllables due to its connection with the ja-ta-ja-ra feet, and having repetition (yamaka) at the beginning and end of all its lines. For it is said in the Vuttodaya: 'They call this Vaṃsaṭṭha, with ja-ta ja-ra.' Its meaning has already been explained below.

Tattha tahiṃ tahinti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave attabhāve vā, buddhavaraṃ paṇidhānato paṭṭhāya tesu tesu bhavesu attabhāvesu vāti attho. Pāramisañcayanti dānādipā ramīnaṃ samūhaṃ. Ettha ca pāramī nāma dānasīlanekkhammapaññā vīriya khantisaccaadhiṭṭhānamettāupekkhāvasena dasavidhā hoti. Vuttañca buddhavaṃse –

Therein, 'tahiṃ tahiṃ' means in this and that existence or individual life; that is, in those various existences or individual lives from the time of making the aspiration for supreme Buddhahood. 'Pāramisañcayaṃ' means the collection of perfections such as generosity. Here, the perfections are tenfold by way of generosity, morality, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity. And it is said in the Buddhavaṃsa:

“Dānaṃ sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññā vīriyena pañcamaṃ;

Khantisaccamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettupekkhāti te dasā”ti.

“Generosity, virtue, and renunciation, wisdom and energy as the fifth; Patience, truthfulness, resolution, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten.”

Ayaṃ pana pāramīsaddassa vacanattho. Dānasīlādiguṇa visesayogena sattuttamatāya mahābodhisatto paramo. Tassa ayaṃ bhāvo kammanti vā pāramī, dānādi kriyāva labbhati. Santakabhāvakammataddhite ṇapaccayo. Itthiliṅgajotaka īpaccayo ca. Atha vā dānādīni pūretīti paramo. Dānādiguṇānaṃ pūrako pālako ca bodhisatto. Pūradhātu amapaccayo. Pare satte mavati attani bandhati guṇavisesayogenāti vā paramo, bodhisatto. Parasaddūpapada mudhātu bandhane kvi. Paraṃ atirekaṃ majjati kilesamalatoti vā paramo. Parasaddūpa pada [M 0.0070] majjadhātu saṃsuddhiyaṃ kvi. Parasaddo atirekattho. Paraṃ seṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ visesena mayati gacchatīti vā paramo. Parasaddūpapada mayadhātu gatiyaṃ kvi. Dhātvantalopo. Para saddo seṭṭhattho. Paraṃ lokaṃ pamāṇabhūtena ñāṇa visesena idhalokamiva munāti paricchindatīti vā paramo. Parasaddūpa pada munadhātu paricchindane kvi. Paraṃ ati viya sīlādiguṇagaṇaṃ attano santāne minoti pakkhipatīti vā paramo. Parasaddūpapada midhātu pakkhipane kvi. Parasaddo atirekavācako. Paraṃ attabhūtadhammakāyato aññaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ vā tadanatthakaraṃ kilesacoragaṇaṃ mināti hiṃsatīti vā paramo, mahābodhisatto. Parasaddūpapada midhātu hiṃsāyaṃ kvi. Parasaddo aññavācako, paṭipakkhavācako vā. Paramassa ayantiādinā vuttanayena pāramīti. Api ca pāre nibbāne majjati sujjhatīti pāramī, mahābodhi satto. Suddhakattusādhanoyaṃ. Pārasaddūpapada majadhātu saṃsuddhiyaṃ kvi. Ī ca. Pāre nibbāne satte majjati sodhetīti vā pāramī, hetukattusādhanoyaṃ.

This, however, is the verbal meaning of the word 'pāramī'. Through connection with the excellence of qualities such as generosity and morality, the Great Bodhisatta is supreme (`paramo`) due to his preeminence among beings. His state or action is called 'pāramī'; it is obtained through actions such as giving. The suffix `ṇa` is used in the taddhita sense of 'state' or 'action', and the suffix `ī` indicates the feminine gender. Alternatively, `parama` is one who fulfills (`pūreti`) generosity and other virtues; the Bodhisatta is the fulfiller and protector of virtues like generosity. From the root `pūr` with the suffix `ama`. Or, `parama` is the Bodhisatta, who binds (`mavati`) other (`pare`) beings to himself through the excellence of his virtues. From the root `mu` (to bind) with the prefix `para-` and the suffix `kvi`. Or, `parama` is one who exceedingly (`paraṃ`) cleanses (`majjati`) the stain of defilements. From the root `majj` (to be pure) with the prefix `para-` (meaning 'exceedingly') and the suffix `kvi`. Or, `parama` is one who goes (`mayati`) specifically to the supreme (`paraṃ`) Nibbāna. From the root `ma` (to go) with the prefix `para-` (meaning 'supreme') and the suffix `kvi`, with elision of the final consonant of the root. Or, `parama` is one who discerns (`munāti`) the other (`paraṃ`) world with special knowledge as if it were this world. From the root `mun` (to discern) with the prefix `para-` and the suffix `kvi`. Or, `parama` is one who places (`minoti`) an exceeding (`paraṃ`) collection of virtues like morality into his own continuum. From the root `mi` (to place) with the prefix `para-` (meaning 'exceeding') and the suffix `kvi`. Or, `parama` is the Great Bodhisatta, who destroys (`mināti`) the other (`paraṃ`) party, the opposing host of thieving defilements that cause harm to his essential Dhamma-body. From the root `mi` (to harm) with the prefix `para-` (meaning 'other' or 'opposing') and the suffix `kvi`. `Pāramī` is also derived as 'that which belongs to the supreme' (`paramassa ayaṃ`). Moreover, `pāramī` can mean the Great Bodhisatta, as in 'he is purified (`majjati`) on the further shore (`pāre`), Nibbāna'. This is a derivation where the agent is the subject. Or, 'he purifies (`majjati`) beings on the further shore, Nibbāna'. This is a derivation where the verb is transitive.

Pārenibbāne satte mavati bandhati yojetīti vā pāramī. Pāraṃ nibbānaṃ mayati gacchati satte ca māyeti gameti vā pāramī. Pāraṃ nibbānaṃ yāthāvato munāti paricchindatīti vā pāramī. Pāre nibbāne satte minoti pakkhipatīti vā pāramī. Midhātu pakkhipane ī. Pāre nibbāne sattānaṃ mināti hiṃsatīti vā pāramī, mahābodhisatto. Tassa ayaṃ bhāvo kammanti dānādikriyā pāramīti. Iminā vuttanayena pāramīsaddassa vacanattho veditabbo. Kiñcāpi pana pāramīsaddassa nibbacanaṃ saṅkhepena vuttaṃ. Sotūnaṃ pana niruttinayakosallatthaṃ vitthārena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Or, `pāramī` is that which binds or yokes beings to the further shore, Nibbāna. Or, `pāramī` is that which goes to the further shore, Nibbāna, and causes beings to go there. Or, `pāramī` is that which truly discerns the further shore, Nibbāna. Or, `pāramī` is that which places beings on the further shore, Nibbāna. The root is `mi` (to place), with the suffix `ī`. Or, `pāramī` is the Great Bodhisatta, who destroys the hindrances of beings on the further shore, Nibbāna. His state or action—the deeds of giving and so on—is `pāramī`. In this way, the verbal meaning of the word `pāramī` should be understood. And although the etymology of the word `pāramī` has been stated concisely, it should be understood that it has been explained in detail for the sake of the listeners' skill in the method of etymology.

Sā pana dasapāramī, dasaupapāramī, dasaparamatthapāramī cāti tividhā hoti. Tattha saviññāṇāviññāṇakaṃ dhanaṃ pariccāgaṃ katvā [M 0.0071] pūritā bodhisambhārā dasapāramiyo nāma. Hattha pāda kaṇṇa nāsādiaṅgapaccaṅgapariccāgaṃ katvā pūritā bodhisambhārā dasaupapāramiyo nāma. Jīvitindriyapariccāgaṃ katvā pūritā bodhisambhārā dasa paramatthapāramiyo nāmāti. Dānādipāramīnaṃ pana attho cariyapiṭakaaṭṭhakathādīsu gahetabbo. Avayavaṃ saṅgahavasena cayati gacchati pavattatīti sañcayo, saṃpubba cidhātu gatiyaṃ ṇa. Sañcinoti avayavanti vā sañcayo, samūho. Pāramīnaṃ sañcayo samūhoti pāramisañcayo, taṃ pāramisañcayaṃ. Taṃ pana cayanti etassa kammaṃ. Cayanti upacitaṃ, parisambhūtanti attho. Cayati upacinātīti cayo, ciyittha upaciyitthāti vā cayo, buddho. Cidhātu upacaye ṇa. Taṃ cayaṃ. Sabbhigatanti sambandho.

These perfections are threefold: the ten pāramī, the ten upapāramī, and the ten paramatthapāramī. Herein, the requisites for enlightenment fulfilled by giving up wealth, both animate and inanimate, are called the ten pāramī. The requisites for enlightenment fulfilled by giving up major and minor limbs such as hands, feet, ears, and nose, are called the ten upapāramī. The requisites for enlightenment fulfilled by giving up the life faculty are called the ten paramatthapāramī. The meaning of the perfections beginning with generosity should be understood from the commentary to the Cariyāpiṭaka and other texts. `Sañcaya` (accumulation) is that which accumulates, goes, or proceeds by way of collecting components; it is from the root `ci` (to go) with the prefix `saṃ-` and the suffix `ṇa`. Or, `sañcaya` is that which collects components; a collection. The accumulation of perfections is `pāramisañcayo`; hence `pāramisañcayaṃ`. This is the object of `cayanti`. `Cayanti` means 'accumulated', 'fully produced'. `Cayo` is one who accumulates; or `cayo` is that which was accumulated, meaning the Buddha. From the root `ci` (to accumulate) with the suffix `ṇa`. That is `cayaṃ`. The connection is with `sabbhigataṃ` (attained by the good).

Tattha sabbhīti santehi sappurisehi. Rāgādikilese samenti upasamentīti santā, sappurisā. Samudhātu upasameta, antapaccayo vā. Santehīti vattabbe smāhismiṃnaṃ mhā bhimhivāti suttena hivibhattiyā bhikāraṃ santasaddassa so bhe bo canteti suttena bhakāre pare santasaddassa sakāraṃ katvā ante ca bakārāgamaṃ katvā sabbhīti vuttaṃ. Tehi sabbhi. Taṃ pana gatanti etassa avuttakattā. Gatanti upagamitabbaṃ. Tañhi devamanussehi gamiyati upagamiyati upasaṅkamiyatīti gatoti vuccati. Taṃ buddhaṃ atthakāmehi sappurisehi devamanussehi sīlādianantaguṇikattā saraṇanti abhimānā payirupāsitabboti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ gataṃ. Sukhappadaṃ padaṃ gatanti sambandho. Tattha sukhappadanti accantasukhassa patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ. Sukhanaṃ sukhaṃ, tassa pajjati tiṭṭhati etthāti sukhappadaṃ, nibbānaṃ. Padanti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi buddhādīhi ariyehi pajjiyati gamiyatīti padanti vuccati. Gatanti agaminti gato, buddho. Dukkhādiasammissassa ekantasukhassa patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena apāpuṇinti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ gataṃ.

Therein, `sabbhīti` means 'by the good,' by the virtuous. Those who pacify or subdue defilements such as greed are called `santā`, virtuous people. The root `sam` is in the sense of pacifying, or it is the suffix `anta`. When `santehi` should be said, the form `sabbhi` is stated, derived by grammatical rules which change the `hi` ending to `bhi` and transform `santa` before it. By them, the good. As for `gataṃ`, this is because it is unstated. `Gataṃ` means 'that which is to be approached.' For it is gone to, approached, and resorted to by gods and humans—thus it is called `gata`. This means it is said that the Buddha, on account of his boundless virtues such as morality, is to be attended upon with the conviction that he is a refuge by virtuous ones, gods, and humans who desire what is beneficial. That is `gataṃ`. The connection is: `sukhappadaṃ padaṃ gataṃ` (gone to the state that gives happiness). Therein, `sukhappadaṃ` means the foundation of ultimate bliss. Happiness is `sukha`; that wherein it is reached or established is `sukhappadaṃ`, Nibbāna. `Pada` means Nibbāna. For it is reached or gone to by the noble ones, such as the Buddhas; thus, it is called `pada`. `Gataṃ` means 'has gone,' hence `gato`, the Buddha. This means it is said that he has attained, by way of making it an object, Nibbāna, which is the foundation of exclusive happiness, unmixed with suffering and so on. That is `gataṃ`.

Narānarānanti [M 0.0072] naraanarānanti padacchedo. Manussadevānanti attho. Pabbajjādiseṭṭhabhāvaṃ narati netīti naro, narīyati sakena kammena niyatīti vā naro, manusso, satto vā. Naradhātu nayane a. Na naro anaro, devo. Naro ca anaro ca narānaro, tesaṃ narānarānaṃ. Taṃ pana sukhasambhavanti pade sambandho.

The word division of `narānarānaṃ` is `nara-anarānaṃ`. The meaning is 'of humans and devas.' One who leads to the supreme state of renunciation and so on is a `naro`; or one who is led by one's own kamma is a `naro`—a human, or a being. The root `nara` is in the sense of leading, with the `a` suffix. Not a `naro` is an `anaro`, a deva. A `naro` and an `anaro` are `narānaro`; of them, `narānarānaṃ`. This, however, is connected with the word `sukhasambhavaṃ`.

Sukhasambhavanti lokiyalokuttarasukhassa kāraṇaṃ. Tividhasukhassa labhanakāraṇabhūtaṃ puññaṃ vā. Sukhayatīti sukhaṃ. Tividhasukhaṃ. Yassa uppajjati, taṃ sukhitaṃ karotīti attho. Atha vā suṭṭhu dukkhaṃ khanatīti sukhaṃ. Supubbakhanudhātu avadhāraṇe a. Sambhavati sukhasaṅkhātaṃ phalaṃ anena puññenāti sambhavaṃ, puññakaraṇaṃ. Saṃpubbabhūdhātu sattāyaṃṇa. Sukhassa sambhavaṃ sukhasambhavaṃ, taṃ pana bhavantipade kammaṃ. Bhavanti nibbattentaṃ. Taṃ sukhasambhavaṃ bhāveti nibbattetīti bhavo, buddho. Taṃ bhavaṃ. So hi mahākaruṇāpubbaṅgamāya dhammadesanāya devamanussānaṃ lokiyalokuttarasukhassa labhanakāraṇabhūtaṃ dānasīlabhāvanāsaṅkhātaṃ puññaṃ kāreti, tasmā bhagavato narānarānaṃ sukhasambhavaṃ bhavanti thometīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

`Sukhasambhavaṃ` means the cause of worldly and supramundane happiness. Or, it is merit which is the cause for obtaining the threefold happiness. It makes happy, thus it is `sukhaṃ`, the threefold happiness. The meaning is that for whomever it arises, it makes that one happy. Alternatively, it thoroughly digs up suffering, thus it is `sukhaṃ`. The root `khan` with the prefix `su` is in the sense of digging out, with the `a` suffix. That by which the fruit called happiness arises from this merit is `sambhavaṃ`, the making of merit. The root `bhū` with the prefix `saṃ` is in the sense of existence, with the `ṇa` suffix. The arising of happiness is `sukhasambhavaṃ`; this, however, is the object of the word `bhavanti`. `Bhavanti` means producing. He who develops or produces that `sukhasambhavaṃ` is `bhavo`, the Buddha. That `bhavaṃ`. For he, through his teaching of the Dhamma preceded by great compassion, causes beings to perform merit—in the form of generosity, virtue, and meditation—which is the cause for humans and devas to obtain worldly and supramundane happiness. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One is praised as 'producing the cause of happiness for humans and non-humans' (`narānarānaṃ sukhasambhavaṃ bhavanti`).

Namānamānanti padassa name anamānanti padacchedo. Nameti ahaṃ namāmīti attho. Ettha ca mivibhattiyā ekārādesoti veditabbo. Anamānanti anamentānaṃ avandantānaṃ anādarānanti attho. Taṃ pana gavantietassa visesanaṃ. Gavanti goṇasadisānaṃ bālānaṃ. Gavanti hi chaṭṭhībahuvacanantanāmapadaṃ. Tato namaṃ patimhālutte ca samāseti sutte samabhiniviṭṭhena caggahaṇena naṃvacanassa aṃ ādesañca goiccetassa okārassa avādesaṃ katvā rūpasiddhi veditabbā. Gacchantīti gāvo, goṇā. Gāvo viyāti gāvo, tesaṃ gavaṃ bālānaṃ. Taṃ pana jinapuṅgavantipade chaṭṭhīkammaṃ. Jinapuṅgavanti jayantapurisuttamaṃ buddhaṃ name namāmīti sambandho. Ettha ca puṅgava saddo [M 0.0073] kammadhārayasamāse seṭṭhatthavācako. Munipuṅgavotiādīsu viya. Vuttañca amarakose –

The word division of `namānamānaṃ` is `name anamānaṃ`. `Name` means 'I bow' (`ahaṃ namāmi`). And here it should be understood that there is a substitution of `e` for the `mi` ending. `Anamānaṃ` means 'of those who do not bow, who do not pay homage, who are disrespectful.' This, however, is an adjective for `gavaṃ`. `Gavaṃ` means 'of fools who are like cattle.' Indeed, `gavaṃ` is a noun in the genitive plural. Then, by the grammatical rule `namaṃ patimhālutte ca samāse`, and by the inclusion of `ca` in that rule, the derivation of the form should be understood by substituting `aṃ` for the ending `naṃ` and substituting `ava` for the `o` of `go`. They go, thus they are `gāvo`, cattle. Like cattle are `gāvo`; of them, `gavaṃ`, of the fools. This, however, is an objective genitive in relation to the word `jinapuṅgavaṃ`. The connection is: `name` (`namāmi`), I bow, to the `jinapuṅgavaṃ`, the conquering, supreme man, the Buddha. Here, the word `puṅgava` in a karmadhāraya compound denotes the meaning of 'foremost,' as in `munipuṅgava` and so on. And it is stated in the Amarakośa:

“Uttarasmiṃ pade byaggha, puṅgavosabhakuñjarā;

Sīhasaddūlanāgādyā, pume seṭṭhatthagocarā”ti.

“In the latter part of a compound, the words ‘byaggha,’ ‘puṅgava,’ ‘usabha,’ ‘kuñjara,’ ‘sīha,’ ‘saddūla,’ ‘nāga,’ and so forth, when in the masculine gender, have the meaning of 'foremost'.”

Tassattho. Kammadhārayasamāse uttarapade vattamānā byagghapuṅgavosabhakuñjarā byagghapuṅgavausabhakuñjarasaddā ca sīha saddūlanāgādyā sīha saddūla nāgāsaddā ca pume seṭṭhattha vācakāti. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho. Go viya buddhaguṇe ajānante anamante aññadiṭṭhike bāle jināti ajinīti vā jino. Pakaṭṭhabhāvaṃ padhānabhāvaṃ vā uddhaṃ gacchatīti puṅgavo. Paupubba gamudhātu gatiyaṃ avapaccayo. Niggahitā gamo. Tassa kavaggantaṃ dhātvantalopañca yadādinā katvā rūpasiddhi veditabbā. Jino ca so puṅgavo cāti jinapuṅgavo, buddho. So pana gunnaṃ viya buddhānaṃ sīlādike appameyyaguṇe ajānantānaṃ anamantānaṃ agāravantānaṃ avandantānaṃ añña diṭṭhigatikānaṃ bālānaṃ asatthena pāramīpuññatejena ajinīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ jinapuṅgavanti.

Its meaning is this: In a karmadhāraya compound, the words `byaggha`, `puṅgava`, `usabha`, `kuñjara`, and the words `sīha`, `saddūla`, `nāga`, and so forth, when occurring in the latter part of the compound, are, in the masculine gender, expressive of the meaning 'foremost.' This is the meaning of the words here. He conquers or has conquered fools who, like cattle, do not know the Buddha's virtues, do not pay homage, and hold other views; thus he is `Jino`. He goes upward to a pre-eminent or principal state, thus he is `puṅgavo`. The root `gamu` with the prefix `pa` is in the sense of going, with the `ava` suffix. A `niggahita` is inserted. The derivation of the form should be understood by making the root end in a guttural and eliding its final consonant, according to the rule beginning `yadādi`. He is both `Jino` and `Puṅgavo`, thus `Jinapuṅgavo`, the Buddha. This means it is said that he, without a weapon, by the power of his perfections and merit, conquered fools who, like cattle, do not know the immeasurable virtues of the Buddhas such as morality, do not pay homage, are disrespectful, do not venerate, and follow other views. That `Jinapuṅgavaṃ`.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Tahiṃ tahiṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave, attabhāve vā, pāramisañcayaṃ dānādipāramīnaṃ samūhaṃ, cayaṃ upacitaṃ parisambhūtaṃ, sabbhi santehi sappurisehi, gataṃ upagamitabbaṃ payirupāsitabbaṃ, sukhappadaṃ accantasukhassa patiṭṭhāna bhūtaṃ, padaṃ nibbānaṃ gataṃ pattaṃ agamiṃ, narānarānaṃ manussadevānaṃ, sukhasambhavaṃ lokiyalokuttarasukhassa kāraṇaṃ tividha sukhassa labhanakāraṇabhūtaṃ puññaṃ vā bhavaṃ nibbattentaṃ, anamānaṃ anamantānaṃ anādarānaṃ avandantānaṃ vā, gavaṃ goṇasadisānaṃ bālānaṃ jinapuṅgavaṃ jayantapurisuttamaṃ buddhaṃ ahaṃ name namāmīti.

Here is the concise syntactical construction. `Tahiṃ tahiṃ`: in this and that existence, or state of being. `Pāramisañcayaṃ`: a collection of perfections such as generosity. `Cayaṃ`: amassed, accumulated. `Sabbhi gataṃ`: by the good, the virtuous, that which is to be approached and attended upon. `Sukhappadaṃ`: the foundation of ultimate happiness. `Padaṃ`: Nibbāna. `Gataṃ`: attained, reached. `Narānarānaṃ`: of humans and devas. `Sukhasambhavaṃ`: the cause of worldly and supramundane happiness. `Bhavaṃ`: producing merit, which is the cause for obtaining the threefold happiness. `Anamānaṃ`: of those who do not pay homage, are disrespectful, or do not venerate. `Gavaṃ`: of fools who are like cattle. `Jinapuṅgavaṃ`: the conquering, supreme man, the Buddha. `Ahaṃ name`: I bow.

Navamavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the ninth verse of homage is concluded.

10.

10.

Maggaṅganāvaṃ [M 0.0074] munidakkhanāviko,

Īhāphiyaṃ ñāṇakarena gāhako;

Āruyha yo tāya bahū bhavaṇṇavā,

Tāresi taṃ buddhamaghappahaṃ name.

I bow to that Buddha, the abandoner of defilements, the sage, the skilled navigator, who, having boarded the boat of the path factors and grasping the oar with the hand of knowledge, ferried many across the ocean of becoming.

10. Evaṃ navamagāthāya buddhaṃ natvā idāni bahū satte tibhavasaṅkhātā saṃsārasamuddato tārentena guṇena ca sattānaṃ dukkhappahānena guṇena ca thomitvā buddhaṃ vanditu kāmo maggaṅganāvantyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana tata jara gaṇehi racitattā dvādasakkharehi yuttā indavaṃsa gāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “sāyindavaṃsā khalu yattha tā jarā”ti.

10. Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the ninth verse, now, desiring to praise and venerate the Buddha by the virtue of his ferrying many beings across the ocean of saṃsāra, known as the three realms, and by the virtue of his abandoning the suffering of beings, he speaks the verse beginning with `Maggaṅganāvaṃ`. This verse, however, being composed with the metrical feet `ta`, `ta`, `ja`, and `ra`, and comprising twelve syllables, should be understood as an Indavaṃsa verse. For it is said in the Vuttodaya: 'That is indeed Indavaṃsā where there are the `ta` feet and `ja`, `ra`.'

Tassattho. Yattha yassaṃ gāthāyaṃ tā tagaṇadvayañca jarā jagaṇa ragaṇā ca ce siyuṃ, sā gāthā khalu ekantaṃ indavaṃsagāthā nāmāti.

Its meaning is this: Wherein, in a verse, there are `tā`—a pair of `ta` feet—and `jarā`—a `ja` foot and a `ra` foot—that verse is indeed certainly named an Indavaṃsa verse.

Tattha yo munidakkhanāvikoti sambandho. Yo buddha saṅkhāto cheko nāvājeṭṭhakoti attho. Tattha munīti ubho loke munāti jānātīti muni, bhagavā. Munadhātu ñāṇe i. Atha vā monaṃ vuccati sabbaññutañāṇaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti muni, bhagavā. Assathyatthe ipaccayo. Vuttañhi ekanipāte vaṇṇapathajātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “munīti monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ. Kāya moneyyādīsu vā aññatarena samannāgatattā puggalo munīti vuccati. So panesa agāriyamuni, anagāriyamuni, sekkhamuni, asekkhamuni, paccekamuni, munimunīti anekavidho. Tattha agāriyamunīti gihi āgataphalo viññātasāsano. Anagāriyamunīti tathārūpova pabbajito. Sekkhamunīti sattasekkhā. Asekkhamunīti khīṇāsavo. Paccekamunīti paccekasambuddho. Munimunīti sammāsambuddho”ti. Idha pana munimuni adhippeto.

Here, the connection is with 'the sage, the skilled navigator'. The meaning is that the Buddha, known as the expert, the chief navigator, is intended. Herein, 'muni' (sage): he is called a sage because he knows (munāti jānāti) both worlds; he is the Blessed One. The root 'mun' is in the sense of knowledge, with the suffix 'i'. Alternatively, 'mona' is said to be omniscient knowledge; because he possesses that, he is called a sage, the Blessed One. The suffix 'i' is in the sense of 'possessing'. For it was said in the commentary on the Vaṇṇapatha Jātaka in the Ekanipāta: “As for ‘muni,’ ‘mona’ is said to be knowledge. Or, a person is called a ‘muni’ because he is endowed with one or another of the forms of sagacity, such as bodily sagacity (kāya moneyya), and so on. But that person is of various kinds: a householder sage (agāriyamuni), a homeless sage (anagāriyamuni), a trainee sage (sekkhamuni), a perfected sage (asekkhamuni), a solitary sage (paccekamuni), and the sage of sages (munimuni). Among these, a householder sage is a layperson who has attained the fruit and understood the teaching. A homeless sage is one who has gone forth, similarly. A trainee sage refers to the seven trainees. A perfected sage is one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavo). A solitary sage is a Paccekabuddha. The sage of sages is the Sammāsambuddha.” Here, however, the sage of sages (munimuni) is meant.

Dakkhoti [M 0.0075] cheko. Samuddataraṇe dakkhati kusalattaṃ gacchatīti dakkho, nāviko. Dakkhadhātu gatiyaṃ a. Atha vā dakkhati kusalakamme aññasmiñca kiccākicce adandhatāya sīghaṃ gacchatīti dakkho, yokoci kusalo puggalo. Dakkhadhātu sīghatthe a. Dakkho viyāti dakkho, buddho. Nītatthena pana buddho sattānaṃ saṃsārasamuddato uddhāraṇassa kāraṇaṃ dakkhati paricchindati ñāṇenāti dakkhoti vuccati. Nāvikoti samuddatīraṃ nāvāya taratīti nāviko, nāvājeṭṭhako. Taratitaddhite ṇiko. Nāviko viyāti nāviko, buddho. Nītatthena pana buddho nibbānaṃ pāraṃ aṭṭhamaggaṅganāvāya taratīti nāvikoti vuccati. Dakkho nāviko dakkhanāviko, muni ca so dakkhanāvikocāti munidakkhanāviko, kammadhārayasamāsoyaṃ. Atha vā dakkhanāviko viya dakkho munīti munidakkhanāviko, buddho. Upamākammadhārayasamāsoyaṃ. Yathā hi samuddataraṇe cheko nāviko manusse samuddapāraṃ neti, evaṃ buddho veneyyasatte nibbānapāraṃ netīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Dakkha' means expert. In crossing the ocean, he is skilled (dakkhati) and attains proficiency (kusalattaṃ gacchati)—thus, 'dakkha,' a navigator. The root 'dakkh' is in the sense of motion, with the suffix 'a'. Alternatively, he is called 'dakkha' because he moves swiftly (sīghaṃ gacchati) without delay in skillful actions and in other matters to be done or not done—any competent person. The root 'dakkh' is in the sense of swiftness, with the suffix 'a'. 'Like a skilled one,' thus 'dakkha,' meaning the Buddha. In its implied sense, however, the Buddha is called 'dakkha' because he discerns (paricchindati) with wisdom the means to raise beings up from the ocean of saṃsāra. 'Nāviko' (navigator): he crosses (tarati) to the ocean shore by boat—thus, 'nāviko,' the chief navigator. The taddhita suffix '-ika' is from 'tarati'. 'Like a navigator,' thus 'nāviko,' meaning the Buddha. In its implied sense, however, the Buddha is called a 'navigator' because he crosses (tarati) to the far shore of Nibbāna by the boat of the eight path factors. 'Dakkho nāviko' (skilled navigator) becomes 'dakkhanāviko.' And since the sage (muni) is that skilled navigator, he is called 'munidakkhanāviko.' This is a kammadhāraya compound. Alternatively, the sage is skilled like a skilled navigator—thus, 'munidakkhanāviko,' meaning the Buddha. This is a kammadhāraya compound based on simile. Just as an expert navigator leads people across the ocean, so too the Buddha leads trainable beings to the far shore of Nibbāna—thus it is said.

Maggaṅganāvaṃ āruyhāti sambandho. Maggaṅganāvanti aṭṭhamaggaṅga saṅkhātaṃ nāvaṃ. Āruyhāti ārohitvāti attho. Kilese mārento ārammaṇakaraṇavasena nibbānaṃ gacchatīti maggo. Mārasaddūpapada gamudhātu kvi. Mārenta goti vattabbe niruttinayena maggoti vuttaṃ. Atha vā nibbānaṃ maggati gavesatīti maggo. Maggadhātu gavesane a. Nibbānatthikehi maggiyati gavesiyatīti vā maggo. Ekantato jāti jarābyādhimaraṇadukkhādīhi pīḷitehi sattehi dukkhakkhayaṃ nibbānaṃ pāpuṇatthāya maggitabbo gavesitabboti maggo, catumaggo. Vuttañhi “maggoti kenaṭṭhena nibbānaṃ magganaṭṭhena nibbānatthikehi magganīyaṭṭhena cā”ti. Aṅgati gacchati phalanibbānaṃ etenāti aṅgaṃ. Agidhātu gamane a. Maggassa aṅgaṃ kāraṇanti maggaṅgaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappa sammāvācā sammākammanta sammāājīva sammāvāyāma [M 0.0076] sammāsati sammāsamādhivasena aṭṭhamaggaṅgaṃ labbhati. Nuyati thavīyatīti nāvā. Nudhātu thaviyaṃ avo. Atha vā orato pāraṃ netīti nāvā, bhāraṃ nayanti etāyāti vā nāvā. Nidhātu nayane avo. Maggaṅgasaṅkhātā nāvā maggaṅganāvā. Atha vā nāvā viya maggaṅganti maggaṅga nāvā. Yathā hi nāvā attani āruḷhe manusse samudda nadīpāraṃ neti, evaṃ aṭṭhamaggaṅgadhammā attānaṃ paṭipajjante nibbāna pāraṃ nentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ maggaṅganāvaṃ.

The connection is with 'having boarded the boat of the path factors'. 'Maggaṅganāvaṃ' refers to the boat known as the eight path factors. 'Āruyha' means 'having boarded'. The 'path' (magga) is so called because, by destroying defilements and making Nibbāna its object, it goes to Nibbāna. It is formed from the root 'gam' with the word 'māra' (killing) as a prefix and the suffix 'kvi'. When 'killing, it goes' (mārenta go) should be said, by linguistic convention it is called 'magga'. Alternatively, the 'path' is that which seeks (maggati) or searches for (gavesati) Nibbāna. The root 'mag' is in the sense of seeking, with the suffix 'a'. Or, it is sought or searched for by those intent on Nibbāna—thus it is called 'magga'. The 'path,' the fourfold path, is to be sought and searched for by beings utterly afflicted by the sufferings of birth, aging, sickness, and death, in order to reach the cessation of suffering, Nibbāna. As it is said: “In what sense is it a path? In the sense of seeking Nibbāna, and in the sense that it is to be sought by those intent on Nibbāna.” 'Aṅga' (factor) is that by which one goes (aṅgati) to the fruit, Nibbāna. The root 'ag' is in the sense of going, with the suffix 'a'. A 'path factor' (maggaṅga) is a cause of the path. The eight path factors are obtained: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. 'Nāvā' (boat) is so called because it is praised (nuyati) or made firm (thavīyati). The root 'nu' is in the sense of praising, with the suffix 'avo'. Alternatively, a 'nāvā' is that which leads (neti) from this shore to the far shore, or that by which a burden is carried (nayanti). The root 'nī' is in the sense of carrying, with the suffix 'avo'. The boat known as the path factors is 'maggaṅganāvā'. Alternatively, the path factors are like a boat—hence 'maggaṅganāvā'. Just as a boat carries the people who have boarded it across an ocean or river to the far shore, so too do the dhammas of the eight path factors carry those who practice them to the far shore of Nibbāna—thus it is said. That is the boat of the path factors.

Īhāphiyanti vīriyasaṅkhātaṃ dabbisārakaṃ. Vuttañhi suttani pātaaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “phiyenāti dabbisārakenā”ti. Īhati ārabbhatīti īhā. Īhati vāyamati cetayati etenāti vā īhā, vīriyaṃ. Saddanītiyaṃ pana “īha cetāya”nti vuttaṃ. Phāti vaḍḍheti udakaṃ etenāti phiyaṃ. Phādhātu vaḍḍhiyaṃ iyo. Phāti ghaṭṭeti udakanti vā phiyaṃ. Atha vā phāyati gacchati nāvaṃ etenāti phiyaṃ. Dabbisārakaṃ. Phāyi dhātu gatiyaṃ a. Ākārassa i. Īhāsaṅkhātaṃ phiyanti īhāphiyaṃ. Phiyaṃ viya īhāti īhāphiyaṃ. Yathā hi phiyena nāvā icchitaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, evaṃ īhāsaṅkhātena vīriyena taṃ taṃ kiccaṃ sādheti, icchitaṃ nibbānaṭṭhānaṃ gacchatīti adhippāyo. Taṃ pana gāhakoti pade kammaṃ. Ñāṇakarenāti sabbaññutañāṇasaṅkhātena hatthena. Sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ jānātīti ñāṇaṃ, sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Taṃ taṃ kammaṃ karotīti karo, hattho. Ñāṇasaṅkhāto karo ñāṇa karo, karaṃ viya ñāṇanti vā ñāṇakaro, tena ñāṇakarena. Gāhakoti daḷhagaṇhamāno hutvā. Tāyāti aṭṭhamaggaṅga saṅkhātāya tāya nāvāya, bahūti aneke veneyyasatte. Bhavaṇṇavāti tibhavasaṅkhātā saṃsāravaṭṭasaṅkhātā vā mahāsamuddato. Tassa pana vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

‘Īhāphiyaṃ’ means the strong oar (dabbisāraka) known as vigor. As it is said in the Suttanipāta commentary: “By ‘phiya’ is meant by the strong oar.” One undertakes (īhati) or begins (ārabbhati), thus it is called effort (īhā). Or, one strives, exerts, or intends by means of this—thus, effort (īhā), which is vigor. In the Saddanīti, it is said: “īha is in the sense of intention.” By this, it makes the water swell (phāti vaḍḍheti), thus it is a ‘phiya’. The root `phā` is in the sense of growth, with the suffix `iyo`. Or, it strikes the water, thus it is a ‘phiya’. Alternatively, by this the boat moves (phāyati gacchati), thus it is a ‘phiya,’ a strong oar. The root is `phāyi` in the sense of movement, with the suffix `a`; the long `ā` becomes `i`. The oar known as effort is ‘īhāphiyaṃ’. Effort is like an oar, thus ‘īhāphiyaṃ’. Just as a boat reaches its desired destination by means of an oar, so too, by means of effort known as vigor, one accomplishes various tasks and reaches the desired destination of Nibbāna—this is the meaning. That (Nibbāna) is the object (kamma) in the word ‘gāhako’ (grasper). ‘Ñāṇakarena’ (by the hand of knowledge) means by the hand known as the knowledge of omniscience. It knows all knowable things, thus it is knowledge (ñāṇa), the knowledge of omniscience. It performs various actions, thus it is a ‘kara,’ a hand. The hand known as knowledge is ‘ñāṇakaro,’ or knowledge is like a hand, thus ‘ñāṇakaro’; by that ‘ñāṇakarena’. ‘Gāhako’ means having firmly grasped. ‘Tāya’ means by that boat, the one known as the eight path factors. ‘Bahū’ means many trainable beings. ‘Bhavaṇṇavā’ means from the great ocean known as the three realms of existence or the cycle of saṃsāra. The meaning of this word, however, has already been explained above.

Tāresīti otiṇṇesi, atikkamesīti attho. Buddhanti paṭividdhacatusaccadhammaṃ. Aghappahanti sattānaṃ dukkhappaja hantaṃ[M 0.0077]. Dukkhaviddhaṃsentanti attho. Atha vā aghappahanti sattānaṃ kilesappajahantaṃ. Kilesaviddhaṃsentanti attho. Ettha hi aghasaddo dukkhe kilese ca vattati. Tattha hi dukkhaṃ aghayati dukkhayatīti aghanti ca, aghayati dukkhākārena pavattatīti vā aghanti ca vuccati. Kileso pana aghayanti pāpaṃ karonti sattā etenāti aghoti vuccati. Aghadhātu pāpakaraṇe a. Aghaṃ pajahati viddhaṃsetīti aghappaho, buddho. Aghasaddūpapadapapubbahādhātu cāge. Buddho veneyyasattānaṃ dukkhañca kilesañca dhammadesanāya apanetīti attho. Ettha ca paṭhamavikappe dukkhassa appahātabbadhammattā maggena appahātabbampi phalūpacārena dukkhappajahantanti vuttaṃ. Tanti munidakkhanāvikaṃ ahaṃ name namāmīti sambandhoti.

‘Tāresi’ (he ferried across) means he caused them to land, he caused them to surpass. ‘Buddhaṃ’ means the one who has penetrated the four noble truths. ‘Aghappahaṃ’ means one who abandons the suffering of beings; that is, one who destroys suffering. Alternatively, ‘aghappahaṃ’ means one who abandons the defilements of beings; that is, one who destroys defilements. Here, the word ‘agha’ applies to both suffering and defilements. For suffering is called ‘agha’ because it afflicts (aghayati) or distresses (dukkhayati), or because it proceeds in the manner of suffering. A defilement, however, is called ‘agha’ because beings do evil (pāpaṃ karonti) through it. The root `agha` is in the sense of doing evil, with the suffix `a`. One who abandons and destroys ‘agha’ is ‘aghappaho,’ the Buddha. This is formed from the root `hā` in the sense of abandoning, preceded by the prefix `pa`, with the word `agha` as its prefix. The meaning is that the Buddha removes the suffering and defilements of trainable beings through the teaching of the Dhamma. Here, in the first explanation, although suffering is a phenomenon not to be abandoned by the path, he is called ‘one who abandons suffering’ by way of a figure of speech concerning the fruit. The connection is: ‘Taṃ’ (that) skilled sage-navigator, ‘ahaṃ name’ (I venerate), which means ‘namāmi’ (I venerate).

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Yo munidakkhanāviko yo buddhasaṅkhāto cheko nāvājeṭṭhako, maggaṅganāvaṃ aṭṭhamaggaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ nāvaṃ āruyha ārohitvā īhāphiyaṃ vīriyasaṅkhātaṃ dabbisārakaṃ, ñāṇakarena sabbaññutañāṇasaṅkhātena hatthena, gāhako daḷhaṃ gaṇhamāno hutvā tāya aṭṭhamaggaṅganāvāya, bahū aneke veneyyasatte bhavaṇṇavā tibhavasaṅkhātamahāsamuddato, tāresi otāresi, buddhaṃ paṭividdhacatusaccadhammaṃ aghappahaṃ sattānaṃ dukkhaviddhaṃsentaṃ kilesa viddhaṃsentaṃ vā taṃ munidakkhanāvikaṃ ahaṃ name namāmīti.

Here is the concise application. The one who is the skilled navigator of the sage, who is designated as the Buddha, the skilled chief of navigators, having boarded the ship of the path factors, the ship designated as the Noble Eightfold Path, having become one who firmly grasps with the hand of knowledge—the hand designated as the knowledge of omniscience—the strong oar, the īhāphiya, designated as vigor; by that ship of the Noble Eightfold Path, he caused many countless trainable beings to cross over, to descend from the great ocean of existence, designated as the three realms of existence. That Buddha, who has penetrated the four noble truths, the destroyer of misery, who destroys the suffering of beings or destroys defilements—to that skilled navigator of the sage, I revere and bow down.

Dasamavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the tenth homage verse is completed.

11.

11.

Samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇaṃ,

Varabodhidume catusaccadasaṃ;

Varamiddhigataṃ naradevahitaṃ,

Tibhavūpasamaṃ paṇamāmi jinaṃ.

I bow to the Victor, who has accumulated the thirty perfections, who under the excellent Bodhi tree realized the four noble truths, who has attained excellent psychic power, benefiting gods and humans, and who brings calm to the three realms.

11. Evaṃ [M 0.0078] dasamagāthāya buddhaṃ vanditvā idāni samatiṃ satipāramisambharaṇādīhi pañcahi guṇehi thomitvā jinaṃ vanditukāmo samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇantyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana catūhi sagaṇehi racitattā dvādasakkharehi yuttā toṭakagāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “iha toṭaka mambudhisehi mita”nti. Tassattho. Yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ ambudhisehi catūhi sagaṇehi mitaṃ pamitaṃ racitaṃ lakkhitaṃ vā vuttaṃ idha jagatichande toṭakaṃ nāmāti.

11. Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the tenth verse, now wishing to honor the Victor by extolling five qualities, beginning with "samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇaṃ," he speaks the verse starting with "samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇaṃ." This verse, however, being composed of four 'sa-gaṇas' and endowed with twelve syllables, should be understood as a toṭaka verse. As stated in the Vuttodaya: "Here, a toṭaka is measured by ambudhisehi." Its meaning is: that composition in which each line is measured, composed, or characterized by four 'sa-gaṇas' is called a toṭaka in this Jagati meter.

Tattha pana samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇanti dasapāramiyo, dasa upapāramiyo, dasa paramatthapāramiyo cāti samatiṃsapāramiyo sambhūtaṃ, paripūritanti attho. Tāsaṃ pana viseso pāramisaddassa ca vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Sambharittha paripūrayitthāti sambharaṇo, jino. Saṃpubbabharadhātu pūraṇe yu. Samatiṃsapāramiyo sambharaṇoti samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇo, jino. Dīpaṅkarabuddhassa pādamūle laddhabyākaraṇato paṭṭhāya kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni samatiṃsapāramiyo pūrayitthāti attho. Taṃ samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇaṃ. Varabodhidumeti uttamabodhirukkhamūle. Ettha ca varabodhisaddassa vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Davati gacchati mūlakhandhatacasākha viṭapa pallava phalehi vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷiṃ vepullaṃ rajata suvaṇṇamaṇi santā rucīhi atisobhanaṃ vā pāpuṇātīti dumo, bodhisattassa vijātadivaseyeva bodhisattena saddhiṃ saha jāto satahatthubbedho asatthadumarājā labbhati. Dudhātu gatimhi amo. Apadānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “dunāti kampatīti dumo. Dumati pūreti ākāsatalanti vā dumo”ti vuttaṃ. Varo bodhi varabodhi, varabodhi ca so dumo cāti varabodhidumo, tasmiṃ.

Here, "samatiṃsatipāramisambharaṇaṃ" means the accumulation or fulfillment of the thirty perfections, namely, the ten perfections, the ten higher perfections, and the ten supreme perfections. The distinction among them, and the meaning of the word "pāramī," has already been explained below. "Sambharaṇo" means "he accumulated" or "he fulfilled"—this refers to the Jina. The root "bhar" with the prefix "saṃ" is in the sense of fulfilling, with the suffix "yu." "Samatiṃsapāramiyo sambharaṇo" means "one who accumulated the thirty perfections"—this refers to the Jina. From the time he received the prediction at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand eons, he fulfilled the thirty perfections—this is the meaning. That is the "accumulation of the thirty perfections." "Varabodhidume" means at the foot of the supreme Bodhi tree. Here, the meaning of the word "varabodhi" has also been explained below. "Dumo" (tree) is so called because it grows ("davati"), spreading with roots, trunk, bark, branches, foliage, sprouts, and fruits, attaining growth, development, and fullness, or it attains magnificent beauty adorned with silver, gold, gems, and radiant colors. On the very day the Bodhisatta was born, the Bodhi tree also arose along with the Bodhisatta—a royal tree, a hundred cubits tall, an assattha tree (Ficus religiosa), is obtained. The root "du" is in the sense of movement, with the suffix "amo." In the Apadāna commentary, it is said: "It is called 'dumo' because it shakes ('dunāti kampatī'). Or, 'dumo' means 'it fills the expanse of the sky' ('dumati pūreti ākāsatalanti')." "Varo bodhi" is the excellent Bodhi tree, and "varabodhi ca so dumo ca" means "varabodhidumo" (the excellent Bodhi tree); `tasmiṃ` means 'in that'.

Catusaccadasanti cattāri ariyasaccāni maggañāṇena paṭivijjhitaṃ. Ettha ca saccasaddo anekesvatthesu dissati. Seyyathidaṃ. Saccaṃ [M 0.0079] bhaṇe na kujjheyyātiādīsu vācāsacce. Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇātiādīsu viratisacce. Kasmā nu saccāni vadanti nānā pavādiyāse kusalāvadānātiādīsu diṭṭhisacce. Ekañhi saccaṃ na dutiyamatthītiādīsu paramatthasacce nibbāne ceva magge ca, catunnaṃ saccānaṃ kati kusalātiādīsu ariyasacce. Svāyamidhāpi ariyasacce vattatīti veditabbo. Sathanaṃ saccaṃ, avitathaṃ. Sathadhātu avitathe ṇyo. Yathā hi aggīnaṃ sabhāvo ekantaṃ uṇhoyeva hoti, na sītalo, evaṃ dukkhādīnaṃ pīḷanādi sabhāvaṃ ekantaṃ saccaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ hoti. Taṃ pana catubbidhaṃ hoti dukkhasaccaṃ, samudayasaccaṃ, nirodhasaccaṃ, maggasaccañcāti. Tattha dukkhasaccanti dukkhacchitaṃ khaṃ tucchanti dukkhaṃ. Kammadhārayasamāsoyaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ saccavibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “duiti ayaṃsaddo kucchite dissati. Kucchitañhi puttaṃ duputtoti vadanti. Khaṃsaddo pana tucche. Tucchañhi ākāsaṃ khanti vuccati. Idañca paṭhamasaccaṃ kucchitaṃ. Anekaupaddavādhiṭṭhānato, tucchaṃbālajanaparikappitadhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitato. Tasmā kucchitattā tucchattā ca dukkhanti vuccatī”ti. Dukkhañca taṃ saccañcāti dukkhasaccaṃ. Tebhūmikavaṭṭaṃ labbhati.

"Catusaccadasaṃ" means one who has penetrated the four noble truths with the knowledge of the path. Here, the word "sacca" is seen in various senses. For example: In "Speak the truth, do not be angry," and so forth, it refers to verbal truth. In "Ascetics and brahmins established in truth," and so forth, it refers to the truth of abstinence. In "Why do the disputants declare various truths, those skilled in assertion?" and so forth, it refers to the truth of views. In "Indeed, there is one truth, there is not a second," and so forth, it refers to the ultimate truth, in Nibbāna and the path. In "How many of the four truths are wholesome?" and so forth, it refers to the noble truths. And here too, it should be understood as referring to the noble truths. Truth is steadfast, not false. The root "sath" is in the sense of "not false," with the suffix "ṇya." Just as the nature of fire is entirely hot and never cold, so too, the nature of suffering and so forth—oppression and the like—is entirely true, real, not false, not otherwise. It is fourfold: the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. Here, "dukkhasacca" (the truth of suffering) means "dukkha" (suffering) which is wretched and empty. This is a karmadhāraya compound. As stated in the Saccavibhaṅgaṭṭhakathā: "The word 'du' appears in the sense of wretchedness. Indeed, they call a wretched son 'duputta' (bad son). The word 'kha', however, is in the sense of emptiness. Indeed, empty space is called 'kha.' And this first truth is wretched because it is the basis of many calamities, and empty because it is devoid of the permanent, beautiful, pleasurable, and self-like nature conceived by foolish people. Therefore, because of being wretched and because of being empty, it is called 'dukkha' (suffering)." That which is suffering and is truth is the truth of suffering. This refers to the cycle of existence in the three realms.

Samudayasaccanti ayati pavattati dukkhaphalaṃ etenāti ayo, lobho. Ayadhātu gatimhi a. Saṃ avasesa paccayasaṃyoge sati u dukkhuppattiyā ayo kāraṇoti samudayo. Chaṭṭhītappurisasamāsoyaṃ. Vutteñhetaṃ sacca vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saṃiti ca ayaṃsaddo samāgamo sametantiādīsu saṃyogaṃ dīpeti. Uiti ayaṃsaddo uppannaṃ uditantiādīsu uppattiṃ. Ayasaddo pana kāraṇaṃ dīpeti. Idañcāpi dutiyasaccaṃ avasesapaccayasamāyoge sati dukkhassuppattikāraṇaṃ. Iti dukkhassa saṃyoge uppattikāraṇattā dukkhasamudayanti vuccatī”ti. Samudayo ca so saccañcāti samudayasaccaṃ, lobhasaṅkhātā taṇhā labbhati[M 0.0080]. Nirodhasaccanti rodhati carati pavattatīti rodho, tebhūmikavaṭṭadhammo. Rodhadhātu caraṇe ṇa. Natthi tebhūmikavaṭṭadhammassa rodho caraṇaṃ etthāti nirodho, nibbānaṃ. Atha vā nirujjhati saṃsāradukkhaṃ etthāti nirodho, nibbānaṃ. Rudhidhātu āvaraṇe ṇa. Vuttañhetaṃ saccavibhaṅgaṭṭha kathāyaṃ “tatiyasaccaṃ pana yasmā nisaddo abhāvaṃ. Rodha saddo cārakaṃ dīpeti. Tasmā abhāvo ettha saṃsāra cārakasaṅkhātassa dukkharodhassa sabbagatisuññattā. Samadhi gate vā tasmiṃ saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa dukkharodhassa abhāvo hoti tappaṭipakkhattātipi dukkhanirodhanti vuccatī”ti. Dukkhassa vā anuppādanirodhapaccayattā dukkhanirodhanti. Nirodho ca so saccañcāti nirodhasaccaṃ. Nibbānaṃ. Maggasaccanti dukkhanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ maggati gacchati etenāti maggo. Aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Maggadhātu gatiyaṃ a. Vuttañhetaṃ sacca vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “catutthasaccaṃ pana yasmā etaṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati ārammaṇavasena tadabhimukhabhūtattā paṭipadā ca hoti dukkhanirodhappattiyā. Tasmā dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadāti vuccatī”ti. Maggo ca so saccañcāti maggasaccaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo labbhati. Yasmā panetāni buddhādayo ariyā paṭivijjhanti, tasmā ariyasaccānītipi vuccanti. Atha vā buddhādīhi ariyehi paṭivijjhiyanti, tasmā ariyasaccānītipi vuccanti.

The truth of origin (samudayasacca) is so called because 'ayo' (greed) is that by which the fruit of suffering proceeds and continues. The root 'aya' is in the sense of 'going.' When the remaining conditions are conjoined, 'u' (arising) of suffering has 'ayo' as its cause; hence, 'samudayo' (origin). This is a sixth-case tatpurisa compound. As it is stated in the Saccavibhaṅga Commentary: "The word 'saṃ' indicates conjunction, as in 'coming together' (samāgamo) or 'meeting' (sameti). The word 'u' signifies arising, as in 'arisen' (uppanna) or 'manifested' (udita). The word 'aya' denotes cause. This second truth is the cause for the arising of suffering when the remaining conditions are conjoined. Thus, because it is the cause for the arising of suffering through conjunction, it is called the 'origin of suffering' (dukkhasamudaya)." And because it is both the origin and a truth, it is called the "truth of origin" (samudayasacca). Here, craving (taṇhā), designated as greed (lobha), is to be understood.

The truth of cessation (nirodhasacca) is so called because 'rodha' means 'that which moves, proceeds, or continues,' referring to the phenomena of the cycle of existence in the three realms. The root 'rodha' is in the sense of 'moving.' Herein, there is no moving or continuation of the phenomena of the cycle of existence in the three realms—hence, 'nirodha' (cessation), which is Nibbāna. Alternatively, because the suffering of saṃsāra ceases herein, it is called 'nirodha' (cessation), which is Nibbāna. The root 'rudhi' is in the sense of 'obstructing.' As it is stated in the Saccavibhaṅga Commentary: "Regarding the third truth, because the term 'ni' denotes absence, and the word 'rodha' denotes a prison, therefore, herein there is the absence of that which is called the prison of saṃsāra, as it is empty of all destinations. Or, when that is attained, there is the absence of that which is called the prison of saṃsāra, because it is its opposite; thus it is also called the 'cessation of suffering' (dukkhanirodha)." Or, because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of suffering, it is called the "cessation of suffering" (dukkhanirodha). And because it is both cessation and a truth, it is called the "truth of cessation" (nirodhasacca), which is Nibbāna.

The truth of the path (maggasacca) is so called because 'maggo' (path) is that by which one seeks or goes to the cessation of suffering, Nibbāna. It is the Eightfold Path. The root 'magga' is in the sense of 'going.' As it is stated in the Saccavibhaṅga Commentary: "The fourth truth is called the 'path leading to the cessation of suffering' (dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā) because it goes toward the cessation of suffering as its object, being oriented toward it, and because it is the practice for attaining the cessation of suffering." And because it is both the path and a truth, it is called the "truth of the path" (maggasacca). Here, the Eightfold Path is to be understood. Since these truths are penetrated by the noble ones (ariyā), beginning with the Buddhas, they are also called the "Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni). Alternatively, because they are to be penetrated by the noble ones, such as the Buddhas, they are also called the "Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni).

Tesaṃ pana lakkhaṇādīni evaṃ veditabbāni. Ettha hi bādhanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, santāpanarasaṃ, pavattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, pabhavalakkhaṇaṃ samudayasaccaṃ, anupacchedakaraṇarasaṃ, palibodhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Santilakkhaṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, accutirasaṃ, animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Niyyānalakkhaṇaṃ maggasaccaṃ, kilesappahāna karaṇarasaṃ, vuṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānanti. Etesu pana catūsu saccesu paṭhamatatiyasaccāni phalāni honti. Dutiya catutthasaccāni hetūni honti. Purimāni dvesaccāni dudda sattā gambhīrāni. Pacchimāni dvesaccāni gambhīrattā duddasāni.

Their characteristics and so forth should be understood thus. Herein, the truth of suffering has the characteristic of affliction, the function of tormenting, and manifests as continuity. The truth of origin has the characteristic of being a source, the function of causing non-cessation, and manifests as an impediment. The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace, the function of immutability, and manifests as the signless. The truth of the path has the characteristic of leading out, the function of causing the abandonment of defilements, and manifests as emergence. Among these four truths, the first and third truths are results, while the second and fourth truths are causes. The first two truths are profound and difficult for beings to see. The latter two truths are difficult to see because of their profundity.

Api [M 0.0081] ca kho pana dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ gambhīrañceva duddasañcāti veditabbaṃ. Ekekassa pana saccassa catunnaṃ catunnaṃ atthānaṃ vasena soḷasa saccaṭṭhā honti. Tena vuttaṃ paṭisambhidā maggapāḷiyaṃ “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho, ime cattāro dukkhassa dukkhaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā. Evaṃ dukkhaṃ tathaṭṭhena saccaṃ. Samudayassa āyūhanaṭṭho nidānaṭṭho saṃyogaṭṭho palibodhaṭṭho, ime cattāro samudayassa samudayaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā. Evaṃ samudayo tathaṭṭhena saccaṃ. Nirodhassa nissaraṇaṭṭho vivekaṭṭho asaṅkhataṭṭho amataṭṭho, ime cattāro nirodhassa nirodhaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā, evaṃ nirodho tathaṭṭhena saccaṃ. Maggassa niyyānaṭṭho hetvaṭṭho dassanaṭṭho adhipateyyaṭṭho, ime cattāro maggassa maggaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā, evaṃ maggo tathaṭṭhena sacca”nti.

Moreover, the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering should be understood as both profound and difficult to see. For each truth, by way of four meanings for each, there are sixteen aspects of the truths. Therefore, it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "For suffering, there is the meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of torment, and the meaning of change. These four are the meanings of suffering as suffering; they are real, not unreal, not otherwise. Thus, suffering is a truth in the sense of reality. For the origin, there is the meaning of accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of conjunction, and the meaning of impediment. These four are the meanings of the origin as an origin; they are real, not unreal, not otherwise. Thus, the origin is a truth in the sense of reality. For cessation, there is the meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, and the meaning of the deathless. These four are the meanings of cessation as cessation; they are real, not unreal, not otherwise. Thus, cessation is a truth in the sense of reality. For the path, there is the meaning of leading out, the meaning of being a cause, the meaning of seeing, and the meaning of dominance. These four are the meanings of the path as a path; they are real, not unreal, not otherwise. Thus, the path is a truth in the sense of reality."

Dassanaṃ dasaṃ, disati passatīti vā dasaṃ, catumaggañāṇaṃ. Disadhātu apekkhane a. Catunnaṃ saccānaṃ dassanaṃ assāti catusaccadaso, jino. Atha vā cattāri saccāni adassi apassīti catusaccadaso, jino. So cattāri saccāni catumaggañāṇena appaṭivijjhīti attho. Taṃ catusaccadasaṃ. Catusaccañāṇaṃ pana duvidhaṃ hoti anubodhañāṇañca, paṭivedha ñāṇañcāti. Tattha anubodhañāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ anussavādivasena nirodhe magge ca pavattati, paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ nirodhamārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccato cattāripi saccāni paṭivijjhati. Yathāha yo bhikkhave dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passati. Dukkhanirodhampi passati, dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭi padampi passatīti sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Catusaccapaṭivedhañāṇaṃ pana anubodhañāṇena vinā na pavattati, tasmā anubodha ñāṇatthāya pubbe catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ paṇḍitena samārambhi tabbanti[M 0.0082]. Nanu ca ariyasāvakā cattāri saccāni paṭivijjhanti. Atha kasmā jinoyeva catusaccadasanti thomitoti. Bhagavā pana ariyasāvakehi visiṭṭhena anaññopadesena arahattamaggañāṇena cattāri saccāni paṭivijjhanti. Tasmā bhagavāyeva catusaccadasanti abhitthavitoti. Tattha pana ṭhapetvā taṇhañca nibbānañca avasesadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ nāma. Aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritā samudayasaccaṃ nāma. Nibbānaṃ nirodha saccaṃ nāma. Aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo maggasaccaṃ nāma. Vuttaṃ pana abhidhammatthasaṅgahe –

Seeing is 'dasaṃ,' or 'dasaṃ' is that which sees or perceives, namely, the knowledge of the four paths. The root 'dis' is in the sense of 'seeing.' One who has the seeing of the four truths is a 'catusaccadaso,' the Victor. Alternatively, because he saw and perceived the four truths, he is a 'catusaccadaso,' the Victor. This means he penetrated the four truths with the knowledge of the four paths. That seer of the four truths. The knowledge of the four truths is of two kinds: knowledge by comprehension (anubodhañāṇa) and knowledge by penetration (paṭivedhañāṇa). Therein, knowledge by comprehension is worldly and proceeds by way of oral tradition and so forth with regard to cessation and the path. Knowledge by penetration is supramundane; taking cessation as its object, it functionally penetrates all four truths. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the path leading to the cessation of suffering"—all of this should be stated. However, the knowledge of penetrating the four truths does not arise without the knowledge of comprehension. Therefore, a wise person should first undertake the meditation subject on the four truths for the sake of knowledge by comprehension. But do not the noble disciples also penetrate the four truths? Then why is only the Victor praised as the 'seer of the four truths'? The Blessed One, however, penetrates the four truths with the distinguished knowledge of the path to arahantship, without instruction from another. Therefore, only the Blessed One is extolled as the 'seer of the four truths.' Therein, setting aside craving and Nibbāna, the remaining phenomena are called the truth of suffering. The one-hundred-and-eight-fold proliferation of craving is called the truth of origin. Nibbāna is called the truth of cessation. The Eightfold Path is called the truth of the path. It is stated in the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha:

“Dukkhaṃ tebhūmakaṃ vaṭṭaṃ, taṇhā samudayo bhave;

Nirodho nāma nibbānaṃ, maggo lokuttaro mato”ti.

"Suffering is the cycle of existence in the three realms; craving is the origin in becoming. Cessation is the name for Nibbāna; the path is considered supramundane."

Varamiddhigatanti varaṃ iddhigataṃ. Uttamaṃ atītabuddhānaṃ iddhiṃ pattanti attho. Atha vā uttamānaṃ iddhīnaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūtanti attho. Ijjhanaṃ samijjhanaṃ iddhi, ijjhati samijjhati nippajjatīti vā iddhi. Iddhividhañāṇañca arahattamaggo ca labbhati. Vuttañhi visuddhimagge “tathā nekkhammaṃ ijjhatīti iddhīti ca arahattamaggo ijjhatīti iddhī”ti ca. Atha vā ijjhanti sattā etāya iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iddhi, aṭṭhasamāpattiyo ca cattāro maggā ca labbhanti. Idhadhātu vuḍḍhiyanti paccayo. Atha vā tapaccayo itthiliṅgajotako īpaccayo ca. Iddhiṃ agaminti iddhigato, jino. Atha vā gacchati patiṭṭhahati etthāti gato, varānaṃ uttamānaṃ iddhīnaṃ gato patiṭṭhānabhūtoti varamiddhigato, jino. Taṃ varamiddhigataṃ. Kiñcāpi pana ariyasāvakā iddhippattā honti, buddhā pana visesato etāya abhiññāya iddhā samiddhā vuddhā atiukkaṃsagatā honti, tasmā buddhoyeva varamiddhigatanti abhitthavituṃ arahatīti veditabbo.

'Varamiddhigata' means 'varaṃ iddhigataṃ' (gone to supreme psychic power). This means having attained the supreme psychic power of past Buddhas. Alternatively, it means being the foundation for supreme psychic powers. Success and accomplishment are called 'iddhi.' Or, it is called 'iddhi' because one succeeds, accomplishes, and is brought to fruition. The knowledge of psychic powers and the path to arahantship are obtained here. As it is stated in the Visuddhimagga: "Thus, 'renunciation succeeds, so it is iddhi,' and 'the path to arahantship succeeds, so it is iddhi.'" Alternatively, beings prosper, grow, and become exalted through this—thus it is called 'iddhi'; the eight attainments and the four paths are obtained here. The root 'idh' has the meaning of 'growth.' Alternatively, there is the 'ti' suffix and the 'ī' suffix which indicates the feminine gender. 'Iddhiṃ agami' means 'iddhigato,' one who has gone to psychic power, the Victor. Alternatively, 'gato' is that wherein one goes and becomes established. Thus, 'varamiddhigato' means one who has gone to and become the foundation of supreme and excellent psychic powers, the Victor. That is 'varamiddhigataṃ.' Although noble disciples may attain psychic powers, the Buddhas are especially prosperous, grown, and supremely exalted through this higher knowledge. Therefore, it should be understood that only the Buddha is worthy of being praised as 'varamiddhigata'.

Naradevahitanti manussadevānaṃ lokiyalokuttara saṅkhātaṃ hitaṃ payojanaṃ dhāraṇaṃ. Tesaṃ pana attho heṭṭhā [M 0.0083] vuttoyeva. Tibhavūpasamanti tibhavaupasamaṃ. Punabbhavābhinibbattiyā abhāvato kāmarūpaarūpasaṅkhātehi tīhi bhavehi tīsu bhavesu punabbhavābhinibbattito vā upasamitaṃ nibbutaṃ niruddhanti attho. Bhavanti sattā etthāti bhavo, tayo bhavā tibhavā, tehi upasamitthāti tibhavūpasamo, jino. Taṃ tibhavūpasamaṃ. Bhagavato pana bodhipallaṅkeva kāmarūpārūpasaṅkhātesu tīsu bhavesu paṭisandhijanakānaṃ avijjātaṇhāmūlakānaṃ puññādisaṅkhārānaṃ arahattamaggañāṇena niravasesaṃ pahīnattā punabbhavābhinibbatti natthi. Tasmā bhagavantaṃyeva visesena tibhavūpasamanti thometīti vuttaṃ hoti. Jinanti pañcamārajayantaṃ buddhaṃ. Paṇamāmīti ahaṃ ñāṇasampayuttacittena ādaraṃ vandāmīti yojanā.

'Naradevahitaṃ' means the welfare, purpose, and support, designated as worldly and supramundane, for humans and gods. Their meaning, however, has been stated previously. 'Tibhavūpasamaṃ' means the pacification of the three existences. Due to the absence of renewed existence, it means pacified, quenched, and ceased from the arising of renewed existence in the three existences—namely, the realms of sensuality, form, and formlessness. 'Beings exist therein,' thus it is 'bhava' (existence). The three existences are 'tibhava.' He is pacified with regard to them, thus he is 'tibhavūpasamo' (one who has pacified the three existences), the Conqueror. That is 'tibhavūpasamaṃ.' For the Blessed One, at the Bodhi seat itself, because the meritorious and other formations rooted in ignorance and craving, which generate rebirth in the three existences of sensuality, form, and formlessness, were completely abandoned without remainder through the knowledge of the Arahant path, there is no renewed existence for him. Therefore, it is said that the Blessed One is especially praised as 'tibhavūpasama.' 'Jinaṃ' means the Conqueror, the Buddha who has vanquished the five Māras. 'Paṇamāmi' means 'I pay homage with reverence, with a mind united with knowledge'—this is the construing.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Samatiṃsati sambharaṇaṃ samatiṃsapāramiyo sambhūtaṃ paripūritaṃ, varabodhidume uttamabodhirukkhamūle, catusaccadasaṃ cattāri ariyasaccāni maggañāṇena passantaṃ paṭivijjhantaṃ, varamiddhigataṃ uttamaṃ atīta buddhānaṃ iddhipattaṃ uttamānaṃ iddhīnaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ vā, naradevahitaṃ manussadevānaṃ lokiyalokuttarasaṅkhātaṃ payojanaṃ dhāraṇaṃ, tibhavūpasamaṃ kāmarūpaarūpasaṅkhātehi tīhi bhavehi upasamitaṃ, kāmarūpārūpasaṅkhātesu tīsu bhavesu punabbhavā bhinibbattito upasamitaṃ nibbutaṃ vā, jinaṃ pañcamārajayantaṃ buddhaṃ paṇamāmi ahaṃ ñāṇasampayuttacittena ādaraṃ vandāmīti.

Here is the concise construing. `Samatiṃsati sambharaṇaṃ` means the thirty perfections fully accomplished and fulfilled. `Varabodhidume` means at the base of the excellent Bodhi tree. `Catusaccadasaṃ` means one who sees and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with the knowledge of the path. `Varamiddhigataṃ` means one who has attained the supreme psychic power of past Buddhas, or one who is the foundation of supreme psychic powers. `Naradevahitaṃ` means one who is the welfare, purpose, and support, designated as worldly and supramundane, for humans and gods. `Tibhavūpasamaṃ` means one who is pacified with regard to the three existences—sensuality, form, and formlessness—or one who is pacified and quenched from the arising of renewed existence in the three existences of sensuality, form, and formlessness. `Jinaṃ` means the Conqueror, the Buddha who has vanquished the five Māras. `Paṇamāmi` means: I respectfully pay homage with a mind united with knowledge.

Ekādasamavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the eleventh verse of homage is complete.

12.

12.

Satapuññajalakkhaṇikaṃ virajaṃ,

Gaganūpamadhiṃ dhitimerusamaṃ;

Jalajūpamasītalasīlayutaṃ,

Pathavīsahanaṃ paṇamāmi jinaṃ.

I bow to the Conqueror, marked with the characteristics born of a hundred merits, unstained, whose wisdom is like the sky, whose steadfastness is like Mount Meru; endowed with morality as cool as a lotus, and as patient as the earth.

12. Evaṃ [M 0.0084] ekādasamagāthāya jinaṃ vanditvā idāni satapuññajalakkhaṇikantyādīhi chahi guṇehi thomitvā jinaṃ vanditu kāmo satapuññajalakkhaṇikantyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana catūhi sa gaṇehi racitattā dvādasakkharehi yuttā toṭakagāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Sādhakaṃ pana anantaragāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva.

12. Having thus paid homage to the Conqueror with the eleventh verse, now, desiring to pay homage to the Conqueror by extolling him with the six qualities beginning with 'marked with the characteristics born of a hundred merits,' he speaks the verse beginning with 'satapuññajalakkhaṇikaṃ.' This, however, should be understood as a Toṭaka verse, endowed with twelve syllables, since it is composed of four sa-gaṇas. The proof, moreover, has been stated in the commentary on the immediately following verse.

Tattha satapuññajalakkhaṇikanti anekapāramīpuññatejena jātena dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇena sampannaṃ. Ettha ca satasaddo anekasaṅkhyāvācako. Satatejo sahassaraṃ sītiādīsu viya. Satena anekena pāramīpuññatejena jātanti satapuññajaṃ, lakkhiyati lakkhitabbaṃ buddhadabbaṃ etehīti lakkhaṇaṃ, dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇādi. Lakkhadhātu dassanaṅkesuyu. Satapuññajañca taṃ lakkhaṇañcāti satapuññaja lakkhaṇaṃ. Taṃ assa atthīti satapuññajalakkhaṇiko, jino. Taṃ. Bhagavā hi anantesu cakkavāḷesu sabbe sattā ekekaṃ puññakammaṃ satakkhattuṃ kareyyuṃ. Ettakehi janehi kataṃ puññakammaṃ bodhisatto ekova ekekaṃ sataguṇaṃ katvā nibbattena pāramīpuññatejena jātehi dvattiṃsa mahāpurisalakkhaṇehi ca asītianubyañjana lakkhaṇe hi ca sampannoti satapuññajalakkhaṇikanti thometīti adhippāyo. Vuttañhi buddhavaṃsaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

Therein, 'satapuññajalakkhaṇikaṃ' means endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, which are born from the power of the merit of numerous perfections. Here, the word 'sata' signifies a countless number, as in 'Satatejo,' 'Sahassaraṃsi,' and so on. 'Satapuññajaṃ' means born from the power of the merit of the perfections, which are a hundred or countless. 'Lakkhaṇaṃ' is that by which the Buddha-substance is marked or should be marked, such as the thirty-two marks of a great man. The root 'lakkh' is used in the sense of 'seeing' and 'marking.' 'Satapuññajaṃ' and that 'lakkhaṇaṃ' together make 'satapuññajalakkhaṇaṃ.' One who possesses that is 'satapuññajalakkhaṇiko,' the Conqueror. Him. That is, if all beings in the infinite world-systems were each to perform a single meritorious deed a hundred times, the Bodhisatta alone, having performed each deed a hundredfold more, is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics, which are born from the power of the merit of perfections thus produced. Thus, he is praised as 'satapuññajalakkhaṇika'—this is the intention. As it is stated in the commentary to the Buddhavaṃsa:

“Satapuñña lakkhaṇoti anantesu cakkavāḷesu sabbe sattā ekekaṃ puññakammaṃ satakkhattuṃ kareyyuṃ, ettakehi janehi katakammaṃ bodhisatto sayameva eko sataguṇaṃ katvā nibbatto. Tasmā satapuññalakkhaṇoti vuccati. Keci pana satena satena puññakammena nibbattaṃ ekekalakkhaṇoti vadanti. Evaṃ sante yo koci buddho bhaveyyāti. Taṃ aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhitta”nti. Pātheyyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sata puññalakkhaṇanti satena satena puññakammena nibbattaṃ ekekaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ[M 0.0085]. Evaṃ sante yo koci buddho bhaveyyāti na rocayiṃsu. Anantesu pana cakkavāḷesu sabbe sattā ekekaṃ kammaṃ satakkhattuṃ kareyyuṃ. Ettakehi janehi kataṃ kammaṃ bodhisatto ekova ekekaṃ sataguṇaṃ katvā nibbatto. Tasmā satapuññalakkhaṇoti imamatthaṃ rocayiṃsū”ti vuttaṃ. Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ pana upari āvibhavissatīti.

"'Satapuññalakkhaṇo' means that if in countless world-systems all beings were to perform a single meritorious act a hundred times each, the Bodhisatta alone is born having made each act done by that many people a hundredfold. Therefore, he is called 'satapuññalakkhaṇo.' Some, however, say that each single mark is produced by a hundred meritorious acts. If this were so, then anyone could become a Buddha. This is rejected in the commentaries." In the Pātheyya commentary, however, it is said: "'Satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ' means that each single mark is produced by a hundred meritorious acts. They did not approve of the view that, if this were so, anyone could become a Buddha. But they did approve of this meaning for 'satapuññalakkhaṇo': in countless world-systems, if all beings were to perform a single act a hundred times each, the Bodhisatta alone is born having made each act done by that many people a hundredfold. Therefore, he is called 'satapuññalakkhaṇo.'" The thirty-two marks of a great man, however, will be made manifest further on.

Virajanti rāgarajādīnaṃ abhāvā vigatarajaṃ. Rañjati sañjati rūpādiārammaṇesūti rajo, rāgādirajo. Ranjadhātu rāge a. Vigato rajo assāti virajo, jino. Taṃ virajaṃ. Jino hi bodhipallaṅkeyeva sabbakilesamāra rajassa jayitattā vigatarajoti attho. Gaganūpamadhinti ettha dhī vuccati sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Tasmā ākāsūpamasabbaññuta ñāṇavantanti attho. Gacchanti ettha vihaṅgamādayoti gaganaṃ, ākāso. Gamudhātu gatiyaṃ yu. Makārassa go. Upamiyate upamā. Bhāvasādhanoyaṃ. Upapubbamādhātu parimāne a.
