The root is 'nī' in the sense of leading, with the suffix 'yu'. That which goes to the beauty of that (eye) is 'nayanasubhagaṃ', a marvel. The word 'nayanasubha' is a pre-pounded word with the root 'gam' in the sense of motion, with the suffix 'kvi'. That is 'nayanasubhagaṃ'.

Ākulaṇṇaggijālanti [M 0.0126] ettha ākulaaṇṇaaggijālanti padacchedo. Parikiṇṇa udakadhāra aggisikhāvantaṃ. Atha vā parisamantato kulaṃ pakiṇṇaṃ aññamaññamissakaṃ yamakaṃ yamakaṃ udakajālaaggijālavantanti attho. Ābhuso kulati udakaggijālaṃ aññamaññamissakaṃ karotīti ākulaṃ, udakaggijālaṃ. Āpubbakuladhātu karaṇe a. Ābhusaṃ kulati bandhati aññamaññanti vā ākulaṃ. Atha vā āsamantato kulati yamakaṃ yamakaṃ udakaggijālaṃ pavattatīti ākulaṃ, udakaggijālaṃ. Udakajālaṃ aggijālena aggijālañca udakajālena sammisso hotīti attho. Ananti jīvanti etena sattāti aṇṇaṃ, udakaṃ. Anadhātu jīvāyaṃ a. Nassa ṇo. Tassa dvittaṃ. Dvibhāvo vā. Atha vā arati gacchati taṃ taṃ ṭhānanti aṇṇaṃ. Aradhātu gatimhito. Tassa annādeso, dhātvantalopo, nnassa ṇṇattaṃ. Aṇṇassa dhāraṃ aṇṇaṃ. Uttarapadalopena. Kuṭilabhāvena ajati gacchatīti aggi, ajadhātu gatiyaṃ i. Jassa ggo. Jalati dibbatīti jālaṃ, sikhaṃ. Jaladhātu dittiyaṃ ṇa. Aggino jālaṃ aggijālaṃ. Aṇṇañca aggijālañca aṇṇaggijālaṃ, ākulaṃ parikiṇṇaṃ aṇṇaggijālaṃ assāti ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ, yamaka pāṭiheraṃ labbhati. Taṃ ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ.

In 'Ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ', the division of words is 'ākula-aṇṇa-aggijālaṃ'. It means possessing scattered streams of water and flames of fire. Alternatively, the meaning is: possessing a mass scattered all around, intermingled in pairs, of nets of water and nets of fire. Because it exceedingly makes the water and fire nets mixed with each other, it is 'ākulaṃ', the water and fire net. This is from the root 'kul' with the prefix 'ā' in the sense of making, with the suffix 'a'. Or, because it exceedingly gathers or binds together, it is 'ākulaṃ'. Alternatively, because the water and fire net proceeds from all sides in pairs, it is 'ākulaṃ', the water and fire net. The meaning is that the net of water is mixed with the net of fire, and the net of fire is mixed with the net of water. 'Aṇṇaṃ' is water, because beings live (ananti) by it. This is from the root 'an' in the sense of living, with the suffix 'a'. The 'n' becomes 'ṇ', and that is doubled. Or it is a doubling. Alternatively, because it goes (arati) to this or that place, it is 'aṇṇaṃ'. This is from the root 'ar' in the sense of motion. 'Anna' is substituted for it, with elision of the end of the root, and 'nn' becomes 'ṇṇ'. 'Aṇṇaṃ' stands for a stream of water (aṇṇadhāraṃ), by elision of the final member of the compound. Because it goes (ajati) crookedly, it is 'aggi' (fire). This is from the root 'aj' in the sense of motion, with the suffix 'i'; 'j' becomes 'gg'. Because it shines (jalati) or blazes, it is 'jālaṃ', a flame. This is from the root 'jal' in the sense of shining, with the suffix 'ṇa'. The flame of fire is 'aggijālaṃ'. Water and the flame of fire are 'aṇṇaggijālaṃ'. Because it has an intermingled, scattered net of water and fire, it is 'ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ'; the Twin Miracle is thereby obtained. That is 'ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ'.

Dujjāladdhaṃsanti duṭṭhu diṭṭhivādasaṅkhātajālaṃ viddhaṃsitaṃ. Duṭṭhu jalati bandhati saṃsāravaṭṭeti dujjālaṃ, diṭṭhivādajālaṃ. Titthiya vādo hi natthi dinnantiādinayapavatto saṃsārato nissaritumappadānavasena jālasadisattā dujjālanti attho. Dupubba jaladhātu bandhane ṇo. Taṃ dhaṃsati viddhaṃsatīti dujjāladdhaṃsaṃ, yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ. Munibhijahitanti munibhi ajahitanti padacchedo. Tattha munibhīti sabbasammāsambuddhehi. Te hi monaṃ vuccati sabbaññutañāṇaṃ, taṃ etesaṃ atthīti munīti vuccanti. Kāyamoneyya vacīmoneyya manomoneyyaṃ etesaṃ atthīti vā [M 0.0127] muni. Assatthitaddhite ṇīpaccayo. Atha vā idhaloka paralokaṃ attahita parahitaṃ hitāhitañca munanti jānantīti munīti vuccanti. Tehi munībhi.

'Dujjāladdhaṃsaṃ' means the net known as wrong views is thoroughly shattered. 'Dujjālaṃ', the net of wrong views, is so called because it badly ensnares and binds one in the round of saṃsāra. For the doctrine of the sectarians, which proceeds by way of such tenets as 'there is nothing given,' is like a net in that it provides no escape from saṃsāra; this is the meaning of 'dujjālaṃ'. This is from the root 'jal' with the prefix 'du-' in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'ṇo'. Because it destroys (dhaṃsati) and shatters (viddhaṃsati) that, it is 'dujjāladdhaṃsaṃ', the Twin Miracle. 'Munibhijahitaṃ' is to be parsed as 'munibhi ajahitaṃ' (not abandoned by the sages). Here, 'munibhi' refers to all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones. For omniscience is called 'monaṃ' (sagacity), and because they possess it, they are called 'munī' (sages). Or, because they possess sagacity of body, sagacity of speech, and sagacity of mind, they are 'munī'. The suffix 'ṇī' is used in the taddhita sense of 'possessing'. Alternatively, because they know (munanti) this world and the next, their own welfare and the welfare of others, the beneficial and the harmful, they are called 'munī'. By those sages.

Ajahitanti avijahitaṃ apariccattaṃ vā, hātabbaṃ cajitabbanti jahitaṃ. Hādhātu cāge ta. Na jahitaṃ ajahitaṃ, pāṭiheraṃ. Taṃ ajahitaṃ. Bhagavato hi sāvatthinagarassa dakkhiṇadvāre kaṇḍambarukkhamūle kataṃ pāṭihāriyañca bhagavā pana tasmiṃ pāṭihāriyāvasāne tāvatiṃsapuraṃ gato, tasmiṃ pārichattakamūlamhi paṇḍukambalanāmake silāsane sannisinno devānaṃ abhidhammakathāya desanā ca sabbasammāsambuddhehi avijahitā dhammatāyeva hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Buddhavaṃsaṭṭhakathāyañhi samatiṃsadhammatāpakāsane sāvatthi nagaradvāre yamakapāṭihāriyakaraṇaṃ. Tāvatiṃse bhavane abhidhammadesanāti dhammatābhāvena vuttaṃ. Tasmā pāṭiheraṃ munībhijahitanti thometi.

'Ajahitaṃ' means unabandoned or unrenounced. What is abandoned or relinquished is 'jahitaṃ'. This is from the root 'hā' in the sense of abandoning, with the suffix 'ta'. Not abandoned is 'ajahitaṃ', the marvel. That is unabandoned. For it is said that both the miracle performed by the Blessed One at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree at the southern gate of the city of Sāvatthī, and the teaching of the Abhidhamma discourse to the devas by the Blessed One, who, at the conclusion of that miracle, went to the city of the Tāvatiṃsa gods and sat on the stone seat named Paṇḍukambala at the foot of the Pārichattaka tree, are unabandoned by all Perfectly Enlightened Ones and are indeed a constant nature. For in the Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭhakathā, in the exposition of the thirty constant natures, the performance of the Twin Miracle at the city gate of Sāvatthī and the teaching of the Abhidhamma in the Tāvatiṃsa realm are stated to be a constant nature. Therefore, the marvel is praised as 'unabandoned by the sages'.

Pāṭiheranti paccanīkapaṭiharaṇavasena pāṭihāriyaṃ, paṭipakkhe titthiye madditvā hinoti pavattatīti pāṭiheraṃ. Paṭipubbahidhātu gatiyaṃ ṇo. Hissa heraṇideso. Atha vā bhagavato ca sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhe titthiye harati apanetīti pāṭiheraṃ, iddhividhañāṇaṃ. Paṭipubbaharadhātu apanayane ṇo. Paṭiharati apaneti sattānaṃ diṭṭhimānopagatāni cittānīti vā pāṭiheraṃ. Appasannānaṃ pasādaṃ āharatīti vā pāṭiheraṃ. Samāhite citte vigatūpakkilese katakiccena paṭipacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti vā pāṭiheraṃ. Paṭīti hi ayaṃsaddo pacchāti etassa atthaṃ bodheti. Tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi añño āgacchi brāhmaṇotiādīsu viya. Atha vā paṭipunappunaṃ udakaggijālaṃ abbocchinnaṃ yamakaṃ yamakaṃ hutvā harati pavattatīti pāṭiheraṃ, yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ. Tañca pana iddhipāṭihāriya, ādesanāpāṭihāriya, anusā sanī [M 0.0128] pāṭihāriyavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Tesu pana idha iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ adhippetanti. Sīghanti khippaṃ āsuṃ lahuṃ vā. Taṃ pana akāsītipade kriyāvisesanaṃ. Seti lahu hutvā pavattatīti sīghaṃ. Sidhātu gatimhi ghapaccayo. Dīgho. Akāsīti akari.

'Pāṭiheraṃ' is a marvel (pāṭihāriyaṃ) by way of repelling the opposition. Because, having crushed the opposing sectarians, it goes forth (hinoti) or proceeds, it is 'pāṭiheraṃ'. This is from the root 'hi' with the prefix 'paṭi-' in the sense of motion, with the suffix 'ṇo'; 'hera' is substituted for 'hi'. Alternatively, because it removes (harati) or dispels (apaneti) the sectarians who are opposed to the Blessed One and his dispensation, it is 'pāṭiheraṃ', the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power. This is from the root 'har' with the prefix 'paṭi-' in the sense of removal, with the suffix 'ṇo'. Or, because it repels and removes the minds of beings that have fallen into wrong views and conceit, it is 'pāṭiheraṃ'. Or, because it brings (āharati) faith to the faithless, it is 'pāṭiheraṃ'. Or, because it is to be brought forth and made to proceed afterwards (pacchā) by one who has completed his task with a concentrated mind free from defilements, it is 'pāṭiheraṃ'. For this word 'paṭi' conveys the meaning of 'afterwards', as in such phrases as, 'While he was engaged in that, another brahmin came.' Alternatively, because it carries on or proceeds repeatedly and uninterruptedly as a twin-pair of water and fire nets, it is 'pāṭiheraṃ', the Twin Miracle. And that is threefold: the marvel of psychic power, the marvel of mind-reading, and the marvel of instruction. Among these, the marvel of psychic power is intended here. 'Sīghaṃ' means quickly, swiftly, or lightly. It is an adverb modifying the verb in the word 'akāsi'. Because it proceeds (seti), being light, it is 'sīghaṃ'. This is from the root 'si' in the sense of motion, with the suffix 'gha', and lengthening of the vowel. 'Akāsi' means 'he did'.

Ettha ca pāṭihāriyamevaṃ veditabbaṃ. Bhagavā hi abhisambodhito sattame saṃvacchare sāvatthinagarassa dakkhiṇadvāre kaṇḍambarukkhamūle devānamindena sakkena āṇāpitena visukammadevaputtena nimmite dvādasayojane ratana maṇḍape bhagavatā nimmite yojanappamāṇe ratanapallaṅke ratanacaṅkame ca nisīditvā tiyojanike dibbasetacchatte dhārayamāne samantato dvādasayojanāya parisāya atthādānaparidīpanaṃ titthiyamaddanaṃ uparimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattati, heṭṭhimakāyato udakadhārā pavattati, heṭṭhimakāyato aggikkhandho, uparimakāyato udakadhārā. Puratthimakāyato aggikkhandho, pacchimakāyato udakadhārā. Pacchimakāyato aggikkhandho, puratthimakāyato udakadhārā, dakkhiṇaakkhito aggikkhandho, vāmaakkhito udakadhārā. Vāmaakkhito aggikkhandho, dakkhiṇaakkhito udakadhārā. Dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotato aggikkhandho, vāmakaṇṇasotato udakadhārā. Vāmakaṇṇasotato aggikkhandho, dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotato udakadhārā. Dakkhiṇa nāsikāsotato aggikkhandho, vāmanāsikāso tato udakadhārā. Vāmanāsikāsotato aggikkhandho, dakkhiṇanāsikāsotato udakadhārā. Dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭato aggikkhandho, vāmaaṃsakūṭato udakadhārā. Vāmaaṃsakūṭato aggikkhandho, dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭato udakadhārā. Dakkhiṇahatthato aggikkhandho, vāmahatthato udakadhārā. Vāmahatthato aggikkhandho, dakkhiṇahatthato udakadhārā. Dakkhiṇapassato [M 0.0129] aggikkhandho, vāmapassato udakadhārā. Vāmapassato aggikkhandho, dakkhiṇapassato udakadhārā. Dakkhiṇapādato aggikkhandho, vāmapādato udakadhārā. Vāmapādato aggikkhandho, dakkhiṇapādato udakadhārā. Aṅgulaṅgulehi aggikkhandho, aṅgulantarikāhi udakadhārā. Aṅgulantarikāhi aggikkhandho, aṅgulaṅgulehi udakadhārā. Ekekalomato aggikkhandho, ekekalomato udakadhārā. Lomakūpato lomakūpato aggikkhandho, lomakūpato lomakūpato udakadhārā pavattati. Channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ nīlānaṃ pītānaṃ lohitakānaṃ odātānaṃ mañjaṭṭhānaṃ pabhassarānaṃ ubbahanabhūtānaṃ yamakā yamakā vaṇṇā pavattanti. Bhagavā caṅkamati, nimmito tiṭṭhati vā nisīdati vā seyyaṃ vā kappeti. Bhagavā tiṭṭhati, nimmito caṅkamati vā nisīdati vā seyyaṃ vā kappeti. Bhagavā nisīdati, nimmito caṅkamati vā tiṭṭhati vā seyyaṃ vā kappeti. Bhagavā seyyaṃ kappeti, nimmito caṅkamati vā tiṭṭhati vā nisīdati vā. Nimmito caṅkamati, bhagavā tiṭṭhati vā nisīdati vā seyyaṃ vā kappeti. Nimmito tiṭṭhati, bhagavā caṅkamati vā nisīdati vā seyyaṃ vā kappeti. Nimmito nisīdati, bhagavā caṅkamati vā tiṭṭhati vā seyyaṃ vā kappeti. Nimmito seyyaṃ kappeti, bhagavā caṅkamati vā tiṭṭhati vā nisīdati vāti vividhaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ titthiyānaṃ maddanatthāya akāsīti. Ettha ca pana yo koci evarūpaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ kātuṃ samattho ce. So āgacchatūti codanāsadisattā vuttaṃ atthādānaparidīpananti. Atthādānañhi anuyogo, paṭipakkhassa atthassa ādānaṃ gahaṇanti katvā, tassa paridīpanaṃ atthādānaparidīpanaṃ. Titthiyamaddananti pāṭihāriyaṃ karissāmāti kuhāyanavasena pubbe uṭṭhitānaṃ titthiyānaṃ maddanaṃ. Tañca tathā kātuṃ asamatthatā sampādanameva. Tadetaṃ padadvayaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyanti etena sambandhitabbanti.

Here, the miracle should be understood thus. In the seventh year after his enlightenment, at the southern gate of the city of Sāvatthī, beneath the Kaṇḍamba tree, in a jeweled pavilion twelve yojanas wide fashioned by the devaputta Visukamma at the command of Sakka, king of the devas, the Blessed One was seated on a jeweled throne upon a jeweled walkway—both created by himself and measuring a yojana in size—while a divine white parasol three yojanas high was held above him, and surrounded by an assembly extending twelve yojanas. For the purpose of illuminating the meaning and crushing the heretics, a mass of fire issued from the upper part of his body while a stream of water flowed from the lower part. From the lower part of his body, a mass of fire issued, while from the upper part, a stream of water flowed. From the eastern part of his body, a mass of fire issued, while from the western part, a stream of water flowed. From the western part of his body, a mass of fire issued, while from the eastern part, a stream of water flowed. From his right eye, a mass of fire issued, while from his left eye, a stream of water flowed. From his left eye, a mass of fire issued, while from his right eye, a stream of water flowed. From his right ear-hole, a mass of fire issued, while from his left ear-hole, a stream of water flowed. From his left ear-hole, a mass of fire issued, while from his right ear-hole, a stream of water flowed. From his right nostril, a mass of fire issued, while from his left nostril, a stream of water flowed. From his left nostril, a mass of fire issued, while from his right nostril, a stream of water flowed. From his right shoulder, a mass of fire issued, while from his left shoulder, a stream of water flowed. From his left shoulder, a mass of fire issued, while from his right shoulder, a stream of water flowed. From his right hand, a mass of fire issued, while from his left hand, a stream of water flowed. From his left hand, a mass of fire issued, while from his right hand, a stream of water flowed. From his right side, a mass of fire issued, while from his left side, a stream of water flowed. From his left side, a mass of fire issued, while from his right side, a stream of water flowed. From his right foot, a mass of fire issued, while from his left foot, a stream of water flowed. From his left foot, a mass of fire issued, while from his right foot, a stream of water flowed. From each finger, a mass of fire issued, while from the spaces between the fingers, a stream of water flowed. From the spaces between the fingers, a mass of fire issued, while from each finger, a stream of water flowed. From each hair, a mass of fire issued, while from each hair, a stream of water flowed. From each hair-pore, a mass of fire issued, while from each hair-pore, a stream of water flowed. Pairs of colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and radiant—arose and manifested. When the Blessed One walked, the created image stood, sat, or lay down. When the Blessed One stood, the created image walked, sat, or lay down. When the Blessed One sat, the created image walked, stood, or lay down. When the Blessed One lay down, the created image walked, stood, or sat. When the created image walked, the Blessed One stood, sat, or lay down. When the created image stood, the Blessed One walked, sat, or lay down. When the created image sat, the Blessed One walked, stood, or lay down. When the created image lay down, the Blessed One walked, stood, or sat. Thus, he performed the manifold Twin Miracle for the purpose of crushing the heretics. Here, 'illuminating the meaning' is said because it is like a challenge, implying, 'If anyone is capable of performing such a miracle, let them come forth!' For 'atthādāna' is a challenge; taking it to mean the grasping of the opponent's position, its illumination is 'atthādānaparidīpana.' 'Crushing the heretics' refers to the suppression of the heretics who had previously risen up with deceitful intention, boasting, 'We will perform a miracle.' This was simply to demonstrate their inability to do so. These two phrases should be understood in connection with the Twin Miracle.

Seṭṭhanti [M 0.0130] pasatthataraṃ. Tassa vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Paramaratijanti devamanussānaṃ uttamaratiṃ janakaṃ. Paramānaṃ uttamasādhūnaṃ cittaramanaṃ janāpetaṃ vā, ettha ca paṭhamavikappe paramasaddo uttamavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko nipāto. Dutiyavikappe sādhuvācako nipphannapāṭipadiko. Devamanussānaṃ paramaṃ uttamaṃ ratiṃ janetīti paramaratijo, munindo. Paramaratisaddūpapada janadhātu janane kvi. Atha vā pakārena saddhamme ramantīti paramā, sādhū labbhanti. Papubba ramudhātu kīḷāyaṃ a. Tesaṃ cittassa ratiṃ ramanaṃ janetīti paramaratijo, munindo. Taṃ paramaratijaṃ. So hi dhamma desanāya ca pāṭihāriyena iddhiyā sarīrasobhagga sampattiādīhi ca devamanussānaṃ cittassa abhiratiṃ abhikkantaṃ janetīti paramaratijanti thometi.

"Seṭṭha" means 'most excellent.' Its meaning has been explained above. "Paramaratija" means 'generator of supreme delight for devas and humans.' Alternatively, it means one who causes delight in the minds of the supreme noble ones. Here, in the first alternative, the word 'parama' is an indeclinable particle signifying 'supreme,' not derived from a verbal root. In the second alternative, it signifies 'noble ones' and is derived from a verbal root. He generates the highest and supreme delight for devas and humans—thus he is "paramaratija," the Lord of Sages. The root 'jan' (to generate) with the suffix 'kvi' and 'paramarati' as the preceding word forms 'paramaratija'. Alternatively, "paramā" are those who delight in the True Dhamma in a special way; they are known as the virtuous ones. The root 'ram' (to delight/play) with the prefix 'pa-' and the suffix 'a' forms this. Thus, he generates delight and joy in their minds—thus he is "paramaratija," the Lord of Sages. That is "paramaratija." For he, through the teaching of the Dhamma, the display of miracles, psychic power, the attainment of physical beauty, and so forth, generates supreme and extraordinary delight in the minds of devas and humans—thus he is praised as "paramaratija."

Iddhidhammehupetanti iddhidhammehi upetanti padacchedo. Iddhi dhammehīti acinteyyaappameyyehi buddhaiddhisaṅkhātaguṇehi. Dhammasaddo hi guṇe vattati buddhadhammātiādīsu viya. Ijjhanaṃ samijjhanaṃ iddhi. Ijjhati samijjhatīti vā iddhi. Ijjhati samijjhati yathicchitattho etāyāti iddhi. Idhadhātu vuddhiyaṃ i, tipaccayo vā. Bhagavā etāya iddhiyā yathicchitattho iddho vuddho ukkaṃsagato hotīti attho. Dhāreti pakāseti taṃsamaṅgino dabbanti dhammo, guṇo. Iddhieva dhammo iddhidhammo, tehi dhammehi. Upetanti samannāgataṃ. Upagacchati sampajjatīti upeto, munindo. Upapubbaidhātu gatiyaṃ ta. Taṃ upetaṃ.

Endowed with supernormal powers: 'iddhi dhammehi upeta' is the word division. 'Iddhi dhammehi' refers to the inconceivable, immeasurable qualities reckoned as the Buddha's supernormal power. The word 'dhamma' indeed functions in the sense of quality, as in 'Buddha-qualities' and so forth. Succeeding, accomplishing is iddhi. Or, that which succeeds, that which accomplishes is iddhi. Or, that through which a desired aim succeeds, accomplishes is iddhi. Here, the root idh is in the sense of growth, with the suffix i, or the suffix ti. The meaning is that the Blessed One, by means of this iddhi, becomes successful in his desired aim, grown, attained to eminence. That which maintains and reveals its possessor is called dhamma, a quality. The iddhi itself is the quality, thus iddhidhamma; by these qualities. 'Upeta' means endowed. That which approaches, that which is accomplished is upeta, the lord of sages. The root i with the prefix upa is in the sense of going, with the suffix ta. That which is endowed.

Iddhi pana adhiṭṭhānā iddhi, vikuppanā iddhi, manomayā iddhi, ñāṇavipphārā iddhi, samādhivipphārā iddhi, ariyā iddhi, kammavipākajā iddhi, puññavato iddhi, vijjāmayā iddhi, tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi cāti dasavidhā hoti. Tattha pakatiyā eko bahukaṃ āpajjati. Sataṃ [M 0.0131] vā sahassaṃ vā āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti bahuko homīti evaṃ vibhajitvā dassitā iddhi adhiṭṭhāna vasena nipphannattā adhiṭṭhānā iddhi nāma. Pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā kumāravaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti nāgavaṇṇaṃ vā supaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ vā yakkhavaṇṇaṃ vā…pe… vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dassetīti evaṃ āgatā iddhi pakativaṇṇavijahanavikāravasena pavattattā vikuppanā iddhi nāma. Idha bhikkhu imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ abhinimmināti rūpaṃ manomayanti iminā nayena āgatā iddhi sarīrabbhantare aññasseva manomayassa sarīrassa nipphattivasena pavattattā manomayā iddhi nāma. Ñāṇuppattito pubbe vā pacchā vā taṅkhaṇe vā ñāṇānubhāvanibbattā visesā ñāṇavipphārā iddhi nāma. Ettha ca āyasmato bākulattherassa ca āyasmato saṃkiccattherassa ca āyasmato bhūtapālattherassa ca ñāṇavipphārā iddhi veditabbā. Samādhito pubbe vā pacchā vā taṅkhaṇe vā samathānubhāvena nibbattā visesā samādhivipphārā iddhi nāma. Ettha ca āyasmato sāriputtattherassa ca āyasmato sañjīvattherassa ca āyasmato khāṇukoṇḍaññattherassa ca uttarāya upāsikāya ca sāmāvatiyā upāsikāya ca samādhivipphārā iddhi veditabbā.

Supernormal power, moreover, is of ten kinds: the power of resolve, the power of transformation, the power of mind-made creation, the power of knowledge-effulgence, the power of concentration-effulgence, the noble power, the power born of kamma-result, the power of the meritorious one, the power consisting of knowledge, and the power in the sense of succeeding due to proper application in various instances. Herein, one who is naturally single becomes many. Having adverted to a hundred or a thousand, one resolves with knowledge, 'May I become many!' The supernormal power thus displayed by way of such differentiation is called the power of resolve because it is accomplished by way of determination. Abandoning one’s natural appearance, one displays the form of a youth, or the form of a nāga, a garuḍa, a yakkha, or even various military formations… The supernormal power that arises in this way is called the power of transformation because it operates by way of abandoning one’s natural appearance and altering it. Here, a bhikkhu creates from this body another body, mind-made, of form. The supernormal power that arises in this way is called the power of mind-made creation because it operates by way of the production of another mind-made body within the physical body. The special phenomena arising from the influence of knowledge, whether before, after, or at the moment of the arising of knowledge, are called the supernormal power of knowledge-effulgence. In this regard, the supernormal power of knowledge-effulgence of the Venerable Bākula, the Venerable Saṃkicca, and the Venerable Bhūtapāla should be understood. The special phenomena arising from the influence of serenity, whether before, after, or at the moment of concentration, are called the supernormal power of concentration-effulgence. In this regard, the supernormal power of concentration-effulgence of the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Sañjīva, the Venerable Khāṇukoṇḍañña, the laywoman Uttarā, and the laywoman Sāmāvatī should be understood.

Paṭikūlādīsu appaṭikūlasaññī vihārādikā pana ariyā iddhi nāma. Pakkhidevādīnaṃ vehāsagamanādikā kamma vipākajā iddhi nāma. Yathāha “katamā vipākajā iddhi. Sabbesaṃ pakkhīnaṃ sabbesaṃ devānaṃ ekaccānaṃ manussānaṃ ekaccā nañca vinipātikānaṃ ayaṃ kammavipākajā iddhī”tiādi. Cakkavattiādīnaṃ vehāsagamanādikā pana puññavato iddhi nāma. Yathāha “katamā puññavato iddhi. Rājā cakkavatti vehāsaṃ gacchati saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya antamaso assabandhagobandhapurise [M 0.0132] upādāya. Jotikassa gahapatissa puññavato iddhi. Jaṭilassa gahapatissa puññavato iddhi. Ghosakassa gahapatissa puññavato iddhi. Meṇḍakassa gahapatissa puññavato iddhi. Pañcannaṃ mahāpuññānaṃ puññavato iddhī”ti. Vijjādharādīnaṃ vehāsagamanādikā pana vijjāmayā iddhi nāma. Ettha ca ādisaddena ākāse antalikkhe hatthimpi dasseti. Assampi…pe… vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dasseti tyādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tena tena sammāpayogena tassa tassa kammassa ijjhanaṃ tattha tattha sammā payogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi nāma.

The noble supernormal power, moreover, is the dwelling and so forth with the perception of non-repulsiveness in repulsive things. The supernormal power born of kamma-result is the going through the air and so forth of winged beings, devas, and others. As it is said: 'What is the supernormal power born of kamma-result? This is the supernormal power born of kamma-result of all birds, all devas, some humans, and some beings in the lower realms,' and so forth. The supernormal power of the meritorious one, moreover, is the going through the air and so forth of wheel-turning monarchs and others. As it is said: 'What is the supernormal power of the meritorious one? A wheel-turning monarch goes through the air together with his fourfold army, including even his horse-trainers and cattle-tenders. The supernormal power of the meritorious one of the householder Jotika, the supernormal power of the meritorious one of the householder Jaṭila, the supernormal power of the meritorious one of the householder Ghosaka, the supernormal power of the meritorious one of the householder Meṇḍaka, the supernormal power of the meritorious one of the five great merit-makers.' The supernormal power consisting of knowledge, moreover, is the going through the air and so forth of knowledge-holders and others. Here, the term 'and so forth' includes displaying an elephant, a horse… in the sky, in the intermediate space… displaying various battle arrays. The success of that particular action through that particular right application, the fact of achieving success in that particular place due to the condition of right application, is called 'supernormal power' in the sense of achieving success.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana paṭisambhidāmagge iddhikathāya ca visuddhimaggaṭṭhakathāya ca gahetabbo. Tāsu pana iddhīsu bhagavato ṭhapetvā vijjāmayiddhiṃ avasesā atthīti veditabbā. Atha vā bhagavato tīhi vijjāhi ca aṭṭhahi vijjāhi ca samannāgatattā sabbā buddhaiddhiyo santīti vijjāmayiddhipi labbhatīti daṭṭhabbā. Taṃ munindaṃ ahaṃ vande vandāmīti sambandho.

Herein is the summary. The detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the discussion on supernormal power in the Paṭisambhidāmagga and from the Visuddhimagga commentary. Among those supernormal powers, it should be understood that all exist for the Blessed One except the supernormal power consisting of knowledge. Alternatively, since the Blessed One is endowed with the three knowledges and the eight knowledges, all the Buddha's supernormal powers exist; thus, it should be seen that even the supernormal power consisting of knowledge is obtained. 'I venerate that lord of sages, I venerate him'—this is the connection.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepatthayojanā. Parahitakaro attanā paresaṃ sabbasattānaṃ atthaṃ payojanaṃ karonto, yo munindo yo yādiso buddho, kaṇḍambaṃmūle kaṇḍanāmikena pasenadikosalarañño uyyānapālena ropitassa setambarukkhassa samīpe sannisinno vasamāno accheraṃ vimhāpanīyaṃ nayanasubhagaṃ devamanussānaṃ pasāda cakkhussa sobhanapattaṃ ākulaṇṇaggijālaṃ parikiṇṇaudaka dhāraaggisikhavantaṃ parisamantato kulaṃ parikiṇṇaṃ aññamañña missakaṃ yamakaṃ yamakaṃ udakajālaaggijālavantaṃ vā, dujjāladdhaṃsaṃ duṭṭhuṃ micchādiṭṭhivādasaṅkhātaṃ jālaṃ viddhaṃsitaṃ, munibhijahitaṃ sabbasammāsambuddhehi avijahitaṃ, pāṭiheraṃ paccanīka paṭihārakaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ udakaggiyamakaṃyamakaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ vā[M 0.0133], sīghaṃ khippaṃ akāsi akari, seṭṭhaṃ pasatthataraṃ, paramaratijaṃ devamanussānaṃ uttamaratiṃ janakaṃ uttamānaṃ sādhūnaṃ cittaramanaṃ janāpetaṃ vā, iddhidhammehi acinteyyaappameyyehi buddhaiddhi guṇehi upetaṃ samannāgataṃ, taṃ munindaṃ ahaṃ sirasā vande vandāmīti.

Herein is the concise explanation of the meaning: The one who works for the welfare of others, himself bringing benefit and purpose to all beings, that Lord of Sages, that Buddha of such qualities—seated near the foot of a white mango tree planted by the park-keeper named Kaṇḍa in the garden of King Pasenadi of Kosala, dwelling there—he swiftly performed a marvelous and astonishing miracle, delightful to the eyes of gods and humans, a beautiful object for the eye of faith, surrounded by a dense net of flames, encircled by streams of water, blazing with tongues of fire, completely encircled, intermingled with one another, pair by pair, having a twin net of water and a twin net of fire—destroying the evil net, the net reckoned as wrong view, shattered, abandoned by sages, but not abandoned by all Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones—a miracle, a counter-miracle, a protective miracle, or the twin miracle of water and fire—the best, the most praised, producing supreme delight for gods and humans, generating supreme delight, or causing the minds of the noble ones to delight—endowed with inconceivable, immeasurable supernormal powers and Buddha-qualities—that Lord of Sages I venerate with my head, I venerate him.

Ekūnavīsatimavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the nineteenth verse of homage is complete.

20. Munindakko yveko dayudayaruṇo ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo, vineyyappāṇoghaṃ kamalakathitaṃ dhammaraṃsīvarehi. Subodhesī suddhe tibhavakuhare byāpitakkittinañca, tilokekaccakkhuṃ dukhamasahanaṃ taṃ mahesiṃ namāmi.

20. The sun of the Lord of Sages, who alone is the dawn of compassion, whose orb of knowledge is widely spread, who fully awakened the flood of beings to be trained with the excellent rays of the Dhamma proclaimed by the lotus, in the pure cavern of the three existences, and whose fame is pervasive, the unique eye of the three worlds, unassailable by suffering—to that great sage I bow.

20. Evaṃ ekūnavīsatimāya gāthāya munindaṃ vanditvā idāni vineyyappāṇoghaṃ dhammadesanāya catusaccadhammaṃ bodhaneyyādīhi navahi guṇehi thomitvā munindakkaṃ vanditukāmo munindakkotyādigāthamāha. Ayaṃ pana ya ma na sa ra ragaṇehi ca ekagarunā ca chayatīhi ca sattayatīhi ca racitattā ekūnavīsatakkharā meghavipphujjitāgāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “rasutvassehi ymā na sa ra ra garū meghavipphujjitā sā”ti. Ayaṃ panettha yojanā. Yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ rasutvassehi cha cha satta yatīhi ymā yagaṇamagaṇā ca na sa rara garū nagaṇa sagaṇa ragaṇa ragaṇa ekagaru ca ce yuttā, sā gāthā meghavipphujjitā megha vipphujjitā gāthā nāmāti. Ettha ca rasānaṃ kasāva titta madhuralavaṇa ambila kaṭukavasena chabbidhattā rasasaddo chasaṅkhyāvācakoti daṭṭhabbo. Utūnaṃ hemanta sisīra vasanta gimhavassānasaradavasena chabbidhattā utusaddo chasaṅkhyāvācakoti. Assasaddo sattasaṅkhyāvācakoti daṭṭhabbo. Assasaddassa hi sattasaṅkhyāvācakabhāvo chandaṭīkāsu vuttoti.

20. Having thus venerated the Lord of Sages with the nineteenth verse, now desiring to venerate the sun of the Lord of Sages by extolling the Dhamma of the four truths for the instruction of beings to be trained, along with its nine qualities such as being worthy of enlightenment, he speaks the verse beginning with 'Munindakko.' This verse, moreover, being composed of the feet ya, ma, na, sa, ra, ra, and one long syllable, with caesuras after the sixth and twelfth syllables, should be understood as the nineteen-syllable Meghavipphujjitā verse. As stated in the Vuttodaya: 'That which has ya, ma, na, sa, ra, ra, and a long syllable, with divisions by taste, season, and horse, is Meghavipphujjitā.' Herein is the explanation: That verse in which each line is endowed with a ya-gaṇa, ma-gaṇa, na-gaṇa, sa-gaṇa, ra-gaṇa, ra-gaṇa, and one long syllable, with caesuras dividing it into segments of six, six, and seven syllables, is called the Meghavipphujjitā verse. Here, moreover, the word 'rasa' (taste) should be understood as denoting the number six, because tastes are sixfold: astringent, bitter, sweet, salty, sour, and pungent. The word 'utu' (season) should also be understood as denoting the number six, because seasons are sixfold: winter, cold season, spring, summer, rainy season, and autumn. The word 'assa' (horse) should be understood as denoting the number seven, for the fact that the word 'assa' denotes the number seven is stated in the commentaries on prosody.

Tattha [M 0.0134] pana dayudayaruṇo ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo eko yo munindakko suddhe tibhavakuhare kamalakathitaṃ vineyyappāṇoghaṃ dhammaraṃsīvarehi subodhesi byāpitakkitti nañca tilokekaccakkhuṃ dukhamasahanaṃ mahesiṃ taṃ munindakkaṃ namāmīti yojanā.

Herein is the construction: 'I bow to that one Lord of Sages, who is the dawn of the rising sun of compassion, whose orb of knowledge is widely spread, who well enlightened the flood of beings to be trained with the excellent rays of the Dhamma proclaimed by the lotus in the pure cavern of the three existences, and whose fame is pervasive, the unique eye of the three worlds, unable to endure suffering, the great sage.'

Imissā gāthāya ca atthakkameneva sukhajānanatthaṃ vaṇṇayissāma, na saddakkamena. Dayudayaruṇotipadassa dayāudayaaruṇoti padavibhāgo kātabbo. Mahākaruṇāsaṅkhātaudayapabbatuggatasūriyāruṇo. Atha vā udayapabbatato uggatasūriyāruṇo viya mahākaruṇā vāti attho. Ettha ca dayāsaddo karuṇāmettāsu vattati. Adayāti vuccati nikkaruṇatanti ettha hi karuṇāyaṃ. Dayāpannoti ettha mettāyaṃ vattati. Mettācittataṃ āpannoti attho. Idha pana karuṇā adhippetā.

For this verse, we shall explain the meaning according to the order of its sense for ease of comprehension, not according to the order of the words. The word 'dayudayaruṇo' should be divided as 'dayā-udaya-aruṇo'. It means 'the dawn of the sun risen from the rising-mountain which is great compassion'. Or alternatively, the meaning is 'great compassion is like the dawn of the sun risen from the rising-mountain'. Here, the word 'dayā' is used in the sense of compassion and loving-kindness. 'Adayā' is called 'lack of compassion' (nikkaruṇatā), and here it is indeed in the sense of compassion. 'Dayāpanna' is used in the sense of loving-kindness, meaning 'endowed with a mind of loving-kindness'. Here, however, compassion is intended.

Ayaṃ pana vacanattho. Dayati hiṃsati kāruṇikaṃ yāva yathādhippetaṃ parassa hitanibbattiṃ na pāpuṇāti tāvāti dayā, mahākaruṇā. Dayadhātu hiṃsāyaṃ a. Dayati anuggaṇhāti pāpajanampi etāyāti vā dayā. Dayadhātu anuggahaṇe. Dayati attano sukhampi pahāya khedaṃ gaṇhātīti vā dayā. Dayadhātu gahaṇe. Atha vā dayanti gaṇhanti etāya bodhisattā saṃsāradukkhañca sabbaññutañāṇañcāti dayā, mahākaruṇā. Mahābodhisattā hi buddhabhāvāya abhinīhārakaraṇakāle hatthagatampi arahatta phalaṃ chaṭṭetvā saṃsārasāgarato satte samuddharitukāmā anassāsakaraṃ atibhayānakaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ pacchimabhave ca saha amatadhātupaṭilābhena anekaguṇasamalaṅkataṃ sabbaññutañāṇañca gaṇhantīti attho. Karuṇāmūlakā hi sabbe buddhaguṇā. Tena vuttaṃ aṅguttaraṭīkāyaṃ “sabbesañca buddhaguṇānaṃ karuṇā ādi, tannidānabhāvato”ti.

Now, this is the verbal meaning. Compassion (dayā) 'harms' (dayati, hiṃsati) the compassionate one so long as it does not attain the intended welfare for others; thus it is 'dayā', great compassion. The root 'daya' is in the sense of harming. Or, it is 'dayā' because by it one supports (anuggaṇhāti) even evil people. The root 'daya' is in the sense of supporting. Or, it is 'dayā' because one abandons even one's own happiness and takes on (gaṇhāti) affliction. The root 'daya' is in the sense of taking. Alternatively, it is 'dayā', great compassion, because by means of it the Bodhisattas 'take up' (dayanti, gaṇhanti) both the suffering of saṃsāra and the knowledge of omniscience. For the great Bodhisattas, at the time of making their aspiration for Buddhahood, having relinquished the fruit of arahantship that was even within their grasp, desiring to rescue beings from the ocean of saṃsāra, take upon themselves the comfortless and extremely terrifying suffering of saṃsāra, and in their final existence, together with the attainment of the deathless element, they also take upon themselves the knowledge of omniscience, adorned with countless qualities—such is the meaning. Indeed, all the qualities of the Buddhas are rooted in compassion. Therefore, it is said in the Aṅguttara Sub-commentary: 'Compassion is the origin of all the Buddha's qualities, because it is their foundation'.

Api [M 0.0135] ca dayanti anurakkhanti satte etāya, sayaṃ vā anuddayati anudayamattameva vā etanti dayā. Dayadhātu anurakkhaṇe apaccayo. Udeti vaḍḍhetīti udayo, pabbato. Udidhātu pasavane ṇa. Āsamantato ālokaṃ karonto uṇati gacchatīti aruṇo, sūriyaraṃsī viseso. Āpubbauṇadhātu gatiyaṃ ṇa. Dayāsaṅkhātato udayapabbatato uggatasūriyassa aruṇo yassāti dayudayaruṇo. Atha vā udayapabbatato uggatasūriyāruṇo viya dayā mahākaruṇā yassāti dayudayaruṇo, munindakko. Yathā hi uggatasūriyassa aruṇo ālokassa ādi hoti, evaṃ bodhisatto dīpaṅkarabuddhassa pādamūle karopayātaṃ nibbānasukhamosajja mahākaruṇāya saṃsārasamuddato satte samuddharitukāmo buddhabhāvāya sudukkarā dānādayo dasa pāramiyo ca pañca mahāpariccāge ca kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni akāsīti karuṇā buddhabhāvāya ādi. Tasmā buddhasseva dayudayaruṇoti abhitthavituṃ arahatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, it is 'dayā' because by means of it they protect (anurakkhanti) beings, or because one is compassionate (anuddayati) oneself, or because it is merely compassion (anudayamatta). The root 'daya' is in the sense of protecting, with the suffix 'a'. It rises (udeti) and grows (vaḍḍheti), thus 'udaya', a mountain. The root 'udi' is in the sense of producing, with the suffix 'ṇa'. Making light all around, it moves (uṇati), thus 'aruṇo', a special solar ray. The root 'uṇa' with the prefix 'ā' is in the sense of motion, with the suffix 'ṇa'. He is 'dayudayaruṇo' who has the dawn of the sun that has risen from the rising-mountain called compassion. Or alternatively, he is 'dayudayaruṇo', the Lord of Sages, for whom great compassion is like the dawn of the sun risen from the rising-mountain. For just as the dawn of the risen sun is the beginning of light, so too the Bodhisatta, at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, having set aside the bliss of Nibbāna which was within his grasp, desiring to rescue beings from the ocean of saṃsāra out of great compassion, for the sake of Buddhahood performed for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more the ten perfections beginning with generosity, and the five great sacrifices. Thus, compassion was the beginning for Buddhahood. Therefore, it is said that only the Buddha is worthy to be praised as 'dayudayaruṇo'.

Ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimboti sabbaññutañāṇasaṅkhāto vitthāra parimaṇḍalo. Vitthāracakkavāḷamaṇḍalaṃ viya vipulārammaṇa sabbaññutañāṇavā. Saṅkhatāsaṅkhatabhedaṃ sabbeñeyyadhammaṃ jānātīti ñāṇaṃ, sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Ñādhātu avabodhaneyu. Visesena tanoti vitthāretīti vitthiṇṇaṃ, ñāṇaṃ. Vipubbatanudhātu vitthāre tapaccayo. Tassa iṇṇādeso. Dhātvantassa lopo, asarūpadvittaṃ. Atha vā vittharati pattharatīti vitthiṇṇaṃ. Tharadhātumevettha viseso. Vamati parimaṇḍalākārena gacchati pavattatīti bimbaṃ, ñāṇamaṇḍalaṃ. Vamadhātu gatiyaṃ bo. Assi. Vassa bo.

'Ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo' means one whose orb of knowledge is expansive. He possesses the knowledge of omniscience whose objects are vast, like the vast orb of the world-system. Because it knows all knowable phenomena, distinguished as conditioned and unconditioned, it is 'ñāṇaṃ', the knowledge of omniscience. The root 'ñā' is in the sense of understanding. Because it spreads (tanoti) and extends (vitthāreti) in a special way (visesena), it is 'vitthiṇṇaṃ', knowledge. This is formed from the root 'tanu' with the prefix 'vi' in the sense of spreading, with the suffix 'ta'. For this, there is the substitution of 'iṇṇa', the elision of the root's final consonant, and the doubling of a dissimilar consonant. Alternatively, because it spreads out (vittharati) and extends (pattharati), it is 'vitthiṇṇaṃ'. Here, the root is simply 'thar' with the prefix 'vi'. Because it is emitted (vamati) and proceeds (gacchati, pavattati) in a circular form, it is 'bimbaṃ', the orb of knowledge. The root 'vam' is in the sense of motion, with the suffix 'bo'.

Ṇvādimoggallāne pana “vama uggiraṇe ba. Vamissa vassa bittaṃ. Vamati uggiratīti bimbaṃ, sarīra”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana bimbasaddassa sarīravācake [M 0.0136] yuttameva. Na parimaṇḍalavācake. Idha pana bimbasaddassa parimaṇḍalavācakattā. Ācariyā pana idha bimbasaddassa atthaṃ cakkamaṇḍalanti vadanti. Taṃ pana vicāretabbaṃ. Kasmā, abhidhānappadīpikāyaṃ “bimbaṃ tu paṭibimbe ca, maṇḍale bimbikāphale”ti ca. Taṭṭīkāyañca “maṇḍale paṭimaṇḍale”ti ca vuttattā. Ñāṇaṃ sabbaññutañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ vitthiṇṇaṃ vitthāraṃ bimbaṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ assāti ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo. Atha vā vitthiṇṇaṃ vitthāraṃ bimbaṃ cakkavāḷaparimaṇḍalaṃ viya vipulārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ sabbaññutañāṇaṃ assāti ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo, munindakko. Yathā hi cakkavāḷassa anantattā cakkavāḷamaṇḍalaṃ vipulaṃ mahantaṃ hoti, eva meva buddhassa sabbaññutañāṇaṃ anantārammaṇattā vipulaṃ mahantaṃ. Tasmā tassa ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimboti thometīti. Yvekoti yo ekoti padacchedo. Yekotipi katthaci pāṭho. Tassa pana yo ekoti padacchedo kātabbo. Taṃ pana pāṭhadvayaṃ yuttameva. Yvekoti hi pāṭhe ādesasandhi hoti. Yekoti pāṭhe pana lopasandhīti ayametesaṃ viseso. Yo munindakkoti sambandho.

In the Moggallāna grammar, however, it is said: 'The root 'vam' is in the sense of emitting. The rule is: For 'vam', 'va' becomes 'bi'. Because it emits (vamati, uggirati), it is 'bimbaṃ', the body.' That, however, is indeed appropriate for the word 'bimba' when it denotes the body, not when it denotes an orb. Here, however, the word 'bimba' is used to denote an orb. Some teachers, however, say that the meaning of the word 'bimba' here is 'cakkamaṇḍala' (a circular disc). That should be examined. Why? Because in the Abhidhānappadīpikā it is stated: 'Bimba is used for a reflection, an orb, and the bimbikā fruit.' And in its sub-commentary: 'in an orb, in a circular area.' He is 'ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo' because his knowledge, designated as the knowledge of omniscience, is an expansive, extensive, round orb. Alternatively, he is 'ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo', the Lord of Sages, because his knowledge, the knowledge of omniscience, has vast objects and is an expansive orb like the orb of the world-system. For just as the orb of the world-system is vast and immense because the world-system is infinite, even so, the Buddha's knowledge of omniscience is vast and immense because its objects are infinite. Therefore, he is praised as 'ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo'. The word division of 'yvekoti' is 'yo eko'. In some places, the reading is 'yekoti'. For that, however, the word division 'yo eko' should be made. Both readings are indeed appropriate. For in the reading 'yvekoti', there is a substitution sandhi, whereas in the reading 'yekoti', there is an elision sandhi—this is the difference between them. The connection is with 'yo munindakko'.

Ekoti asahāyo, adutiyako eka buddhabhūtoti attho. Ettha ca ekasaddo aññaseṭṭhāsahāya saṅkhyādīsu dissati. Tathāhesa sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantītiādīsu aññatthe dissati. Cetaso ekodibhāvantiādīsu seṭṭhe. Eko vūpakaṭṭhotiādīsu asahāye. Ekova kho bhikkhave khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyāyātiādīsu saṅkhyāyaṃ. Idha pana asahāye adhippeto. Ayaṃ panassa vacanattho. Asahāyo hutvā eti gacchati pavattatīti eko, adutiyako hutvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ eti jānāti paṭivijjhatīti vā eko, munindakko. Edhātu idhātu vā ñāṇagatīsu ṇvu. Atha vā eko bhagavā pabbajjasaṅkhātena eko. Adutiyaṭṭhena eko, taṇhāya pahānaṭṭhena eko[M 0.0137], ekantavītarāgoti eko, ekantavītadosoti eko, ekantavītamohoti eko, ekantanikkilesoti eko, ekāya maggaṃ gatoti eko, anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti ekotiādinā āgatena mahāniddesanayenapettha attho veditabbo.

'Eko' means 'alone', 'without a second', 'the one who has become a Buddha'—such is the meaning. Here, the word 'eka' is seen in the senses of 'other', 'foremost', 'without a companion', 'number', and so forth. For instance, in passages such as 'some (eke) assert thus: "This self and the world are eternal, this alone is true, all else is false,"' it is seen in the sense of 'other'. In passages such as 'the unification (ekodibhāva) of the mind,' it is in the sense of 'foremost'. In expressions such as 'dwelling alone (eko),' it is in the sense of 'without a companion'. In sayings such as 'Indeed, monks, there is but one (eko) moment, one occasion for the holy life,' it is in the sense of 'number'. Here, however, it is intended in the sense of 'without a companion'. This is its verbal meaning: He is 'eko' because, being without a companion, he goes (eti), proceeds, and continues; or alternatively, he is 'eko', the Lord of Sages, because, being without a second, he comes to (eti), knows, and penetrates the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. The root 'e' or 'i' is in the sense of knowledge and going, with the suffix 'ṇvu'. Alternatively, the Blessed One is 'eko' in the sense of the going forth; he is 'eko' in the sense of being without a second; 'eko' in the sense of having abandoned craving; 'eko' as being utterly free from lust; 'eko' as being utterly free from hatred; 'eko' as being utterly free from delusion; 'eko' as being utterly free from defilements; 'eko' as having gone by the one path; 'eko' as having awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—the meaning here should be understood according to the method of the Mahāniddesa.

Api ca anantacakkavāḷesuyeva ekova buddho eti uppajjati vikasati vāti eko. Vuttañhi ekanipāta aṅguttara pāḷiyaṃ “aṭṭhānametaṃ bhikkhave anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyuṃ, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ṭhānañca kho etaṃ bhikkhave vijjati, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā ekova arahaṃ sammāsambuddho uppajjeyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjatī”ti. Tadaṭṭhakathāyañca “ekissā lokadhātuyāti dasasahassilokadhātuyā. Tīṇi hi khettāni jātikkhettaṃ āṇakkhettaṃ visayakkhettanti. Tattha jātikkhettaṃ nāma dasasahassilokadhātu. Sā hi tathāgatassa mātukucchiṃ okkamanakāle nikkhamanakāle sambodhikāle dhammacakkappavattane āyu saṅkhāravossajjane parinibbāne ca kampati, koṭisatasahassa cakkavāḷaṃ pana āṇakkhettaṃ nāma. Āṭānāṭiyaparitta moraparittadhajaggaparitta ratanaparittādīnañhi ettha āṇā pavattati. Visayakkhettassa pana parimāṇaṃ natthi. Buddhānañhi yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Ñāṇapariyantikaṃ ñeyyaṃ, ñeyyapariyantikaṃ ñāṇanti vacanato avisayo nāma natthi. Imesu pana tīsu khettesu ṭhapetvā imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhā uppajjantīti suttaṃ natthi. Na uppajjantīti pana atthi. Tīṇi hi piṭakāni vinayapiṭakaṃ, suttantapiṭakaṃ, abhidhammapiṭakaṃ. Tisso saṃgītiyo mahākassapattherassa saṃgīti, yasattherassa saṃgīti, moggaliputtattherassa saṃgīti, imā tisso saṃgītiyo [M 0.0138] āruḷhe tepiṭake buddhavacane imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ muñcitvā aññattha buddhā uppajjantīti suttaṃ natthi. Na uppajjantīti pana atthī”ti.

Moreover, in the infinite world-systems, only one Buddha comes forth, arises, and flourishes. As stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Ekanipāta: “Bhikkhus, this is impossible, there is no possibility that two Arahants, Fully Self-Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously in a single world-system; such a possibility does not exist. But, bhikkhus, it is possible, it is conceivable, that a single Arahant, a Fully Self-Enlightened One, should arise in a single world-system; this is a possibility.” Its commentary explains: “‘In a single world-system’ means in a ten-thousandfold world-system. There are three domains: the birth-domain (jātikkhetta), the authority-domain (āṇakkhetta), and the range-domain (visayakkhetta). Among these, the birth-domain is the ten-thousandfold world-system. For it trembles when the Tathāgata enters his mother’s womb, at his birth, at his full enlightenment, when he sets the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, when he relinquishes the life-formation, and at his final Nibbāna. The authority-domain, however, extends to a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, for the authority of protective chants such as the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, the Mora Paritta, the Dhajagga Paritta, and the Ratana Paritta operates there. The range-domain, however, has no limit. For the Buddhas’ knowledge extends as far as the knowable, and the knowable extends as far as their knowledge. Since the knowable is bounded by knowledge and knowledge by the knowable, there is no ‘unreachable domain.’ Among these three domains, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system apart from this one. But there is one stating they do not arise elsewhere. There are three Piṭakas: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. There were three Councils: the Council of the Elder Mahākassapa, the Council of the Elder Yasa, and the Council of the Elder Moggaliputta. In these three Councils, where the Tipiṭaka of the Buddha’s word was established, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise outside this world-system. But there is one stating they do not arise elsewhere.”

Ettha ca ekissā lokadhātuyāti dasasahassi lokadhātuyāti idaṃ jātikkhettaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dasasahassilokadhātu hi imaṃ lokadhātuṃ parivāretvā ṭhitā hoti. Tattakānaṃyeva jātikkhettabhāvo dhammatā vasena veditabbo. Imesu pana tīsu khettesūti iminā dasasahassilokadhātusaṅkhāte jātikkhette koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷasaṅkhāte āṇakkhette anantacakkavāḷa saṅkhāte visayakkhette cāti imesu tīsu buddhakkhettesu ito cakkavāḷato aññesu anantacakkavāḷesu buddhā nuppajjantīti dasseti. Tividhañhi buddhakkhettaṃ dassetvā imesu pana tīsu khettesūti ādhārabhāvena vuttaṃ, na niddhāraṇabhāvena. Kasmā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ niddhāraṇīyapadassa abhāvato. Sati hi aṭṭhakathācariyo tassa padassa niddhāraṇatthe adhippete imesu tīsu khettesu āṇakkhette ṭhapetvā imaṃ cakkavāḷantiādi vucceyya. Na. Tasmā tassa padassa ādhāratthoyeva gahetabbo. Pubbanissayā cariyehi ca tassa padassa ādhārabhāvena atthayojanā katāti. Tatheva pana abhidhammañāṇavibhaṅgapāḷiyañca, tadaṭṭhakathāyañca uparipaṇṇāse bahudhātusuttapāḷiyañca, tadaṭṭhakathāyañca nettipāḷiyañca tadaṭṭhakathāyañca taṃ kāraṇaṃ āgatamevāti. Taṃ aṅguttaraṭīkāyaṃ pana “na uppajjantīti pana atthīti na me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me navijjatītiādi. Imissā lokadhātuyā ṭhatvā vadantena bhagavatā kiṃpanāvuso sāriputta atthetarahi añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā samasamo sambodhiyanti evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ bhante noti vadeyyanti vatvā tassa [M 0.0139] kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyunti imaṃ suttaṃ āharantena dhamma senāpatinā ca buddhakkhettabhūtaṃ imaṃ lokadhātuṃ ṭhapetvā aññattha anuppatti vuttā hotīti adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Tatheva pana ñāṇavibhaṅgamūlaṭīkāyaṃ, uparipaṇṇāsabahudhātu suttaṭīkāyañca vuttaṃ. Ettha ca imaṃ lokadhātuṃ ṭhapetvā aññattha anuppatti vuttā hotīti iminā buddhakkhettabhūtato ito cakkavāḷato aññesu anantacakkavāḷesu buddhānaṃ anuppatti dassitā hoti. Aññatthāti hi sāmaññena vuttepi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttena imesu tīsu khettesūti saddantarasannidhānena anantacakkavāḷabhūto visesattho gahetabbo. Sāmaññavacanopi hi saddo saddantarasannidhānena visesavisayoti.

Here, the phrase “in a single world-system” means “in a ten-thousandfold world-system,” referring to the birth-domain. For a ten-thousandfold world-system stands surrounding this world-system. The fact that only that is the birth-domain should be understood as by way of natural law. Now, with “in these three domains,” it shows that in these three Buddha-domains—namely, the birth-domain reckoned as a ten-thousandfold world-system, the authority-domain reckoned as a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, and the range-domain reckoned as infinite world-systems—Buddhas do not arise in other infinite world-systems apart from this world-system. Indeed, having shown the threefold Buddha-domain, “in these three domains” is stated as a location, not as a determination. Why? Because there is no word implying determination in the commentary. If the commentator had intended a meaning of determination for that phrase, he would have said something like: ‘Among these three domains, setting aside the authority-domain, [it is] in this world-system...’ But he did not. Therefore, that phrase should be taken only in the sense of a location. And earlier teachers have applied the meaning of that phrase as a location due to the previous authority. Similarly, that reason has been stated in the Abhidhamma Ñāṇavibhaṅga Pāḷi and its commentary, in the Bahudhātuka Sutta Pāḷi of the Uparipaṇṇāsa and its commentary, and in the Netti Pāḷi and its commentary. However, in the Aṅguttara Ṭīkā it says: “‘But there is one stating they do not arise elsewhere’ refers to such statements as ‘I have no teacher; there is no one equal to me.’ When the Blessed One, standing in this world-system, asked, ‘What do you think, friend Sāriputta, is there now another ascetic or brahmin equal to the Blessed One in supreme enlightenment?’ and when asked thus, one should answer, ‘No, venerable sir,’ then, in order to show the reason, by bringing forth this sutta, ‘Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is inconceivable, that two Arahants, Fully Self-Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously in a single world-system; such a possibility does not exist,’ the Dhamma General implies that non-arising elsewhere is stated, setting aside this world-system, which is a Buddha-domain.” Similarly, it is stated in the Mūlaṭīkā to the Ñāṇavibhaṅga and in the Ṭīkā to the Bahudhātu Sutta in the Uparipaṇṇāsa. Here, by “setting aside this world-system, non-arising elsewhere is stated,” it is shown that Buddhas do not arise in other infinite world-systems apart from this world-system, which is a Buddha-domain. For even though “elsewhere” is stated generally, due to the presence of the other term “in these three domains” mentioned in the commentary, the specific meaning of ‘infinite world-systems’ should be taken. For even a general statement, due to the presence of another term, can relate to something specific.

Ayaṃ panettha aparo nayo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutte buddhā hi uppajjamānā imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe uppajjanti. Uppajjanaṭṭhāne pana vārite ito aññesu cakkavāḷesu nuppajjantīti vāritameva hotītiettha vākye imasmiṃ yevātipade samabhiniviṭṭho evasaddo nivattāpanāvadhāraṇattho. Etena aññesu anantacakkavāḷesu aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ uppattiṃ nivatteti. Yadipi hi aññesu anantacakkavāḷesu aññe buddhā uppajjeyyuṃ. Evaṃ santesu saṅkhatāsaṅkhatabhedaṃ sabbadhammaṃ jānanto passanto amhākaṃ bhagavā aññacakkavāḷesu aññe buddhā uppajjantīti evaṃ vucceyya. Na. Taṇhaṅkarādayo hi aṭṭhavīsati sambuddhā ito cakkavāḷato aññesu cakkavāḷesu uppajjantītivacanaṃ tepiṭake buddhavacane natthi, tathā aṭṭhakathā ṭīkāsu ca. Tasmā ito cakkavāḷato aññesu ananta cakkavāḷesu aññe buddhā nuppajjantīti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ suttantamahāvaggaṭṭhakathāyaṃ mahāsamayasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ –

Here, moreover, is another approach. According to the commentary, Buddhas, when arising, arise only in this very world-system. When the place of arising is thus restricted, it is thereby established that they do not arise in other world-systems apart from this one. In this sentence, the particle eva in the phrase “in this very” is firmly established, having the meaning of exclusion and determination. By this, the arising of other Buddhas in other infinite world-systems is excluded. Even if other Buddhas were to arise in other infinite world-systems, our Blessed One, who knows and sees all phenomena, with the distinction of conditioned and unconditioned, would have said, “Other Buddhas arise in other world-systems.” But he did not. For the statement that the twenty-eight Buddhas, beginning with Taṇhaṅkara, arise in other world-systems apart from this world-system is not found in the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha’s word, nor in the commentaries and sub-commentaries. Therefore, it should be understood that other Buddhas do not arise in other infinite world-systems apart from this world-system. This was stated in the commentary to the Suttanta Mahāvagga, in the explanation of the Mahāsamaya Sutta—

“Athassa [M 0.0140] etadahosi mādiso buddhoyeva sakkuṇeyya. Atthi pana katthaci añño buddhoti anantāsu lokadhātūsu anantañāṇaṃ pattharitvā olokento aññaṃ buddhaṃ na addasa. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ idāni attanā samaṃ na passeyya. Yo jātadivasepi brahmajālasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena attanā samaṃ apassanto aggohamasmi lokassāti appaṭivattiyaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadi. Evaṃ aññaṃ attanā samaṃ apassitvā cintesī”ti. Tathevetaṃ. Purābhedasutta mahāniddesaṭṭhakathāyañca, taṃ mahāsamayasuttaṭīkāyañca ekissā lokadhātuyāti sutte āgatanayena sabbattheva pana apubbaṃ acarimaṃ dve buddhā nāma na honteva. Tenevāha “anantāsu loka dhātūsu…pe… na addasā”ti saṃvaṇṇeti.

“Then it occurred to him: ‘Only a Buddha like myself would be capable. But is there another Buddha anywhere?’ Surveying the infinite world-systems with infinite knowledge, he saw no other Buddha. And this was no wonder, that he did not now see one equal to himself. For even on the day of his birth, as described in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta, not seeing one equal to himself, he roared the unassailable lion’s roar: ‘I am the foremost in the world!’ Thus, not seeing another equal to himself, he reflected.” So it is. As stated in the commentary on the Mahāniddesa on the Purābhedasutta and in the sub-commentary on the Mahāsamayasutta, in a single world-system—according to the way it is mentioned in the sutta—there are never two Buddhas, neither one before nor one after. Therefore, it is said: “Surveying the infinite world-systems… he saw no other,” and this is explained.

Apaṇṇakajātakaṭṭhakathāyañca “satthā upāsakā heṭṭhā avīciṃ upari bhavaggaṃ paricchedaṃ katvā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu sīlādīhi guṇehi buddhena sadiso nāma natthi. Kuto adhikataro…pe… āhā”ti vuttaṃ. Imāsu dvīsu aṭṭhakathāsu ca anantāsu lokadhātūsūti ca aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsūti ca anantaaparimāṇa saddena vuttaṃ. Tehi dvīhi saddehi ṭīkāvacanena ca anantāsu lokadhātūsu aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ anuppattiṃ dasseti.

In the commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka, it is said: “The Teacher said: ‘Lay followers, having set the boundaries with Avīci below and the pinnacle of existence above, in countless world-systems there is no one equal to the Buddha in virtues such as morality. How then could there be one superior?… thus it is said.’ In these two commentaries, the terms ‘infinite world-systems’ and ‘countless world-systems’ are used. By these two words and the statement in the sub-commentary, the non-arising of other Buddhas in infinite world-systems is shown.

Sammohavinodanīaṭṭhakathāya yojanāyaṃ pana imesu panātiādinā koṭisatasahassa cakkavāḷato aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhā na uppajjantīti ñāpeti. Mayaṃ pana evaṃ vitakkayāma. Aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷeti ito cakkavāḷato aññesu sabbesupi tīsu buddhakkhettesūti atthe gayhamāne sati koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷato aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhā na uppajjantīti viññāyati. Yadi pana aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷeti ito aññasmiṃ jātiāṇākhettabhūte cakkavāḷeti atthe [M 0.0141] gahite koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷato aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhānaṃ uppatti bhaveyyāti viññāyati. “Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā”tiādipāḷiyā ca. “Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve rājāno cakkavattī”tiādipāḷiyā saddhiṃ kathanato koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷato buddhānaṃ anuppatti viya aññissā lokadhātuyā cakkavattirañño anuppatti bhaveyya. Kathāvatthuppakaraṇe ca koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷato aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhānaṃ uppatti na paṭisedhitā. Tasmā āṇakkhettabhūtato koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷato aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhassa bhaveyyāti ayaṃ amhākaṃ khanti. Vīmaṃsetvā gahetabbanti vuttaṃ.

In the Yojanā on the Sammohavinodanī-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is indicated by means of the phrase 'imesu pana' and so on, that Buddhas do not arise in a world-system apart from the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems. We, however, reflect thus: If 'in another world-system' is understood to mean 'in all three Buddha-fields apart from this world-system,' then it is understood that Buddhas do not arise in a world-system apart from the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems. But if 'in another world-system' is taken to mean a world-system that is another sphere of birth and authority, then it would be understood that Buddhas could arise in a world-system beyond the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems. The Pāli texts state: 'It is impossible, it cannot happen, that in one world-element two Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones should arise,' and similarly, 'It is impossible, it cannot happen, that in one world-element two wheel-turning monarchs should arise.' From such statements, it seems that just as Buddhas do not arise outside the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, so too a wheel-turning monarch would not arise in another world-element. Moreover, in the Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa, the arising of Buddhas in a world-system beyond the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems is not prohibited. Therefore, our inclination is that a Buddha could arise in a world-system beyond the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems that constitute the sphere of authority. It is said that this should be examined and then accepted.

Ettha ca yaṃ kathāvatthuppakaraṇe ca…pe… na paṭisedhitāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana kathāvatthupāḷiyaṃ nattheva. Imissā pana sabbadisākathāyaṃ paravādīnaṃ parikappavacanamattameva atthi. Tena vuttaṃ tassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “sabbadisā buddhā tiṭṭhantīti. Āmantā. Puratthimāya disāya buddho tiṭṭhatīti. Nahevaṃ vattabbe…pe… puratthimāya disāya buddho tiṭṭhatīti. Āmantā. Kinnāmo so bhagavā kiṃjacco kiṃgotto, kinnāmā tassa bhagavato mātāpitaro, kinnāmaṃ tassa bhagavato sāvakayugaṃ, ko nāmo tassa bhagavato upaṭṭhako, kiṃdisaṃ cīvaraṃ dhāreti, kiṃdisaṃ pattaṃ dhāreti. Katarasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā nagare vā raṭṭhe vā janapade vāti. Nahevaṃ vattabbe”tyādi.

Here, regarding what was said, that in the Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa... it is not prohibited. That, however, is not found in the Kathāvatthu Pāḷi itself. But in this 'discussion of all directions', there is only the mere speculative assertion of the opponents. Therefore, it is said in that Pāḷi text: 'Do Buddhas exist in all directions?' 'Yes.' 'Does a Buddha exist in the eastern direction?' 'It should not be said so… Does a Buddha exist in the eastern direction?' 'Yes.' 'What is the name of that Blessed One? What is his birth? What is his clan? What are the names of that Blessed One’s parents? What is the name of that Blessed One’s pair of disciples? Who is the name of that Blessed One’s attendant? What kind of robe does he wear? What kind of bowl does he carry? In which village, or market town, or city, or state, or country?' 'It should not be said so,' and so on.

Tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “idāni sabbadisākathā nāma hoti. Tattha catūsu disāsu heṭṭhā uparīti samantato lokadhātusannivesaṃ sabbalokadhātūsu ca buddho atthīti attano vikappasippaṃ uppādetvā sabbadisāsu buddhā tiṭṭhantīti yesaṃ…pe… [M 0.0142] seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa. Paṭiññā itarassa. Puratthimāyāti puṭṭho sakyamuniṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho laddhivasena aññalokadhātuyaṃ ṭhitaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Kinnāmo so bhagavātiādi sace tvaṃ jānāsi. Nāmādivasena naṃ kathehīti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca catūsu disāsu…pe… seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānanti iminā paravādīnaṃ laddhiṃ dasseti. Tattha pana catūsu disāsu ca heṭṭhā ca upari ca iti evaṃ samantato lokadhātusannivesaṃ atthīti yojanā. Yesaṃ…pe… mahāsaṅghikānanti yesaṃ paravādīnaṃ laddhi hoti. Kesaṃ laddhi viya. Mahāsaṅghikānaṃ laddhi seyyathāpīti attho. Te sandhāyāti te paravādīpuggale sandhāya ñāṇena dhāretvā sallakkhetvāti attho. Pucchā sakavādissāti sakavādissa sabbadisāsu buddhā tiṭṭhantīti pucchā hoti. Paṭiññā itarassāti paravādissa paṭijānanā hoti. Puratthimāyāti puṭṭhoti sakavādinā puratthi māyātiādinā pucchite sati. Sakyamuninti sakyavaṃsa khattiyajātibhūtaṃ amhākaṃ gotamabuddhaṃ sandhāya. Paṭikkhipatīti paravādīpuggalo apaneti. Puna puṭṭhoti sakavādinā puna puratthimāya buddho tiṭṭhatīti pucchite sati. Laddhivasenāti attano aññalokadhātuyaṃ buddho atthi ca uppajjati cāti micchāladdhivasena paṭijānātīti paravādī puggalo paṭijānāti. Yadi pana aññalokadhātuyaṃ buddho tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ sati tassa nāmagottādiṃ tvaṃ kathehīti sakavādissa codanāvacanaṃ dassetuṃ kinnāmo so bhagavātiādimāha. Iminā ca ito cakkavāḷato aññesu anantacakkavāḷesu aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ abhāvaṃ dasseti. Tena vuttaṃ kathāvatthupāḷiyaṃ “kinnāmo so bhagavā kiṃjacco…pe… janapadevāti. Nahevaṃ vattabbe”ti.

In its commentary, it is said: 'Now, this is called the discussion about all directions. Therein, it concerns the arrangement of world-systems in the four directions—below, above, and all around. Having generated their own speculative idea, some say, ‘In all world-systems, a Buddha exists,’ and ‘Buddhas stand in all directions’… as, for example, the Mahāsāṅghikas. The question is directed toward them by the proponent. The admission is by the opponent. When asked, ‘In the east?’—referring to the Śākyamuni—he denies it. But when asked again, he admits, based on his own doctrine, that a Buddha exists in another world-system. ‘What is the name of that Blessed One?’ and so on—‘if you know, then tell his name and so forth.’ This is said for the purpose of a challenge. By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere.’ Here, ‘in the four directions… as, for example, the Mahāsāṅghikas’—this shows the doctrine of the opponents. Therein, it connects to the arrangement of world-systems, saying that it exists in the four directions, below, and above—thus, all around. ‘Of whom… as, for example, the Mahāsāṅghikas’—this means those of other schools have such a doctrine. Like whose doctrine? The meaning is: just as it is the doctrine of the Mahāsāṅghikas. ‘Directed toward them’—this means considering and reflecting on those individuals of other schools, holding them in mind with knowledge. ‘The question is by the proponent’ means that the proponent asks, ‘Do Buddhas stand in all directions?’ ‘The admission is by the opponent’ means that the opponent makes an admission. ‘When asked, “In the east?”’ means when the proponent asks, ‘In the east?’ and so on. ‘Referring to the Śākyamuni’ means referring to our Gotama Buddha, who is of the Śākya clan, of khattiya birth. ‘He denies it’ means the opponent rejects it. ‘But when asked again’ means when the proponent asks again, ‘Does a Buddha stand in the east?’ ‘Based on his own doctrine’ means the opponent admits based on his own false doctrine that a Buddha exists and arises in another world-system. To show these words of challenge from the proponent, ‘But if a Buddha stands in another world-system, then, in that case, you tell his name, clan, and so forth,’ he says, ‘What is the name of that Blessed One?’ and so on. By this, he demonstrates the absence of other Buddhas in infinite world-systems other than this world-system. Therefore, it is said in the Kathāvatthu Pāḷi: 'What is the name of that Blessed One? Of what birth?… In what country? It should not be said thus.'

Ettha [M 0.0143] ca pana sakavādinā kinnāmotyādinā pucchite paravādīpuggalo attano laddhiyā sabbalokadhātūsu uppajjamānānaṃ buddhānaṃ nāmādiṃ ajānanto apassanto na hevaṃ vattabbeti paṭikkhipati. Tasmā panettha sakavādī puggalassa laddhiyā aññesu anantacakkavāḷesu aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ uppajjanābhāvo viññāyati. Yadipi hi aññānantacakkavāḷesu aññabuddhā uppajjeyyuṃ. Evaṃ santesu buddhassa matiṃ yathābhūtato jānanto passanto mahāpañño iddhimā dibbacakkhuādīhi chaḷabhiññehi sampanno paṭisambhidā patto satthārā dinnamātikānayena kathāvatthupāḷiṃ desento āyasmā mahāmoggaliputtatthero aññānantacakkavāḷesu aññabuddhānaṃ uppattiṃ katheyya ca. Nāti. Tasmā ayaṃ kathāvatthupāḷi ca tadaṭṭhakathāvacanañca aññānantacakkavāḷesu aññabuddhānaṃ abhāvadīpane sabbaṭṭhakathāṭīkāsu vuttavacanehi daḷhataraṃ padhānavacanameva hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, when the person of the opposing view is questioned by the proponent with 'What is the name?' and so on, that person, not knowing or seeing the names and so on of the Buddhas arising in all world-systems according to his own doctrine, rejects it by saying, 'It should not be said thus.' Therefore, it is understood here that, according to the doctrine of the proponent, there is no arising of other Buddhas in other infinite world-systems. For if other Buddhas were to arise in other infinite world-systems, the Venerable Mahāmoggaliputta Thera—being one of great wisdom who knows and sees the Buddha's intention as it truly is, endowed with psychic power, possessed of the six higher knowledges including the divine eye, having attained the analytical knowledges, and expounding the Kathāvatthu Pāḷi in accordance with the matrix given by the Teacher—would have spoken of the arising of other Buddhas in other infinite world-systems. But he did not. Therefore, this Kathāvatthu Pāḷi and the word of its commentary, in indicating the absence of other Buddhas in other infinite world-systems, should be seen as a stronger and more primary statement than the statements found in all the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

Na pana buddhāeva aññānantacakkavāḷesu na uppajjeyyuṃ, atha kho laddhabyākaraṇā mahābodhisattā ca paccekabodhi sattā aggasāvakamahāsāvakabodhisattā paripākindriyā sāvakabodhisattā ca buddhakkhettabhūte imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe uppajjanti, na aññattha. Kasmā, tesu buddhānaṃ anuppannattā, tesaṃ pana abhinīhāro pāramīsambharaṇaṃ ñāṇaparipācanañca tasmiṃeva samijjhati, na aññattha. Tena vuttaṃ mahāpadāna suttaṭīkāyaṃ –

It is not only that Buddhas do not arise in other infinite world-systems, but also that great Bodhisattvas who have received a prediction, Paccekabodhisattas, chief disciple and great disciple Bodhisattvas, and disciple Bodhisattvas with ripened faculties arise only in this very world-system, which is a Buddha-field, and not elsewhere. Why? Because Buddhas have not arisen in those other world-systems; for them, the aspiration, the accumulation of perfections, and the ripening of wisdom succeed only in this one, not elsewhere. Therefore, it is said in the sub-commentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta—

“Purimabuddhānaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca nibbattiyā sāvakabodhisattānaṃ sāvakabodhiyā abhinīhāro sāvakapāramiyā sambharaṇaṃ paripācanañca buddhakkhettabhūte imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe jambudīpeeva ijjhati, na aññatthā”ti. Tathevetaṃ ekanipātaaṅguttaraṭīkāyañcāti.

The arising of the great Bodhisattvas of former Buddhas and of Paccekabuddhas, the aspiration of disciple Bodhisattvas for disciple-enlightenment, and the accumulation and maturation of the disciple perfections—these succeed only in this world-system, which is a Buddha-field, in Jambudīpa, and not elsewhere. Likewise, this is also stated in the sub-commentary to the Ekanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

Etarahi [M 0.0144] pana apare ācariyā “āṇakkhettabhūtato koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷato aññesu cakkavāḷesu buddhā uppajjantī”ti vadanti. Tesaṃ pana vacanaṃ ayuttameva. Kasmā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutte aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷeti ettha aññasaddassa ṭhapetvā imaṃ cakkavāḷantipadato aññassa apādānassa asambhavato ca anantacakkavāḷesu bahūsu buddhesu uppannesu buddhassa anacchariyattā ca. Acchariyamanusso hi sammāsambuddho. Vuttañhi ekanipāta aṅguttarapāḷiyaṃ

Now, however, other teachers say, 'Buddhas arise in other world-systems beyond the one hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems that constitute the sphere of authority.' But their statement is indeed improper. Why? Because in the commentary, regarding the phrase 'in another world-system,' it is impossible for the word 'another' to have a point of reference other than 'this world-system,' and because if many Buddhas were to arise in infinite world-systems, the Buddha would not be a wondrous being. For a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is indeed a wondrous human being. As it is said in the Ekanipāta of the Aṅguttara Pāḷi:

“Ekapuggalo bhikkhave loke uppajjamāno uppajjati acchariyamanusso. Katamo ekapuggalo, tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. Ayaṃ kho bhikkhave ekapuggalo loke uppajjati acchariyamanusso”ti. Aññaṃ pana kāraṇaṃ mayā heṭṭhā vuttanayenapi viññūhi viññātabbanti. Aññe pana ācariyā buddhaapadānapāḷiyaṃ –

'Monks, one individual arising in the world arises as a wondrous human being. Which individual? The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. This, monks, is the individual who arises in the world as a wondrous human being.' Moreover, other reasons should be understood by the wise through the method stated previously. Other teachers, however, in the Buddha Apadāna Pāḷi—

“Disā dasavidhā loke, yāyato natthi antakaṃ;

Tasmiñca disābhāgamhi, buddhakkhette asaṅkhayā;

Pabhā pakittitā mayhaṃ, yamakā raṃsivāhanā;

Etthantare raṃsijālaṃ, āloko vipulo bhave”ti.

'In the world, there are ten directions, to which there is no end for one who travels. And in that region of the directions, the Buddha-fields are innumerable. My radiance has been proclaimed, twin-like and carrying rays. Within this space, a net of rays, a vast light, would arise.'

Vuttāsu dvīsu gāthāsu paṭhamagāthāya atthaṃ buddhassa anādhippāyena gahetvā micchāñāṇena aññānantacakkavāḷesu uppajjamānā buddhā asaṅkhayāti vadanti. Tesaṃ panetaṃ ayuttameva asundarameva. Kasmā, pāḷiyā ca aṭṭhakathāṭīkāvacanehi ca viruddhattā ca tassā gāthāya atthaggahaṇassa micchattā ca. Imāya hi pāḷiyā gāthāya vā aññānantacakkavāḷesu aññe buddhā uppajjantīti atthe gayhamāne aṭṭhakathāsu imesu pana tīsu khettesu ṭhapetvā imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ aññasmiṃ cakkavāḷe buddhā uppajjantīti suttaṃ natthi, na uppajjantīti pana atthīti vuttavacanena ca, tīṇi hi [M 0.0145] piṭakāni…pe… imā tisso saṃgītiyo āruḷhe tepiṭake buddhavacane…pe… suttaṃ natthi. Na uppajjantīti pana atthīti vuttavacanena ca ujukaṃ virujjhati ca. Bhaddantamahā buddhaghosādayo aṭṭhakathācariyā taṃ pāḷiṃ na passantīti attano duggahitena aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ abbhakkhānaṃ āpajjati ca. Kiṃ panete tipiṭakadharā tikkhavisadajavana gambhīrādiñāṇikā aṭṭhakathācariyā na passeyyuṃ. Passeyyuṃ eva. Tasmā ayuttameva. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana āgataṃ suttaṃ natthītiādivacanameva yuttataraṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding the two verses mentioned, some, taking the meaning of the first verse contrary to the Buddha's intention and with wrong knowledge, say that innumerable Buddhas arise in other infinite world-systems. But this is indeed improper and unfitting. Why? Because it contradicts the Pāḷi, the commentaries, and the sub-commentaries, and because their interpretation of that verse is wrong. For if the meaning of this Pāḷi verse were taken to be that other Buddhas arise in other infinite world-systems, it would directly contradict the statement made in the commentaries: 'apart from this world-system, there is no sutta declaring that Buddhas arise in other world-systems, but there is one stating that they do not arise.' And it would directly contradict the word of the Buddha, contained in the Tipiṭaka and established in these three recensions, where it is stated that 'there is no sutta to that effect, but there is one stating that they do not arise.' Furthermore, by asserting through one's own wrong grasp that the venerable great commentators like Buddhaghosa did not see that Pāḷi text, one incurs the fault of slandering the commentators. How could these commentators, who uphold the Tipiṭaka and possess sharp, clear, swift, and profound wisdom, not have seen it? They surely would have seen it. Therefore, that assertion is improper. Instead, the statement found in the commentaries, 'there is no sutta,' and so on, should be seen as the more fitting one.

Ettha ca buddhakkhettetipadaṃ tasmiñca disābhāgamhītipade visesanaṃ, asaṅkhayātipadaṃ dutiyagāthāya pabhātipadassa visesananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha yojanā. Loke cakkavāḷaloke dasavidhā dasa koṭṭhāsā disā honti. Tattha koṭṭhāse yāyato yāyantassa gacchantassa me antakaṃ pariyosānaṃ natthi. Buddhakkhette buddhassa dasasahassisaṅkhātajātikkhettabhūte tasmiñca disābhāgamhi mayhaṃ asaṅkhayā saṅkhārahitā yamakā yugaḷā yugaḷā hutvā raṃsivāhanā raṃsivahantā raṃsimuñcamānā vā pabhā cakkaratanamaṇiratanādīnaṃ ālokā pakittitā pākaṭā pattharitā vā. Etthantare dasasahassacakkavāḷantare raṃsijālaṃ raṃsisamūhena vipulo bahutaro āloko bhave ahosinti. Ayamattho cakkindābhisirīsaddhamma dhajamahādhammarājādhirājagurūtiladdhalañchitena ācariyabudhena likhitoti daṭṭhabbo.

Here, the term 'buddhakkhette' should be understood as a qualifier for the phrase 'tasmiñca disābhāgamhi,' and the term 'asaṅkhayā' as a qualifier for the word 'pabhā' in the second part of the verse. This is the construction here: In the world, the world-system, there are ten kinds, ten portions, of directions. In that portion, for me traveling and going, there is no end or limit. In the Buddha-field—the birth-field known as the ten-thousandfold world-system—in that very region of direction, my innumerable (countless), paired (twin-like), ray-carrying (ray-bearing or ray-emitting) radiances—the lights of the Wheel-Treasure, the Jewel-Treasure, and so on—are proclaimed (made manifest or spread out). Within this—within the ten-thousandfold world-system—a net of rays, a vast and abundant light, arose from the multitude of rays. This meaning, it should be understood, was written by the teacher Acariya Buddha, who was honored with the title Cakkindābhisirīsaddhamma-dhaja-mahādhammarājādhirājaguru.

Bhagavā hi imāhi gāthāhi cakkavattirājakāle mayhaṃcakkaratanamaṇīratanādīnaṃ asaṅkhayā pabhā buddhakkhettabhūte dasasahassicakkavāḷe pākaṭā pattharitāti dasseti. Na anantacakkavāḷesu uppajjanabuddhānaṃ asaṅkhayabhāvanti.

Indeed, by these verses, the Blessed One shows that during the time he was a Wheel-Turning Monarch, his innumerable radiances from the Wheel-Treasure, Jewel-Treasure, and so forth, were made manifest and spread throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system, which is the Buddha-field. He does not show the innumerability of Buddhas arising in infinite world-systems.

Vuttañhetaṃ [M 0.0146] buddhaapadānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “disā dasavidhā loketi cakkavāḷaloke dasavidhā dasakoṭṭhāsā disā honti. Tattha koṭṭhāse yāyato yāyantassa gacchantassa antakaṃ natthīti attho. Cakkavattikāle tasmiṃ mayā gataṭṭhāne disābhāge vā buddhakkhette buddhavisayā asaṅkhayā saṅkhārahitā. Pabhā pakittitāti tadā cakkavatti rājakāle mayhaṃ pabhā cakkaratanamaṇiratanādīnaṃ pabhā ālokā yamakā yugaḷā yugaḷā hutvā raṃsivāhanā raṃsimuñcamānā pakittitā pākaṭā. Etthantare dasasahassacakkavāḷantare raṃsijālaṃ raṃsisamūhaṃ āloko vipulo bahutaro bhave ahosinti attho”ti. Ettha ca paṭhamagāthāya pubbaḍḍhassa ekavākyabhāvato disā dasavidhā loketi cakkavāḷaloke…pe… antakaṃ natthīti atthoti vuttaṃ. Aparaḍḍhassa dutiyagāthāyaṃ antogadhattā cakkavattikāle…pe… asaṅkhayā saṅkhārahitā pabhā pakittitāti tadā cakkavattikāle…pe… bhave ahosinti atthoti vuttaṃ. Tasmā asaṅkhayātipadaṃ dutiyagāthāya pabhātipadassa visesananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

This is stated in the commentary on the Buddha's Apadāna: '“The world has ten directions”—meaning that in the world of the universe, there are ten kinds of divisions, ten sectors of directions. In those sectors, for one who goes on and on, there is no end—such is the meaning. During the time of the Wheel-Turning Monarch, in the place where I had gone, in that region or direction, within the Buddha-field, the Buddha's domains were countless, immeasurable. “Radiance was proclaimed”—meaning that at that time, during the time of the Wheel-Turning Monarch, my radiance—the radiance of the wheel-treasure, the gem-treasure, and so on—being in pairs, bearing rays, emitting rays, was proclaimed and made manifest.
