In the space of the ten-thousandfold world-system, a net of rays, a mass of rays, a vast and abundant light would arise—such is the meaning.’ Here, because the first half of the first verse is a single sentence, it is said: ‘“The world has ten directions”—meaning in the world of the universe… there is no end—such is the meaning.’ And because the latter half of the first verse is included in the second verse, it is said: ‘During the time of the Wheel-Turning Monarch… countless, immeasurable radiance was proclaimed’ means ‘during the time of the Wheel-Turning Monarch… there would be an abundance—such is the meaning.’ Therefore, the word ‘countless’ should be understood as a qualifier for the word ‘radiance’ in the second verse.

Jinālaṅkāraṭīkāyaṃ pana evamassa sabbadhammesu appaṭihata ñāṇācāraṃ dassetvā idāni loke tādisassa aññassa abhāvaṃ dassento āha.

In the Jinālaṅkāraṭīkā, however, having shown his unimpeded knowledge and conduct in all phenomena, it now states, to show the absence of another such being in the world:

“Anantasattesu ca lokadhātusu,

Ekova sabbepi samā na tenā”ti.

“And in infinite world-systems of beings, not even one is equal to him, much less all.”

Tattha anantalokadhātūsu ekekissaṃ lokadhātuyā anantasattesu tena tathāgatena samo ekopi natthi. Sace eko pana samo na bhaveyya. Sabbe sattā ekajjhaṃ hutvā samā bhaveyyunti ce. Tathāpi natthi, sabbe ekajjhaṃ hutvāpi iminā ekakena samā na hontīti adhippāyoti [M 0.0147] vuttaṃ. Ettha ca anantalokadhātusūtiādinā ito cakkavāḷato aññesu anantacakkavāḷesu aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ abhāvaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ pana mayā pathavojaṃ uddharitvā dassito viya dassitehi atidaḷhatarehi sādhakavacanehi ito cakkavāḷato aññacakkavāḷesu buddhā uppajjantīti micchāvādo sūriyo andhakāraṃ paṭihanati viya paṭihaniyati apaniyatīti saddhahakaṃ daṭṭhabboti.

In those infinite world-systems, in each world-system with infinite beings, there is not even one equal to that Tathāgata. If there were not even one equal, and suppose all beings were to come together and become equal, even then they would not be equal to this single one—this is the intended meaning. Here, by the phrase 'in the infinite world-systems' and so on, it shows the absence of other Buddhas in other infinite world-systems beyond this world-system. Thus, just as the sun dispels darkness, so too is the false view that Buddhas arise in other world-systems beyond this world-system refuted and removed by these extremely firm words of proof, as if I had extracted the earth's essence and shown it. This should be understood by the faithful.

Munindakkoti muninda akkoti padacchedo. Buddhādiccoti attho. Sabbadhamme manati jānātīti muni. Manadhātu ñāṇe i. Makāre assuttaṃ. Atha vā munāti sabbadhamme saka sāmaññalakkhaṇādinā paṭivijjhatīti muni. Munati hitāhitaṃ paricchindatīti vā muni, bhagavā. Munadhātu paṭivijjhane, catusaccadhamme munāti jānātīti vā monaṃ. Catumaggañāṇaṃ. Vuttañhi saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “monanti catumaggañāṇaṃ. Tañhi munātīti monaṃ, catusaccadhamme jānātīti attho”ti. Monaṃ assa atthīti muni, bhagavā. Muni ca so indati veneyyasatte dhammena abhibhavati indo cāti munindo, bhagavā. Atha vā munīnaṃ pañcamunīnaṃ indoti munindo, bhagavā. Na kamati na gacchati pādena attano puññajavimānena gacchatīti akko, ādicco. Napubba kamudhātu gatiyaṃ kvi. Dhātvantalopo. Kassa dvittaṃ. Atha vā yugandharubbedhappamāṇe ākāse arati gacchatīti akko. Aradhātu gamane kapaccayo. Kassa dvittaṃ. Taṃ taṃ rāsito taṃ taṃ rāsiṃ arati yātīti vā akko. Atha vā mahantajutatāya akkiyati abhitthaviyati tappasannehi janehīti akko, ādicco. Akkadhātu thavane a. Munindo ca so akko cāti munindakko, akko ādicco viya vā munindoti munindakko, buddho. Yathā hi sūriyo attano [M 0.0148] sahassaraṃsiyā ekacakkavāḷe timirandhakāraṃ vidhametvā dine dine navayojanasatasahassappadesaṃ koṭisahassappadesaṃ vā dasadisaṃ vā obhāsetvā virocamāno carati, evameva bhagavāpi attano saddhammaraṃ siyā buddhakkhettabhūtesu dasasahassacakkavāḷesu vineyyānaṃ avijjandhakāraṃ vidhametvā dine dine tasmiṃ tasmiṃ disābhāge veneyyasattasamūhaṃ catusaccadhammobhāsena jotayamāno virocanaṃ caratīti ṭhānānurūpaṃ munindakkoti thometi. Ayaṃ samāsopamā hīnūpamāti daṭṭhabbā.

The word 'Munindakka' is a compound of 'Muninda' and 'Akka'. Its meaning is 'Buddha-sun'. One who knows, who discerns all phenomena, is called a 'muni'. The root 'man' is used in the sense of knowledge, with the suffix 'i', and the 'm' is not heard. Alternatively, a 'muni' is one who penetrates all phenomena by their specific and universal characteristics, etc. Or, a 'muni' is the Blessed One who discerns what is beneficial and harmful. The root 'mun' is used in the sense of penetration. Or, 'monaṃ' is the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths; it is the fourfold path-knowledge. As stated in the Saṃyuttaṭṭhakathā: '“Monaṃ” refers to the fourfold path-knowledge. It is called “monaṃ” because it comprehends; the meaning is that it knows the Four Noble Truths.' One who possesses 'monaṃ' is a 'muni'—the Blessed One. He is a 'muni' and also an 'inda' (lord), for he overcomes trainable beings through the Dhamma; thus, he is 'Muninda'—the Blessed One. Alternatively, 'Muninda' means the lord of the sages, of the five sages—the Blessed One. 'Akka' means 'one who does not walk or go by foot,' for he travels by his merit-born celestial mansion; it also means 'the sun.' The root 'kam' (to move) is prefixed by 'na', with the suffix 'kvi', the end of the root is dropped, and the 'k' is doubled. Alternatively, 'Akka' is one who traverses the sky to the height of the Yugandhara mountain. The root 'ara' (to go) is used with the suffix 'ka', and the 'k' is doubled. Or, 'Akka' is one who moves from one constellation to another. Alternatively, 'Akka' is the sun, so called because he is praised by devoted people due to his great radiance. The root 'akk' is used in the sense of praise, with the suffix 'a'. He is the Muninda and also the Akka, thus 'Munindakka'. Or, the Muninda is like the sun (ādicca), thus 'Munindakka', the Buddha. For just as the sun, with its thousand rays, dispels the darkness in a single world-system and illuminates a region of nine hundred thousand yojanas or a thousand koṭis of regions in the ten directions each day, shining brilliantly as it moves—even so, the Blessed One, with the rays of his true Dhamma, dispels the darkness of ignorance in the ten-thousand world-systems that are Buddha-fields. Each day, in various regions, he illuminates assemblies of trainable beings with the radiance of the Four Noble Truths, shining as he moves. Thus, in accordance with the context, he is praised as 'Munindakka'. This is a compound simile, an inferior simile, and should be understood as such.

Suddheti rāgādimalehi visuddhe. Sujjhati visujjhatīti suddho, tibhavo. Sudhadhātu soceyyeti. Tibhava kuhareti tibhavasaṅkhātakamalasare. Kamalasaraṃ viya tibhavasmiṃ vā bhavanti sattā etthāti bhavo. Bhūdhātu sattāyaṃ ṇa. Tayo bhavā tibhavā, kāmarūpārūpabhūmi labbhati. Kuṃ vuccati udakaṃ, taṃ haratīti kuharo. Kupubbaharadhātu haraṇe a. Tayo bhavā ca te kuharo cāti tibhavakuharo, kuharo viya tayo bhavāti vā tathā. Tasmiṃ tibhavakuhare. Kamala kathitanti uppalanti kathetabbaṃ kaṃ jalaṃ alayati vibhūsayatīti kamalaṃ, uppalaṃ. Kaṃsaddūpapada aladhātu vibhūsane a. Atha vā kamiyati icchiyatīti kamalaṃ. Kamudhātu icchāyaṃ alapaccayo. Kamalanti uppalanti kathiyatīti kamalakathitaṃ. Vineyyappāṇoghanti vineyyapāṇaoghanti padavibhāgo. Vinetabbasattasamūhanti attho. Vinetabbo dametabbo satthārāti vineyyo, satto. Vipubbanidhātu damane ṇyo. Paṇanti jīvanti sattā anenāti pāṇaṃ, jīvitindriyaṃ. Paṇadhātu jīvāyaṃ ṇa. Taṃ assa atthi tasmiṃ vā vijjatīti pāṇo, satto. Assatthitaddhite ṇapaccayo. Vineyyo ca so pāṇo cāti vineyyappāṇo. Avayavena [M 0.0149] saha hanati gacchati pavattatīti ogho, samūho. Avapubba hanadhātu gatiyaṃ ṇo. Avassa o. Hanassa gho. Vineyyappāṇānaṃ ogho samūhoti vineyyappāṇogho, taṃ.

The word `suddhe` means: in that which is pure, purified from defilements such as lust. `Suddho` (pure) means 'is purified, is thoroughly purified,' referring to the three realms. The root 'sudh' means 'to cleanse.' 'Tibhavakuhare' (in the hollow of the three realms) refers to the lotus-pond that is the three realms. Just as beings exist in a lotus-pond, so do they exist in the three realms; thus, 'bhava' (existence). The root 'bhū' (to be) with the suffix 'ṇa' is in the sense of 'being'. The three realms are the three existences, namely, the planes of sensuality, form, and formlessness. 'Ku' is said to be water; that which carries it is 'kuhara' (hollow). The root 'har' preceded by 'ku' is in the sense of carrying, with the suffix 'a'. The three realms and that hollow are 'tibhavakuharo', or alternatively, the three realms are like a hollow. In that hollow of the three realms. 'Kamala' (lotus) is said to be 'uppala' (water lily); 'kaṃ' (water) it adorns and beautifies, thus 'kamala', the water lily. The root 'al' (to adorn) with the suffix 'a', is preceded by the word 'kaṃ'. Alternatively, that which is desired is 'kamala'. The root 'kam' (to desire) is used with the suffix 'ala'. 'Kamala' is said to be 'uppala', thus 'kamalakathitaṃ' (spoken of as lotus). 'Vineyyappāṇoghaṃ' is a division of words: 'vineyya-pāṇa-ogha'. The meaning is 'a multitude of beings to be tamed'. One to be tamed, to be disciplined by the Teacher, is a `vineyyo`, a being. The root 'nī' (to lead) with the prefix 'vi' is in the sense of taming, with the suffix 'ṇya'. 'Pāṇaṃ' (life) means beings live by this, thus it is the life faculty. The root 'paṇ' (to live) is used with the suffix 'ṇa'. That which has it or in which it exists is a `pāṇo`, a living being. The suffix 'ṇa' is added in the sense of 'having' in a possessive derivative. That which is both `vineyyo` and `pāṇo` is `vineyyappāṇo`. That which strikes, goes, or proceeds along with its parts is an `ogho` (flood), a multitude. The root 'han' (to strike) with the prefix 'ava' is in the sense of going, with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Ava' becomes 'o', 'han' becomes 'gho'. The flood or multitude of beings to be tamed is `vineyyappāṇogho`, that.

Dhammaraṃsivarehīti uttamadhammasaṅkhātaraṃsīhi. Ettha ca dhammoti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne satte catūsu apāyesu vaṭṭadukkhesu ca apatamāne katvā dhāretīti dhammo. Dharadhātu dhāraṇe rammapaccayo. Dhāreti ca apāyādinibbattakakilesaṃ viddhaṃsetīti attho. Caturiyamaggo ca nibbānañca nippariyāyato labbhati. Kasmā, ariyamaggassa kilesānaṃ samucchedappahānavasena samucchedakattā, nibbānassa ca nissaraṇappahānavasena tassa ārammaṇabhāvaṃ patvā tadatthasiddhihetuttā. Caturiyaphalañca pariyattidhammo ca pariyāyato labbhati. Kasmā, phalassa maggena viddhaṃsi tabbānaṃ kilesānaṃ paṭippassambhanappahānavasena maggānukūlappa vattattā. Pariyattidhammassa ca tadaṅgappahānavasena tadadhigama hetuttā. Atha vā kilese dhunāti kampati calati viddhaṃsetīti dhammo, caturiyamaggo. Dhunadhātu kampane rammo. Ariyehi dhāriyati paṭivijjhiyati sacchikariyati ārammaṇa karaṇavasenāti dhammo, nibbānaṃ. Dharadhātu ñāṇe. Dhaṃseti paṭippassambheti maggappahīnakilesavāsananti dhammo, ariyaphalaṃ. Dhaṃsadhātu viddhaṃsane. Attano sabhāvaṃ dhāreti ca dhāriyati ca paṇḍitehi na bālehīti dhammo, pariyattidhammo. Dhammo ca dhammo ca dhammo ca dhammo cāti dhammo eka sesanayena, dasavidho dhammo labbhati. Vuttañhetaṃ chattavimāne –

'By the excellent rays of the Dhamma' (Dhammaraṃsivarehi) means by the rays designated as the supreme Dhamma. Here, 'Dhamma' refers to that which holds beings, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery and the suffering of the cycle of existence, as they practice according to what has been taught. The root 'dhar' means 'to hold,' with the 'ramma' suffix. And 'it holds' means that it destroys the defilements that lead to rebirth in states of misery. The fourfold Noble Path and Nibbāna are taken in the primary sense. Why? Because the Noble Path cuts off defilements by way of eradication, and Nibbāna, by way of abandoning through escape, having become its object, is the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose. The fourfold Noble Fruit and the Dhamma of the scriptures are taken in a secondary sense. Why? Because the fruit, by way of abandoning through tranquillization the defilements destroyed by the path, acts in conformity with the path. And the Dhamma of the scriptures, by way of abandoning by substitution of opposites, is the cause for its attainment. Alternatively, 'Dhamma' is that which shakes, agitates, moves, and destroys defilements, namely, the fourfold Noble Path. The root 'dhun' means 'to shake,' with the 'ramma' suffix. Nibbāna is called 'Dhamma' because it is held, penetrated, and realized by the Noble Ones by way of being made an object. The root 'dhar' here is in the sense of knowledge. The Noble Fruit is called 'Dhamma' because it destroys and pacifies the residual impressions of defilements abandoned by the path. The root 'dhaṃs' means 'to destroy.' The Dhamma of the scriptures is called 'Dhamma' because it holds its own nature and is held by the wise, not by fools. Thus, by the method of 'ekasesa' (retention of one), 'Dhamma' is understood in ten ways. As stated in the Chatta Vimāna:

“Rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ,

Dhammamasaṅkhatamappaṭikūlaṃ;

Madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ,

Dhammamimaṃ saraṇattamupehī”ti.

Free from lust, without agitation, sorrowless, the unconditioned Dhamma, unobjectionable; this sweet, excellent, well-divided Dhamma, go to this Dhamma for refuge.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0150] panettha yojanā. Māṇava rāgavirāgaṃ rāgavigataṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ maggadhammañca anejaṃ ejāsaṅkhātataṇhāvirahitaṃ asokaṃ sokavirahitaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ phaladhammañca, asaṅkhataṃ saṅkhatavirahitaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ nibbānadhammañca. Appaṭikūlaṃ avirodhanaṃ madhuraṃ atthabyañjana sampannattā madhuraṃ, paguṇaṃ pakaṭṭhaguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ suṭṭhu vibhajitabbaṃ, imaṃ dhammaṃ pariyattidhammañca saraṇattaṃ saraṇabhāvaṃ upehi upagacchāhīti.

Herein is the explanation. O young man, go for refuge to this Dhamma: the path-Dhamma, which is 'rāgavirāga,' meaning devoid of lust; the fruit-Dhamma, which is 'aneja,' meaning devoid of the craving called agitation, and 'asoka,' meaning devoid of sorrow; the Nibbāna-Dhamma, which is 'asaṅkhata,' meaning devoid of the conditioned; and the scriptural Dhamma, which is 'appaṭikūla,' meaning non-opposing, 'madhura,' meaning sweet because it is endowed with meaning and expression, 'paguṇa,' meaning possessing excellent qualities, and 'suvibhatta,' meaning to be thoroughly analyzed. 'Go for refuge' (`upehi`) means to attain the state of being a refuge (`saraṇabhāvaṃ upagacchāhi`).

Ettha hi kāmarāgādibhedo sabbopi rāgo virajjati pahiyati etenāti rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Ejāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāya antonijjhānalakkhaṇassa ca sokassa taduppattiyā sabbaso parikkhīṇattā anejama sokanti phalaṃ kathitaṃ. Kenaci paccayena asaṅkhatattā dhammamasaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ. Avirodhadīpanato pana atthabyañjanassa sampannatāya pakaṭṭhaguṇavibhāvanato suṭṭhu vibhajitattā ca appaṭikūlantiādinā sabbopi pariyatti dhammo kathito. Vuttañhi tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ettha hi rāgavirāganti maggo kathito. Anejamasokanti phalaṃ. Dhammamasaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ. Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattanti piṭakattayena vibhattā sabbadhammakkhandhā”ti. Idha pana sāmaññato dasavidho dhammo. Visesato pana pariyatti dhammo adhippeto. Kasmā, subodhesīti vuccamānattā. Raṃsīti rasiyanti assādiyantīti raṃsī, rasanti assādenti sattā etāyāti vā raṃsī, rasadhātu assādane a ca ī ca. Atha vā rasiyati sinehiyati taṃ janehīti raṃsī. Rasadhātu sinehe. Niggahītāgamo.

Here, indeed, all lust, such as sensual lust, fades away and is abandoned by this; thus, 'rāgavirāga' (the fading away of lust) is said to be the path. Because craving, called agitation, and sorrow, characterized by inner burning, are completely exhausted by its arising; thus, 'aneja' (without agitation) and 'asoka' (sorrowless) are said to be the fruit. Because it is unconditioned by any cause, 'Dhamma-asaṅkhata' (the unconditioned Dhamma) is said to be Nibbāna. Moreover, because it illuminates non-opposition, is endowed with meaning and expression, manifests excellent qualities, and is thoroughly divided; thus, all the Dhamma of the scriptures is said to be 'appaṭikūla' (unobjectionable) and so forth. As stated in its commentary: 'Here, indeed, 'rāgavirāga' is said to be the path. 'Anejamasoka' is the fruit. 'Dhamma-asaṅkhata' is Nibbāna. 'Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ' (unobjectionable, sweet, excellent, well-divided) refers to all the aggregates of Dhamma divided into the three Pitakas.' Here, however, Dhamma is generally taken in ten ways. But specifically, the Dhamma of the scriptures is intended. Why? Because it is said to be 'subodhesi' (you illuminated well). 'Raṃsī' (rays) means they are savored, delighted in. Or, beings savor and delight through them, thus 'raṃsī'. The root 'ras' is in the sense of savoring, with 'a' and 'ī'. Alternatively, 'raṃsī' means it is cherished by people. The root 'ras' is in the sense of affection. The 'niggahīta' (nasal sound) is an augment.

Varoti uttamo, varitabbo patthitabboti varo, varati nivāreti hīnanti vā varo. Varadhātu patthane nivāraṇe vā a. Dhammo ca so raṃsi cāti dhammaraṃsi, dhammassa vā raṃsi dhammaraṃsi. Ayaṃ pana samāso abhedūpacārena vutto[M 0.0151]. Varo ca so dhammaraṃsi cāti dhammaraṃsivaro, tehi dhammaraṃsivarehi. Subodhesīti catusaccadhammaṃ paṭivijjhayamānena suṭṭhu pabodhesi vikāsetīti attho. Yathā hi sūriyo attano raṃsiyā phusayitvā kuhara saṅkhāte sare jātaṃ uppalaṃ vikāseti, evameva bhagavāpi attano dhammadesanāsaṅkhātaraṃsiyā kamalasarasaṅkhāte bhavattaye vasantaṃ puññūpanissayaṃ paṭivijjhārahaṃ kamala saṅkhātaṃ vineyyappāṇoghaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ paṭivijjhayamāno phaladhammena pabodhesi vikāsetīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Vara' (excellent) means supreme; it should be chosen, desired, thus 'vara'; or it wards off the inferior, thus 'vara'. The root 'var' is in the sense of desiring or preventing, with 'a'. That which is both Dhamma and a ray is 'dhammaraṃsi', or the ray of the Dhamma is 'dhammaraṃsi'. This compound, however, is stated by way of the figure of speech of non-difference. That which is both 'vara' and 'dhammaraṃsi' is 'dhammaraṃsivara'; by those 'dhammaraṃsivara' (excellent rays of the Dhamma). 'Subodhesi' (you illuminated well) means, by penetrating the Dhamma of the four Noble Truths, you thoroughly awakened and unfolded it. Just as the sun, by touching with its rays, causes the lotus born in a pond to bloom, even so the Blessed One, by the ray called his Dhamma-teaching, penetrating the Dhamma of the four Noble Truths, awakened and unfolded by means of the fruit-Dhamma the multitude of beings to be tamed, who are like lotuses, dwelling in the three existences which are like lotus-ponds, and are worthy of penetration through the support of merit. Thus, it is said that he awakened and unfolded them.

Byāpitakkittinañcāti tiloke patthaṭaparikittanaṃ. Sīlādiguṇehi patthaṭathutighosikanti attho. Casaddo cettha padapūraṇamattoyeva. Visesena vividhaṃ vā āpati vaḍḍhatīti byāpito. Vipubbaāpadhātu byāpane vaḍḍhane vā ta. Byāpanaṃ vā byāpitaṃ. Kittiyate abhitthaviyate kittinaṃ. Bhāvasādhanoyaṃ. Thutikriyā labbhati. Kittiyati abhitthaviyati devamanussehīti kittinaṃ, thutighoso. Kittadhātu abhitthavane yu. Byāpito patthaṭo kittano thutighoso yassa soti byāpitakkittino, munindakko. Taṃ. Bhagavato hi tiloke devamanussehi sīlādiguṇehi ca arahaṃ sammāsambuddhotyādīhi guṇehi ca thomito kittisaddo yāva bhavaggaṃ abbhuggacchatīti byāpitakkittinanti thometīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Byāpitakkittinañca' (and of widespread fame) means one whose praise is widespread in the three worlds. The meaning is 'one whose sound of praise is spread by virtues such as morality'. Here, the particle 'ca' is merely an expletive. 'Byāpita' means that which spreads and increases in various ways. It is from the root 'āp' preceded by 'vi' in the sense of spreading or increasing, with the 'ta' suffix. Or, the act of spreading ('byāpana') is 'byāpita'. Praising or extolling is 'kittinaṃ'. This is a noun formed in the sense of an action, referring to the act of praising. That which is praised or extolled by gods and humans is 'kittinaṃ', the sound of praise. It is from the root 'kitt' in the sense of extolling, with the 'yu' suffix. He whose sound of praise is widespread is 'byāpitakkittino', the chief of sages. To him (`taṃ`). Indeed, the sound of praise for the Blessed One, extolled by gods and humans in the three worlds for virtues such as morality and for qualities such as being an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, rises up to the highest state of existence; thus, it is said that he is praised as 'byāpitakkittino'.

Tilokekaccakkhunti tiloke ekacakkhūti padacchedo. Kāmarūpa arūpasaṅkhātānaṃ tilokānaṃ ekaṃ paññācakkhubhūtanti attho. Tayo lokā tilokaṃ. Tassa cakkhu viya eka bhūtaṃpaññācakkhu yassa soti tilokekaccakkhu, munindakko. Ettha ca ekacakkhusaddassa lopo hoti brahmassarotiādīsu viya. Atha vā tilokassa ekaṃ paññācakkhuṃ bhūto pattoti tilokekaccakkhu, munindakko. Tilokekaccakkhubhūtanti vattabbe chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ bhūtasaddalopaṃ katvā [M 0.0152] tilokekaccakkhunti vuttaṃ. Atha vā tilokassa ekabhūto paññācakkhu hutvā sabbadhamme cakkhati passatīti tilokekaccakkhu, munindakko. Taṃ. Bhagavā hi paññācakkhu mayattā sattesu ca taduppādanato tilokassa cakkhubhūto ñāṇabhūto dhammabhūto brahmabhūto hoti. Vuttañhi madhupiṇḍikasutte “so hāvuso bhagavā jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passati cakkhubhūto ñāṇabhūto dhammabhūto brahmabhūto vattā pavattā atthassa ninnetā amatassa dātā dhammassāmī tathāgato”ti. Tasmā tilokekaccakkhunti thometi.

“Tilokekaccakkhu” is a compound of “tiloke ekacakkhu,” meaning “the one eye in the three worlds.” The meaning is that he has become the one eye of wisdom for the three worlds, designated as the realms of sensuality, form, and formlessness. The three worlds are “tiloka.” He is “tilokekaccakkhu,” the chief of sages, because for him the eye of wisdom has become the one eye for the three worlds. Here, there is an elision of the word `ekacakkhu`, as in phrases like `brahmassaro`. Alternatively, he is “tilokekaccakkhu,” the chief of sages, because he has become and attained the one eye of wisdom for the three worlds. Though it should be said “tilokekaccakkhubhūta” (one who has become the one eye of the three worlds), the word “bhūta” is omitted to preserve the meter, so it is said “tilokekaccakkhu.” Or, he is “tilokekaccakkhu,” the chief of sages, because, having become the one eye of wisdom for the three worlds, he sees and beholds all phenomena. To him (`taṃ`). Indeed, the Blessed One, being constituted of the eye of wisdom and because he gives rise to it in beings, becomes the eye for the three worlds, becomes knowledge, becomes Dhamma, becomes Brahma. As it is said in the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta: “Friends, the Blessed One, knowing, knows; seeing, sees. He is the eye, knowledge, Dhamma, Brahma—the speaker, the expounder, the guide to the meaning, the giver of the deathless, the master of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.” Therefore, he is praised as “the one eye of the three worlds.”

Dukhamasahananti puthujjanehi atidukkhamitaṭṭhānaṃ khamanaṃ. Puthujjanehi dukkhena kasirena khamitabbanti dukhamaṃ, iṭṭhāniṭṭhādi ārammaṇaṃ. Dukkhamanti vattabbe gajjabandhattā chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ kakāralopaṃ katvā dukhamanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ sahati khamatīti dukhamasahano, munindakko. Sahadhātu parisahane yu. Taṃ dukhamasahanaṃ. Bhagavā hi puthujjanehi sudukkhamitaṃ iṭṭhā niṭṭhādiārammaṇaṃ sītuṇhādiṃ lābhālābhayasāyasa nindapasaṃsasukhadukkhasaṅkhātaṃ lokadhammañca ativiya khamati adhivāseti, tasmā dukhamasahananti thometi.

“Dukhamasahana” means the endurance of that which is extremely difficult for ordinary people to bear. That which ordinary people endure with difficulty and hardship is “dukhamaṃ,” namely, desirable and undesirable objects, and so on. When “dukkham” should be said, due to the constraints of the verse and to preserve the meter, the syllable “ka” is elided, and thus it is said “dukham.” He bears that, he endures it—thus, he is “dukhamasahano,” the Lord of Sages. The root sah is in the sense of enduring, with the suffix yu. That is “dukhamasahana.” Indeed, the Blessed One exceedingly endures and tolerates what is extremely difficult for ordinary people to bear—desirable and undesirable objects, and so on; cold and heat; and the worldly conditions known as gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. Therefore, he is extolled as “dukhamasahana.”

Mahesinti mahantaṃ sīlakkhandhādiṃ pariyesamānaṃ mahantaṃ nibbānaṃ gavesamānaṃ vā mahante sīlakkhandhādike esati gavesati pariyesatīti mahesī, munindakko. Mahantasaddūpa pada esadhātu gavesane ī. Vuttañhi mahāniddese “mahesīti mahesī. Bhagavā mahantaṃ sīlakkhandhaṃ esi gavesi pariyesīti mahesī. Mahantaṃ samādhikkhandhaṃ mahantaṃ paññākkhandhaṃ mahantaṃ vimuttikkhandhaṃ mahantaṃ vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhaṃ esī gavesī pariyesīti mahesī”ti. Mahante sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiya dhamme esati gavesatīti vā mahesī, mahantaṃ nibbānaṃ esati gavesatīti vā mahesī. Vuttañhi mahāniddese “mahante satipaṭṭhāne mahante sammappadhāne mahante iddhipāde mahantāni indriyāni [M 0.0153] mahantāni balāni mahante bojjhaṅge mahantaṃ ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ mahantaṃ paramatthaṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ esī gavesī pariyesīti mahesī”ti. Atha vā mahesakkhehi sattehi esiyati gavesiyati pariyesiyati amhākaṃ kahaṃ buddhoti mahesī. Vuttañhi mahāniddese “mahesakkhehi vā sattehi esito gavesito kahaṃ buddho”tyādi. Taṃ mahesiṃ. Tanti munindakkaṃ. Ahaṃ sirasā namāmīti sambandho.

“Mahesī” means one who seeks the great aggregate of virtue and so on, or who seeks the great Nibbāna; or, he seeks and searches for the great things such as the aggregate of virtue—thus, he is the great sage, the lord of sages. The word is formed from “mahanta” (great) as a prefix to the root es (to seek) in the sense of “gavesana” (searching), with the suffix ī. As stated in the Mahāniddesa: “Mahesī means a great sage. The Blessed One sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue—thus, he is a great sage. He sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of concentration, the great aggregate of wisdom, the great aggregate of liberation, the great aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—thus, he is a great sage.” Or, he seeks and searches for the great thirty-seven aids to enlightenment—thus, he is a great sage. Or he seeks and searches for the great Nibbāna—thus, he is a great sage. As stated in the Mahāniddesa: “He sought, searched for, and pursued the great foundations of mindfulness, the great right efforts, the great bases of spiritual power, the great faculties, the great powers, the great enlightenment factors, the great Noble Eightfold Path, the great ultimate goal, the deathless Nibbāna—thus, he is a great sage.” Alternatively, he is sought after, searched for, and pursued by beings of great power, who wonder, “Where is our Buddha?”—thus, he is a great sage. As stated in the Mahāniddesa: “Or he is sought after and searched for by beings of great power, wondering, ‘Where is the Buddha?’” and so on. To that great sage, that is, to the lord of sages—the connection is with “I bow my head.”

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Dayudayaruṇo mahākaruṇāsaṅkhātaudayapabbatuggatasūriyāruṇo, udayapabba tato uggatasūriyāruṇo viya mahākaruṇā vā, ñāṇa vitthiṇṇabimbo sabbaññutañāṇasaṅkhāto vitthāraparimaṇḍalo, vitthāracakkavāḷamaṇḍalaṃ viya vipulārammaṇasabbaññutañāṇavā, eko asahāyo ekabuddhabhūto, yo yādiso munindakko buddhādicco suddhe rāgādimalehi visuddhe tibhava kuhare tibhavasaṅkhātakamalasare, kamalakathitaṃ uppalanti kathetabbaṃ, vineyyappāṇoghaṃ vinetabbasattasamūhaṃ, dhammaraṃ sīvarehi uttamadhammasaṅkhātaraṃsīhi, subodhesi catusaccadhammaṃ paṭivedhayamānena suṭṭhu pabodhesi vikāsesi, byāpitakkittinaṃ tiloke patthaṭaparikittanaṃ, sīlādiguṇehi patthaṭathutighosikaṃ vā, tilokekaccakkhuṃ kāmarūpaarūpa saṅkhātānaṃ tilokānaṃ ekaṃ paññācakkhubhūtaṃ, dukhamasahanaṃ puthujjanehi atidukkhamitaṭṭhānaṃ khamanaṃ, mahesiṃ mahantaṃ sīlakkhandhādiṃ pariyesamānaṃ mahantaṃ nibbānaṃ gavesamānaṃ vā, taṃ munindakkaṃ ahaṃ sirasā namāmi vandāmīti.

Here is the concise application. “Dayudayaruṇa”: the crimson glow of the sun rising from the eastern mountain, which is great compassion; or, great compassion is like the crimson glow of the sun rising from the eastern mountain. “Ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimba”: the vast orb, which is the knowledge of omniscience, possessing omniscient knowledge with a vast object, like the broad circle of the universe. He is “eko,” alone, without a companion, the one Buddha. That “munindakko,” the Lord of Sages, the “buddhādicco,” the Buddha-sun, in the “suddhe tibhava kuhare,” the pure hollow of the three realms—pure, being free from defilements like lust—which is like a lotus pond; here, what is called “kamala” (lotus) should be understood as “uppala” (water lily). He “subodhesi,” thoroughly awakened and caused to blossom, the “vineyyappāṇoghaṃ,” the multitude of beings to be trained, with the “dhammaraṃsīvarehi,” the rays of the supreme Dhamma, by causing the penetration of the four noble truths. He is “byāpitakkittinaṃ,” one whose fame is spread throughout the three worlds, or whose praise is proclaimed on account of virtues such as morality. He is “tilokekaccakkhuṃ,” the one eye for the three worlds, the eye of wisdom for the three worlds comprising the realms of sensuality, form, and formlessness. He is “dukhamasahanaṃ,” one who endures what is extremely difficult for ordinary people to bear. He is “mahesiṃ,” the great sage, one who seeks the great aggregate of virtue and so on, or who seeks the great Nibbāna. To “taṃ munindakkaṃ,” that Lord of Sages, “ahaṃ sirasā namāmi,” I bow with my head, I venerate.

Vīsatimavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty homage stanzas is completed.

21.

21.

Yo [M 0.0154] jino anekajātiyaṃ saputtadāramaṅgajīvitampi;

Bodhipemato alaggamānaso adāsiyeva atthi kassa;

Dānapāramiṃ tato paraṃ apūri sīlapāramādikampi;

Tāsamiddhiyopayātamaggataṃ tamekadīpakaṃ namāmi.

That Victor who, in many a birth, with mind unattached out of love for enlightenment, gave up even his children, wife, limbs, and life—to whom did he not give?

Having fulfilled the perfection of giving, he then fulfilled the perfection of morality and the others;

To that sole beacon who reached the supreme state through the success of these perfections, I bow.

21. Evaṃ vīsatimāya gāthāya munindakkaṃ vanditvā idāni pubbe anekajātiyaṃ bodhisattakāle jīvitapariccāgādīhi ca dānādidasapāramiyo pūrentehi guṇehi ca thometvā jinaṃ vanditukāmo yo jino tyādimāha. Ayaṃ pana raja raja raja gaṇehi ca garulahūhi ca racitattā vīsatakkharehi lakkhitā vuttagāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “vutta mīdisantu nāmato rajā rajā rajā garullahū cā”ti.

21. Having thus paid homage to the Lord of Sages with twenty verses, now, desiring to praise and pay homage to the Victor by extolling the virtues with which he, in many past births during his time as a Bodhisatta, fulfilled the ten perfections such as giving by means of sacrificing his life and so forth, the author begins with ‘Yo jino’ and so on. This verse, however, should be understood as a vutta verse, characterized by twenty syllables, as it is composed of raja feet and heavy and light syllables. For it is stated in the Vuttodaya: ‘A verse of this kind is known by the name vutta; it has rajā, rajā, rajā, and a heavy and a light syllable.’

Ayaṃ panettha yojanā. Yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ rajā rajagaṇā ca rajā rajagaṇā ca rajā rajagaṇā ca garullahū ca ce siyyuṃ, īdisantu īdisaṃ pana gāthā nāmato nāmena vuttaṃ vutta gāthā nāmāti.

Here is the explanation of it. If in each quarter of a verse there are a raja foot, and a raja foot, and a raja foot, and a heavy and a light syllable, then such a verse is called by the name vutta, a vutta verse.

Tattha pana yo jinoti yo buddho. So hi devaputtakilesābhisaṅkhārakhandhamaccuvasena pañcamāre ajini jināti jinissatīti jinoti vuccati. Nanu ca buddhasāvakāpi pañcamāre jinattā jinā nāmāti ce. Na bhagavato parūpa nissayavirahaniratisayavasena pañcamārajinattā bhagavāyeva jino nāmāti. Vuttañhi dhātukathāmūlaṭīkāyaṃ –

Here, ‘Yo jino’ means ‘he who is the Buddha.’ For he conquered, conquers, and will conquer the five Māras—the Māra of celestial beings, the Māra of defilements, the Māra of volitional formations, the Māra of aggregates, and the Māra of death—thus he is called ‘Jina’ (the Victor). If it is asked whether the Buddha’s disciples are also called ‘Jina’ because they too conquer the five Māras, the answer is no. Only the Blessed One is called ‘Jina’ because his conquest of the five Māras is unsurpassed and without reliance on others. As stated in the Dhātukathāmūlaṭīkā:—

“Tattha balavidhamana visayātikkamavasena devaputtamārassa, apavattikaraṇavasena kilesābhisaṅkhāramārānaṃ, samudayappahānapariññāvasena khandhamārassa, maccumārassa, ca bodhimūle eva bhañjitattā parūpanissayarahitaṃ niratisayaṃ taṃ bhañjanaṃ upādāya bhagavāeva mārabhañjanoti thomito”ti.

“Therein, the Blessed One is praised as ‘Mārabhañjana’—the Crusher of Māra—because at the foot of the Bodhi tree he crushed the Māra of celestial beings by destroying his power and overcoming his sphere; the Māras of defilements and volitional formations by causing them not to arise again; and the Māra of the aggregates and the Māra of death by fully understanding their origin and abandoning them. On account of that crushing being unsurpassed and without reliance on another, the Blessed One alone is extolled as ‘Mārabhañjana.’”

Anekajātiyanti [M 0.0155] anekasaṃsārabhave. Ettha hi ayaṃ jātisaddo anekattho. Tathā hesa ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyoti ettha bhave āgato. Atthi visākhe nigaṇṭhā nāma samaṇajātīti ettha nikāye. Tiri nāma tiṇajāti nābhiyā uggantvā nabhaṃ āhacca ṭhitā ahosīti ettha paññattiyaṃ. Jāti dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahitāti ettha saṅkhatalakkhaṇe. Yaṃ mātukucchiyaṃ paṭhamaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ paṭhamaṃ viññāṇaṃ pātubhūtaṃ. Tadupādāya sāvassa jātīti ettha paṭisandhiyaṃ. Sampatijāto ānanda bodhisattoti ettha pasūtiyaṃ. Anupakuṭṭho jātivādenāti ettha kule. Yatohaṃ bhagini ariyāya jātiyā jātoti ettha ariyasīle. Idha panāyaṃ bhave vattati. Tasmā anekasaṃsārabhaveti attho viññātabbo. So hi jāyati yoni gatiādi vibhāgoti jātīti vuccati. Atha vā jāyanti nibbattanti ettha khandhādayoti jāti, bhavo. Janidhātu nibbattaneti. Na ekā anekā, anekā ca sā jāti cāti aneka jāti. Tassaṃ anekajātiyaṃ.

“Anekajātiyaṃ” means in many existences in saṃsāra. Here, indeed, this word ‘jāti’ has many meanings. For example, it is used in the sense of existence, as in ‘one birth, two births.’ It is used in the sense of a group, as in ‘Visākhā, there are ascetics called Nigaṇṭhas, a class of ascetics.’ It is used in the sense of a kind or designation, as in ‘A kind of grass called Tiri grew upward from the navel, reaching the sky and stood there.’ It is used in the sense of a conditioned characteristic, as in ‘Birth is included under two aggregates.’ It refers to rebirth-linking, as in ‘The first consciousness that has arisen in the mother’s womb, the first cognition that has appeared—on account of that, it is his birth.’ It is used in the sense of delivery, as in ‘Ānanda, the Bodhisatta is newly born.’ It refers to lineage, as in ‘unblemished by claims of birth.’ It denotes noble conduct, as in ‘Sister, from when I was born into the noble birth.’ Here, however, it is used in the sense of existence. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as ‘in many existences in saṃsāra.’ For it is called ‘jāti’ because one is born into various divisions of wombs, destinations, and so forth. Alternatively, ‘jāti’ is existence, that wherein aggregates and so forth arise and are produced. The root jani is in the sense of producing. Not one is many. That which is many is ‘many births.’ In that, ‘in many births…’

Saputtadāranti puttena ca bhariyāya ca sahitaṃ. Attano kulaṃ punāti pavati sodhetīti vā putto. Pudhātu pavane ta. Mātāpitūnaṃ manaṃ pūretīti vā putto. Pūradhātu pūraṇe ta. Putto ca dhītā ca putto. Virūpeka sesoyaṃ. Sāmikena dhariyateti dāro. Dharadhātu dhāraṇe ṇo. Dhassa do. Atha vā purisena bhogaṃ dīyatīti dāro. Dādhātu dāne rapaccayo. Dākucchitā kārena purisena ramiyati etthāti vā dāro, bhariyā. Dāpubbaramudhātu ramane kvi. Dāsaddo kucchitattho. Abhidhānaṭīkāyaṃ pana “dārayante yenāti dāro, dara vidāraṇe. Akattari ca kārake saññāyaṃ ṇo”ti vuttaṃ. Putto ca dāro ca puttadāro. Samāhāradvandepi hi [M 0.0156] pulliṅgaṃ icchanti ācariyā. Tena saha vattati yassāti saputtadāro, puttadārapariccāgo. Taṃ saputtadāraṃ. Aṅgajīvitampīti hatthapādakaṇṇanāsacakkhādisarīrāvayavañca jīvitindriya paṭibaddhasakalasarīrañca aṅgati gacchati kāyeti aṅgo, cakkhādisarīrāvayavo. Agidhātu gatiyaṃ a. Jīvanti sattā etenāti jīvitaṃ, jīvitindriyaṃ. Jīvadhātu pāṇadhāraṇe ta. Aṅgo ca jīvitañca aṅgajīvitaṃ. Ettha ca pisaddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena dhanaraṭṭhapariccāgaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Vuttañhi sīlakkhandhaṭṭha kathāyaṃ –

“Saputtadāraṃ” means “together with a son and a wife.” A son (putto) is so called because he purifies (punāti, pavati) or cleanses (sodheti) his own family. (From the root “pu” in the sense of purifying, with the suffix “ta”.) Or, a son is so called because he fills the minds of his parents. (From the root “pūr” in the sense of filling, with the suffix “ta”.) Both a son and a daughter are called 'putto'. This is a virūpekasesa compound. A wife is called “dāra” because she is supported by her husband. (From the root “dhar” in the sense of supporting, with the suffix “ṇo,” and “dha” changing to “da.”) Alternatively, “dāra” is so called because enjoyment is given by the man. (From the root “dā” in the sense of giving, with the suffix “ra.”) Or, a wife is called “dāra” because she is delighted in by a man in a contemptible manner. (From the root “ram” in the sense of delighting, with “dā” as a prefix and the suffix “kvi”; the word “dā” here means contemptible.) However, in the Abhidhānaṭīkā, it is said: “That by which one is torn apart is called 'dāra', from the root 'dara' in the sense of tearing apart. The suffix 'ṇo' is used in the sense of a non-agentive case in conventional usage.” A son and a wife are 'puttadāro'. Indeed, teachers prefer the masculine gender even in a collective dvanda compound. Thus, “saputtadāro” means “one who is together with a son and a wife,” and the phrase indicates the abandonment of son and wife. That is 'saputtadāraṃ'. “Aṅgajīvitampi” means both the bodily limbs such as hands, feet, ears, nose, eyes, etc., and the entire body connected with the life faculty. A limb (aṅga) is so called because it goes (aṅgati, gacchati) in the body (kāye); it is a bodily limb like the eye, etc. (From the root “agi” in the sense of going, with the suffix “a.”) 'Jīvita' means “that by which beings live,” i.e., the life faculty. (From the root “jīv” in the sense of sustaining life, with the suffix “ta.”) A limb and life form 'aṅgajīvita'. Here, the particle 'pi' has the meaning of aggregation. Thus, it aggregates the abandonment of wealth, kingdom, and so forth. For it is said in the commentary on the Sīlakkhandhavagga—

“Aṅgapariccāgaṃ jīvitadhanarajjaputtadārapariccāganti ime pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajitvā”ti. Atha vā sambhāvanattho. Tena bhagavā sabbaññutañāṇahetupi puttadāraaṅgajīvitampi alaggamānaso pariccajeti, pageva dhanādibāhiravatthu pariccāgepīti sambhāveti.

“Having abandoned these five great abandonments: the abandonment of limbs, life, wealth, kingdom, and son and wife…” Alternatively, the particle ‘pi’ is used in the sense of possibility. Therefore, one should consider that the Blessed One, for the sake of omniscient knowledge, relinquished even son, wife, limbs, and life with an unattached mind; how much more so external things like wealth and so forth.

Bodhipematoti arahattamaggasabbaññutañāṇasaṅkhātāya bodhiyā piyamānattā, hetvatthe hi topaccayo. Cattāri saccāni bujjhatīti bodhi, arahattamaggañāṇaṃ. Sabba ñeyyadhamme bujjhatīti bodhi, sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Budhadhātu ñāṇe ṇa. Itthiliṅgajotako īpaccayo ca. Vuttañhi abhidhānappadīpikāyaṃ – “bodhi sabbaññutañāṇe, ariyamagge ca nāriya”nti. Bodhi ca bodhi ca bodhi sarūpekase savasena. Piyanaṃ pemo, piyāyitabboti vā pemo. Pīdhātu tappanakantīsu manipaccayo. Bodhiyā pemo bodhipemo, tato bodhipemato. Bhagavatā hi puttadāraaṅgajīvitehipi sataguṇena sahassaguṇena sata sahassaguṇenapi bodhiñāṇameva piyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttañhi vessantarajātake –

“Bodhipemato” means “because of love for enlightenment,” which is designated as the knowledge of the path to arahantship and omniscient knowledge; for the suffix “to” here is in the sense of cause. Enlightenment (bodhi) is so called because one understands the Four Noble Truths—this is the knowledge of the path to arahantship. Enlightenment (bodhi) is so called because one understands all knowable phenomena—this is omniscient knowledge. (From the root 'budh' in the sense of knowing, with the suffix 'ṇa,' and the suffix 'ī' which indicates the feminine gender.) As stated in the Abhidhānappadīpikā: “Bodhi, a feminine noun, refers to omniscient knowledge and also to the noble path.” The two instances of 'bodhi' become one 'bodhi' by way of a sarūpekasesa compound. 'Pema' means 'love' (piyanaṃ), or 'that which is to be loved' (piyāyitabbaṃ). (From the root 'pī' in the sense of satisfying and delighting, with the suffix 'maṇi'.) Love for enlightenment is 'bodhipema'; from that, 'bodhipemato'. Indeed, it is said that for the Blessed One, the knowledge of enlightenment was a hundred times, a thousand times, and a hundred thousand times dearer than even sons, wives, limbs, and life. As stated in the Vessantara Jātaka—

“Na me dessā ubho puttā, maddī devī na dessiyā;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā piye adāsaha”nti.

“Neither are my two sons displeasing to me, nor is Queen Maddī displeasing; Omniscience is dear to me, therefore I gave up what was dear.”

Alaggamānasoti [M 0.0157] puttadāraaṅgajīvitādīsu anallīyana citto hutvā laganaṃ saṅganaṃ laggo, lagati saṅgati allayati vāti laggo. Lagadhātu saṅge allīyane vā gapaccayo. Na laggo alaggo, natthi laggo ettha puttadāra aṅgajīvitādīsūti vā alaggo. Manati jānāti ārammaṇanti mano. Soyeva mānaso. Alaggo mānaso yassa soti alaggamānaso, jino. Atthikassāti putta dārādiṃ kāmikassa, yācakassa paṭiggāhakassa vāti attho. Attho kāmo assa atthīti atthiko, ṇiko. Tassa atthikassa. Adāsiyevāti pūjānuggahakāmatāya ñāṇasampayuttapariccāgacetanāya adāsievāti attho. Bodhisatto hi pāramīpūraṇa kāle sarāgasadosasamohasseva sato āgatā gatānaṃ yācakānaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ sīsaṃ kantitvā galalohitaṃ nīharitvā suañjitāni akkhīni uppāṭetvā kulavaṃsappadīpaṃ puttaṃ manāpacāriniṃ bhariyañca kheḷapiṇḍamiva anapekkho pariccajitvā dīyamānova sammāsambodhiñāṇaṃ laddhuṃ sakkā, na puttadāraaṅgajīvitampi apariccajitvā. Pañca hi mahāpariccāge apariccajitvā buddhabhūtapubbā nāma natthi. Paccekabuddhāriyasāvakā pana puttadāraaṅgajīvitaṃ apariccajantāpi paccekabuddhāriyasāvakabodhiñāṇaṃ laddhuṃ samatthāva. Tasmāyeva bhagavantaṃyeva saputtadāramaṅgajīvitampi bodhipemato alaggamānaso adāsiyeva atthi kassāti thometi. Vuttañhetaṃ vessantarajātakaṭṭha kathāyaṃ “sabbabodhisattā dhanapariccāgaṃ, puttapariccāgaṃ, bhariyapariccāgaṃ, aṅgapariccāgaṃ, jīvitapariccāganti ime pañca mahāpariccāge apariccajitvā buddhabhūtapubbā nāma natthī”ti.

“Alaggamānaso” means “having a mind not clinging” to sons, wives, limbs, life, and so forth. “Laggo” means “clinging” or “attachment,” or “that which clings, attaches, or sinks.” (From the root “lag” in the sense of clinging or sinking, with the suffix “ga.”) “Na laggo” means “not clinging,” hence “alaggo.” Or, “alaggo” means “there is no clinging here” regarding sons, wives, limbs, life, and so forth. “Mano” means “that which knows or perceives an object.” That itself is “mānaso.” One whose mind is unattached is “alaggamānaso,” the Conqueror. “Atthikassa” means “for one who has need,” i.e., for one desirous of sons, wives, etc., or for a beggar or a recipient. (“Atthiko” means “one who has desire” (attho being desire), with the suffix “ṇiko.”) For such a one who has need. “Adāsiyeva” means “he gave indeed” with the intention of generosity linked with wisdom, out of a desire for honor and compassion. Indeed, the Bodhisatta, while fulfilling the perfections, even when still possessing desire, aversion, and delusion, when approached by beggars, would cut off his adorned and prepared head, extract blood from his neck, pluck out his beautified eyes, and relinquish his son, the lamp of his lineage, and his charming wife, without concern, as if spitting out a lump of phlegm. Only by such giving could he attain perfect enlightenment, not without relinquishing even sons, wives, limbs, and life. Indeed, there has never been a Buddha who became a Buddha without relinquishing the five great abandonments. However, Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples are capable of attaining their respective enlightenments even without relinquishing sons, wives, limbs, and life. Therefore, the Blessed One himself is praised thus: “Because of his love for enlightenment, with an unattached mind, he gave indeed even his son, wife, limbs, and life to one in need.” As stated in the Vessantara Jātaka commentary: “All Bodhisattas have never become Buddhas in the past without relinquishing these five great abandonments: the abandonment of wealth, the abandonment of sons, the abandonment of wives, the abandonment of limbs, and the abandonment of life.”

Evaṃ pañcahi mahāpariccāgaguṇehi bhagavato thomanaṃ katvā idāni dānādipāramīpūraṇaguṇena thomanaṃ kattu kāmo dānapāramintiādimāha. Tattha dānanti tividhaṃ hoti [M 0.0158] cāgacetanā ca, virati ca, deyyadhammo cāti. Saddhā hiriyaṃ kusalañca dānanti āgataṭṭhāne hi cāgacetanā dānaṃ nāma. Abhayaṃ detīti āgataṭṭhāne viratī dānaṃ nāma. Dānaṃ deti annaṃ pānanti āgataṭṭhāne deyyadhammo dānaṃ nāma. Tattha cāgacetanā deti vā deyyadhammaṃ denti vā etāya deyyadhammanti dānaṃ. Virati avakhaṇḍanaṭṭhena lavanaṭṭhena vā dānaṃ. Sā hi uppajjamānā bhayabheravasaṅkhātaṃ dussilyaṃ cetanaṃ dāti lunāti cāti dānaṃ, deyyadhammo diyyatīti dānaṃ. Idha pana tividhaṃ dānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Pāramīsaddassa vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Atha vā pāraṃ nibbānaṃ eti gacchati etāyāti pārami. Pārasaddūpapada idhātu gatiyaṃ kvi. Pāraṃ itīti padacchedo kātabbo. Dānameva pāramī dānapāramī, taṃ dānapāramiṃ. Tatoti dānapāramito. Paranti aññaṃ. Sīlapāramādikampīti sīlatīti sīlaṃ. Sīla dhātu samādhimhi a. Kāyavacīkammāni samādahati samādhapetīti attho. Sīlati samādhiyati kāyakammādīnaṃ susilyavasena na vippakiratīti vā sīlaṃ, sīlanti samādahanti cittaṃ etenāti vā sīlaṃ. Atha vā sīlayati upadhāretīti sīlaṃ, sīladhātu upadhāraṇe a. Kusala dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhānabhāvena ābhuso dhāretīti attho. Sīlenti vā etena kusale dhamme upadhārenti sādhavoti sīlaṃ, sīliyati upadhāriyati sappurisehi hadayamaṃsantaraṃ upanetvāti vā sīlaṃ, sīleti upadhāreti taṃ samaṅgī puggalaṃ apāyesu uppattinīvāraṇavasena suggati nibbānanti vā sīlaṃ, sīlameva pāramī sīlapāramī, sā ādi yāsanteti sīlapāramādikā. Ettha ca ādisaddena nekkhammapaññā vīriyakhantisaccaadhiṭṭhānamettāupekkhāpāramiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Vuttañhetaṃ buddhavaṃsapāḷiyaṃ –

Having thus praised the Blessed One with the five great qualities of abandonment, now wishing to praise him with the quality of fulfilling the perfections beginning with giving, he says 'the perfection of giving' and so forth. Herein, giving is threefold: the intention of relinquishing, abstention, and the object to be given. Indeed, in passages where 'faith, shame, and wholesome states are giving' occurs, the intention of relinquishing is called giving. In passages where 'one gives fearlessness' occurs, abstention is called giving. In passages where 'one gives a gift, food, drink' occurs, the object to be given is called giving. Herein, the intention of relinquishing is called giving because it gives, or because by it one gives the object to be given. Abstention is called giving in the sense of cutting off or severing. For when it arises, it cuts off or severs the immoral intention designated as fear and terror—thus it is called giving. The object to be given is called giving because it is given. Here, however, the threefold giving is intended. The meaning of the word 'pāramī' has already been stated below. Alternatively, 'pāramī' means 'that by which one goes to the far shore, Nibbāna'. (From the root 'i' in the sense of going, with 'pāra' as a prefix, and the suffix 'kvi'. The word division should be made as 'pāraṃ iti'.) Giving itself is the perfection, the perfection of giving; that perfection of giving (`dānapāramiṃ`). 'Tato' means 'from the perfection of giving'. 'Paraṃ' means 'another'. 'Sīlapāramādikaṃ' means 'virtue' (sīla) is so called because it composes (sīlati). (The root 'sīla' is in the sense of composing, with the suffix 'a'. The meaning is that it composes or causes bodily and verbal actions to be composed.) Or, 'sīla' is so called because it composes, and through good habit, bodily actions and so forth are well-composed and not scattered; or 'sīla' is so called because by it, they compose the mind. Alternatively, 'sīla' is so called because it bears or upholds (sīlayati); (the root 'sīla' is in the sense of upholding, with the suffix 'a'.) The meaning is that it firmly supports wholesome states as their foundation. Or, 'sīla' is so called because the virtuous uphold wholesome states with it; or 'sīla' is so called because it is upheld by good people, having brought it into the inner heart; or 'sīla' is so called because it protects that person who possesses it, preventing rebirth in the lower realms and leading to happy destinies and Nibbāna. Virtue itself is the perfection, the perfection of virtue; that which has virtue as its beginning is 'sīlapāramādikā'. Here, by the word 'beginning', the perfections of renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity are included. For it is said in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi:

“Dānaṃ sīlañca nekkhammaṃ, paññā vīriyena pañcamaṃ;

Khantisaccamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, mettupekkhā imā dasā”ti.

“Generosity, virtue, and renunciation, wisdom, with energy as the fifth; patience, truthfulness, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these ten.”

Pisaddo [M 0.0159] cettha sampiṇḍanattho. Tena pañca mahāpariccāge sampiṇḍeti.

Here, the particle 'pi' has the meaning of aggregation. By it, he aggregates the five great abandonments.

Apūrīti sammāsambodhatthāya pūraṇaṃ akāsīti attho. Bhagavato hi dīpaṅkarapādamūle aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā buddhatthāya abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya anekajātīsu sammāsambodhiṃ paṭivijjhituṃ vāyamanto adinnadānaṃ nāma natthi, arakkhitasīlaṃ nāma natthi. Apūritā pāramī nāma natthi. Atibahumpi pūraṇaṃ akāsiyeva. Bhagavā hi bodhisatta bhūto catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakaṃ parājetvā adhikaṃ lohitadānamakāsi. Sakalapathaviyā paṃsuṃ parājetvā adhikaṃ maṃsamadāsi. Sinerupabbatarājaṃ parājetvā adhikaṃ sīsadānamadāsi. Ākāse tārakasamūhaṃ parājetvā adhikaṃ nayanamadāsi.

'Apūrī' means 'he fulfilled', that is, he performed the fulfillment for the sake of perfect enlightenment. Indeed, for the Blessed One, from the time he made the aspiration for Buddhahood at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, having combined the eight qualities, striving through many lives to penetrate perfect enlightenment, there was no gift ungiven, no virtue unguarded. There was no perfection unfulfilled. Indeed, he performed the fulfillment in great abundance. For the Blessed One, when he was a Bodhisatta, gave more blood than the water in the four great oceans. He gave more flesh than the dust of the entire earth. He gave more heads than Mount Sineru, the king of mountains. He gave more eyes than the multitude of stars in the sky.

Tena vuttaṃ jinālaṅkāre –

Thus it was said in the Jinālaṅkāra:

“So sāgare jaladhikaṃ rudhiraṃ adāsi,

Bhūmiṃ parājiya samaṃsamadāsi dānaṃ;

Meruppamāṇamadhikañca samoḷisīsaṃ,

Khe tārakādhikataraṃ nayanaṃ adāsī”ti.

“He gave blood more than the ocean’s water; having surpassed the earth, he gave his own flesh as a gift; and heads with diadems exceeding the measure of Meru; in the sky, he gave eyes more numerous than the stars.”

Vasantatilakagāthā.

A Vasantatilaka verse.

Tattha ca soti so evaṃvidho bodhisatto. Sāgareti catūsu mahāsamuddesu. Jaladhikanti udakato adhikaṃ katvā. Rudhiraṃ adāsīti lohitadānamadāsi. Bhūmiṃ parājiyāti paṃsupathaviyā paṃsuṃ parājetvā attano sarīramaṃsaṃ adhikaṃ adāsi. Meruppamāṇamadhikanti yojana aṭṭhasaṭṭhisatasahassubbedhassa girirājassa pamāṇatopi adhikaṃ katvā. Samoḷisīsanti moḷiyā saha abhisittasīsaṃ adāsi. Kheti cakkavāḷapabbatapariyante ākāse. Tārakādhikataranti nakkhattāditārakarūpatopi adhikaṃ katvā[M 0.0160]. Nayanaṃ adāsīti nettadānaṃ adāsīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, “so” refers to such a bodhisatta. “Sāgare” means in the four great oceans. “Jaladhikaṃ” means having made it more than water. “Rudhiraṃ adāsi” means he gave a gift of blood. “Bhūmiṃ parājiya” means having surpassed the dust of the earth, he gave more of his own body’s flesh. “Meruppamāṇamadhikaṃ” means having made it more than the measure of the king of mountains, which is 168,000 yojanas in height. “Samoḷisīsaṃ” means he gave his consecrated head with the diadem. “Khe” means in the sky at the boundary of the Cakkavāḷa mountains. “Tārakādhikataraṃ” means having made it more than the forms of the stars, constellations, and so on. “Nayanaṃ adāsi” means he gave a gift of eyes—this is the meaning to be understood here.

Tāsamiddhiyopayātamaggatanti tāsaṃ iddhiyā upayātaṃ aggatanti padacchedo. Tāsanti tāsaṃ pāramīnaṃ. Iddhiyāti samiddhiyā, hetvatthe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Upayātanti upagataṃ. Aggatanti sabbasattānaṃ uttamabhāvaṃ, seṭṭhabhūtaṃ buddhattanti attho. Taṃ pana padaṃ upayātantipade kammaṃ. Aggasaddo cettha uttamavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko. Atha vā aggati uttamabhāvaṃ seṭṭhabhūtaṃ vā buddhabhāvaṃ pāpuṇātīti aggo, jino. Aggadhātu gatiyaṃ a. Aggassa bhāvo aggataṃ. Bhagavā hi anantalokadhātūsu sabba sattānaṃ aggo uttamataro seṭṭhataroti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ dasanipāta aṅguttarapāḷiyaṃ –

“Tāsamiddhiyopayātamaggataṃ” is to be divided as “tāsaṃ iddhiyā upayātaṃ aggataṃ.” “Tāsaṃ” refers to those perfections. “Iddhiyā” means by success—here it is an instrumental case indicating cause. “Upayātaṃ” means attained. “Aggataṃ” means the supreme state of all beings, the highest state of Buddhahood—this is the meaning. That word is the object of the word “upayātaṃ.” The word “agga” here denotes the supreme, an underived nominal stem. Alternatively, one who attains (`aggati`) the supreme state or the highest state of Buddhahood is `aggo`, the Victor. The root `agg` is in the sense of ‘going,’ and takes the suffix `a`. The state of being `agga` is `aggataṃ`. For the Blessed One is the highest, the most excellent, the supreme among all beings in infinite world-systems—this is the meaning. As it is said in the Aṅguttara Pāḷi, in the Book of the Tens:

“Yāvatā bhikkhave sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā catuppadā vā bahuppadā vā rūpino vā arūpino vā saññino vā asaññino vā nevasaññīnāsaññino vā, tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti.

“Monks, as far as there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or with neither perception nor non-perception—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared the foremost among them.”

Tamekadīpakanti taṃ ekadīpakanti padacchedo. Tanti jinaṃ. Ekadīpakanti sabbasattānaṃ ekapaṭisaraṇabhūtaṃ patiṭṭhabhūtaṃ vā. Dīpakasaddo hi paṭisaraṇapatiṭṭhavācako nipphannapāṭipadiko. Vuttañhi saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “patiṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena dīpa”nti. Dīpanti patiṭṭhahanti paṭisaraṇabhāvena sattā etthāti vā dīpako, jino. Dīpadhātu patiṭṭhāyaṃ ako. Ekasaddo saṅkhyāvācako. Eko ekabhūto dīpakoti ekadīpako, jino. Atha vā ekadīpakanti manussānaṃ paṭisaraṇabhūtaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ samuddadīpakamiva sabbasattānaṃ paṭisaraṇabhūtaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ ekabuddhabhūtaṃ.

The phrase `tamekadīpakanti` is analyzed as `taṃ ekadīpakaṃ iti`. `Taṃ` refers to the Victor. `Ekadīpakaṃ` means the one refuge and foundation for all beings. The word `dīpaka` signifies refuge and support, being a derived nominal stem. As stated in the Saṃyuttaṭṭhakathā: “An island (`dīpa`) in the sense of establishing.” Beings find footing (`patiṭṭhahanti`) and take refuge in it (`dīpanti`), thus it is an island (`dīpako`), the Victor. The root `dīp` is in the sense of ‘being a support,’ and takes the suffix `ako`. The word `eka` is a numerical term. `Eko`, one or unique, combined with `dīpako` forms `ekadīpako`, the one island, the Victor. Alternatively, `ekadīpakaṃ` means the refuge and foundation for all beings, just as an island in the ocean is a refuge and foundation for humans—the one Buddha.

Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho. Jalamajjhe dippatīti dīpo. Dvidhā āposandati etthāti vā dīpo. Soyeva dīpako. Soviya [M 0.0161] eko buddho hutvā eti gacchati pavattatīti ekadīpako, jino. Yathā hi mahāsamudde bhinnanāvānaṃ manussānaṃ samuddadīpo paṭisaraṇo patiṭṭho hoti, evaṃ jino saṃsārasāgare alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhe osīdantānaṃ sabbasattānaṃ ekabuddhabhūto paṭisaraṇo patiṭṭho hotīti ekadīpakanti thometi. Taṃ jinaṃ ahaṃ namāmīti sambandhoti.

Here is the meaning of the expression: “That which shines (`dippati`) in the midst of water is a lamp (`dīpo`).” Or, “that where water (`āpo`) flows on two sides (`dvidhā sandati`) is an island (`dīpo`).” That very one is the `dīpaka`. Like that, the one Buddha, having become, comes, goes, and proceeds; thus he is the `ekadīpako`, the Victor. For just as, in the great ocean, an island is a refuge and support for shipwrecked humans, so too the Victor, in the ocean of saṃsāra where beings sink without obtaining a secure footing, having become the one Buddha, is a refuge and support for all beings. Thus, he is praised as the `ekadīpako`. “I bow to that Victor”—this is the connection.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Yo jino aneka jātiyaṃ anekasaṃsārabhave, saputtadāraṃ puttena ca bhariyāya ca sahitaṃ, aṅgajīvitampi aṅgapaccaṅgajīvitindriyampi. Atha vā hatthapādakaṇṇanāsacakkhādisarīrāvayavañca jīvitindriya paṭibaddhasakalasarīrañca, bodhipemato arahattamagga sabbaññutañāṇasaṅkhātāya bodhiyā piyamānattā, alagga mānasoti puttadāraaṅgajīvitādīsu anallīyanacitto hutvā, atthikassa puttadārādiṃ kāmikassa yācakassa adāsiyeva pariccāgacetanāya adāsieva. Dānapāramimpi tato dānapāramito paraṃ aññaṃ sīlapāramādikampi sīlapāramīādikampi, apūri sammāsambodhatthāya pūraṇaṃ akāsi, tāsaṃ pāramīnaṃ iddhiyā samiddhiyā aggataṃ uttama bhāvaṃ seṭṭhabuddhattaṃ vā, upayātaṃ upagataṃ, ekadīpakaṃ sabbasattānaṃ ekapaṭisaraṇabhūtaṃ ekapatiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ vā, dīpakamiva ekapaṭisaraṇabhūtaṃ patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ vā taṃ jinaṃ tīhi dvārehi namāmīti.

Here is the concise explanation. The Victor, through countless births and cycles of existence, together with his children and wife—that is, with son and spouse—and even his limbs and life, his major and minor limbs and the life faculty. Or, his hands, feet, ears, nose, eyes, and other bodily parts, along with his entire body bound to the life faculty, out of love for awakening—that is, out of his cherishing of awakening, which is designated as the path to Arahantship and omniscient knowledge. With a mind unattached—that is, with a mind not clinging to children, wife, limbs, life, and the like—he gave them away to one in need, to one who desired them, to a beggar, with the very intention of relinquishment. And he fulfilled the perfection of giving, and beyond that perfection of giving, the other perfections such as virtue and so on—the perfections of virtue and the rest—for the sake of perfect enlightenment. By the power and success of those perfections, he attained the highest state, the supreme state, or supreme Buddhahood; he became the one lamp for all beings, their one refuge, their one foundation, or like a lamp, the one refuge and foundation. To that Victor, I pay homage through the three doors.

Ekavīsatimavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-first homage verse is concluded.

22.

22.

Devādevātidevaṃ nidhanavapudharaṃ mārabhaṅgaṃ abhaṅgaṃ,

Dīpaṃ dīpaṃ pajānaṃ jayavarasayane bodhipattaṃdhipattaṃ;

Brahmābrahmāgatānaṃ varagirakathikaṃ pāpahīnaṃ pahīnaṃ,

Lokālokābhirāmaṃ satatamabhiname taṃ munindaṃ munindaṃ.

I ever bow to that Lord of Sages, the Lord of Sages,

who is the god beyond gods, the bearer of a final body,

the breaker of Māra, the unbreakable;

a refuge, a lamp for all beings,

who attained mastery of enlightenment on the excellent seat of victory;

the speaker of excellent speech to Brahmā and those who have gone to the Brahmā-world,

free from evil, utterly devoid of it,

the delight of the world and its light, I ever pay homage to that Lord of Sages, the Lord of Sages.

22. Evaṃ [M 0.0162] ekavīsatimāya gāthāya jinaṃ vanditvā idāni devādevātidevantyādīhi dasahi guṇehi thometvā munindaṃ vanditukāmo devādevātidevantiādimāha. Ayaṃ pana ma ra bha na ya ya gaṇehi ca timuniyatīhi ca racitattā ekavīsatakkharehi yuttā ādyantayamakā saddharā gāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi vuttodaye “mrā bhnā yo yotra yena timuniyatiyutā saddharā kittitāya”nti.

22. Having thus paid homage to the Victor with the twenty-first verse, now, desiring to praise the Lord of Sages with ten qualities such as “god beyond gods,” he speaks the verse beginning “Devādevātidevaṃ.” This, however, should be understood as a Saddharā verse with yamaka at the beginning and end, composed of twenty-one syllables, formed with the gaṇas ma, ra, bha, na, ya, and ya, and having three caesurae at the seventh syllable. For it is said in the Vuttodaya: “The Saddharā is acclaimed where there are m, r, bh, n, y, y, and y, with a caesura after every seven syllables.”

Ayaṃ panettha yojanā. Yassaṃ paṭipādaṃ mrā maragaṇā ca bhnā bhanagaṇā ca yogaṇo ca yena yagaṇena saha yogaṇo ca timuniyatiyutā sattamakkharantetīhi yatīhi yuttā ca ce siyuṃ. Atra imasmiṃ pakati chande ayaṃ gāthā saddharāgāthāti kittitāti. Ettha ca munisaddo sattasaṅkhyāvācakoti daṭṭhabbo. Ekasmiṃ pāde sattamakkharante sattamakkharante yatīnaṃ tiparivattattā timuniyatiyutāti vuttaṃ. Ekavīsatakkharavantoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Here is the explanation of that verse: If in each line there are the gaṇas ma, ra, bha, and na, along with three ya-gaṇas, and it is endowed with three caesurae at the seventh syllable, then in this standard meter, this verse is called a Saddharā verse. Here, the word ‘muni’ should be understood as denoting the number seven. In one line, because the caesura occurs three times at the seventh syllable, it is called ‘timuniyatiyutā’ (endowed with three ‘muni’ caesurae). This means it has twenty-one syllables.

Tattha ca devādevātidevanti rājasaṅkhātasammutideva catumahārājādikaupapattidevānaṃ atiuttamaṃ atiseṭṭhaṃ visuddhidevabhūtaṃ. Ettha hi devāti sammutidevā. Te hi mānussaissariyasampattīhi dibbantīti manussarājadevī kumārā devāti vuccanti. Puna devāti upapattidevā. Te hi dibbaissariyasampattīhi dibbantīti catumahārājikā devā vuccanti, dibbanti kāmaguṇādīhi kīḷanti laḷanti, tesu vā viharanti, vijayasamatthatāyogena paccatthike vijetuṃ icchanti, issariyadhanādisakkāradānaggahaṇaṃ taṃ taṃ atthānusāsanañca karontā voharanti. Puññātisayayogānubhāvappattāya jutiyā jotanti. Yathādhippetañca visayaṃ appaṭighātena gacchanti. Yathicchitanipphādane ca sakkontīti devāti visuddhimaggamahāṭīkāyaṃ āgatanayenapi veditabbo. Atidevanti [M 0.0163] tesaṃ devānaṃ atiuttamaṃ atiseṭṭhaṃ vā visuddhi devabhūtaṃ bhagavantanti attho. So hi tesaṃ sammuti upapattidevānaṃ sīlādiguṇehi atirekattā atireko devoti bhagavā atidevoti vuccati. Devo devānaṃ atireko atiuttamo atiseṭṭho ativisiṭṭho devo devādevātidevo, visuddhidevabhūto munindo labbhati. Taṃ devādevātidevaṃ.

Therein, ‘devādevātideva’ means the one who is a pure divine being, most supreme and most excellent among the conventional gods, designated as kings, and the gods by rebirth, such as the Four Great Kings and so on. Here, ‘devā’ refers to conventional gods. Human kings, queens, and princes are called ‘devā’ because they shine with human sovereignty and fortune. Again, ‘devā’ refers to gods by rebirth. The gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings and above are called ‘devā’ because they shine with divine sovereignty and fortune; they sport and delight in sensual pleasures and so on, or they dwell among them; they desire to conquer their enemies by their capacity for victory; they conduct themselves by giving and receiving honor, wealth, and so on, and by giving various instructions. They glow with the radiance attained through the power of their abundant merit. They travel unobstructed to their desired destinations. And they are able to accomplish whatever they wish. This is to be understood according to the method found in the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā. ‘Atideva’ means the Blessed One, who is a pure divine being, most supreme and most excellent among those gods. For the Blessed One is called ‘atideva’ because he surpasses those conventional gods and gods by rebirth in virtues such as morality. A god who surpasses the gods, a most supreme, most excellent, most distinguished god is a ‘devādevātideva.’ The Lord of Sages, being a pure divine being, is thus obtained. To that ‘god beyond gods’.

Vuttañhi dhammahadayavibhaṅge “devāti tayo devā sammuti devā, upapattidevā, visuddhidevā. Sammutidevā nāma rājāno deviyo rājakumārā. Upapattidevā nāma catumahārājike deve upādāya tadupari devā. Visuddhidevā nāma arahanto vuccantī”ti.

For it is said in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga: “Deva means three kinds of devas: conventional devas, devas by rebirth, and devas by purity. Conventional devas are kings, queens, and royal princes. Devas by rebirth are the devas beginning with those of the Four Great Kings and those above them. Devas by purity are said to be the Arahants.”

Bhagavā pana nirātisayāya abhiññākīḷāya uttamehi dibbabrahmaariyavihārehi saparasantānagatapañcavidhamāravija yicchānipphattiyācittissariya sattadhanādi sammāpaṭipatti aveccappasādasakkāradānaggahaṇasaṅkhātena dhammasabhāvapuggalajjhāsayānurūpānusāsanīsaṅkhātena ca vohārātisayena paramāya paññāsarīrappabhāsaṅkhātāya jutiyā anaññasādhāraṇāya ñāṇasarīragatiyā māravijaya sabbaññuguṇaparahita nipphādanesu appaṭihatāya sattiyā ca samannāgatattā sadevakena lokena saraṇanti gamanīyato abhitthavanīyato bhattivasena kamanīyato ca sabbe te deve tehi guṇehi abhibhuyya ṭhitattā tesaṃ devānaṃ atiseṭṭho atiuttamo devoti devādevātidevoti visuddhimagga mahāṭīkāyaṃ āgatanayenapi veditabbo.

The Blessed One, however, is endowed with the unparalleled sport of the higher knowledges; with the supreme divine, brahma, and noble abodes; with the fulfillment of his wish to conquer the five kinds of Māra affecting his own and others’ mental continuities; with sovereignty over the mind; with the seven treasures and so on; with right practice; with unwavering confidence; with the acceptance of honor and gifts; with surpassing excellence in discourse, designated as instruction that is suitable for the nature of the teaching and the dispositions of individuals; with the supreme radiance, designated as the splendor of the wisdom-body; with the unique course of the knowledge-body; and with the unobstructed power to conquer Māra and to accomplish the qualities of an omniscient one and the welfare of others. Because he is to be gone to for refuge, to be praised, and to be sought with devotion by the world with its gods, and because he stands having surpassed all those devas with these qualities, he is the most excellent, most supreme deva among those devas. Thus, he is a ‘devādevātideva,’ the god beyond gods. This is to be understood according to the method found in the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā.

Nidhanavapudharanti antimakāyadhāraṇaṃ. Ettha ca nidhanasaddo pariyosānavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko. Atha vā nidheti pariyosānaṃ karoti etenāti nidhanaṃ. Nidheti vināseti bhavanti vā nidhanaṃ, antimakāyo labbhati. Nipubba dhā dhātu [M 0.0164] nāse yu. Vapati kusalākusalabījametthāti vapu, kāyo. Vapadhātu bījasantāne u. Nidhanañca taṃ vapu cāti nidhanavapu, taṃ dhāretīti nidhanavapudharo, munindo. Taṃ nidhanavapudharaṃ. So hi anamataggasaṃsārabhavesu nibbattentānaṃ sabbakilesānaṃ bodhimaṇḍe aggamaggañāṇasatthena samucchindi tattā punabbhavābhinibbatti natthi. Ayañhi buddhabhāvajāti antima bhavo hoti, tasmā visesena munindameva nidhanavapudharanti thometi. Vuttañhetaṃ aṅguttarapāḷiyaṃ “buddho antima dharo”ti.

‘Nidhanavapudharaṃ’ means the bearer of the final body. Here, the word ‘nidhana’ signifies the end and is an underived stem. Alternatively, that by which one brings an end is ‘nidhana.’ Or, that which destroys or puts an end to existence is ‘nidhana’; thus, the final body is meant. It is formed from the root ‘dhā’ with the prefix ‘ni-’ and the suffix ‘yu’ in the sense of destruction. That in which the seeds of the wholesome and unwholesome are sown is ‘vapu,’ the body. It is from the root ‘vap’ with the suffix ‘u’ in the sense of the continuity of seeds. The final body is ‘nidhanavapu,’ and he who bears it is the ‘nidhanavapudharo,’ the Lord of Sages. To that ‘bearer of the final body.’ For he, at the seat of enlightenment, utterly cut off with the sword of the knowledge of the supreme path all the defilements that cause rebirth in the beginningless round of existence; therefore, there is no further becoming or rebirth for him. This birth into the state of a Buddha is his final existence. Therefore, he praises the Lord of Sages specifically as the ‘bearer of the final body.’ For this is stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: “The Buddha is the bearer of the final body.”

Mārabhaṅganti devaputtādipañcamāre viddhaṃsanaṃ. Mārasaddattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Pañcamāre bhañjati abhañji bhañjissatīti mārabhaṅgo, munindo. Mārasaddūpapada bhanjadhātu avamaddane tapaccayo. Tassa saha dhātvantena goādeso. Nakārassa niggahitādeso. Tassa kavaggantādeso. Taṃ mārabhaṅgaṃ. Abhaṅganti mārasenāya bhañjituṃ viddhaṃsituṃ asamatthaṃ, bhañjiyate bhaṅgo. Nabhaṅgo abhaṅgo. Atha vā mārasenāya na bhañjiyatīti abhaṅgo. Mārasenāya bhañjituṃ na arahatīti attho. Mārasenā bhañjituṃ na samatthoti vā abhaṅgo, munindo. Taṃ abhaṅgaṃ.

'Mārabhaṅga' means the destroyer of the fivefold Māra, including the devaputta Māra. The meaning of the word 'Māra' has already been explained above. He who breaks, has broken, or will break the fivefold Māra is 'mārabhaṅga', the Lord of Sages. The term is formed from the root 'bhañj' in the sense of crushing (avamaddane), with the word 'Māra' as the preceding element (upapada) and the suffix 'ta'. This suffix, along with the final part of the root, is replaced by 'ga'. The letter 'n' is replaced by a niggahīta, which is then replaced by the final letter of the guttural class (ṅ). This is 'mārabhaṅga'. 'Abhaṅga' means unable to be broken or destroyed by Māra's army. That which is broken is 'bhaṅga'; 'na bhaṅga' (not broken) is 'abhaṅga'. Alternatively, 'abhaṅga' means 'not broken by Māra's army'; the meaning is that he is not fit to be broken by Māra's army. Or, 'abhaṅga' means Māra's army is not able to break him, the Lord of Sages. This is 'abhaṅga'.

Dīpaṃdīpaṃ pajānanti ettha pajānaṃ dīpaṃ dīpanti sambandho. Tattha pajānanti sattānaṃ. Tehi kammakilesehi pajāyanti nibbattiyanti, pakārena vā jāyanti nibbattanti paṭisandhicutivasenāti pajāti vuccanti. Dīpanti paññāpadīpaṃ. Tañhi kusalākusale dhamme vibhajitvā dīpeti pakāseti jotetīti dīpanti vuccati. Atha vā dippati jotetīti dīpo. Andhakāraṃ vidhametvā ālokaṃ pakāsetīti attho. Dīpadhātu dittiyaṃ a. Dīpamivāti dīpā, paññā. Yathā hi padīpo andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokaṃ pakāseti, evaṃ paññā avijjandhakāraṃ hantvā dhammālokaṃ pakāsetīti [M 0.0165] vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ dīpaṃ. Puna dīpanti dīpakaṃ pakāsentanti attho. So hi dīpeti pakāsetīti dīpoti vuccati. Munindo hi payirupāsanavasena gatāgatānaṃ vineyyasattānaṃ dhammadesanāya catumaggañāṇādipaññāpadīpaṃ pakāsetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ dīpaṃ.

Here, the connection is 'illuminating the lamp for beings' (`pajānaṃ dīpaṃ dīpan ti`). Therein, 'of beings' (`pajānaṃ`) means 'of living beings' (`sattānaṃ`). They are called 'pajā' (beings) because they are born (`pajāyanti`) or produced by those actions and defilements, or because they are born (`jāyanti`) or produced in various ways through rebirth-linking and death. 'Lamp' (`dīpaṃ`) means the lamp of wisdom. For it is called a 'lamp' because it divides wholesome and unwholesome states and illuminates, reveals, and makes them shine. Alternatively, that which shines (`dippati`) or illuminates (`joteti`) is a 'lamp' (`dīpo`). The meaning is that it dispels darkness and reveals light. The root 'dīp' is in the sense of shining, with the suffix 'a'. 'Like a lamp' (`dīpamiva`) means a lamp (`dīpā`), that is, wisdom. For it is said: just as a lamp dispels darkness and reveals light, so wisdom destroys the darkness of ignorance and reveals the light of the Dhamma. That is the lamp. Again, 'lamp' (`dīpaṃ`) means the illuminator, the one who reveals. For he is called a 'lamp' (`dīpo`) because he illuminates and reveals. It is said that the Lord of Sages, by teaching the Dhamma to the trainable beings who come and go to attend upon him, reveals the lamp of wisdom, such as the knowledge of the four paths. That is the lamp.

Jayavarasayaneti pañcamāravijayantaṭṭhānabhūte uttama bodhipallaṅkāsane. Pañcamāre jināti etthāti jayo, bodhirukkhapallaṅko. Jidhātu jaye ṇa. Varitabbo patthi tabboti varo, varadhātu patthane a. Varati nivāreti hīnanti vā varo. Varadhātu nivāraṇe a. Buddhena seviyati bhajiyati etthāti sayano. Sidhātu sevāyaṃyu. Varo uttamo sayano varasayano, jayoeva varasayano jayavarasayano, bodhirukkhapallaṅko. Tasmiṃ.

On the excellent victorious seat (`jayavarasayane`), which has become the place of victory over the five Māras, the supreme seat of the Bodhi-dais. Because he conquers the five Māras here, it is 'jaya' (victory), that is, the dais at the foot of the Bodhi-tree. The word is formed from the root 'ji' in the sense of victory, with the suffix 'ṇa'. That which is to be desired (`varitabbo`), to be longed for (`patthitabbo`), is 'vara' (excellent). The word is formed from the root 'var' in the sense of desiring, with the suffix 'a'. Or, because it wards off (`vāreti`) or prevents (`nivāreti`) what is inferior (`hīnaṃ`), it is 'vara'. The word is formed from the root 'var' in the sense of preventing, with the suffix 'a'. Because it is frequented (`seviyati`) or resorted to (`bhajiyati`) by the Buddha, it is a 'sayana' (seat). The word is formed from the root 'si' in the sense of frequenting, with the suffix 'yu'. An excellent (`varo`), supreme (`uttamo`) seat (`sayano`) is a 'varasayana'. Victory (`jayo`) itself is the excellent seat, hence 'jayavarasayana', which is the dais at the foot of the Bodhi-tree. On that (`tasmiṃ`).

Bodhipattaṃdhipattanti bodhipattaṃ adhipattanti padacchedo. Bodhipattanti arahattamaggasabbaññutañāṇaṃ gataṃ. Ettha ca bodhisaddo rukkhamaggañāṇasabbaññutañāṇanibbānesupi vattati. Tathā hesa bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddhotiādīsu rukkhe vattati. Bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇantiādīsu magge. Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrī medhasotiādīsu sabbaññutañāṇe. Patvāna bodhiṃ amataṃ asaṅkhatantiādīsu nibbāne. Idha pana bhagavato arahattamaggasabbaññutañāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Cattāri saccāni bujjhatīti bodhi, arahatta maggañāṇaṃ. Sabbañeyyadhamme bujjhatīti bodhi, sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. Budhadhātu ñāṇe ṇa ī ca. Bodhi ca bodhi ca bodhi sarūpekasesavasena. Taṃ apajjiṃ agaminti bodhi patto, munindo. Taṃ bodhipattaṃ. Adhipattanti sadevake loke sabbadevamanussānaṃ jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ gatanti attho. Sabbadevamanussānaṃ adhikaṃ jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ vuḍḍhatarabhāvaṃ patto gatoti adhipatto, munindo. Taṃ adhipattaṃ. Yathā hi kukkuṭapotakānaṃ [M 0.0166] yo kukkuṭapotako aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā abhinibbhido, so tesaṃ jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ vuḍḍhatarabhāvaṃ gato, evameva bhagavā sadevake loke avijjā gatāya pajāya taṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā paṭhamataraṃ ariyāya jātiyā jātattā ca sīlasamādhipaññādi sabbaguṇehi adhikattā ca appaṭisamattā ca sabbadevamanussānaṃ jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ vuḍḍhatarabhāvaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ appaṭisamabhāvañca patto gatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā adhipattanti thometi.

The word division is 'bodhipattaṃ' and 'adhipattaṃ'. 'Bodhipattaṃ' means having attained the knowledge of the Arahant path and omniscience. Here, the term 'bodhi' is used in the sense of the tree, the path, knowledge, omniscience, and Nibbāna. For instance, in 'He first attained supreme enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree,' it refers to the tree. In 'Bodhi is called the knowledge in the four paths,' it refers to the path. In 'The one of great wisdom reaches the supreme bodhi,' it refers to omniscience. In 'Having attained bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned,' it refers to Nibbāna. Here, however, what is intended is the Blessed One’s knowledge of the Arahant path and omniscience. 'Bodhi' is so called because one awakens to the Four Truths; this is the knowledge of the Arahant path. 'Bodhi' is so called because one awakens to all knowable things; this is the knowledge of omniscience. It is formed from the root 'budh' in the sense of knowing, with the suffixes 'ṇa' and 'ī'. The two instances of 'bodhi' are reduced to one by the principle of retaining one of similar forms (sarūpekasesa). He attained that bodhi, he went to it; thus he is 'bodhipatta' (one who has attained bodhi), the Lord of Sages. That is 'bodhipattaṃ'. 'Adhipattaṃ' means having attained the state of being foremost among all gods and humans in the world with its deities. He has attained a superior, foremost, and greater status among all gods and humans; thus he is 'adhipatta', the Lord of Sages. That is 'adhipattaṃ'. Just as among chicks, the one that first breaks the eggshell and emerges attains the foremost and greater status among them, so too the Blessed One, in this world with its deities, for the sake of beings caught in ignorance, broke open the eggshell of ignorance and was the very first to be born with the noble birth. And because he is superior in all qualities—such as virtue, concentration, and wisdom—and is incomparable, it is said that he has attained the foremost, greater, supreme, and incomparable status among all gods and humans. Therefore, he is praised as 'adhipatta'.

Brahmābrahmāgatānanti brahma abrahma āgatānanti padacchedo. Āgatānaṃ payirupāsanavasena āgatānaṃ brahma devamanussaparisānanti attho. Tattha brahmāti brahmapārisajjādi brahmā. Te hi jhānādiguṇehi brūhanti vaḍḍhantīti brahmāti vuccanti, abrahmāti devamanussā. Te hi na brahmā abrahmāti vuccanti, āgacchanti payirupāsanavasenāti āgatā, brahmā brahmāno labbhanti. Āpubbagamudhātu gatiyaṃ ta. Āgatā brahmā ca abrahmā cāti brahmābrahmāgatā, tesaṃ. Visesana paranipātapadametaṃ agyāhitotiādīsu viya. Taṃ pana padaṃ varagirakathikantipade sampadānaṃ. Payirupāsanānaṃ brahma devamanussaparisānanti attho.

'Brahmābrahmāgatānaṃ' is divided as 'brahma-abrahmā-āgatānaṃ'. 'Of those who have come' (`āgatānaṃ`) means of the assemblies of Brahmās, devas, and humans who have come for the purpose of attendance. Herein, 'brahmā' refers to the Brahmās of Brahmā's retinue and others. They are called 'brahmā' because they grow (`brūhanti`) and increase (`vaḍḍhanti`) through qualities such as jhāna. 'Abrahmā' refers to devas and humans. They are called 'abrahmā' because they are not Brahmās. They are 'āgatā' (those who have come) because they come (`āgacchanti`) for the purpose of attendance. The term is formed from the root 'gam' in the sense of movement, with the prefix 'ā-' and the suffix 'ta'. Those who have come who are Brahmās and non-Brahmās are 'brahmābrahmāgatā'; 'of them' (`tesaṃ`). This is an adjectival term placed after its noun, as in cases like 'agyāhito'. This term, however, functions as a dative in relation to the word 'varagirakathikaṃ' (the speaker of the excellent speech). The meaning is: for the assemblies of Brahmās, devas, and humans who have come to attend upon him.
