Varagirakathikanti uttamaṃ dhammavācaṃ desentaṃ. Seṭṭhavācāya dhammaṃ desamānaṃ vā, gāyati kathiyatīti girā, vācā. Gādhātu sadde īro. Varā seṭṭhā girā vācā varagirā. Tāya dhammaṃ kathetīti varagirakathiko, munindo. Uttamāya manāpabhūtavācāya dhammaṃ desetīti attho. Taṃ.

'Varagirakathikaṃ' means him who teaches the supreme Dhamma-speech, or him who teaches the Dhamma with the best speech. 'Girā' (speech) is so called because it is sung (`gāyati`) or spoken (`kathiyati`); it means speech (`vācā`). It is formed from the root 'gā' in the sense of sound, with the suffix 'īra'. Excellent (`varā`), best (`seṭṭhā`) speech (`girā`) is 'varagirā'. He who speaks the Dhamma with that excellent speech is 'varagirakathika', the Lord of Sages. The meaning is that he teaches the Dhamma with supreme and pleasing speech. Him.

Pāpahīnanti lāmakaakusalakilesaṃ. Tañhi apāyādi dukkhaṃ pāpetīti pāpoti vuccati. Akusalakileso. Papubbaapadhātu pāpuṇane. Kusaladhammena hātabbaṃ caji tabbanti hīnanti vuccati. Lāmakadhammo. Hādhātu cāge tapaccayo, tassino. Pāpoeva hīnaṃ pāpahīnaṃ. Pahīnanti [M 0.0167] arahattamaggañāṇena susamucchinnaṃ. Pajahatīti pahīno, munindo. Papubbahādhātu cāge ino. Sabbe akusaladhamme aggamaggañāṇena samucchindatīti attho.

'Pāpahīnaṃ' means the base, unwholesome defilement. It is called 'pāpa' (evil) because it leads (`pāpeti`) to suffering, such as in the lower realms; it is the unwholesome defilement. The word is formed from the root 'āp' in the sense of attaining, with the prefix 'pa-'. It is called 'hīna' (base) because it is to be given up (`hātabbaṃ`) and relinquished (`cajitabbaṃ`) by wholesome states; it is an inferior quality. The word is formed from the root 'hā' in the sense of abandoning, with the suffix 'ta', which takes the form 'ina'. That which is evil (`pāpa`) is itself base (`hīna`); thus it is 'pāpahīna'. 'Pahīnaṃ' means utterly uprooted by the knowledge of the Arahant path. He who abandons (`pajahati`) is 'pahīna', the Lord of Sages. The word is formed from the root 'hā' in the sense of abandoning, with the prefix 'pa-' and the suffix 'ina'. The meaning is that he eradicates all unwholesome states with the knowledge of the highest path.

Lokālokābhirāmanti lokaalokaabhirāmanti padacchedo. Manussalokadevabrahmalokānaṃ abhirāmaṭṭhānabhūtanti attho. Lokoti manussa loko, so hi lokayati patiṭṭhahati pavattati vā ettha puññāpuññaṃ tabbipāko cāti loko, manussa loko. Lokadhātu patiṭṭhāyaṃ a. Na loko aloko. Devabrahmaloko. Loko ca aloko ca lokālokā, tesaṃ sattalokānaṃ abhiadhikaṃ ramanti etthāti lokālokābhirāmo. Munindo, taṃ. So hi tilokānaṃ pūjānuggahādikaraṇavasena abhirāmaṭṭhānaṃ hotīti lokālokābhirāmanti thometi. Satatanti niccaṃ. Rattidivaṃ abhiṇhanti attho. Munindanti pañcamunissaraṃ, taṃ munindaṃ. Abhinameti ahaṃ abhisakkaccaṃ namāmīti sambandhoti.

'Lokālokābhirāmaṃ' is divided as 'loka-aloka-abhirāmaṃ'. The meaning is: he who has become a place of delight for the human world, the deva world, and the Brahmā world. 'Loka' means the human world; it is called 'loka' because merit and demerit and their results are seen (`lokayati`), established (`patiṭṭhahati`), or proceed (`pavattati`) therein. The word is formed from the root 'lok' in the sense of establishing, with the suffix 'a'. That which is not the human world is 'aloka', meaning the deva and Brahmā worlds. 'Loka' and 'aloka' together are 'lokāloka'. He in whom the beings of these worlds exceedingly delight (`abhiramanti`) is 'lokālokābhirāma', the Lord of Sages; him. For he is a place of delight for the three worlds, being an object of their worship and a source of their support; thus he is praised as 'lokālokābhirāma'. 'Satataṃ' means constantly; the meaning is day and night, frequently. 'Munindaṃ' means the supreme lord of sages; that Lord of Sages. The connection is: 'abhinameti' (he bows down) implies 'I respectfully pay homage' (`ahaṃ abhisakkaccaṃ namāmi`).

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Devādevātidevaṃ sammutidevaupapattidevānaṃ atiuttamaṃ visuddhidevabhūtaṃ nidhanavapudharaṃ antimakāyadhāraṇaṃ, mārabhaṅgaṃ devaputtādipañcamāre viddhaṃsanaṃ abhaṅgaṃ mārasenāya bhañjituṃ asamatthaṃ, mārasenā bhañjanārahaṃ vā, pajānaṃ sattānaṃ dīpaṃ paññāpadīpaṃ, kammabhūtaṃ dīpaṃ dīpakaṃ pakāsentaṃ, jayavarasayane pañcamāravijayantaṭṭhānabhūte uttamabodhipallaṅkāsane ādhārabhūte, bodhipattaṃ arahattamaggasabbaññutañāṇaṃ gataṃ adhipattaṃ sadevake loke sabbadevamanussānaṃ jeṭṭhabhāvaṃ gataṃ, brahmā brahmāgatānaṃ payirupāsanavasena āgatānaṃ brahmadeva manussaparisānaṃ varagirakathikaṃ seṭṭhavācāya dhammaṃ desamānaṃ pāpahīnaṃ lāmakaakusalakilesaṃ pahīnaṃ arahattamagga ñāṇena [M 0.0168] susamucchinnaṃ lokālokābhirāmaṃ manussa lokadevabrahmalokānaṃ abhirāmabhūtaṃ, munindaṃ pañcamunissaraṃ taṃ munindaṃ satataṃ niccaṃ abhiṇhaṃ ahaṃ abhiname abhisakkaccaṃ namāmīti.

Herein is the concise explanation. He is the God of gods, supreme among conventional gods and gods by rebirth, a pure divine being, bearing his final body, his last physical form; the destroyer of Māra, who crushed the five Māras including the Māra of divine sons, unbreakable, incapable of being shattered by Māra’s army, or worthy of shattering Māra's army; a refuge for beings, the lamp of wisdom, illuminating the island that is the ground of kamma; seated on the supreme throne of enlightenment, the foundation, which is the excellent victory seat, the place of victory over the five Māras; who attained the knowledge of the path to Arahantship and omniscience, who attained supremacy among all gods and humans in the world with its deities; the supreme speaker who, with excellent speech, delivers the Dhamma to assemblies of Brahmās, gods, and humans who have approached him for service; who has abandoned evil, having forsaken base, unwholesome defilements, thoroughly uprooted by the knowledge of the Arahant path; delightful to the world and the non-world, pleasing to the human world, the world of gods, and the Brahmā world—that Lord of Sages, lord of the five sages—him I constantly, ceaselessly, and repeatedly revere with deep respect, I bow down.

Dvāvīsatimavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-second verse of homage is completed.

23.

23.

Buddho nigrodhabimbo mudukaracaraṇo brahmaghoseṇijaṅgho,

Kosacchādaṅgajāto punarapi sugato suppatiṭṭhitapādo;

Mūdodātuṇṇalomo athamapi sugato brahmujuggattabhāvo,

Nīlakkhī dīghapaṇhī sukhumamalachavī thomyarasaggasaggī.

The Buddha, with a body of banyan-like proportion, with soft, tender hands and feet, with a Brahma-like voice and antelope-like calves; with genitals concealed in a sheath, and again the Fortunate One with well-set feet; with a soft, white uṇṇā-curl, and also the Fortunate One with a Brahma-like upright body; with deep blue eyes, with long heels, with delicate and pure skin, possessing the supreme sense of taste.

24.

24.

Cattālīsaggadanto samakalapanajo antaraṃsappapīno,

Cakkenaṅkitapādo aviraḷadasano mārajussaṅkhapādo;

Tiṭṭhanto nonamantobhayakaramudunā jaṇṇukānāmasanto,

Vaṭṭakkhandho jino gotaruṇapakhumako sīhapubbaḍḍhakāyo.

He has forty excellent teeth, even teeth, and is full between the shoulders; his feet are marked with wheels, his teeth are without gaps, and he has prominent ankles; standing upright without bending, he can touch his knees with his soft, tender hands; with rounded shoulders, the Victor, with eyelashes like a young ox, and the forepart of his body like a lion.

25.

25.

Sattappīno ca dīghaṅguli matha sugato lomakūpekalomo,

Sampannodātadāṭho kanakasamataco nīlamuddhaggalomo;

Sambuddho thūlajivho atha sīhahanuko jālikappādahattho,

Nātho uṇhīsasīso itiguṇasahitaṃ taṃ mahesiṃ namāmi.

He is well-fleshed in seven places, with long fingers, and the Fortunate One has a single hair in each pore; with perfectly white canine teeth, a golden-hued skin, and dark blue hair curling upwards; the Fully Enlightened One has a broad tongue, a lion-like jaw, and webbed fingers and toes; the Protector with a protuberance on the crown of his head—endowed with these virtues—to that great sage I bow.

23. Evaṃ [M 0.0169] dvāvīsatimāya gāthāya munindassa paṇāmaṃ katvā idāni buddho nigrodhabimbotyādīhi tīhi gāthāhi buddhassa dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasampannehi guṇehi thomitvā mahesiṃ vanditukāmo buddho nigrodhabimbotyādigāthāttayamāha. Taṃ pana gāthāttayaṃ saddharāgāthāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sādhakaṃ pana heṭṭhā vuttameva.

23. Having thus paid homage to the Lord of Sages with the twenty-second verse, now, desiring to venerate the Great Sage by praising the Buddha with the virtues endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, he speaks the three verses beginning 'Buddho nigrodhabimbo.' These three verses, moreover, should be understood as Saddharā verses. The justification, however, is as stated below.

Tattha paṭhamagāthāyaṃ buddhoti paṭividdhacatusaccadhammo paṭividdhaniravasesasabbadhammo vā. Taṃ pana padaṃ nigrodhabimbo tyādīsu padesu tulyaliṅgattabhāvena sambandhitabbaṃ. So hi cattāri saccāni bujjhati abujjhi bujjhissatīti ca, niravasesasabbadhamme bujjhati abujjhi bujjhissatīti ca buddhoti vuccati. Tesu pana dvīsu vikappesu paṭhamavikappe budhadhātussa vāccaṃ catusaccadhammapaṭivijjhanaṃ arahattamaggañāṇaṃ mukhyena labbhati. Heṭṭhā maggaphalañāṇañca vipassanāñāṇañca pāramīñāṇañca phalūpacārena. Arahattaphalañāṇañca sabbaññutañāṇādipacchimapacchimañāṇāni ca kāraṇūpacārena. Tapaccayassa vāccaṃ tena mukhyopacārena upalakkhito aparimitaguṇagaṇālaṅkāraṃ khandhapañcakaṃ paṭicca buddhobuddhoti paññatto sattaviseso labbhati. Dutiya vikappe budhadhātussa vāccaṃ sabbañeyyadhammapaṭivijjhanasamatthaṃ sabbaññutañāṇaṃ mukhyena labbhati. Catumaggaphalañāṇañca vipassanā pāramīñāṇañca phalūpacārena. Āsayānusayañāṇādipacchima pacchimañāṇāni kāraṇūpacārena. Tapaccayassa vāccaṃ tena mukhyopacārena upalakkhito aparimāṇaguṇoghālaṅkataṃ khandhapañcakaṃ paṭicca buddhobuddhoti paññatto sattaviseso labbhati. Kiṃpanettha budhadhātussa vāccabhūtaṃ ñāṇameva buddho nāma hoti. Udāhu tapaccayassa vāccabhūto khandhasantāno buddho nāmāti. Ñāṇena pana malakara kilesānaṃ savāsanānaṃ niravasesaṃ pahīnattā citta santāno suddho hoti. Tassa pana suddhattā tassa nissayabhūto [M 0.0170] rūpakāyopi suddho hoti. Tasmā tapaccayassa vāccabhūto arahattamaggañāṇādīnaṃ ādhārabhūto khandhasantāno nāmapaññattivohārena buddho nāmāti. Tena vuttaṃ paṭisambhidāmaggaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

In the first verse, 'Buddha' means one who has penetrated the Four Noble Truths, or one who has penetrated all phenomena without remainder. That term, moreover, should be connected to words like 'nigrodhabimba' and so on, due to their similar gender. For he understands, has understood, and will understand the Four Noble Truths; and he understands, has understood, and will understand all phenomena without remainder—thus he is called 'Buddha.' Among these two alternatives, in the first alternative, the primary meaning of the root 'budh' is taken as the knowledge of the Arahant path, which penetrates the Four Noble Truths. By extension, the knowledge of the lower paths and fruitions, the knowledge of insight, and the knowledge of perfections are obtained by way of result (phalūpacāra). And the knowledge of Arahantship-fruition and the subsequent ultimate knowledges such as omniscience are obtained by way of cause (kāraṇūpacāra). The meaning of the suffix 'ta' (in Buddha), on the other hand, refers to a special being designated as 'Buddha' in dependence on the five aggregates, which are adorned with immeasurable qualities, characterized by that primary meaning and its extensions. In the second alternative, the primary meaning of the root 'budh' is taken as omniscient knowledge, which is capable of penetrating all knowable phenomena. And the knowledge of the four paths and fruitions, the knowledge of insight, and the knowledge of perfections are obtained by way of result. The subsequent ultimate knowledges such as the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies are obtained by way of cause. The meaning of the suffix 'ta', on the other hand, refers to a special being designated as 'Buddha' in dependence on the five aggregates, which are adorned with a stream of boundless qualities, characterized by that primary meaning and its extensions. Now, here, is it the knowledge itself—which constitutes the essential meaning of the root 'budh'—that is called 'Buddha'? Or is it the continuum of aggregates, which constitutes the essential meaning of the suffix 'ta', that is called 'Buddha'? By knowledge, moreover, the stain-making defilements along with their latent tendencies are completely abandoned without remainder, and thus the mental continuum becomes purified. Due to that purity, moreover, the physical body dependent on it also becomes pure. Therefore, the continuum of aggregates—which constitutes the essential meaning of the suffix 'ta' and serves as the basis for the knowledge of the Arahant path and so on—is called 'Buddha' by way of conventional designation (nāmapaññatti). Hence, it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga commentary—

“Sabbesu dhammesu appaṭihatañāṇa nimittānuttaravimokkhādhigamaparibhāvitaṃ khandhasantānaṃ upādāya paṇṇattiko sabbaññutapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā saccābhisambodhimupādāya paṇṇattiko sattaviseso buddho”ti.

"A special being is designated as 'Buddha' based on the continuum of aggregates, which is imbued with the attainment of the unsurpassed liberation that is the sign of unhindered knowledge regarding all phenomena; or, a special being is designated as 'Buddha' based on the full awakening to the truths, which is the basis for omniscience."

Paramatthabhūte hi khandhasantāne vohārasukhatthaṃ satta puggalādivohāro āropito. Evaṃ vohārappatto satto yāva bodhiñāṇatthāya na vāyamati, paṇidhānaṃ na karoti. Tāva sattotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Yato pana paṭṭhāya bodhiñāṇatthāya vāyamati, paṇidhānaṃ karoti, tadā bodhisatto nāma vohāro hoti. So pana yadā bodhiñāṇaṃ labhati, tadā buddho nāma vohāro hoti. Tasmā paññattisaṅkhāto khandhasantāno buddho nāmāti daṭṭhabbo. Vuttañhi mahāniddese “buddhoti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ, na pitarā kataṃ, na bhātarā kataṃ, na bhaginiyā kataṃ, na mittāmaccehi kataṃ, na ñātisā lohitehi kataṃ, na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṃ, na devatāhi kataṃ, vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutañāṇassa paṭilābhā sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ buddhoti taṃ buddha”nti. Atha vā paṭṭhānanayena vā nānantarikanayena vā ñāṇappadhāno suvisuddhakhandhasantāno buddho nāmāti atthopi yujjatevāti.

Indeed, on the continuum of aggregates, which is ultimate reality, conventional terms like 'being' or 'person' are imposed for the sake of ease in communication. So long as a being, thus conventionally designated, does not strive for the knowledge of awakening or make an aspiration, that being is reckoned merely as a 'being.' But from the moment that being begins striving for the knowledge of awakening and makes an aspiration, that being is then conventionally termed a 'bodhisatta.' And when that being attains the knowledge of awakening, that being is then conventionally termed a 'Buddha.' Therefore, the continuum of aggregates, which is a conventional designation, should be understood as being what is named 'Buddha.' As stated in the Mahāniddesa: "'Buddha'—this name is not given by a mother, not by a father, not by a brother, not by a sister, not by friends or companions, not by relatives or kin, not by ascetics or brahmins, not by deities. This is an empirically realized designation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, at the culmination of liberation, at the root of enlightenment, together with the attainment of omniscient knowledge—that is, 'Buddha.'" Alternatively, by the method of conditionality or the method of proximity, the thoroughly purified continuum of aggregates, with wisdom as foremost, is also rightly understood to be 'Buddha.'

Nigrodhabimboti nigrodharukkhassa parimaṇḍalo viya parimaṇḍalasarīro. Adhobhāgaṃ rundhatīti nigrodho, vaṭarukkho. Nipubbarudhadhātu āvaraṇe ṇa, usso gāgamo. Vamati [M 0.0171] uggiratīti bimbo, sarīro. Vamudhātu uggiraṇe bo. Vamissa vassa bittaṃ. Nigrodhassa parimaṇḍalo viya parimaṇḍalo bimbo sarīro yassāti nigrodhabimbo, buddho. Nigrodhaparimaṇḍalabimboti vattabbe parimaṇḍalasaddalope nevaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā hi paṇṇāsahatthatāya vā satahatthatāya vā samakkhandhasākho nigrodho dīghatopi vitthāratopi ekappamāṇova hoti, evaṃ kāyatopi byāmatopi ekappamāṇo. Yathā aññesaṃ kāyo vā dīgho hoti, byāmo vā na evaṃ visamappamāṇoti attho. Vuttañhi brahmāyusutte “nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo kho pana bhavaṃ gotamo. Yāvatakvāssa kāyo, tāva takvāssa byāmo. Yāvatakvāssa byāmo, tāva takvāssa kāyo”ti.

'Nigrodhabimba' means 'with a perfectly round body like the circumference of a nigrodha tree'. It is called 'nigrodha' (banyan tree) because it obstructs the lower part; it is a banyan tree. The root 'rudh' preceded by 'ni' is in the sense of covering, with the affix 'ṇa' and the augment 'usso'. 'Bimba' means 'body', as it emits or pours forth. The root 'vam' is in the sense of emitting, with the affix 'bo'. The 'va' of 'vam' becomes 'ba'. He whose perfectly round body is like the circumference of a nigrodha tree is 'Nigrodhabimba', the Buddha. Though one might say 'Nigrodhaparimaṇḍalabimba', it is stated thus with the omission of the word 'parimaṇḍala'. For just as a nigrodha tree with branches spreading fifty or a hundred cubits is uniform in height and breadth, so too is his body and his fathom of uniform measure. Unlike others, whose body may be long while their fathom is not, or whose fathom is long while their body is not, his proportions are not uneven—this is the meaning. As stated in the Brahmāyusutta: "Indeed, the venerable Gotama is of perfect proportions. As long as his body is, so long is his fathom. As long as his fathom is, so long is his body."

Mudukaracaraṇoti saṇhahatthapādo. Ettha ca mudusaddo saṇhasukhumavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko. Atha vā mudeti modayati satteti mudu, saṇhahatthapādo. Mudadhātu modane hāse vā u. Taṃ taṃ kammaṃ karoti etenāti karo, hattho carati gacchati etena taṃ taṃ ṭhānanti caraṇo, pādo. Caradhātu gatiyaṃ yu. Mudukaro ca caraṇo ca yassāti mudukaracaraṇo, buddho. Sappi maṇḍe osāritvā ṭhapitaṃ satavāraṃ vihatakappāsapaṭalaṃ viya mudujātamattakumārassa viya ca niccakālaṃ muduhattha pādoti attho.

"Mudukaracaraṇo" means one with soft hands and feet. Here, the word "mudu" conveys softness and subtlety, not being a regularly formed word. Alternatively, "mudu" means that which delights or pleases beings, hence soft hands and feet. The root 'mud' (to delight, to be joyful) takes the suffix 'u'. 'Karo' is that by which one performs various actions, referring to the hand. 'Caraṇo' is that by which one moves and goes to various places, referring to the foot. The root 'car' (to move) takes the suffix 'yu'. Thus, "mudukaracaraṇo" describes the Buddha, whose hands and feet are always soft, like the cream of clarified butter that has been strained and set aside, like a hundred-times-beaten layer of cotton, or like a newly born prince.

Brahmaghoseṇijaṅghoti brahmaghoso eṇijaṅghoti padacchedo. Brahmaghosoti brahmuno saro viya aṭṭhaṅga sampannasaravantoti attho. Jhānādiguṇehi brūhati vaḍḍhatītibrahmā. Brūhadhātu manipaccayo. Ghusiyati saddiyati kathiyatīti ghoso, saro. Ghusadhātu sadde ṇa. Brahmuno ghoso saro brahmaghoso, so viya ghoso [M 0.0172] saro yassāti brahmaghoso, buddho. Yathā hi mahābrahmuno pittasemhehi apalibuddhattā saro visuddho hoti, evameva tathāgatenapi kataṃ kammaṃ vatthuṃ sodheti, vatthussa suddhattā nābhito paṭṭhāya samuṭṭhahanto saro visuddho aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatoti attho. Tasmā brahmaghoso viya aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatasaravantoti thometi.

"Brahmaghoseṇijaṅgho" is to be divided as "brahmaghoso" and "eṇijaṅgho." "Brahmaghoso" means one who has a voice like that of Brahmā, possessing the eight qualities. Brahmā is one who grows or increases through qualities such as jhāna; the root 'brūh' takes the suffix 'maṇi'. 'Ghoso' is that which is sounded, resounded, or spoken, a voice; the root 'ghus' (to sound) takes the suffix 'ṇa'. The voice of Brahmā is 'brahmaghoso'; one whose voice is like that is 'brahmaghoso', the Buddha. Just as the great Brahmā’s voice is pure because it is unhindered by bile and phlegm, so too the Tathāgata's voice, arising from a purified physical basis—the kamma performed by the Tathāgata purifies the basis—is pure, originates from the navel upwards, and is endowed with eight qualities. Therefore, he is praised as having a voice like Brahmā's, complete with eight attributes.

Eṇijaṅghoti eṇimigassa jaṅghā viya suvaṭṭajāṇuko. Eti gacchatīti eṇi, migo. Idhātu gatiyaṃ ṇi. Jāyati kamanametāyāti jaṅgho, jāṇu. Janadhātu janane gho. Nassa niggahitādeso. Eṇimigassa jaṅgho viya jaṅgho yassa soti eṇijaṅgho, buddho. Yathā hi eṇimigassa jaṅgho suvaṭṭo hoti, evameva buddhassa maṃsussadena paripuṇṇajaṅgho. Na ekato bandhapiṇḍikamaṃso. Samantato samasaṇṭhitena maṃsena parikkhittāhi suvaṭṭitāhi sāli gabbhayavagabbhasadisāhi jaṅghāhi samannāgatoti attho. Tasmā eṇimigajaṅghasadiso suvaṭṭajāṇukoti thometi.

"Eṇijaṅgho" means having shanks like those of an antelope, with well-rounded knees. "Eṇi" means antelope, a creature that goes; the root 'i' (to go) takes the suffix 'ṇi'. 'Jaṅgho' is that by which one moves, the shin or knee; the root 'jan' (to be born, to produce) takes the suffix 'gho'. There is a substitution for 'na'. One whose shanks are like those of an antelope is 'eṇijaṅgho', the Buddha. Just as the shanks of an antelope are well-rounded, so too are the Buddha's shanks, full of flesh, not a mass of bunched muscle in one place, but endowed with shanks surrounded by evenly distributed flesh, well-rounded, and similar to the core of a rice stalk or barley stalk. Therefore, he is praised as having well-rounded knees similar to an antelope's shanks.

Kosacchādaṅgajātoti kosacchādaaṅgajātoti padacchedo. Usabhavāraṇādīnaṃ aṅgajāto viya suvaṇṇapaduma kaṇṇikasadisena vatthakosena paṭicchannena guyhaṅgajātena samannāgatoti attho. Kusati tiṭṭhati etthāti koso. Kusadhātu gatiyaṃ ṇa. Chādiyatīti chādo. Chadadhātu paṭicchanne ṇa. Kosena chādo kosacchādo. Aṅge sarīrāvayave jātanti aṅgajātaṃ. Kosacchādaṃ aṅgajātaṃ byañjanaṃ yassāti kosacchādaṅgajāto, buddho. Bhagavato hi usabhavāraṇādīnaṃ aṅgajāto viya suvaṇṇapadumakaṇṇi kasadisena kosohitavatthaguyhena byañjanena samannāgatoti attho. Tasmā kosacchādaṅgajātasampannoti thometi. Punarapīti puna apīti padacchedo. Rakārā gamo[M 0.0173]. Punāti eso atthantaratthe nipāto. Apisaddo sampiṇḍanattho. Sugatoti buddho. So hi sundaraṃ nibbānaṃ gacchatīti sugatoti vuccati.

The term "kosacchādaṅgajāto" is to be divided as "kosacchāda aṅgajāto." The meaning is that he is endowed with a concealed private organ, covered by a sheath, like the pericarp of a golden lotus, similar to the private organs of a bull or an elephant. 'Koso' is that in which one stands or remains; the root 'kus' (to move) takes the suffix 'ṇa'. 'Chādo' is that which is covered; the root 'chad' (to cover) takes the suffix 'ṇa'. 'Kosacchādo' is the covering sheath. 'Aṅgajātaṃ' refers to what is born or produced on a limb or body part. "Kosacchādaṅgajāto" means one whose private organ ('byañjanaṃ') is covered by a sheath—this refers to the Buddha. For the Blessed One is endowed with a private organ concealed in a sheath, like the pericarp of a golden lotus, similar to the private organs of a bull or an elephant. Therefore, he is praised as being endowed with a sheathed private organ. "Punarapīti" is to be divided as "puna api." The 'ra' is an insertion. "Puna" is a particle indicating another meaning. The word "api" serves the purpose of conjunction. "Sugato" refers to the Buddha. He is called "Sugato" because he goes beautifully to Nibbāna.

Suppatiṭṭhitapādoti suvaṇṇapādukatalamiva bhūmiyaṃ samaṃ suṭṭhu patiṭṭhitapādo. Samaṃ suṭṭhu bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhatīti suppatiṭṭhito, pādo. Su pati pubbo ṭhā dhātu gatinivattiyaṃ ta. Pajjati gacchati etenāti pādo. Padadhātu gatimhi ṇa. Suppatiṭṭhito pādo yassāti suppatiṭṭhitapādo, sugato. Yathā hi aññesaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pādaṃ ṭhapentānaṃ aggatalaṃ vā paṇhiṃ vā passaṃ vā paṭhamaṃ phusati vemajjhaṃ vā pana chiddaṃ hoti, ukkhipantānampi aggatalādīsu ekakoṭṭhāsova paṭhamaṃ uṭṭhahati, na evaṃ tassa. Tassa pana suvaṇṇapādukatalaṃ viya ekappahāreneva sakalapādatalaṃ bhūmiṃ phusati, bhūmito uṭṭhahati. Sacepi hi bhagavā anekasataporisaṃ narakaṃ akkamissāmīti pādaṃ nīharati, tāvadeva ninnaṭṭhānaṃ vātapūritaṃ viya kammārabhastaṃ unnamitvā pathavīsamaṃ hoti, unnataṭṭhānampi anto pavisati, dūre akkamissāmīti abhinīharantassa sineruppamāṇopi pabbato seditavetthaṅkuro viya namitvā pādasamīpaṃ āgacchati. Tathā hissa yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ katvā yugandharapabbataṃ akkamissāmīti pāde abhinīharato pabbato namitvā pādasamīpaṃ āgato. So taṃ akkamitvā dutiyapādena tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ akkami. Na hi cakkalakkhaṇena patiṭṭhātabbaṭṭhānaṃ visamaṃ bhavituṃ sakkoti. Khāṇu vā kaṇḍako vā sakkharakathalā vā uccārapassāvo vā kheḷasiṅghaṇikādīni vā purimatarāva apagacchanti. Tattha tattheva pathaviṃ pavisanti. Tathāgatassa hi sīlatejena paññātejena dhammatejena dasannaṃ pāramīnaṃ ānubhāvena ayaṃ mahāpathavī samā mudu pupphākiṇṇā honti. Tatra tathāgato samaṃ pādaṃ nikkhipati. Samaṃ uddharati, sabbāvantehi pādatalehi [M 0.0174] bhūmiṃ phusati, tasmā suppatiṭṭhitapādoti thometi.

"Suppatiṭṭhitapādo" means one whose feet are well and evenly planted on the ground, like the soles of golden sandals. That which is well and evenly planted on the ground is a 'suppatiṭṭhita' foot. The root 'ṭhā' (to stand), preceded by 'su' and 'pati', is in the sense of stopping motion, taking the suffix 'ta'. 'Pāda' (foot) is so called because one moves ('pajjati', goes) by means of it. The root 'pad' (to go) takes the suffix 'ṇa'. One whose feet are firmly planted is 'suppatiṭṭhitapādo', the Sugata. For when others place their feet on the ground, the ball of the foot, the heel, or the side touches first, or there is a gap in the middle; and when lifting them, only one part, such as the ball of the foot, rises first. Not so for him. For him, like the sole of a golden sandal, the entire sole of his foot touches the ground at once and lifts from it at once. Even if the Blessed One were to think, "I will step upon a hell many hundreds of men deep," the moment he extends his foot, the low ground would rise as if inflated by wind like a blacksmith’s bellows, becoming level with the earth. High ground would sink inward. If he were to intend, "I will step far away," even a mountain as vast as Sineru would bend like a tender vetta shoot and come near his foot. Indeed, when he performed the Twin Miracle and resolved to step upon the Yugandhara mountain, the mountain bent and came to his foot. Having stepped there, he then placed his second foot upon the Tāvatiṃsa realm. No place where the wheel-marked foot is set can remain uneven. Stumps, thorns, gravel, excrement, urine, spit, mucus—all such things vanish beforehand or sink into the earth right there. For by the power of the Tathāgata’s virtue, wisdom, and the Dhamma, and by the might of the ten perfections, this great earth becomes even, soft, and strewn with flowers. There, the Tathāgata places his foot evenly, lifts it evenly, and touches the ground with the entire sole. Therefore, he is praised as having firmly planted feet.

Mūdo dātuṇṇalomoti muda odāta uṇṇalomoti padacchedo. Bhamukantare jāto saṇhasukhumo seto suddho uṇṇalomavantoti attho. Ettha ca mudasaddo saṇhasukhumavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko. Atha vā mudeti mudayati satteti mudo, sukhumo. Mudadhātu modane a. Avadāyati khaṇḍiyatīti odāto. Avapubba dādhātu avakhaṇḍane ta. Atha vā avadāyati sujjhatīti odāto, yathā vodānanti. Mudo ca odāto ca mudodāto, uṇati uddhaṃ gacchatīti uṇṇā, lomo. Uṇṇasaddo hi loke lomasaddapariyāyoti vadanti ācariyā. Maṃsassa upari pavattatīti attho. Uṇadhātu gatiyaṃ ṇa. Maṃsacammāni lunāti chindatīti lomo. Ludhātu chindane manipaccayo. Lunitabboti vā lomo, uṇṇā ca sā lomo cāti uṇṇalomo, lomaviseso. Mudo dāto uṇṇalomo yassa soti mudodātuṇṇa lomo, sugato. Uṇṇālomaṃ pana bhagavato dvinnaṃ bhamukānaṃ vemajjhe nāsimatthakeyeva jātaṃ. Uggantvā pana nalāṭamajjhe jātaṃ. Sappimaṇḍe osāretvā ṭhapitasata vitatakappāsapaṭalaṃ viya mudaṃ. Parisuddhaosadhitārakavaṇṇaṃ viya ca sippalitūlalatātūlaṃ viya ca vigatamalena odātaṃ uṇṇālomaṃ atthi, na aññesanti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ brahmāyusutte –

“Mūdodātuṇṇalomo” is to be divided as “muda odāta uṇṇalomo.” The meaning is that he possesses an uṇṇaloma (a hair between the eyebrows) that is born between the eyebrows, soft, subtle, white, and pure. Here, the word `muda` conveys softness and subtlety, not being a regularly formed word. Alternatively, `mudo` is that which delights or soothes beings, hence subtle. The root `mud` (to delight) takes the suffix `a`. `Odāta` is that which is cleansed or purified. The root `dā` (to cut/cleanse), preceded by `ava`, is in the sense of cutting/cleansing, taking the suffix `ta`. Or, `odāta` is that which is purified, as in `vodāna`. `Mudo` and `odāta` together are `mudodāta`. `Uṇṇā` is that which goes upwards, i.e., `loma` (hair). Indeed, teachers say that in common parlance, the word `uṇṇā` is a synonym for `loma`. The meaning is that it exists above the flesh. The root `uṇa` (to go) takes the suffix `ṇa`. `Loma` is that which cuts or divides flesh and skin. The root `lud` (to cut) takes the suffix `maṇi`. Or, `loma` is that which should be cut. `Uṇṇā` and `loma` together mean `uṇṇaloma`, a special kind of hair. One whose `uṇṇaloma` is soft and white is `mudodātuṇṇalomo`, the Sugata. Now, the Blessed One's `uṇṇāloma` was born precisely in the middle between the two eyebrows, at the top of the nose. Having emerged, it was situated in the center of the forehead. It was soft, like a layer of cotton teased out a hundred times and spread with the cream of ghee. And like the color of a purified morning star, or like the fiber of a sippali creeper, it was white and free from impurities. The meaning is that he has this `uṇṇāloma`, and others do not. This is stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta:

“Uṇṇā kho panassa bhoto gotamassa bhamukantare jātā odātā mudu tūlasannibhā”ti.

“Indeed, between the eyebrows of Master Gotama, a tuft of hair has grown that is white, soft, and like cotton.”

Taṃ panetaṃ koṭiyaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhiyamānaṃ upaḍḍha bāhuppamāṇaṃ hoti. Vissaṭṭhaṃ dakkhiṇāvaṭṭavasena āvaṭṭitvā uddhaggā hutvā santiṭṭhati. Suvaṇṇaphalakamajjhe ṭhapitarajata pupphuḷakaṃ [M 0.0175] viya, suvaṇṇaghaṭato nikkhammamānaṃ khīradhāraṃ viya aruṇappabhārañjite gaganatale osadhitārakaṃ viya ca atimanoharāya siriyā virocati, tasmā mūdodātuṇṇalomoti thometi.

But when it is grasped by the tip and drawn out, it becomes half an arm's length. Released, it coils clockwise and stands upright with its tip raised. Like a silver stamen placed on a golden plate, like a stream of milk pouring from a golden pot, and like the morning star in the sky tinged with the red glow of dawn—it shines with exceedingly delightful splendor. Therefore, he is praised as `mudodātuṇṇaloma`.

Athamapīti tadaññaṃ api. Sugatoti buddho. So hi sundaravācaṃ gadati vadatīti sugatoti vuccati. Brahmujuggattabhāvoti brahmaujuuggataattabhāvoti padavibhāgo. Brahmuno uju uggataattabhāvo viya ujumeva uggataattabhāvo dīghasarīroti attho. Brahmāyusutte pana “brahmujugatto”tipāṭho. Tadaṭṭhakathāyañca brahmujugattoti brahmā viya ujugatto ujumeva uggatadīghasarīroti vivarati. Taṃ pana sandhāya brahmujuggattabhāvoti vuttaṃ.

“Athamapi” means “also something else.” “Sugata” refers to the Buddha. He is called “Sugata” because he speaks and utters beautiful words. The phrase “brahmujuggattabhāvo” is analyzed as “brahmā uju uggata attabhāvo.” It means having a straight and lofty self, like the straight and lofty self of Brahmā—that is, a tall body. In the Brahmāyu Sutta, however, the reading is “brahmujugatto.” And in the commentary to that, “brahmujugatto” is explained as “straight like Brahmā,” meaning “having a straight, upright, and tall body.” It is with reference to that that “brahmujuggattabhāvo” is stated.

Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho. Jhānādiguṇehi uparūparibrūhati vaḍḍhatīti brahmā. Brūhadhātu vaḍḍhane ma, arati avaṅkabhāvena pavattatīti uju, avaṅko. Aradhātu gatiyaṃ jupaccayo. Arissa uādeso. Uddhaṃ gacchati pāpuṇātīti uggato. Upubba gamudhātu gatiyaṃ to. Āhito āropito ahaṃ māno etthāti attā, sarīro. Āpubba dhā dhātu ropane manipaccayo tupaccayo vā. Dhassa to. Massa to. Atha vā sukhadukkhaṃ adati anubhavatīti attā. Adadhātu anubhavane manipaccayo. Kaccāyanasaddasatthe pana “sukhadukkhaṃ adati bhakkhatīti attā, jātijarāmaraṇādīhi adiyate bhakkhiyateti vā attā. Ātumā”ti vuttaṃ. Khyādīhi manimaca tovāti suttena padasiddhi veditabbā. Attāti abhidhānaṃ buddhi ca bhavanti etasmāti attabhāvo, rūpakāyo. Anuṭīkāyaṃ pana “āhito ahaṃ māno etthāti attā, soeva bhavati uppajjati na paraparikappito viya niccoti attabhāvo. Attāti vā diṭṭhigatikehi gahetabbākārena bhavati pavattatīti attabhāvo”ti vuttaṃ[M 0.0176]. Brahmuno ujumeva uggato attabhāvo viya ujumeva uggato attabhāvo yassa soti brahmujuggattabhāvo, sugato. Yebhuyyena hi sattā khandhe kaṭiyaṃ jāṇusūti tīsu ṭhānesu namanti. Thokaṃ kaṭiyaṃ namantā pacchato namanti. Itaresu dvīsu ṭhānesu purato. Dīghasarīrā paneke passā vaṅkā honti, eke mukhaṃ unnametvā nakkhattāni gaṇayantā viya caranti, eke appamaṃsalohitā sūlasadisā honti, pavedhamānā gacchanti, tathāgato pana ujumeva uggantvā dīghappamāṇo devanagare ussitasuvaṇṇa toraṇaṃ viya hoti. Tasmā brahmujuggattabhāvoti thometi.

Here is the meaning of the statement. He is called Brahmā because he grows and excels through the qualities of jhāna and so forth. The root `brūh` is in the sense of increasing, with the suffix `ma`. Moreover, he is called `uju` (straight) because his conduct proceeds without crookedness. The root `ar` is in the sense of going, with the suffix `ju`; the `ari` is substituted with `u`. He is called `uggata` (uplifted) because he rises upward and attains. The root `gam` (to go), preceded by `u`, takes the suffix `ta`. He is called `attā` (self) because the conceit 'I' is implanted or established therein, referring to the body. The root `dhā` (to place), preceded by `ā`, takes the suffix `maṇi` or `tu`; the `dh` becomes `t`, and the `m` becomes `t`. Alternatively, he is called `attā` because he experiences pleasure and pain. The root `ad` is in the sense of experiencing, with the suffix `maṇi`. In the Kaccāyana grammar, however, it is said: 'He is called “attā” because he consumes pleasure and pain, or because he is consumed by birth, aging, and death. He is also called “ātumā.”' The formation of the word should be understood according to the rule, 'Khyādīhi manimaca tovā.' The designation 'attā' (self) and intellect arise from this, hence 'attabhāvo' (individual existence), which is the physical body. In the Anuṭīkā, it is said: 'He is called “attā” because the conceit “I” is implanted therein. This very being arises, not being eternal as conceived by others, hence “attabhāvo.” Or, “attabhāvo” is so called because “attā” exists or proceeds in the manner grasped by those holding wrong views.' 'Brahmujuggattabhāvo' means one whose individual existence is straight and uplifted like Brahmā’s—thus, Sugato. For most beings, their bodies bend at three places: the shoulders, waist, and knees. Some bend slightly at the waist and lean backward. Others bend forward at the other two places. Some long-bodied beings are crooked sideways. Some walk with their faces upturned as if counting stars. Others, with little flesh and blood, are like spears, trembling as they go. But the Tathāgata, having risen up straight, is of great stature, like a raised golden archway in a celestial city. Therefore, he is praised as 'Brahmujuggattabhāvo.'

Nīlakkhīti nīlaakkhīti padacchedo. Atinīlanettena samannāgatoti attho. Ikkhati passati anena rūpārammaṇaṃ samavisamaṃ vāti akkhi, nettaṃ. Ikkhadhātu dassane i. Issa attaṃ. Nīlā atinīlā akkhi nettā yassāti nīlakkhi, sugato. Bhagavato hi na sakalanīlakkhiva hoti. Nīlayuttaṭṭhāne panassa ummārapupphasadisena ativisuddhena nīlavaṇṇena samannāgatāni akkhīni honti. Pītayuttaṭṭhāne kaṇikārapupphasadisena lohitavaṇṇena. Lohitayuttaṭṭhāne bandhujīvakapupphasadisena lohitavaṇṇena. Seta yuttaṭṭhāne osadhitārakasadisena setavaṇṇena. Kāḷa yuttaṭṭhāne addāriṭṭhakasadisena kāḷavaṇṇena samannāgatāni suvaṇṇavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇisīhapañjarasadisāni khāyanti. Vuttañhi mahāniddese “maṃsacakkhumhi bhagavato pañcavaṇṇā saṃvijjanti. Nīlo ca vaṇṇo, pītako ca vaṇṇo, lohitako ca vaṇṇo, kaṇho ca vaṇṇo, odāto ca vaṇṇo akkhilomāni ca bhagavato, yattha ca akkhi lomāni patiṭṭhitāni. Taṃ nīlaṃ hoti sunīlaṃ pāsādikaṃ dassaneyyaṃ ummārapupphasamānaṃ. Tassa parato pītakaṃ hoti [M 0.0177] supītakaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ pāsādikaṃ dassaneyyaṃ kaṇikārapupphasamānaṃ. Ubhato akkhikuṭāni bhagavato lohitakāni honti sulohikāni pāsādikāni dassaneyyāni indagopakasamānāni. Majjhe kaṇhaṃ hoti sukaṇhaṃ alūkhaṃ suddhaṃ pāsādikaṃ dassaneyyaṃ addāriṭṭhaka samānaṃ. Tassa parato odātaṃ hoti suodātaṃ setaṃ paṇḍaraṃ pāsādikaṃ dassaneyyaṃ osadhitārakasamāna”nti. Bhagavā pana tena maṃsacakkhunā caturaṅgasamannāgate andhakārepi samantā yojanaṃ passati divā ceva rattiñca.

The word 'nīlakkhīti' is split as 'nīla-akkhīti.' It means endowed with exceedingly blue eyes. The word 'akkhi' (eye) is derived from the root 'ikkha,' meaning 'to see,' because through it one sees visible objects, whether even or uneven. 'Nīlakkhi' means one whose eyes are blue or exceedingly blue, the Sugata. For the Blessed One, it is not as if his entire eye is blue. In the places where blue is appropriate, his eyes possess an exceedingly pure blue color, like the blossom of the flax plant. In the places where yellow is appropriate, they are yellow like the kaṇikāra flower. In the places where red is appropriate, they are red like the bandhujīvaka flower. In the places where white is appropriate, they are white like the morning star. In the places where black is appropriate, they are black like the `addāriṭṭhaka` gem. They appear like opened jeweled windows in a golden palace. As stated in the Mahāniddesa: 'In the Blessed One’s physical eye, five colors are found: blue, yellow, red, black, and white. The eyelashes of the Blessed One, and where the eyelashes are set, are blue, deep blue, delightful, and pleasing to behold, resembling the flax flower. Beyond that, the yellow is bright yellow, golden in color, delightful, and pleasing to behold, like the kaṇikāra flower. On both sides, the eye-sockets of the Blessed One are red, very red, delightful, and pleasing to behold, like the indagopaka insect. In the middle, the black is deep black, not rough, pure, delightful, and pleasing to behold, like the `addāriṭṭhaka` gem. Beyond that, the white is very white, bright, radiant, delightful, and pleasing to behold, like the morning star.' Moreover, with that physical eye, the Blessed One, even in darkness endowed with four factors, can see for a yojana all around, both day and night.

Vuttañhi mahāniddese –

For it was said in the Mahāniddesa:

“Tena bhagavā pākatikena maṃsacakkhunā attabhāva pariyāpannena purimasucaritakammābhinibbattena samantā yojanaṃ passati divā ceva rattiñca. Yadāpi caturaṅgasamannāgato andhakāro hoti, sūriyo ca atthaṅgamito hoti, kāḷapakkho ca uposatho hoti, tibbo ca vanasaṇḍo hoti, mahā ca kāḷamegho abbhuṭṭhito hoti, evarūpepi caturaṅgasamannāgate andhakāre samantā yojanaṃ passati. Natthi so kuṭṭo vā kavāṭaṃ vā pākāro vā pabbato vā gaccho vā latā vā āvaraṇaṃ rūpānaṃ dassanāyā”ti. Tasmā upalakkhaṇanayena nīlakkhīti thometi.

'With that natural fleshy eye, which pertains to his own being and has arisen as a result of past good conduct, the Blessed One sees a yojana all around, both day and night. Even when there is darkness endowed with four factors—when the sun has set, it is the dark fortnight, the Uposatha day, and there is a dense forest, and a great dark cloud has arisen—even in such darkness endowed with four factors, he sees a yojana all around. There is no wall, door-leaf, rampart, mountain, bush, or creeper that obstructs the sight of forms.' Therefore, he praises him as 'blue-eyed' by way of characteristic indication.

Dīghapaṇhīti āyatapaṇhi. Paripuṇṇapaṇhīti attho. Pasati bādhati anena paresanti paṇhi, pādassa pacchābhāgo. Pasadhātu bādhane ṇi. Sassa ho. Ṇvādimoggallāne pana “paṇa byavahārathutīsu hi paṇiyati vohāriyatīti paṇhi, pādassa pacchābhāgo”ti vuttaṃ. Dīghā paṇhi yassa soti dīghapaṇhi, sugato. Yathā hi aññesaṃ agga pādo dīgho hoti. Paṇhimatthake jaṅghā patiṭṭhāti paṇhiṃ [M 0.0178] tacchetvā ṭhapitā viya hoti. Na evaṃ tathāgatassa. Tathāgatassa pana catūsu koṭṭhāsesu dve koṭṭhāsā aggapādā honti. Tatiye koṭṭhāse jaṅghā patiṭṭhāti. Catutthe koṭṭhāse āraggena vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitā viya rattakambale geṇḍukasadisā paṇhi hoti. Tasmā dīghapaṇhīti thometi.

'Long-heeled' means having a long heel. The meaning is 'perfectly formed heel.' It presses or obstructs with this, hence 'paṇhi,' the back part of the foot. The root 'pas' is in the sense of obstructing, with the suffix 'ṇi.' The 's' becomes 'h.' However, in Moggallāna's grammar, it is said: 'It is used or dealt with in transactions and praises, hence "paṇhi," the back part of the foot.' One whose heel is long is called 'long-heeled,' the Sugata. For others, the forepart of the foot is long. The shin rests on the top of the heel, as if it were placed after shaping the heel. Not so for the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata, of four parts, two parts are the forepart of the foot. On the third part, the shin rests. On the fourth part, the heel is rounded at the end, like a ball placed on a red blanket. Therefore, he is praised as 'long-heeled.'

Sukhumamalachavīti sukhuma amala chavīti padacchedo. Saṇhamalavisuddhataco saṇhamalavirahitataco vāti attho. Ettha ca sukhumasaddo saṇhavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko. Atha vā sukhayati saṇhabhāvenāti sukhumaṃ, saṇhaṃ. Sukhadhātu takkariyaṃ umapaccayo. Taṃsamaṅgīpuggalaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ malati dhāretīti malaṃ, rajādimalaṃ. Maladhātu dhāraṇe a, natthi malametissāti amalā, chavī. Maṃsaṃ chādetīti chavī. Chada dhātu saṃvaraṇe ravapaccayo īpaccayo ca. Sukhumā saṇhā amalā malavirahitā chavī yassāti sukhumamalachavī, sugato. Bhagavato hi suvaṇṇasiniddhasaṇhasarīrattā kañcanasannibha tacattā ca rūpakāye padumapalāse udakabindhu viya rajojallaṃ vā malaṃ vā na limpati. Vuttañhi majjhimapaṇṇāse brahmāyusutte –

'With delicate and blemishless skin' is the word division: 'sukhuma, amala, chavīti.' It means having soft and pure skin or having skin free from impurities. Here, the word 'sukhuma' is a synonym for 'saṇha' (soft) and is an underived nominal stem. Alternatively, that which delights by its softness is 'sukhuma,' meaning soft. The root 'sukha' in the sense of 'doing that' takes the suffix 'uma.' That which bears stains or impurities in a person endowed with it is called 'mala' (blemish), such as dust and other impurities. The root 'mala' is in the sense of bearing, with the suffix 'a.' 'Blemishless' means free from blemishes: 'amalā, chavī.' That which covers the flesh is called 'chavī' (skin). The root 'chada' in the sense of covering takes the suffix 'rava' and the suffix 'ī.' One whose skin is delicate, soft, and free from blemishes is 'with delicate and blemishless skin,' the Sugata. For the Blessed One, due to his body being smooth and soft like gold, and his skin resembling gold, dust or dirt or impurity does not adhere to his physical body, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. As stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya:

“Sukhumacchavī kho pana bhavaṃ gotamo sukhumattā chaviyā rajojallaṃ kāye na upalimpatī”ti. Tasmā sukhuma malachavīti thometi.

'Indeed, the Venerable Gotama has delicate skin; because of the delicacy of his skin, dust and dirt do not adhere to his body.' Therefore, he is praised as 'having delicate and blemishless skin.'

Thomyarasaggasaggīti thomyarasa gasa aggīti padacchedo. Thomitabba rasaharaṇasattasahassanhārū uddhaggikāti attho. Thomiyatīti thomyo, nhāru. Thomadhātu sīlāghāyaṃ ṇyo. Madhurādibhedaṃ rasaṃ gasenti anto pavesentīti rasaggasā, nhāru. Rasasaddūpapadagasadhātu adane a. Atha vā rasaṃ gasati harati etehīti rasaggasā[M 0.0179], nhāru. Gasadhātu haraṇe a. Dhātusaddo hi anekattho. Rasaggasānaṃ aggāti rasaggasaggā, te ettha santīti rasaggasaggī, nhāru. Assathyatthe īpaccayo. Thomyo rasaggasaggī yassa soti thomyarasaggasaggī, sugato. Tathāgatassa hi sattarasaharaṇisahassāni uddhaggāni hutvā gīvāyameva paṭimukkāni. Tilaphalamattopi āhāro jivhagge ṭhapito sabbaṃ kāyaṃ anupharati. Teneva mahāpadhānaṃ padahantassa ekataṇḍulādīhipi kaḷāyayūsapasatenapi kāyassa yāpanaṃ hoti. Aññesaṃ pana tathā abhāvā na sakalakāyaṃ ojā pharati. Tena te bahvābādhā honti. Idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ appābādhatāsaṅkhātassa nissandaphalassavasena pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmā thomyarasaggasaggīti thometi.

'Thomyarasaggasaggī' is split as 'thomya-rasa-gasa-aggī.' The meaning is that the seven thousand taste-carrying tendons are to be praised and are supreme, pointing upwards. That which is praised is 'thomyo,' a tendon. The root 'thom' in the sense of praise takes the suffix 'ṇyo.' Those that consume or bring inside tastes of various kinds, such as sweet, are called 'rasaggasā,' tendons. The root 'gas' with 'rasa' as its prefix, in the sense of eating, takes the suffix 'a.' Alternatively, 'rasaggasā' are those by which taste is carried, hence tendons. The root 'gas' in the sense of carrying takes the suffix 'a.' Indeed, a root has many meanings. The foremost of the 'rasaggasā' are 'rasaggasaggā.' One who possesses these is 'rasaggasaggī.' The suffix 'ī' is in the sense of 'possessing.' He who possesses the praised supreme taste-channels is called 'thomyarasaggasaggī,' the Sugata. For the Tathāgata, indeed, seven thousand taste-carrying tendons, pointing upwards, are attached only at the neck. Even a piece of food the size of a sesame seed placed on the tip of the tongue permeates the entire body. Therefore, when he was undertaking the great striving, his body was sustained even by a single grain of rice or by a measure of bean soup. For others, however, since this is not the case, nutritive essence does not spread throughout the entire body. Therefore, they suffer many ailments. This characteristic becomes manifest by way of its resultant fruit, which is known as freedom from illness; therefore, he is praised as 'thomyarasaggasaggī.'

Tevīsatimavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Twenty-Third Verse of Homage is Completed.

24. Dutiyagāthāyaṃ jinoti pañcamārajitavā buddho. Tassa pana padassa samacattālīsaggadantotyādīhi padehi tulyaliṅgattabhāvena sambandho. Cattālīsaggadantoti cattālīsaaggadantoti padacchedo. Samacattālīsa uttamadantoti attho. Ettha ca aggasaddo uttamavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko. Atha vā uttamabhāvaṃ ajati gacchatīti aggo, danto. Daṃsati vidaṃsati bhojjamanenāti danto. Daṃsadhātu daṃsane ta. Tassa nto dhātvantalopo. Samacattālīsaṃ aggo uttamo danto yassāti cattālīsaggadanto, jino. Uparimahanuke patiṭṭhitā dantā vīsati heṭṭhime vīsatīti samacattālīsadantā hontīti attho. Aññesañhi paripuṇṇadantānampi dvattiṃsadantā honti. Tathā gatassa pana cattālīsaṃ. Tasmā cattālīsaggadantoti thometi.

24. In the second verse, 'jino' refers to the Buddha, who has conquered the five Māras. The connection of this word is established through its agreement in gender with terms such as 'cattālīsaggadanto.' 'Cattālīsaggadanto' is analyzed as 'cattālīsa-aggadanto.' The meaning is 'forty even, supreme teeth.' Here, the word 'agga' signifies 'supreme' and is an underived nominal stem. Alternatively, 'agga' means 'that which goes to the highest state.' 'Danto' means 'tooth,' because food is bitten and chewed by it. The root 'daṃs' is in the sense of biting, with the suffix 'ta'. For this root, the suffix is 'nta' and the end of the root is elided. He who has forty even, supreme, excellent teeth is 'cattālīsaggadanto,' the Victor. The meaning is that twenty teeth are situated in the upper jaw and twenty in the lower, thus there are forty even teeth. For others, even those with a full set of teeth, there are only thirty-two teeth. But for the Tathāgata, there are forty. Therefore, he is praised as 'cattālīsaggadanto' (one with forty supreme teeth).

Samakalapanajoti [M 0.0180] kakacena chinditvā ṭhapito viya samadantoti attho. Lapati vadati etenāti lapanaṃ, mukhaṃ. Lapadhātu vadane yu. Tasmiṃ lapane mukhe jātoti lapanajo, danto. Tappurisasamāsoyaṃ, samako lapanajo danto yassāti samakalapanajo, jino. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “samadanto”ti pāṭho atthi. Ayamevattho. Aññesañhi keci dantā uccā, keci nīcāti visamā honti. Tathāgatassa pana ayapaṭṭachinnasaṅkhapaṭalaṃ viya samā honti. Tasmā samakalapanajoti thometi.

'Samakalapanajo' means 'samadanto' (having even teeth), that is, the teeth are even, as if cut and placed by a saw. That by which one speaks is 'lapana,' the mouth. The root 'lap' is in the sense of speaking, with the suffix 'yu'. That which is born in that 'lapana,' the mouth, is 'lapanajo,' the tooth. This is a dependent-determinative compound. He whose teeth born in the mouth are even is 'samakalapanajo,' the Victor. In the Pāli Canon, however, there is the reading 'samadanto.' This has the same meaning. For others, some teeth are high and some are low, thus they are uneven. But the Tathāgata’s teeth are even, like a row of conch-shell plates cut by an iron blade. Therefore, he is praised as 'samakalapanajo'.

Antaraṃsappapīnoti antaraaṃsapīnoti padavibhāgo. Gāthābandhavasena chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ pakārāgamaṃ katvā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Dvinnaṃ aṃsānaṃ khandhānaṃ antaraṃ vemajjhe paripuṇṇapiṭṭhitaloti attho. Ettha ca aṃsasaddo khandhatthe vattati. Vuttañhetaṃ abhidhānappadīpikāyaṃ “aṃso nitthi bhujasiro, khandho tassandhi jattu ta”nti.

The word division for 'antaraṃsappapīno' is 'antaraṃsa-pīno.' It is stated thus by adding the augment 'p' for the sake of preserving the meter in the verse composition. The meaning is: the space between the two 'aṃsas' (shoulders) is a full back surface. Here, the word 'aṃsa' is used in the sense of 'khandha' (shoulder). Indeed, it is stated in the Abhidhānappadīpikā: ''Aṃsa' (shoulder), not feminine, is the head of the arm; 'khandha' (shoulder); its joint is the 'jattu' (collarbone).'

Anati jīvati etenāti aṃso, khandho. Anadhātu pāṇe sopaccayo. Nassa niggahitādeso. Sarīrassa avayavabhāvena anati gacchati pavattatīti vā aṃso, dvinnaṃ aṃsānaṃ khandhānaṃ antaraṃ vemajjhanti antaraṃso, piṇati pūratīti pīno, piṭṭhitalaṃ. Piṇadhātu pinane pūraṇe vā ṇa. Ṇassa no. Dvinnaṃ aṃsānaṃ khandhānaṃ antaraṃ vemajjhe pīnaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ piṭṭhitalaṃ yassāti antaraṃsappapīno, jino. Uttarapadalopabahubbīhisamāsoyaṃ. Aññesañhi taṃ ṭhānaṃ ninnaṃ hoti, dve piṭṭhikoṭṭā pāṭiekkaṃ paññāyanti. Tathāgatassa pana kaṭito paṭṭhāya maṃsapaṭalaṃ yāva khandhā uggamma samussitasuvaṇṇaphalakaṃ viya piṭṭhiṃ chādetvā patiṭṭhitaṃ. Tasmā antaraṃsappapīnoti thometi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “citantaraṃso”ti pāṭho. Tadaṭṭhakathāyañca “citantaraṃ soti [M 0.0181] antaraṃsaṃ vuccati dvinnaṃ koṭṭānamantaraṃ. Taṃ paripuṇṇa massāti antaraṃso”ti vuttaṃ.

That by which one lives or breathes is 'aṃsa,' the shoulder. The root 'ana' is in the sense of breathing, with the suffix 'sa'; there is a substitution of the niggahita for 'n'. Or, 'aṃsa' is so called because it moves, goes, and proceeds as a part of the body. The middle space between the two 'aṃsas' (shoulders) is 'antaraṃsa.' That which fills or completes is 'pīna,' the back surface. The root 'piṇa' is in the sense of filling or completing, with the suffix 'ṇa'; the 'ṇa' becomes 'no'. He whose middle space between the two 'aṃsas' (shoulders) is plump and completely full, with a full back surface, is 'antaraṃsappapīno,' the Victor. This is a Bahubbīhi compound with the elision of the latter part. For others, that place is hollow, and the two shoulder blades are visible separately. But for the Tathāgata, from the waist upwards, a layer of flesh rises up to the shoulders and covers the back, established like a raised golden plate. Therefore, he is praised as 'antaraṃsappapīno.' In the Pāli text, however, there is the reading 'citantaraṃso.' And in its commentary, it is stated: 'Citantaraṃso' means 'antaraṃsa,' which is the space between the two shoulder blades. That space is full of flesh for him—thus, he is 'antaraṃso'.

Cakkenaṅkitapādoti cakkena aṅkitapādoti padacchedo. Aṭṭhasatapādacakkalakkhaṇena lakkhitapādataloti attho. Cakkena aṭṭhasatapādacakkena aṅkito lakkhito pādo yena soti cakkenaṅkitapādo, jino. Tatiyābahubbīhi samāsoyaṃ. Aññesañhi pādatale aṭṭhasatapādacakka lakkhaṇaṃ natthi. Tathāgatassa pādataleeva vicitraṃ aṭṭhasata pādacakkalakkhaṇaṃ atthi. Tasmā cakkenaṅkitapādoti thometi.

The word division for 'cakkenaṅkitapādo' is 'cakkena aṅkitapādo.' The meaning is: the soles of his feet are marked with the characteristic sign of the wheel with one hundred and eight spokes. He whose feet are marked with the wheel, with the wheel of one hundred and eight spokes, is 'cakkenaṅkitapādo,' the Victor. This is a Tatiyā-Bahubbīhi compound. For others, the soles of the feet do not bear the characteristic sign of the wheel with one hundred and eight spokes. But on the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet, there is the exquisite characteristic sign of the wheel with one hundred and eight spokes. Therefore, he is praised as 'cakkenaṅkitapādo'.

Vuttañhi brahmāyusutte “heṭṭhā kho pana tassa bhoto gotamassa pādatalesu cakkāni jātāni sahassārāni sanemikāni sanābhikāni sabbākāraparipūrānī”ti. Aṭṭhasatapādacakkalakkhaṇasarūpaṃ pana yo pādapaṅkajamuduttalarā jikehīti gāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttamevāti.

Indeed, it is stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta: 'Below, on the soles of the venerable Gotama’s feet, wheels have arisen, with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in all respects.' The nature of the characteristic mark of the wheel with one hundred and eight spokes on the feet, however, is indeed mentioned in the commentary on the verse beginning 'yo pādapaṅkajamuduttalarājikehīti'.

Aviraḷadasanoti avivaradanto. Avivaradantena sampannoti attho. Vivarati phullatīti viraḷo. Varadhātu phullaneḷo. Assi. Na viraḷo aviraḷo, natthi viraḷo etassāti aviraḷo, danto. Daṃsati vidaṃsati khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā etenāti dasano, danto. Daṃsadhātu daṃsane yu. Niggahitalopo. Aviraḷo dasano danto yassāti aviraḷadasano, jino. Aññesañhi kumbhilānaṃ viya dantā viraḷā honti. Macchamaṃsādīni khādantānaṃ dantantaraṃ pūrati. Tathāgatassa pana kanakalatāya samussāpitavajira panti viya aviraḷā tulikāya dassitaparicchedā viya dantā honti, tasmā aviraḷadasanoti thometi.

'Aviraḷadasano' means having teeth without gaps. The meaning is: endowed with teeth that have no gaps. That which opens or blooms is 'viraḷo.' The root 'vara' is in the sense of blooming, with the suffix 'ḷo.' It exists. Not gapped is 'aviraḷo'; he for whom there are no gaps is 'aviraḷo,' referring to the teeth. That by which one bites or chews edible or consumable food is 'dasano,' a tooth. The root 'daṃs' is in the sense of biting, with the suffix 'yu'; the niggahita is elided. He whose teeth are without gaps is 'aviraḷadasano,' the Victor. For others, their teeth are gapped, like those of crocodiles. For those who eat fish, meat, and so on, the spaces between their teeth get filled. But the Tathāgata’s teeth are without gaps, like a row of diamonds set on a golden creeper, or like teeth whose divisions are marked as if by a painter's brush; therefore, he is praised as 'aviraḷadasano'.

Mārajussaṅkhapādoti māraji ussaṅkhapādoti padacchedo. Ettha ca mārajīti pañcamārajitavā buddho kattubhūto. So [M 0.0182] hi pañcamāre jitavāti mārajīti vuccati. Ussaṅkhapādoti pādassa upari ṭhitena saṅkhasadisattā saṅkhanāmikena gopphakena samannāgatoti attho. Saṃsuṭṭhuṃ pathaviṃ khanatīti saṅkhe. Saṃpubbakhanudhātu avadāraṇe kvi. Apadānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “saṃsuṭṭhuṃ khādanto khaṇanto gacchatīti saṅkhe. Samuddajalapariyante caramāno gacchati caratīti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Saṅkhe viyāti saṅkhe, gopphako. Pādassa uddhaṃ upari ṭhitaṃ saṅkhasadisaṃ gopphaka massāti ussaṅkhapādo, jino. Vuttañhi brahmāyusuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “uddhaṃ patiṭṭhitagopphakattā ussaṅkhā pādā assāti ussaṅkhapādo”ti. Aññesañhi piṭṭhipāde gopphakā honti. Tena tesaṃ pādā āṇibaddhā viya baddhā honti. Na yathāsukhaṃ parivattanti. Gacchantānaṃ pādatalāni na dissanti. Tathāgatassa pana abhirūhitvā upari gopphakā patiṭṭhahanti. Tenassa nābhito paṭṭhāya uparimakāyo nāvāya ṭhapita suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya niccalo hoti. Adhokāyova iñjati. Sukhena pādā parivattanti. Puratopi pacchato ubhayapassesupi ṭhatvā passantānaṃ pādatalāni paññāyanti. Na hatthīnaṃ viya pacchatoyevāti. Tasmā ussaṅkhapādoti thometi.

'Mārajussaṅkhapādo' is divided as 'māraji ussaṅkhapādo.' Herein, 'mārajī' refers to the Buddha, the agent who conquered the five Māras. Indeed, he is called 'mārajī' because he conquered the five Māras. The meaning of 'ussaṅkhapādo' is: endowed with ankles (gopphaka) which are named 'saṅkha' because they are situated above the foot and resemble a conch. It digs the earth thoroughly, hence 'saṅkha.' The root 'khanu' with the prefix 'saṃ' is in the sense of splitting, with the suffix 'kvi.' In the Apadāna commentary, however, it is stated: 'Saṅkha' means moving while thoroughly chewing or digging. The meaning is: it moves and wanders along the edge of the ocean. Like a conch, it is 'saṅkha,' the ankle. He whose conch-like ankles are situated high above the foot is 'ussaṅkhapādo,' the Victor. Indeed, it is stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta commentary: 'Because his ankles are situated high up, his feet are 'ussaṅkhā,' hence he is 'ussaṅkhapādo.' For others, the ankles are on the back of the feet. Therefore, their feet are bound as if tied with a peg. They do not turn easily. When they walk, the soles of their feet are not visible. But for the Tathāgata, the ankles are raised and situated high up. Therefore, his upper body, from the navel upwards, is motionless like a golden statue placed on a ship. Only the lower body moves. His feet turn easily. For those standing and looking from the front, back, or both sides, the soles of his feet are visible, unlike elephants, whose soles are only seen from behind. Hence, he is praised as 'ussaṅkhapādo'.

Tiṭṭhanto nonamantobhayakaramudunā jaṇṇukānāma santoti ettha tiṭṭhanto no namanto ubhaya karamudunā jaṇṇukāni āmasantoti padavibhāgo. Tiṭṭhantoti ṭhitakova. Nonamantoti anamamāno hutvā. Ubhaya karamudunāti sukhumena hatthadvayena. Jaṇṇukānīti jaṅghāni. Jāyati gamanāgamanaṃ anenāti jaṇṇu, janadhātu janane ṇu. Soeva jaṇṇukā, jaṅghorūnaṃ sandhi labbhati. Tāni. Āmasantoti parimajjituṃ sakkonto. Ettha ca tiṭṭhanto nonamantoti iminā tathāgatassa akhujjaavāmanabhāvo dīpito[M 0.0183]. Avasesajanā hi khujjā vā honti vāmanā vā. Khujjānaṃ uparimakāyo aparipuṇṇo hoti vāmanānaṃ heṭṭhimakāyo. Te aparipuṇṇakāyattā na sakkonti nonamanto jaṇṇukāni parimajjituṃ. Tathāgato pana paripuṇṇaubhayakāyattā sakkoti, tasmā tiṭṭhanto…pe… jaṇṇukā nāmasantoti thometi.

Herein, the word division for 'tiṭṭhanto nonamantobhayakaramudunā jaṇṇukānāmasanto' is 'tiṭṭhanto no namanto ubhaya karamudunā jaṇṇukāni āmasanto.' 'Tiṭṭhanto' means while standing. 'Nonamanto' means without bending. 'Ubhaya karamudunā' means with both soft hands. 'Jaṇṇukāni' means the knees. That by which coming and going is produced is 'jaṇṇu,' from the root 'jan' in the sense of producing, with the suffix 'ṇu.' The same is 'jaṇṇukā,' the joint of the shanks and thighs; it is these that are meant. 'Āmasanto' means being able to stroke. Herein, by 'tiṭṭhanto nonamanto,' the Tathāgata’s state of not being hunchbacked or dwarfish is indicated. Other people are either hunchbacked or dwarfish. For the hunchbacked, the upper body is incomplete; for the dwarfish, the lower body is incomplete. Because their bodies are incomplete, they cannot stroke their knees without bending. But the Tathāgata, having both parts of his body complete, is able to do so; therefore, he is praised with the words, 'standing... he touches his knees'.

Vaṭṭakkhandhoti suvaṇṇāliṅgo viya samavaṭṭitagaliko. Vuttañhi brahmāyusutte “samavaṭṭakkhandho”ti. Parimaṇḍalā kārena vaṭṭati pavattatīti vaṭṭo, parimaṇḍalo. Vaṭṭadhātu vaṭṭane a. Bhojanaṃ khādati etena galenāti khandho, galo. Khādadhātu khādane bhakkhane vā kvipaccayo. Khādāmagamānaṃ khandhandhagandhāti suttena padasiddhi veditabbā. Abhidhānaṭīkāyaṃ pana “kaṃ matthakaṃ dadhātīti kandho. Soeva kakārassa khakārakaraṇavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Vaṭṭo samaparimaṇḍalo khandho galo yassāti vaṭṭakkhandho, jino. Yathā hi eke koñcā viya bakā viya varāhā viya ca dīghagalā vaṅkagalā puthugalā ca honti. Kathanakāle sirājalaṃ paññāyati. Mando saro nikkhamati, na evaṃ tassa. Tathāgatassa pana suvaṭṭitasuvaṇṇāliṅgasadiso khandho galo hoti. Kathanakāle sirājalaṃ na paññāyati. Meghassa viya gajjato saro mahā hoti. Tasmā vaṭṭakkhandhoti thometi.

'Vaṭṭakkhandho' means one with a perfectly rounded neck like a golden shaft. As stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta: 'one with a perfectly rounded neck.' It is called 'vaṭṭa' (round), or 'parimaṇḍala' (circular), because it turns or proceeds with a circular form. The root 'vaṭṭ' is in the sense of turning, with the suffix 'a'. 'Khandho' refers to the neck (galo), as by it one eats food. The root 'khād' is in the sense of eating or chewing, with the suffix 'kvip.' The formation of the word should be understood according to the grammatical rule, 'Khādāmagamānaṃ khandhandhagandhāti'. In the Abhidhānaṭīkā, however, it is stated: 'It supports (dadhāti) the head (kaṃ matthakaṃ), hence 'kandho.' The same word becomes 'khandho' by means of changing the letter 'ka' to 'kha'.' He whose neck is round and perfectly symmetrical is 'vaṭṭakkhandho,' the Victor. For some have long necks like cranes, crooked necks like herons, or broad necks like boars. When they speak, a web of veins becomes visible, and a weak voice emerges. It is not so for him. The Tathāgata’s neck is like a well-rounded golden shaft. When he speaks, no web of veins is visible, and his voice is great, like that of a thundering cloud. Therefore, he is praised as 'vaṭṭakkhandho'.

Puna jinoti buddho kattubhūto. Tassa pana padassa gotaruṇapakhumakotyādīhi padehi tulyaliṅgattabhāvena sambandho. Gotaruṇapakhumakoti taṃmuhuttajātaratta vacchassa cakkhubhaṇḍo viya vippasannacakkhubhaṇḍo, vippasannacakkhubhaṇḍena samannāgato vā. Ettha ca pakhumakoti sakalaṃ cakkhubhaṇḍaṃ adhippetaṃ. Cakkhubhaṇḍanti cakkhuparivāraṃ. Cakkhubhaṇḍanti akkhidalanti keci. Akkhidalapattanti vadanti aññe. Akkhidale hi [M 0.0184] pana saddhiṃ akkhibimbanti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho. Patati cakkhuṃ parivāreti etenāti pakhumaṃ, pamhādiparivāraṃ. Patadhātu parivāre umo. Takārassa kho. Atha vā akkhino pakkhadvaye jātanti pakhumaṃ, pamhaṃ. Jātataddhite umo. Pakkhumanti vattabbe kakāralopavasena pakhumanti vuccati. Pakhumaṃyeva pakhumako. Gotaruṇassa taṃmuhuttajātarattavacchassa pakhumaṃ viya pakhumaṃ yassa soti gotaruṇapakhumako, jino. Gotaruṇassa taṃmuhuttajātarattavacchassa pakhumasadisaṃ vippasannacakkhubhaṇḍaṃ atthīti attho. Aññesañhi akkhibhaṇḍo aparipuṇṇo hoti. Hatthimūsikakākādīnaṃ akkhisadisehi viniggatehi gambhīrehipi akkhīhi samannāgatā. Tathāgatassa pana dhovitvā majjitvā ṭhapitamaṇiguḷikā viya mudusiniddhanīla sukhumapakhumācitāni akkhīni honti. Tasmā gotaruṇapakhumakoti thometi.

Again, 'Jina' (the Victor) refers to the Buddha, who is the agent. That term is connected with words like 'gotaruṇapakhumako' by having the same grammatical gender. 'Gotaruṇapakhumako' means one whose eye is as clear as the eye of a newborn red calf at that very moment, or one endowed with such a clear eye. Here, 'pakhumako' is intended to mean the entire eye. 'Cakkhubhaṇḍa' means the surroundings of the eye. Some say 'cakkhubhaṇḍa' means the eyelid; others say it is the eyelid-covering. However, it should be understood as the eyelid together with the eyeball. This is the etymological meaning here: 'Pakhuma' is that by which the eye is surrounded—the eyelashes and the like. The root 'pat' is in the sense of 'to surround,' with the suffix 'uma'; the 't' becomes 'kh'. Alternatively, 'pakhuma' is what is born on the two sides ('pakkha') of the eye—the eyelashes ('pamha'). The suffix 'uma' is used in a taddhita sense of 'born from'. Though it should be 'pakkhuma,' it is said as 'pakhuma' through the elision of a 'k'. 'Pakhumako' is simply 'pakhuma.' Thus, 'gotaruṇapakhumako' means one whose eye is like that of a newborn red calf—the Victor. The meaning is that he possesses a very clear eye, like that of a newborn red calf. For the eyes of others are imperfect. They are endowed with protruding or sunken eyes, like those of elephants, mice, and crows. But the Tathāgata’s eyes are soft, smooth, deep blue, and adorned with fine eyelashes, like a gemstone bead that has been washed, polished, and set. Therefore, he is praised as 'gotaruṇapakhumako.'

Sīhapubbaḍḍhakāyoti sīhassa pubbaḍḍhakāyo viya paripuṇṇakāyo. Vātātapādiparissayaṃ sahati khamatīti sīho, sahadhātu khamane a. Īkārāgamo. Atha vā sūkaramahiṃsādayo satte hiṃsatīti sīho. Hiṃsadhātu hanane ṇa. Hiṃsoti vattabbe akkharavipariyāyena sīhoti vuccati. Atha vā sabbiriyāpathesu daḷhavīriyattā suṭṭhu īhati vāyamatīti sīho, kesarasīho. Supubba īhadhātu cetāyaṃ a. Tena vuttaṃ saddanītiyaṃ “sahahiṃsa īhāvasā, sīhasaddagatiṃ vade”ti. Sīhassa pubbaḍḍhe jāto kāyo viya paripuṇṇakāyo yassāti sīhapubbaḍḍhakāyo, jino. Yathā hi sīhassa pubbaḍḍhakāyova paripuṇṇo hoti, na evaṃ tassa. Tathāgatassa pana kāyo sabbaparipuṇṇoti attho. Sīhassa pana purimakāyova paripuṇṇo hoti, pacchima kāyo [M 0.0185] aparipuṇṇo. Tathāgatassa pana sīhassa pubbaḍḍhakāyoiva sabbo kāyo paripuṇṇo. Sopi sīhasseva na tattha tattha vinatunnatādivasena dussaṇṭhita visaṇṭhito. Dīghayuttaṭṭhāne pana dīgho. Rassakisathūla anuvaṭṭitayuttaṭṭhānesu tathāvidhova hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ “manāpiye ca kho bhikkhave kammavipāke paccupaṭṭhite yehi aṅgehi dīghehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni thūlāni saṇṭhahanti. Yehi aṅgehi kisehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni kisāni saṇṭhahanti. Yehi aṅgehi vaṭṭehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni vaṭṭāni saṇṭhahantī”ti. Iti nānācittena puññacittena cittito dasahi pāramīhi sajjito tathāgatassa attabhāvo tassa loke sabbasippino vā iddhimanto vā patirūpakampi kātuṃ na sakkonti. Tasmā sīhapubbaḍḍhakāyoti thometi.

"One with a body like the forepart of a lion" means having a body as fully developed as the forepart of a lion. He endures and withstands afflictions such as wind and sun, hence he is called a lion ('sīha'). The root is 'sah,' meaning 'to endure,' with the suffix 'a' and the insertion of the vowel 'ī.' Or, because he harms beings like boars and buffaloes, he is called a lion. The root is 'hiṃs,' meaning 'to harm,' with the suffix 'ṇa.' Instead of 'hiṃsa,' it is called 'sīha' by transposition of letters. Alternatively, because of his firm vigor in all postures, he strives excellently ('suṭṭhu īhati'), hence he is a lion ('sīha'), the maned lion. The root is 'īh,' meaning 'to strive,' preceded by 'su,' with the suffix 'a.' Thus, it is said in the Saddanīti: "'Sah' (to endure), 'hiṃs' (to harm), 'īhā' (to strive) are the bases; from these the derivation of the word 'sīha' should be stated." "One with a body like the forepart of a lion" refers to the Victor, whose body is as fully developed as the forepart of a lion. For just as only the forepart of a lion's body is fully developed, it is not so for him. The meaning is that the Tathāgata's entire body is fully developed. A lion's forepart is fully developed, but its hind part is not. The Tathāgata's entire body, however, is as fully developed as the forepart of a lion. His body, like a lion's, is not ill-formed or misshapen with depressions and protrusions. Where length is fitting, it is long; where shortness, thinness, thickness, or roundness is fitting, it is accordingly so. As it is said: "Monks, when a pleasant karmic result manifests, the limbs that should be long appear long, those that should be thick appear thick, those that should be thin appear thin, and those that should be rounded appear rounded." Thus, the Tathāgata's physical form, adorned by a meritorious mind of diverse thoughts and prepared by the ten perfections, cannot be replicated even in semblance by all the skilled artisans or those with psychic powers in the world. Therefore, he is praised as "one with a body like the forepart of a lion."

Catuvīsatimavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The Explanation of the Twenty-Four Homage Verses is Complete.

25. Tatiya gāthāyaṃ sugatoti buddho kattubhūto. Tassa pana padassa sattappīnotyādīhi padehi tulyaliṅgattabhāvena sambandho. Sattappīnoti dvihatthapāda aṃsakūṭa ekagalavasena sattasu ṭhānesu paripuṇṇamaṃsikoti attho. Ācariyā pana paripuṇṇadvihatthapāda aṃsakūṭa khandhasaṅkhātasattaṭṭhānoti atthaṃ vadanti. Maṃsena pīṇati paripūratīti pīno. Pīṇate paripūrate vā pīno. Pīṇadhātu pīṇane, pūraṇe vā ṇa. Ṇassa no. Dve hatthapiṭṭhiyo dve pādapiṭṭhiyo dve aṃsakūṭāni ekagalo cāti sattasu ṭhānesu pīno paripuṇṇo maṃso assāti sattapīno, sugato labbhati. Aññesañhi hatthapādapiṭṭhīsu nhārujālā paññāyanti aṃsakūṭagalesu aṭṭhikoṭiyo. Te manussā petā viya khāyanti. Na tathāgato. Tathāgato pana sattasu ṭhānesu [M 0.0186] paripuṇṇamaṃsussadattā niguḷanhārujālehi hatthapiṭṭhādīhi vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitasuvaṇṇavaṇṇāliṅgasadisena galena sīlārūpakaṃ viya cittakammarūpakaṃ viya ca khāyati, tasmā sattappīnoti thometi.

25. In the third verse, 'Sugato' refers to the Buddha, who is the agent. The connection of this term with words like 'sattappīno' is established through their shared grammatical gender. 'Sattappīno' means one with flesh full and prominent in seven places: the two backs of the hands, the two backs of the feet, the two shoulders, and the neck. Some teachers, however, say the seven places are the two backs of the hands, the two backs of the feet, the two shoulders, and the trunk ('khandha'). 'Pīno' means filled or plump with flesh. One is 'pīno' because one is filled ('pīṇati') or full ('paripūrati'). It is from the root 'pīṇ' in the sense of 'to be plump' or 'to be full,' with the suffix 'ṇa,' which becomes 'no.' He whose flesh is full and prominent in seven places—the two backs of the hands, the two backs of the feet, the two shoulders, and the one neck—is 'sattapīno'; this quality is obtained by the Sugato. For in others, a network of sinews is visible on the backs of their hands and feet, and the points of bone are visible on their shoulders and necks. Such people appear like ghosts. It is not so for the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata, on account of his full and prominent flesh in these seven places, with the network of sinews on the backs of his hands and so forth being concealed, and with a neck like a well-rounded golden image, appears like a stone sculpture or a painting. Therefore, he is praised as 'sattappīno.'

Brahmāyusutte pana “sattussado”ti pāṭho. Tassa pana sattasu ṭhānesu paripuṇṇamaṃsussadoti attho daṭṭhabbo.

In the Brahmāyusutta, however, the reading is "sattussado." The meaning of this should be understood as "having prominent flesh in seven places."

Dīghaṅgulīti dīghaaṅgulīti padacchedo. Samaāyatahattha pādaṅgulīti attho. Aṅgati uddhaṃ gacchatīti aṅguli. Aṅgati taṃ taṃ kāyaṅgaṃ parāmasati etāyāti vā aṅguli, karasākhā. Agidhātu gatiyaṃ ulipaccayo. Atha vā aṅgaṃ kāyaṅgaṃ ulati gacchati parāmasati etāyāti aṅguli, karasākhā. Aṅga saddūpapadauladhātu gatiyaṃ i. Samadīghā aṅguli hattha pādaṅguli yassa soti dīghaṅguli, sugato. Samadīghā hatthapādaṅguli atthīti attho. Yathā hi aññesaṃ kāci aṅguli dīghā hoti kāci rassā, na evaṃ tathāgatassa. Tathāgatassa pana makkaṭasseva dīghahatthapādaṅguliyo mūle thūlā anupubbena gantvā agge tanukā niyyāsatelena madditvā vaṭṭitaharitālavaṭṭasadisā honti. Tasmā dīghaṅgulīti thometi. Mathāti maathāti padacchedo. Makāro hi padasandhikaro. Athāti atthantare nipāto. Tadaññanti attho.

'Dīghaṅgulī' (long-fingered) is divided into the words 'dīgha-aṅgulī.' The meaning is having evenly long fingers and toes. 'Aṅguli' (finger/toe) is so called because it goes ('aṅgati') upward. Or, it is that by which one touches ('parāmasati') various limbs ('kāyaṅgaṃ'), hence 'aṅguli,' a branch of the hand. The root is 'ag' in the sense of movement, with the suffix 'uli.' Alternatively, it is that by which one goes to ('ulati,' 'gacchati') or touches ('parāmasati') a limb ('aṅgaṃ'), hence 'aṅguli,' a branch of the hand. Here, the word 'aṅga' is a prefix to the root 'ul' in the sense of movement, with the suffix 'i.' He whose fingers and toes are evenly long is 'dīghaṅguli,' the Sugato. The meaning is that he has evenly long fingers and toes. For while with other people some fingers are long and some are short, it is not so for the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata’s fingers and toes, like those of a monkey, are long; they are thick at the base and gradually taper to slender tips, resembling rounded sticks of yellow orpiment that have been rubbed with resin oil. Therefore, he is praised as 'dīghaṅguli.' As for 'mathā,' the word division is 'ma-athā.' The letter 'm' is a euphonic consonant for sandhi. 'Athā' is a particle indicating a different matter. The meaning is 'other than that.'

Lomakūpekalomoti lomakūpaekalomoti padacchedo. Ekekalomakūpe ekekajātalomoti attho. Cammamaṃsaṃ lunāti chindatīti lomo, vaḍḍhamānaṃ lunitabbanti vā lomo, lūdhātu chedane manipaccayo. Kuvuccati udakaṃ, taṃ pāti rakkhatīti kūpo. Kupubbapādhātu rakkhane kvi. Ussa dīgho. Kūpo viyāti kūpo, atha vā [M 0.0187] kuvuccati lomaṃ, taṃ pāti rakkhatīti kūpo. Abhidhānaṭīkāyaṃ pana “kusadde po. Dīghādi. Kūpo. Kena ubhatīti vā kūpo. Bhassa po”ti vuttaṃ. Lomassa kūpo lomakūpo. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ jāto ekeka lomo yassāti lomakūpekalomo, sugato. Yathā hi aññesaṃ ekekasmimpi lomakūpe anekāni lomāni jāyanti, na evaṃ tathāgatassa. Tathāgatassa pana ekekasmiṃ lomakūpe ekekalomo jāyati. Vuttañhi brahmāyusutte “ekekalomo kho pana bhavaṃ gotamo. Ekekāni lomāni lomakūpesu jātā nī”ti. Tasmā lomakūpekalomoti thometi.

"Lomakūpekalomo" is the division of words for "lomakūpa-ekalomo." The meaning is: in each hair-pore, a single hair is born. It cuts the skin and flesh, thus it is called 'loma' (hair); or, because it is cut as it grows, it is called 'loma.' This is from the root 'lū', meaning 'to cut', with the suffix 'mani'. Water is called 'ku'; that which protects it is a 'kūpa' (well). This is from the root 'pā', meaning 'to protect', preceded by 'ku', with the suffix 'kvi', and the 'u' is lengthened. It is like a well, thus it is a 'kūpa'. Alternatively, a hair is called 'ku'; that which protects it is a 'kūpa'. In the Abhidhānaṭīkā, however, it is said: “With the root ku, meaning sound, the suffix is po. There is lengthening at the beginning, giving kūpo. Or, from kena ubhati, giving kūpo, where bha becomes po.” The pore of the hair is 'lomakūpa'. He for whom a single hair is born in each and every pore is 'lomakūpekalomo', the Sugata. For while in the case of others many hairs grow in each single hair-pore, it is not so for the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata, in each single hair-pore, a single hair is born. For it is said in the Brahmāyu Sutta: “The Venerable Gotama has single hairs; single hairs are born in his hair-pores.” Therefore, he is praised as 'lomakūpekalomo'.

Sampannodātadāṭhoti sampannoodātadāṭhoti padacchedo. Sampannasukkadāṭhoti attho. Sampajjatīti sampanno. Saṃpubbapadadhātu gatiyaṃ ta. Tassa anno. Avadāyati avakhaṇḍiyati aññavaṇṇobhāsanti odāto. Avapubba dādhātu avakhaṇḍane ta. Daṃsati odanādiṃ etāyāti dāṭho, dantaviseso. Daṃsadhātu daṃsane ṭho. Daṃsissa dā. Sampanno ca odāto ca dāṭho yassāti sampanno dātadāṭho, sugato. Aññesañhi pūtidantā uṭṭhahanti. Tena kāci dāṭhā kāḷāpi vivaṇṇāpi honti. Tathāgato pana sukkadāṭho osadhitārakampi atikkamma virocamānāya pabhāya samannāgatadāṭho hoti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “susukkadāṭho”ti pāṭho. Ayamevattho. Tasmā sampannodātadāṭhoti thometi.

"Sampannodātadāṭho" is the division of words for "sampanno-odāta-dāṭho." The meaning is "possessed of perfectly white teeth." "Sampanno" means "perfected." It is from the root 'pad', meaning 'to go', with the prefix 'saṃ' and the suffix 'ta', which becomes 'anna'. "Odāto" means pure, unblemished, and shining with a distinct color. It is from the root 'dā', meaning 'to cleanse', with the prefix 'ava' and the suffix 'ta'. "Dāṭho" is a special kind of tooth, that by which one bites food and so on. It is from the root 'daṃs', meaning 'to bite', with the suffix 'ṭha'; 'daṃs' becomes 'dā'. He whose teeth are perfect and pure is 'sampannodātadāṭho', the Sugata. For others, decayed teeth arise, and because of that, some teeth are black or discolored. But the Tathāgata has perfectly white teeth, endowed with a radiance that, shining forth, surpasses even the morning star. In the Pāḷi canon, however, the reading is "susukkadāṭho." This has the same meaning. Therefore, he is praised as "sampannodātadāṭho".

Kanakasamatacoti suvaṇṇena sadisacammo. Kanati dibbati obhāsenāti kanakaṃ. Kaniyati icchiyati manusse hīti vā kanakaṃ, suvaṇṇaṃ. Kanadhātu dittigatikantīsu akapaccayo, saṃsadisena amati gacchati pavattatīti samaṃ. Saṃpubbaamadhātu gatiyaṃ a. Tacati maṃsaṃ chādeti saṃvarati vāti [M 0.0188] taco, tacati dibbati suvaṇṇobhāsenāti vā taco, cammaṃ. Tacadhātu saṃvaraṇadittīsu a. Kanakena suvaṇṇena samo sadiso taco yassāti kanaka samataco, sugato. Yathā hi aññesaṃ taco koci nīlataco setataco pītataco hoti, na evaṃ tathāgatassa. Tathāgatassa pana jātihiṅgulakena majjitvā nisadāya ghaṃsitvā gerukaparikammaṃ katvā ṭhapita ghanasuvaṇṇarūpakaṃ viya kañcanasadisataco hoti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco”ti vutto. Ettha ca suvaṇṇavaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo yassāti suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, kañcanena sannibhaṃ sadisaṃ tacamassāti kañcanasannibhattacoti vacanattho kātabbo. Ettha ca suvaṇṇavaṇṇanti iminā tathāgatassa ghanasiniddhasaṇhasarīrataṃ dasseti. Kañcanasannibhattacoti iminā chavivaṇṇaṃ dasseti. Atha vā vevacanametaṃ padadvayaṃ. Tasmā kanakasamatacoti thometi.

"Kanakasamataco" means having skin similar to gold. "Kanaka" (gold) is so called because it shines and gleams with radiance; or, because it is desired by people. It is from the root 'kan', in the senses of shining, moving, and desiring, with the suffix 'aka'. "Sama" is so called because it goes, moves, or proceeds together with what is similar. It is from the root 'am', meaning 'to go', with the prefix 'saṃ' and the suffix 'a'. "Taco" (skin) is so called because it covers and conceals the flesh; or, because it shines with the radiance of gold. It is from the root 'tac', in the senses of covering and shining, with the suffix 'a'. He whose skin is 'sama', similar, to 'kanaka', gold, is 'kanakasamataco', the Sugata. For while the skin of others may be blue, white, or yellow, it is not so for the Tathāgata. Rather, the Tathāgata’s skin is like a solid golden image that has been polished with the finest cinnabar, rubbed with a touchstone, and prepared with red ochre. In the Pāḷi canon, however, he is described as "suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco" (of golden color, with skin like gold). Here, the meaning of the words should be understood as: 'suvaṇṇavaṇṇo' is he whose color is like the color of gold, and 'kañcanasannibhattaco' is he whose skin is 'sannibha', resembling, gold. And here, by 'suvaṇṇavaṇṇo', the solid, lustrous, and fine nature of the Tathāgata's body is shown. By 'kañcanasannibhattaco', the complexion of his skin is shown. Or, these two terms are synonyms. Therefore, he is praised as 'kanakasamataco'.

Nīlamuddhaggalomoti nīlaṃ uddhaṃ aggalomoti padacchedo. Nīlaṃ uddhaṃ aggā koṭi hutvā mukhasobhaṃ ullokayamāno viya ṭhitalomo, nīlāni uddhaṃ aggāni koṭīni hutvā ṭhitāni lomāni yassāti nīlamuddhaggalomo, sugato. Yathā hi aññesaṃ lomāni heṭṭhā aggāni hutvā tiṭṭhanti, na evaṃ tathāgatassa. Tathāgatassa pana lomāni āvaṭṭapariyosāne uddhaṃ aggāni hutvā mukhasobhaṃ ullokayamānāni viya tiṭṭhanti. Vuttañhetaṃ brahmāyusutte “uddhaggalomo bhavaṃ gotamo. Uddhaggāni lomāni jātāni nīlāni añjanavaṇṇāni kuṇḍalāvaṭṭāni padakkhiṇāvaṭṭakajātānī”ti. Tasmā nīlamuddhaggalomoti thometi.
