"Nīlamuddhaggalomo" is the division of words for "nīlaṃ-uddhaṃ-agga-lomo." This means having hairs that stand with their blue tips turned upward, as if gazing upon the beauty of the face. He whose hairs are blue and stand with their tips turned upward is 'nīlamuddhaggalomo', the Sugata. For while the hairs of others stand with their tips pointing downward, it is not so for the Tathāgata. Rather, the Tathāgata’s hairs, at the end of their coils, stand with their tips turned upward, as if gazing upon the beauty of the face. For this is said in the Brahmāyu Sutta: “The Venerable Gotama has upward-pointing hairs. His hairs are born pointing upward, blue-black like collyrium, coiled in rings, turning to the right.” Therefore, he is praised as 'nīlamuddhaggalomo'.

Sambuddhoti tathāgato. So hi anaññabuddho hutvā sāmaṃyeva cattāri saccāni bujjhatīti sambuddhoti vuccati. Tassa [M 0.0189] pana padassa thūlajivhotyādīhi tīhi padehi tulyaliṅgattabhāvena sambandho.

The Perfectly Enlightened One is the Tathāgata. For he, not enlightened by another, awakens to the four truths by himself; thus he is called the Perfectly Enlightened One. Moreover, this word is connected with the three terms beginning with 'Thūlajivho' due to their having the same grammatical gender.

Thūlajivhoti mududīghaputhula jivhāya sampannoti attho. Gāthābandhavasena hi mududīghasaddalopaṃ katvā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “mudujivhā dīghā thūlā vaṇṇa sampannā”ti. Thūlati brūhatīti thūlā, jivhā. Thūladhātu buddhiyaṃ a. Jīvati pāṇaṃ dhāretīti jivhā, rasanā. Jīvadhātu pāṇadhāraṇe hapaccayo. Jīvanti sattā etena rasenāti jīvitaṃ, chabbidharaso. Taṃ avhāyatīti jivhā, jivhāpasādarūpaṃ. Sambhārajivhā ṭhānūpacārena labbhati. Jīvitasaddūpapada avhadhātu avhāyane a. Jīvitaavhāti vattabbe niruttinayena vitasaddalopaṃ katvā jivhāti vuttaṃ. Thūlā mahantā dīghā mudukā jivhā yassāti thūlajivho, sambuddho. Aññesañhi jivhā thūlāpi hoti kisāpi rassāpi thaddhāpi visamāpi. Tathāgatassa pana mudujivhā dīghā puthulā vaṇṇa sampannā hoti. So taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ pariyesituṃ āgatānaṃ brahmāyubrāhmaṇādīnaṃ kaṅkhāvinodanatthaṃ jivhāya mudukattā taṃ jivhaṃ kathinasūci viya vaṭṭetvā ubhopi nāsikāsotāni parāmasati, dīghattā ubho kaṇṇasotāni parāmasati, puthulattā kesantapariyosānaṃ kevalampi nalāṭaṃ paṭicchādeti, evaṃ tassā mududīghaputhulabhāvaṃ pakāsento kaṅkhāvinodeti, evaṃ tilakkhaṇasampannaṃ jivhaṃ sandhāya thūla jivhoti thometi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “pahūtajivho”ti pāṭho. Ayamevattho.

"Thūlajivho" means endowed with a soft, long, and broad tongue. It is stated thus due to the constraints of the verse, the words 'soft' and 'long' having been omitted. Therefore, it is said in the commentary: “The tongue is soft, long, broad, and endowed with beauty.” "Thūlā" is so called because it grows large. This is from the root 'thūl', meaning 'to grow', with the suffix 'a'. "Jivhā" (tongue) is so called because it sustains life; it is the organ of taste. This is from the root 'jīv', meaning 'to sustain life', with the suffix 'ha'. Beings live by this taste, which is 'jīvita' (life)—the six kinds of taste. That which calls for it is the 'jivhā', the sensitive matter of the tongue. The physical tongue is obtained by extension from its functional basis. The word 'jivhā' is formed from the root 'avhā', meaning 'to call', with the prefix 'jīvita'. Although it should be 'jīvita-avhā', the syllable 'vita' is elided by etymological rule, resulting in 'jivhā'. He whose tongue is large, long, and soft is 'thūlajivho', the Perfectly Enlightened One. For the tongues of others may be broad, thin, short, stiff, or uneven. But the Tathāgata’s tongue is soft, long, broad, and endowed with beauty. To dispel the doubt of the brahmin Brahmāyu and others who came to investigate this characteristic, he, by the softness of his tongue, rolls it out like a stiff needle and touches both his nostrils; by its length, he touches both his ears; and by its breadth, he covers his entire forehead up to the hairline. Thus, by displaying its softness, length, and breadth, he dispels their doubt. Referring to the tongue endowed with these three characteristics, he is praised as 'thūlajivho'. In the Pāḷi canon, however, the reading is "pahūtajivho" (ample tongue). This has the same meaning.

Athāti atthantaratthe nipāto. Tadaññanti attho. Sīhahanukoti sīhassa heṭṭhā hanu viya paripuṇṇa hanuko. Sīhasaddattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Hanati odanādīnaṃ vaṇṇavisesaṃ nāsetīti hanu. Hanadhātu hiṃsāyaṃ u. Sīhassa heṭṭhā hanu viya hanu yassāti sīhahanuko[M 0.0190], sambuddho. Samāsante ko. Sīhassa hi heṭṭhimahanumeva paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, na uparimaṃ. Tathāgatassa pana sīhassa heṭṭhimaṃ viya dvepi paripuṇṇāni dvādasiyaṃ pakkhassa candasadisāni honti. Tasmā sīhahanukoti thometi.

"Atha" is a particle in the sense of a different matter. The meaning is "other than that." "Sīhahanuko" means one whose jaw is as full as a lion’s lower jaw. The meaning of the word 'sīha' has been explained previously. "Hanu" (jaw) is so called because it destroys the distinct form of food and so on. It is from the root 'han', meaning 'to harm', with the suffix 'u'. He whose jaw is like a lion’s lower jaw is 'sīhahanuko', the Perfectly Enlightened One. The 'ko' is a suffix at the end of the compound. For a lion, only the lower jaw is full, not the upper one. But for the Tathāgata, both jaws are full like a lion’s lower jaw, resembling the moon on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight. Therefore, he is praised as 'sīhahanuko'.

Jālikappādahatthoti kusalena vaḍḍhakinā vātapāne sammāyojitajālaṃ viya cammena appaṭibaddhahatthapādaṅgulantaro. Jalati dibbatīti jālaṃ, jaladhātu dittiyaṃ ṇa. Jālaṃ assa atthi tasmiṃ vā vijjatīti jālikaṃ, vātapānaṃ. Assathyatthe ṇiko. Atha vā jālaṃ eva jālikaṃ. Pajjati gacchati etenāti pādo, caraṇo. Padadhātu gamane ṇa. Taṃ taṃ bhāraṃ haratīti hattho, karo. Haradhātu haraṇe tho. Jālikaṃ viya hatthapādaṅgulantaraṃ yassāti jālikappādahattho, sambuddho. Kusalena vaḍḍhakinā vātapāne sammāyojitāni jālasadisāni hatthapādaṅgulantarāni honti. Na ca cammena paṭibaddhaaṅgulantarānīti attho. Ettha jālikappādahatthaṅgulantaranti vattabbe uttarapadalopena evaṃ vuttaṃ. Cammena paṭibaddhahatthapādaṅgulantaro hi phaṇahatthako purisadosena upahato pabbajjampi na labhati. Tathāgatassa pana catasso hatthaṅguliyo pañcapi pādaṅguliyo ekappamāṇā honti. Tāsaṃ ekappamāṇa tāya yavalakkhaṇaṃ aññamaññaṃ paṭivijjhitvā tiṭṭhati. Athassa hatthapādā kusalena vaḍḍhakinā sammāyojitajālavāta pānasadisā honti, tasmā jālikappādahatthoti thometi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “jālahatthapādo”ti pāṭho. Ayamevattho.

“Jālikappādahattho” means one whose hands and feet have spaces between the digits like a net, not bound by skin, just as a net is properly fitted by a skilled craftsman in a window. “Jāla” means to shine or glow, derived from the root 'jal' (to shine), with the suffix 'ṇa'. “Jālika” refers to that which has a net or in which a net exists—here, the window. The suffix 'ṇika' conveys the sense of possession. Alternatively, 'jālika' simply means the net itself. “Pāda” means that by which one moves or walks, derived from the root 'pad' (to go), with the suffix 'ṇa'. “Hattha” means that which carries burdens, the hand, derived from the root 'har' (to carry), with the suffix 'tha'. Thus, “Jālikappādahattho” refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One, whose spaces between the fingers and toes are like a net. The spaces between his fingers and toes are like a net skillfully constructed by a craftsman in a window, not bound by skin. Here, though it should be said “jālikappādahatthaṅgulantara,” it is expressed concisely by eliding the final word. For if a person's fingers and toes were webbed, like a cobra's hood, it would be a physical defect, and such a person would not even be able to go forth into monastic life. But in the case of the Tathāgata, the four fingers of the hand and the five toes of the foot are of equal length. Due to their being of equal length, they stand interpenetrating one another, like the characteristic of barleycorns. Thus, his hands and feet resemble a well-constructed net-like window made by a skilled craftsman. Therefore, he is praised as “Jālikappādahattho.” In the Pāli canon, however, the reading is “jālahatthapādo” (net-like hands and feet). This has the very same meaning.

Nāthoti buddho kattuvasena. So hi nāthati vineyyānaṃ hitapaṭipattiṃ yācati, parasantānagataṃ vā kilesabyasaṃ upatāpeti, paramena cittissariyena samannā gato[M 0.0191]. Sabbasatte vā guṇehi īsati abhibhavati, veneyyānaṃ hitasukhaṃ vā āsīsatīti nāthoti vuccati. Vuttañhi saddanītiyaṃ “nāthadhātu yācane upatāpe issariye āsisane cāti catūsvatthesu pavattatī”ti.

Why is the Buddha called 'Nātha'? For he requests the beneficial practice for those who are to be trained; or he afflicts the disaster of defilements that has gone to the mental continuum of others; and he is endowed with supreme mastery of mind. Or, he is called 'Nātha' because he masters or surpasses all beings by means of his virtues, or because he wishes for the welfare and happiness of those who are to be trained. As it is said in the Saddanīti: 'The root nāth functions in four meanings: requesting, afflicting, exercising mastery, and wishing.'

Tassa pana padassa uṇhīsasīsotipadena tulyaliṅgattabhāvena sambandho. Uṇhīsasīsoti rañño baddhauṇhīsa paṭṭo viya virocamāno pakatimaṃsapiṇḍasaṅkhāto uṇhīsapaṭṭasīso. Nalāṭe nahiyati bandhiyatīti uṇhīso. Upubbanahadhātu bandhane, īso. Vaṇṇavikāro. Vuttañhi jāliniyaṃ –

Moreover, this word is connected with the term “uṇhīsasīsa” due to their having the same grammatical gender. “Uṇhīsasīsa” means one who has a head with a protuberance, that protuberance being a natural mass of flesh, shining like a king's bound turban-band. “Uṇhīsa” is so-called because it is bound or fastened on the forehead. It comes from the root 'nah' (to bind) with the prefix 'u' and the suffix 'īsa', with an alteration of a letter. As it is said in the Jālinī:—

“Vaṇṇāgamo vaṇṇavipariyāyo,

Dve cāpare vaṇṇavikāranāsā;

Dhātūnamatthātisayena yogo,

Taduccate pañcavidhaṃ nirutti”nti.

“Addition of a letter, transposition of letters, and two others, alteration and loss of letters; the application of roots with an extended meaning—this is called the fivefold Nirutti.”

Tattha ca avijjamānassa āgamā vaṇṇāgamo nāma. Vijjamānaakkharānaṃ heṭṭhupariyāyavasena vaṇṇavipariyāyo nāma. Aññakkharassa aññakkharāpajjanatā vaṇṇavikāro nāma. Vijjamānakkharavināso vaṇṇavināso nāma. Tattha tattha yathāyogaṃ visesatthayogo dhātūnaṃ atthātisaya yogo nāmāti adhippāyo. Ettha pana nakārassa ṇakāraṃ katattā vaṇṇavikāroti daṭṭhabbo. Mālādiṃ siyati bandhiyatīti sīso, uttamaṅgo. Sidhātu bandhane īso. Rājūnaṃ uṇhīsapaṭṭena veṭhitasīso viya sīso yassāti uṇhīsasīso. Atha vā rājūnaṃ uṇhīsaṃ viya sabbattha parimaṇḍalasīso yassāti uṇhīsasīso, nātho.

Therein, the arrival of a non-existent letter is called 'vaṇṇāgamo' (letter addition). The inversion of existing letters, by way of their order, is called 'vaṇṇavipariyāyo' (letter transposition). The substitution of one letter for another is called 'vaṇṇavikāro' (letter alteration). The destruction of an existing letter is called 'vaṇṇavināso' (letter loss). The application of a special meaning or the application of an extended meaning to roots, here and there as is suitable, is the intention of 'atthātisayayogo' (application of extended meaning). Here, because 'ṇ' is made from 'n', it should be understood as 'vaṇṇavikāro' (letter alteration). 'It binds a garland, etc.'—thus, 'sīso', the head, the highest part. The root 'si' is in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'īsa'. 'One whose head is like the head of kings wound with a turban-band'—thus, 'uṇhīsasīso' (turban-headed). Or alternatively, 'one whose head, like the turban of kings, is round on all sides'—thus, 'uṇhīsasīso' (turban-headed), the Protector.

Vuttañhi brahmāyusuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “uṇhīsasīsoti idaṃ paripuṇṇanalāṭañceva paripuṇṇasīsañcāti dve atthavase paṭicca vuttaṃ. Tathāgatassa hi dakkhiṇakaṇṇacūḷikato paṭṭhāya maṃsapaṭaṃ [M 0.0192] uṭṭhahitvā sakalaṃ nalāṭaṃ chādayamānaṃ pūrayamānaṃ gantvā vāmakaṇṇacūḷikāya patiṭṭhitaṃ. Rañño baddhauṇhīsapaṭṭo viya virocati. Pacchimabhavikabodhisattānaṃ kira imaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ viditvā rājūnaṃ uṇhīsapaṭṭaṃ akaṃsu. Ayaṃ tāva eko attho. Aññe pana janā aparipuṇṇasīsā honti. Keci kapisīsā, keci phalasīsā, keci aṭṭhisīsā, keci tumba sīsā, keci pabbhārasīsā. Tathāgatassa pana āraggena vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitaṃ viya suparipuṇṇaṃ udakapupphulasadisaṃ sīsaṃ hoti. Tattha purimanayena uṇhīsaveṭhitasīso viyāti uṇhīsasīso. Dutiyanayena uṇhīsaṃ viya sabbattha parimaṇḍala sīsoti uṇhīsasīso”ti. Taṭṭīkāyañca “dve attha vase paṭicca vuttanti, yasmā buddhā cakkavattino ca paripuṇṇa nalāṭatāya paripuṇṇasīsabimbatāya uṇhīsasīsāti vuccanti. Tasmā te dve atthavase paṭicca uṇhīsasīsoti vutta”nti vaṇṇeti. Tasmā uṇhīsasīsoti thometi.

In the commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta, it is stated: “The term 'uṇhīsasīso' is used with reference to two matters: having a fully developed forehead and having a perfectly rounded head. For the Tathāgata, a fold of flesh rises from the top of the right ear, covering and filling the entire forehead before settling at the top of the left ear. It shines like a king's bound turban-band. It is said that, having seen this mark on Bodhisattas in their final existence, people fashioned turban-bands for kings. This is the first meaning. Other people, however, have imperfectly shaped heads. Some have heads like monkeys, some like fruits, some like bones, some like water pots, and some like mountain slopes. But the Tathāgata’s head is perfectly rounded, like a water bubble, as if shaped on a lathe. Thus, according to the first method, he is called 'uṇhīsasīso' because his head appears as if wrapped in a turban. According to the second method, his head is entirely circular like a turban, hence 'uṇhīsasīso.'” And in the subcommentary it is explained: “'It is said with reference to two matters'—because Buddhas and wheel-turning monarchs are called 'uṇhīsasīso' on account of their fully developed foreheads and their perfectly rounded head-orbs. Therefore, the term 'uṇhīsasīso' is used with reference to these two matters.” Thus, he is praised as “uṇhīsasīso.”

Itiguṇasahitanti iminā vuttappakārena nigrodhabimbotyādinā dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaguṇena sampannaṃ. Itievaṃ vuttappakāraṃ guṇaṃ itiguṇaṃ. Tena saha ito pattoti itiguṇasahito, mahesī. Aññe hi dvattiṃsa mahāpurisalakkhaṇehi sampannā na honti, cakkavattirājāno mahāpurisalakkhaṇehi sampannāpi ṭhapetvā kosohitavattha guyhalakkhaṇaṃ avasesehi sampannā honti. Tathāgatoyeva sabbamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato. Tasmā bhagavantaṃyeva itiguṇasahitanti thomanaṃ arahatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ mahesinti sīlakkhandhādike ca nibbānañca esati gavesatīti mahesī. Taṃ mahesiṃ ahaṃ tīhi dvārehi namāmi vandāmīti sambandho.

Endowed with such virtues: this means endowed with the qualities of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, in the manner described by such phrases as 'having the proportions of a banyan tree,' and so on. A quality described in this way is an 'itiguṇa' (such a virtue). He who has attained this is 'itiguṇasahito' (endowed with such virtues), the Great Seeker. For others are not endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; even wheel-turning monarchs, though endowed with the marks of a Great Man, are endowed with the remaining marks only after excluding the mark of the male organ being concealed in a sheath. Only the Tathāgata is endowed with all the marks of a Great Man. Therefore, it is said that the praise 'endowed with such virtues' is fitting only for the Blessed One. That 'Great Seeker' (mahesī) means one who seeks and searches for the aggregates of virtue and so on, and for Nibbāna. 'To that Great Seeker I bow, I pay homage with the three doors'—this is the connection.

Pañcavīsatimavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the twenty-fifth homage verse is complete.

23. Ayaṃ [M 0.0193] pana imāsu tīsu gāthāsu saṅkhepatthayojanā. Buddho kattubhūto nigrodhabimbo nigrodhassa parimaṇḍalo viya parimaṇḍalasarīro mudukaracaraṇo saṇhahatthapādo, brahmaghoso brahmuno saro viya aṭṭhaṅgasampannasaravanto, eṇijaṅghā eṇimigassa jaṅghā viya suvaṭṭajāṇuko, kosacchādaṅgajāto usabhavāraṇā dīnaṃ aṅgajāto viya suvaṇṇapadumakaṇṇikasadisena vatthakosena paṭicchannena guyhaṅgajātena samannāgato, punarapi punaapi, sugato buddho suppatiṭṭhitapādo suvaṇṇa pādukatalamiva bhūmiyaṃ samaṃ suṭṭhu patiṭṭhitapādo, mūdo dātuṇṇalomo bhamukantare jāto saṇhasukhumo seto suddho uṇṇalomavanto, athamapi tadaññaṃapi, sugato buddho, brahmujuggattabhāvo brahmuno ujuuggata attabhāvo viya ujumeva attabhāvo, nīlakkhī atinīlanettena samannāgato, dīghapaṇhi āyatapaṇhi paripuṇṇapaṇhi vā, sukhumamalachavī saṇhamalavisuddhataco saṇhamala virahitataco vā, thomyarasaggasaggī thomitabbasattara saharaṇasahassanhāruuddhaggikā.

23. Now, this is the concise syntactical explanation of the meaning of these three verses. The Buddha, the agent, has the proportions of a banyan tree, his body being rounded like the circumference of a banyan tree; he has soft hands and feet, and delicate hands and feet. His voice is like Brahmā’s, possessing a voice endowed with eight components. His calves are like an antelope's, with well-rounded knees. His male organ is concealed in a sheath, being endowed with a private organ covered by a fleshy sheath resembling the pericarp of a golden lotus, like the generative organ of bulls, elephants, and so on. Furthermore, the Sugata, the Buddha, has well-established feet, his feet being well and evenly placed on the ground like the sole of a golden sandal. He possesses the ūrṇā-hair, a soft, fine, white, and pure hair that grows between his eyebrows. And also, the Sugata, the Buddha, has a body as straight as Brahmā's, his posture being perfectly upright like the upright posture of Brahmā. He has deep blue eyes, being endowed with intensely blue eyes. He has long heels, or projecting heels, or full heels. His skin is fine and unblemished, being delicate and pure, free from any subtle impurity. His body has seven convexities and upward-pointing body hairs.

24. Jino pañcamārajitavā buddho, cattālīsaggadanto samacattālīsauttamadanto, samakalapanajo kakacena chinditvā ṭhapito viya samadanto, antaraṃsappapīno dvinnaṃ aṃsānaṃ khandhānaṃ antaraṃ vemajjhe paripuṇṇapiṭṭhitalo, cakkenaṅkitapādo aṭṭhasatapādacakkalakkhaṇena lakkhita pādatalo, aviraḷadasano avivaradantena sampanno, māraji pañcamārajitavā buddho, ussaṅkhapādo pādassa upari ṭhitena saṅkhasadisattā saṅkhanāmikena gopphakena samannāgato, tiṭṭhanto ṭhitakova nonamanto anamamāno hutvā ubhayakaramudunā sukhumena hatthadvayena jaṇṇukāni jaṅghāni āmasanto parimajjituṃ sakkonto, vaṭṭakkhandho suvaṇṇāliṅgo [M 0.0194] viya samavaṭṭitagaliko, gotaruṇa pakhumako taṃmuhuttajātarattavacchassa cakkhubhaṇḍo viya vippasannacakkhubhaṇḍo, vippasannacakkhubhaṇḍena samannāgato vā, sīhapubbaḍḍhakāyo sīhassa pubbaḍḍhakāyo viya paripuṇṇakāyo.

24. The Victorious One, the Buddha, has conquered the five Māras. He has forty supreme and evenly set teeth, as if cut and placed with a saw. The space between his shoulders is perfectly filled. The soles of his feet are marked with a wheel, possessing the sign of a wheel with one hundred and eight spokes. His teeth are without gaps. The conqueror of Māra, the Buddha, has conquered the five Māras. His ankles are prominent like conch shells. While standing erect, without bending, he is able to touch and stroke his knees with both of his soft and delicate hands. His neck is perfectly rounded like a golden drum. His eyelashes are like those of a young bull, and his eyes are exceedingly clear, like those of a newborn red calf. The front half of his body is like a lion's, his torso full and majestic.

25. Sugato buddho, sattapīno dvihatthapādaaṃsakūṭaekagalavasena sattasu ṭhānesu paripuṇṇamaṃsiko, dīghaṅguli samaāyatahatthapādaṅguli, atha tadaññaṃ loma kūpekalomo ekekalomakūpe ekekajātalomo, sampannodātadāṭho sampannasukkadāṭho, kanaka samataco suvaṇṇena sadisacammo nīlamuddhaggalomo nīlaṃ uddhaṃ aggā koṭi hutvā mukhasobhaṃ ullokayamāno viya ṭhitalomo, sambuddho tathāgato, thūlajivho mududīghaputhulajivhāya sampanno, atha tadaññaṃ, sīhahanuko sīhassa heṭṭhāhanu viya paripuṇṇahanuko, jālikappāda hattho kusalena vaḍḍhakinā vātapāne sammāyojita jālaṃ viya cammena appaṭibaddhahatthapādaṅgulantaro, nātho buddho, uṇhīsasīso rañño uṇhīsapaṭṭo viya virocamāno pakatimaṃsapiṇḍasaṅkhāto uṇhīsapaṭṭasīso, iti guṇasahitaṃ evaṃ iminā vuttappakārena dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaguṇena samannāgataṃ taṃ mahesiṃ buddhaṃ tīhi dvārehi ahaṃ namāmi vandāmīti.

25. The Well-Gone One, the Buddha, is full in seven places—his two hands, two feet, two shoulders, and his trunk—being perfectly fleshy in these seven areas. His fingers and toes are long and of equal length. He has one hair per pore, with a single hair growing from each hair pore. He is endowed with perfectly white canine teeth. His skin has a golden hue, like that of fine gold. The hair on his head is dark blue with tips that curl upwards, as if gazing upon the beauty of his face. The Fully Enlightened One, the Tathāgata, is endowed with a soft, long, and broad tongue. His jaw is full, like that of a lion. His hands and feet are webbed, the skin between his fingers and toes being connected like a net skillfully fitted in a window by a master carpenter. The Protector, the Buddha, has a head with a cranial protuberance, radiant like a king's turban, appearing as a natural crown of flesh. Thus, endowed with these qualities, possessing the thirty-two marks of a great man as described, I bow down and pay homage to that Great Sage, the Buddha, through the three doors of action.

Tīsu gāthāsu saṅkhepatthayojanā samattā.

The brief explanation of the meaning in these three verses is complete.

Imissaṃ pana namakkārapāḷiyaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ buddhavacanapāḷiyaṃ āgatanayānukkamena na vuttaṃ. Gāthābandhavasena chandānurakkhaṇatthameva pana nigrodhabimbotyādinā akkamena vuttaṃ. Tasmā pātheyyavagge lakkhaṇasutte vuttaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇakkamaṃ [M 0.0195] saṅkhepena dassayissāma bahussutapaññāvaḍḍhanatthaṃ.

In this Pāli text of homage, however, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are not stated in the sequential order found in the Pāli of the Buddha's word. Rather, on account of the verse composition and for the sake of preserving the meter, they are stated out of order, beginning with 'nigrodhabimbo,' and so forth. Therefore, for the purpose of increasing the wisdom of the learned, we will briefly present the sequence of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man as stated in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta of the Pātheyyavagga.

1

1

. Buddho suppatiṭṭhitapādo 2. heṭṭhāpādatalesu cakkajāto 3. āyatapaṇhi 4. dīghaṅguli 5. mudutaluna hatthapādo 6. jālahatthapādo 7. ussaṅkhapādo 8. eṇijaṅgho 9. ṭhitakova anonamanto ubhohi pāṇitalehi jāṇukāni parimasati 10. kosohita vatthaguyho 11. suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco 12. sukhumacchavī 13. ekekalomakūpesu ekekalomo 14. nīlamuddhaggalomo 15. brahmujugatto 16. sattussado 17. sīhapubbaḍḍhakāyo 18. citantaraṃso 19. nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo 20. samavaṭṭakkhandho 21. rasaggasaggī 22. sīhahanuko 23. cattālīsadanto 24. samadanto 25. aviraḷadanto 26. susukkadāṭho 27. pahuta jivho 28. brahmasaro 29. abhinīlanetto 30. gopa khumo 31. uṇṇā bhamukantare jātā odātā mudutūla sannibhā 32. uṇhīsasīsoti dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇassa kamo veditabbo. Imāni pana bhagavato dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni pāramīpuññakammena yathārahaṃ kammasarikkhakaṃ labbhantīti veditabbāni. Tāni pana kammāni pātheyyavagge lakkhaṇasutte vuttāni, tāni panettha oloketvā gahetabbānīti.

1. The Buddha has well-planted feet. 2. On the soles of his feet, wheels are present. 3. His heels are long. 4. His fingers and toes are long. 5. His hands and feet are soft and tender. 6. His hands and feet are webbed. 7. His ankles are prominent. 8. His calves are like those of an antelope. 9. Standing erect, without bending, he can touch and stroke his knees with both palms. 10. His male organ is concealed in a sheath. 11. His complexion is golden, his skin like burnished gold. 12. His skin is delicate. 13. In each hair pore, there is a single hair. 14. The hair on his head is dark blue and curls upwards. 15. His body is as upright as Brahmā's. 16. He is well-fleshed in seven places. 17. The front part of his body is like a lion’s. 18. The space between his shoulder blades is filled out. 19. His proportions are like those of a banyan tree. 20. His shoulders are evenly rounded. 21. He possesses the supreme sense of taste. 22. His jaw is like a lion’s. 23. He has forty teeth. 24. His teeth are even. 25. His teeth are without gaps. 26. His canine teeth are exceedingly white. 27. His tongue is large. 28. His voice is like Brahmā’s. 29. His eyes are deep blue. 30. His eyelashes are like a cow’s. 31. Between his eyebrows grows the ūrṇā, white and soft like cotton down. 32. His head has a cranial protuberance. Thus the sequence of the thirty-two marks of a great man should be understood. Furthermore, it should be known that these thirty-two marks of the Blessed One are obtained through the meritorious deeds of the perfections, each in accordance with its corresponding action. These actions are described in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta of the Pātheyyavagga; they should be examined and understood from there.

Tisso vandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the three verses of homage is concluded.

26.

26.

Buddhobuddhotighoso atidulabhataro kā kathā buddhabhāvo,

Loke tasmā vibhāvī vividhahitasukhaṃ sādhavo patthayantā;

Iṭṭhaṃ atthaṃ vahantaṃ suranaramahitaṃ nibbhayaṃ dakkhiṇeyyaṃ,

Lokānaṃ nandivaḍḍhaṃ dasabalamasamaṃ taṃ namassantu niccaṃ.

The proclamation 'A Buddha! A Buddha!' is exceedingly rare; what then to say of the state of Buddhahood? Therefore, let the wise and good in the world, desiring various kinds of welfare and happiness, ever pay homage to Him—who brings the desired goal, is honored by gods and men, is fearless and worthy of offerings, who increases the joy of the worlds, the unequalled one possessing the ten powers.

26. Evaṃ [M 0.0196] sugatantiādīhi pañcavīsativandanagāthāhi buddhassa paṇāmaṃ katvā idāni tassa vandane uyyojanaṃ karonto āha buddho buddhotighoso tyādigāthaṃ. Ayaṃ pana saddharāgāthāti daṭṭhabbo.

26. Having thus paid homage to the Buddha with the twenty-five verses of veneration beginning with 'Evaṃ sugata,' now, making an exhortation to pay homage to him, the author recites the verse starting with 'Buddho buddhotighoso.' This should be understood as the Saddharāgāthā.

Tattha pana loke buddho buddhoti ghoso atidulabhataro buddhabhāvo kā kathāti sambandho. Ettha ca loketi manussaloke tiloke vā anantacakkavāḷa loke vā. Buddho buddhotighosoti buddho buddho iti kittisaddo thutisaddo vā. Ghusanaṃ ghoso. Ghusiyati kathiyatīti vā ghoso, kittisaddo. Ghusadhātu sadde ṇa. Atha vā ghusiyati thaviyatīti ghoso, thutisaddo. Tena vuttaṃ pārājikaṇḍaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “kittisaddoti kittieva. Thutighoso vā”ti. Buddho buddho iti pavatto ghoso thutighosoti buddhobuddhotighoso. Atidulabhataroti ativiya dullabhatamo. Dullabhataroti hi vattabbe chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ lakāralopena dulabhataroti vuttaṃ. Dukkhena labhiyatīti dullabho. Dupubbalabhadhātu labhane a. Atha vā labhassa asamiddhanti dullabho, dubbhijāneyya abyayībhāvasamāsoyaṃ. Dusaddo asamiddhattho, yathā dubbhikkhoti. Ati viya dullabhoti atidulabho. Tesaṃ visesena atidullabhoti atidulabhataro. Buddhā hi loke kadāci karahaci uppajjanti. Tasmā buddho buddhoti ghoso atidulabhataroti vuttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ cūḷavaggakhandhake “ghosopi kho eso gahapati dullabho lokasmiṃ, yadidaṃ buddho buddho”ti. Yathā ca hi loke udumbarikapupphaṃ dullabhaṃ. Candamhi sasakaṃ hatthena gaṇhituṃ. Vāyasānaṃ khīraṃ, evaṃ buddhabhāvo atidullabhataroti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ pana hīnūpamāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ apadānapāḷiyaṃ –

Therein, the syntactical connection is as follows: 'In the world, the proclamation "A Buddha! A Buddha!" is exceedingly rare; what then to say of the state of Buddhahood?' Here, 'in the world' refers to the human world, the three worlds, or the infinite cosmos. 'The proclamation "A Buddha! A Buddha!"' refers to the sound of fame or praise, 'A Buddha! A Buddha!' A proclamation (`ghoso`) is an announcement. Or, that which is proclaimed or spoken of is a `ghoso`, a sound of fame. The root is `ghusa`, 'to sound,' with the suffix `ṇa`. Alternatively, that which is praised is a `ghoso`, a sound of praise. Thus it is said in the commentary to the Pārājika: 'A sound of fame is fame itself, or a sound of praise.' The utterance 'A Buddha! A Buddha!' is a proclamation of praise; hence, `buddhobuddhotighoso`. 'Exceedingly rare' (`atidulabhataro`) means most exceedingly rare. Although `dullabhataro` ('rarer') should have been said, for the sake of preserving the meter, `dulabhataro` is stated with the elision of the letter 'l'. 'Difficult to obtain' (`dullabho`) is that which is obtained with difficulty. It is formed from the prefix `du-` and the root `labha` ('to obtain') with the suffix `a`. Alternatively, `dullabho` means 'the non-attainment of gain.' The prefix `du-` has the meaning of non-attainment or scarcity, as in `dubbhikkho` ('famine'). 'Exceedingly difficult' (`atidullabho`) means very rare. 'Most exceedingly rare' (`atidulabhataro`) means especially rare among those. For Buddhas arise in the world only from time to time. Therefore, it is said that the proclamation 'A Buddha! A Buddha!' is exceedingly rare. And this was stated in the Khandhaka of the Cūḷavagga: 'Householder, even this proclamation is rare in the world—that is, "A Buddha! A Buddha!"' And just as the udumbara flower is rare in the world, or catching the hare on the moon with one's hand, or the milk of crows, so too is the state of Buddhahood said to be exceedingly rare. This, however, should be understood as an inferior simile. And this was stated in the Pāli of the Apadāna—

“Udumbarikapupphaṃva[M 0.0197], candamhi sasakaṃ yathā;

Vāyasānaṃ yathā khīraṃ, dullabhaṃ lokanāyaka”nti ca;

Dullabho buddhuppādo lokasmi”nti ca;

"Like an udumbara flower, like the hare in the moon, like milk from crows, so rare is a leader of the world." And: "Rare is the arising of a Buddha in the world."

Kiñcāpi hi loke cakkavattirājūnaṃ uppajjamāno dullabho. Ekasmimpi pana kappe cakkavattirājāno anekā uppajjanti. Tathāgatā pana loke uppajjamānāpi ekasmiṃ kappe eka dviti catu pañca buddhāyeva uppajjanti, na taduttari. Yasmā hi asaṅkhyeyyepi kappe tathāgatasuñño hoti. Tasmā tathāgatasseva kadāci karahaci uppajjanato buddhobuddhotighoso atidulabhataro kā kathā buddhabhāvoti vutto. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā mahāparinibbānasamaye “devatā ānanda ujjhāyanti. Durāvatamhā āgatā tathāgataṃ dassanāya kadāci karahaci tathāgatā loke uppajjanti arahanto sammāsambuddhā. Ajja rattiyā paccūsasamaye tathāgatassa parinibbānaṃ bhavissati. Ayañca mahesakkho bhikkhu bhagavato purato ṭhito ovārento otarento vā na mayaṃ labhāma pacchime kāle tathāgataṃ dassanāyā”ti.

Although in the world the arising of a wheel-turning monarch is rare, yet in a single eon many wheel-turning monarchs arise. However, regarding Tathāgatas, even though they arise in the world, in one eon only one, two, four, or five Buddhas arise, not more than that. For in incalculable eons the world is empty of a Tathāgata. Therefore, because a Tathāgata arises only occasionally, the proclamation "Buddha! Buddha!" is exceedingly rare; what is to be said of Buddhahood itself? This was also stated by the Blessed One at the time of the Great Final Nibbāna: "Ānanda, the deities are complaining, 'We have come from afar to see the Tathāgata, for only occasionally do Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, arise in the world. Yet tonight, in the last watch, the Tathāgata's final Nibbāna will take place. And this eminent monk stands before the Blessed One, screening him, so that we cannot get to see the Tathāgata in this final hour!'"

Buddhabhāvoti buddhassa bhāvo. Kā kathāti kiṃ vattabboevāti attho. Kasmā pana buddho atidullabhataroti ca, buddho kadāci karahaci uppajjantīti ca vuttaṃ. Nanu buddhā loke anekā uppajjantīti. Saccametaṃ. Buddho nāma pana anekāsaṅkhyeyyavārena vā anekāsaṅkhyeyyadivasamāsasaṃvaccharaṃ vā anekāsaṅkhyeyyakappaṃ vā dasapāramiyo ca pañcamahāpariccāge ca pūretvāva bhavituṃ sakkoti, na ekekavārādinā. Atha kho pana antamaso kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni dasapāramiyo ca pañca mahāpariccāge ca pūretvāva buddho [M 0.0198] bhavituṃ sakkoti. Tasmā buddho atidullabhataroti ca, buddhā kadāci karahaci uppajjantīti ca vuttanti.

"Buddhahood" is the state of a Buddha. "What is to be said?" means "what is there to say?" But why is it said that a Buddha is exceedingly rare and that a Buddha arises only occasionally? Is it not so that many Buddhas arise in the world? That is true. However, one can become a Buddha only after fulfilling the ten perfections and the five great sacrifices over many incalculable instances, or many incalculable days, months, and years, or many incalculable eons; not by a single instance and so on. Furthermore, one can become a Buddha only after fulfilling the ten perfections and the five great sacrifices for at least four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand more eons. Therefore, it is said that a Buddha is exceedingly rare and that Buddhas arise only occasionally.

Evaṃ buddhassa atidullabhatarattā ca kadāci karahaci uppannattā caeva buddhobuddhoti kittayantassa mahapphalaṃ hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ apadāne –

Thus, because a Buddha is exceedingly rare and arises only occasionally, for one who proclaims "Buddha! Buddha!" there is great fruit. This is stated in the Apadāna:

“Buddhoti kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti;

Varameva hi sā pīti, kasiṇenapi jambudīpassā”ti.

"The joy that arises in the body of one who proclaims 'Buddha'—indeed, that joy is superior even to the whole of Jambudīpa."

Tasmāti yasmā buddho buddhoti ghoso atidullabhataro, buddhabhāvo kā kathā. Tasmā. Vibhāvīti medhāvī. Te hi hitāhitaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ vā visesena bhāveti pakāsetīti vibhāvā, paññā. Vipubba bhūdhātu sattāyaṃ ṇa. Sā etesaṃ atthīti vibhāvīti vuccanti, sādhavo labbhati. Taṃ pana sādhavoti pade visesanaṃ.

Therefore: because the proclamation 'Buddha! Buddha!' is exceedingly rare, what is to be said of Buddhahood? Therefore. `Vibhāvī` means wise. For they make clear with distinction what is beneficial and harmful, or cause and non-cause; hence this is `vibhāvā`, wisdom. It is from the root `bhū` with the prefix `vi` in the sense of 'being,' with the suffix `ṇa`. Because they possess that wisdom, they are called `vibhāvī` (discerning); this refers to the virtuous (`sādhavo`). That word, however, is an adjective for the word `sādhavo`.

Vividhahitasukhanti nānappakāraṃ lokiyalokuttara saṅkhātaṃ hitasukhaṃ. Tassa pana attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Taṃ pana patthayantātipade kammaṃ. Sādhavoti sappurisā. Te hi saparahitaṃ sādheti nibbattetīti sādhavoti vuccati. Sādhadhātu saṃsiddhiyaṃ avo. Tassa pana padassa namassantūti padena kattubhāvena sambandho. Patthayantāti yācantā. Vividhahitasukhaṃ patthayanti yācantīti patthayantā, sādhavo. Patthadhātu yācane anto. Yakārāgamo. Taṃ pana sādhavotipade visesanaṃ. Iṭṭhanti kāmayamānaṃ. Icchitabbaṃ kamitabbanti iṭṭhaṃ. Isudhātu icchā kantīsu tapaccayo. Tassa raṭṭho, dhātvantalopo. Atthanti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikādiatthaṃ. Atthiyati patthiyatīti attho, vipākānisaṃsaphalaṃ. Atthadhātu yācanāyaṃ a[M 0.0199]. Atha vā asati bhavati phalabhāvenāti attho. Asadhātu bhuvimhi tha. Taṃ pana padadvayaṃ vahantantipade kammaṃ. Vahantanti dhārakaṃ. Vahati haratīti vahanto, buddho. Vahadhātu vahane pāpuṇane vā anto. Buddho hi sattānaṃ lokiyalokuttarahitasukhaṃ dhammadesanāya dhāretīti attho.

Various kinds of welfare and happiness (`vividhahitasukhaṃ`) means the manifold welfare and happiness designated as worldly and supramundane. Its meaning, however, has been stated below. That word is the object of `patthayantā`. The virtuous (`sādhavo`) means good people. They are called 'virtuous' because they accomplish and bring about their own and others' welfare. The root `sādha` is in the sense of accomplishment, with the suffix `avo`. That word is connected as the agent to the word `namassantū`. Desiring (`patthayantā`) means requesting. Because they desire and request various kinds of welfare and happiness, they are `patthayantā`, the virtuous. The root `pattha` is in the sense of requesting, with the suffix `anta` and the augment `ya`. That word, however, is an adjective for the word `sādhavo`. Wished for (`iṭṭhaṃ`) means desired. What is to be wished for and desired is `iṭṭhaṃ`. The root `isu` is in the senses of wishing and desiring, with the suffix `ta`. Benefit (`atthaṃ`) refers to benefits in this life and the next, and so on. It is `attho` because it is desired and sought; it is the result, benefit, and fruit. The root `attha` is in the sense of desiring, with the suffix `a`. Alternatively, it is `attho` because it exists as a result. The root `asa` is in the sense of being, with the suffix `tha`. That pair of words is the object of the word `vahantaṃ`. The bearer (`vahantaṃ`) means the supporter. He carries and bears, thus he is `vahanto`, the bearer, the Buddha. The root `vaha` is in the sense of carrying or reaching, with the suffix `anta`. For the Buddha supports the worldly and supramundane welfare and happiness of beings through the teaching of the Dhamma; this is the meaning.

Suranaramahitanti devehi ca manussehi ca catupaccayādīhi pūjitaṃ. Idaṃ panettha nibbacanaṃ. Issariyakīḷādīhi suranti dibbantīti surā, devā. Suradhātu dittiyaṃ. Atha vā suranti īsanti devissariyaṃ pāpuṇanti virocanti cāti surā, devā. Sundarā rā vācā etesanti vā surā, devā. Khandhasantānaṃ naranti nentīti narā, manussā. Naradhātu nayane a. Surā ca narā ca suranarā. Tehi mahitabbā pūjitabbāti suranaramahito, buddho. Mahadhātu pūjāyaṃ ta. Taṃ suranaramahitaṃ. Nibbhayanti abhayaṃ. Bhiyate bhayaṃ. Natthi bhayaṃ etassāti nibbhayo, buddho. Taṃ nibbhayaṃ. Tathāgatassa aṭṭhasu parisāsu kenaci kāraṇena bhayaṃ hadayacalanaṃ kampanaṃ natthīti attho.

'Honored by gods and humans' means worshipped by gods and humans with the four requisites and so on. Herein is the etymological explanation. Gods (`devā`) are called `surā` because they shine (`suranti`) or sport (`dibbanti`) with sovereignty, play, and so on. The root `sur` is in the sense of shining. Alternatively, gods (`devā`) are called `surā` because they shine (`suranti`), exercise lordship (`īsanti`), attain divine sovereignty, and radiate. Or they are called `surā` because they have beautiful speech. Humans (`manussā`) are called `narā` because they lead the continuity of the aggregates. The root `nar` is in the sense of leading, with the suffix `a`. Gods and humans are `suranarā`. He who is to be honored and worshipped by them is `suranaramahito`, honored by gods and humans, that is, the Buddha. The root `mah` is in the sense of worship, with the suffix `ta`. That one honored by gods and humans. 'Fearless' means without fear. Fear is that by which one is frightened. He for whom there is no fear is `nibbhayo`, the fearless one, that is, the Buddha. That fearless one. The meaning is that for the Tathāgata there is no fear, no trembling of heart, no shaking in the eight assemblies for any reason whatsoever.

Dakkhiṇeyyanti paralokaṃ saddahitvā dātabbauttamadānārahaṃ. Dātabbāti dakkhiṇā, deyyadhammavatthu. Dādhātu dānekkhiṇapaccayo. Atha vā dakkhanti vaḍḍhanti etāya sattā yathādhippetāhi sampattīhīti dakkhiṇā, paralokaṃ saddahitvā dātabbadānaṃ. Dakkhadhātu vaḍḍhaneyu, taṃ arahatīti dakkhiṇeyyo, buddho. Arahatitaddhite ṇeyyo. Atha vā dakkhiṇāya hitaṃ anurūpaṃ mahapphalakaraṇatāya visodhetīti dakkhiṇeyyo, buddho. Visodhetitaddhitāyaṃ. Buddhoyeva hi dakkhiṇāya mahapphalakaraṇavasena ca, visodhanavasena ca, devasakkabrahmehi ca, kosalarājādīhi ca, anāthapiṇḍikaseṭṭhādīhi ca paralokaṃ saddahitvā dātabbaṃ uttamadānaṃ visesena arahati, tasmā dakkhiṇeyyanti thometi.

'Worthy of offerings' means worthy of the supreme gift that should be given with faith in the world beyond. What is to be given is an offering (`dakkhiṇā`), an object that is a religious gift. The root `dā` in the sense of giving takes the suffix `khiṇa`. Alternatively, an offering (`dakkhiṇā`) is so called because by it beings prosper (`dakkhanti`) and grow (`vaḍḍhanti`) with the attainments they desire; it is a gift to be given with faith in the world beyond. The root `dakkh` is in the sense of prospering. He who is worthy of that is `dakkhiṇeyyo`, worthy of offerings, that is, the Buddha. The taddhita suffix `ṇeyya` is in the sense of 'worthy of'. Alternatively, he is `dakkhiṇeyyo` because he purifies the offering, making it beneficial, suitable, and greatly fruitful. The taddhita suffix here is in the sense of 'purifying'. For it is the Buddha alone who, by way of making the offering greatly fruitful and by way of purifying it, is especially worthy of the supreme gift to be given with faith in the world beyond by gods, Sakka, Brahmā, the king of Kosala and others, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and others. Therefore he is praised as 'worthy of offerings'.

Lokānanti [M 0.0200] sattalokānaṃ. Tassa pana attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Nandivaḍḍhanti pītiyā vaḍḍhāpentaṃ. Nandiyate nandi. Bhāvasādhanoyaṃ. Nandadhātu samiddhiyaṃ nandane vā i. Pītiyā adhivacanametaṃ. Sā vaḍḍheti buddhetīti nandivaḍḍho, buddho. Nandisaddūpapadavaḍḍhadhātu vaḍḍhane a. Buddho hi dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāsītānubyañjanalakkhaṇasampannena ca sabbaññutañāṇādiguṇasampannena dhammadesanāya ca loke sabbasattānaṃ pītiṃ vaḍḍhetīti attho. Sabbasattānañhi buddhadassane dhammasavane ca titto natthi, tasmā lokānaṃ nandivaḍḍhanti thometi. Vuttañhetaṃ apadānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “pakatiyāeva hi buddhadassane puṇṇacandasamuddarājadassane atitto lokoti. Kathaṃ pana sabbasattānaṃ buddhadassane atitto hotī”ti. Buddhassa pana bāttiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇādīhi sīlādiasādhāraṇaguṇehi ca adhika sampanno hutvā sabbadevamanussehi ativirocamānattā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā tāvatiṃse –

'Of the worlds' means of the world of beings. But its meaning has already been stated. 'Increaser of joy' means one who makes joy increase. Joy (nandi) is that by which one rejoices. This is a derivation in the abstract sense. The root 'nand' is in the sense of prospering or delighting, with the suffix 'i'. This is a synonym for joy (pīti). He increases or awakens that joy, thus he is 'Nandivaḍḍha,' the increaser of joy, that is, the Buddha. The root 'vaḍḍh,' meaning to increase, is preceded by the word 'nandi' and takes the suffix 'a'. The meaning is that the Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the qualities of omniscience and so on, increases the joy of all beings in the world through his teaching of the Dhamma. For no beings are ever satiated by seeing the Buddha or hearing the Dhamma. Therefore, he is praised as 'the increaser of joy for the worlds.' This has been said in the commentary to the Apadāna: 'By nature, the world is never satiated by seeing the Buddha, just as it is not satiated by seeing the full moon or the ocean.' 'But how is it that all beings are never satiated by seeing the Buddha?' Because the Buddha, being endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and so on, and with unique qualities such as moral virtue, shines forth exceedingly among all gods and humans. This was stated by the Blessed One in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven:

“Na koci devo vaṇṇena, sambuddhaṃ atirocati;

Sabbe deve adhiggayha, sambuddhova virocatī”ti.

'No god surpasses the Perfectly Enlightened One in splendor; having surpassed all the gods, the Perfectly Enlightened One alone shines forth.'

Dasabalanti aññehi paccekabuddhāriyasāvakehi asādhāraṇena dasakāyabalena ca dasañāṇabalena sampannaṃ. Tañhi kehici viruddhehi kāraṇehi balanti na kampentīti balanti vuccati. Atha vā balanti jīvitaṃ kappenti etenāti balaṃ, kāyabalaṃ. Baladhātu pāṇe a. Balanti bhāraṃ vahituṃ sakkuṇantīti vā balaṃ, balanti jānanti sabbadhammanti balaṃ, ñāṇa balaṃ. Dasabalañca dasabalañca dasabalāni ekasesanayena. Tāni yassa soti dasabalo, buddho. Idha pana sāmaññavasena vuttopi visesaṭṭhāniyattā bhagavato dasakāyabalāni ca, dasañāṇabalāni ca adhippetāni. Tesaṃ pana sarū patthaṃ nayanasubhagakāyaṅgantyādi gāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttameva.

'Possessor of the Ten Powers' means endowed with the ten bodily powers and the ten powers of knowledge, which are not shared with other Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples. It is called 'power' (bala) because it cannot be shaken by any opposing causes. Alternatively, 'power' is that by which one lives or maintains life; this is bodily power. The root 'bal' is in the sense of living, with the suffix 'a'. Or 'power' is the ability to bear a burden; or 'power' is that by which one knows all dhammas; this is the power of knowledge. 'Ten powers and ten powers' becomes 'ten powers' (dasabalāni) by the principle of ellipsis. He who possesses these is 'Dasabalo,' the Possessor of the Ten Powers, that is, the Buddha. Here, however, although spoken of in a general way, what is specifically intended are the ten bodily powers and the ten powers of knowledge of the Blessed One. But their nature and purpose have already been described in the commentary on the verse beginning 'nayanasubhagakāyaṅgaṃ'.

Asamanti [M 0.0201] sīlādiguṇehi kenaci asadisaṃ. Natthi samo sadiso puggalo etassāti asamo, buddho. Taṃ asamaṃ. Tanti tādisaṃ guṇasampannaṃ buddhaṃ. Niccanti satataṃ samitaṃ sabbakālaṃ nirantaranti attho. Namassantūti abhivandantūti.

'Unequaled' means not similar to anyone in respect of qualities such as moral virtue. There is no person equal or similar to him, thus he is 'asamo,' the Unequaled One, that is, the Buddha. That Unequaled One. 'That one' (taṃ) means that Buddha, so endowed with qualities. 'Always' (niccaṃ) means constantly, continually, at all times, without interruption. 'Let them pay homage' (namassantu) means 'let them revere'.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Loke tiloke manussaloke vā, buddhobuddhotighoso buddho buddhoiti kittisaddo thutisaddo vā, atidulabhataro ativiya dullabhatamo, buddhabhāvo buddhassa bhāvo, kā kathā kiṃvattabbo eva, tasmā buddhobuddhoti ghosassa atidullabhatarattā, vibhāvī medhāvī vividhahitasukhaṃ nānappakāraṃ lokiyalokuttarasaṅkhātaṃ hitasukhaṃ patthayantā yācantā, sādhavo sappurisā iṭṭhaṃ kāmayamānaṃ, atthaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikādiatthaṃ, vahantaṃ dhārakaṃ, suranaramahitaṃ devamanussehi pūjitaṃ, nibbhayaṃ abhayaṃ asantāsaṃ vā, dakkhiṇeyyaṃ paralokaṃ saddahitvā dātabbauttamadānārahaṃ, lokānaṃ sattalokānaṃ nandivaḍḍhaṃ pītiyā vaḍḍhāpanentaṃ. Dasabalaṃ asādhāraṇena dasakāyañāṇabalena sampannaṃ, asamaṃ sīlādiguṇehi kenaci asadisaṃ taṃ tādisaṃ guṇasampannaṃ buddhaṃ niccaṃ satataṃ samitaṃ sabbakālaṃ nirantaraṃ, namassantu abhivandantūti.

Herein is the concise construction: In the world—or in the three worlds, or in the human world—the cry 'A Buddha! A Buddha!' or the sound of his fame and praise, is exceedingly rare, most difficult to find. What then needs to be said of the state of Buddhahood itself? Therefore, because the cry 'A Buddha! A Buddha!' is exceedingly rare, let discerning and wise people, good and virtuous people who desire and seek various kinds of welfare and happiness—both worldly and supramundane—always, constantly, continually, at all times, without interruption, pay homage to that Buddha who is: the bearer of the desired goal, that is, the goal of this life and the life to come; honored by gods and humans; fearless, without dread or terror; worthy of offerings, worthy of the supreme gift to be given with faith in the world beyond; the increaser of joy for the worlds, for the world of beings; the Possessor of the Ten Powers, endowed with the ten unshared bodily and knowledge powers; the Unequaled One, dissimilar to any other in respect of qualities such as moral virtue.

Chabbīsatimavandanagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-sixth verse of homage is completed.

27.

27.

Puññenetena sohaṃ nipuṇamati sato samparāye ca titto,

Dakkho diṭṭhujjupañño avikalavīriyo bhogavā saṃvibhāgī;

Tikkho [M 0.0202] sūro dhitatto saparahitadharo dīghajīvī arogo,

Dhañño vaṇṇo yasassī atibalavadharo kittimā khantupeto.

By this merit, in the future life may I be of subtle intellect, mindful, and content; skilled, of upright view and wisdom, of unimpaired energy, wealthy, and one who shares; sharp, heroic, resolute, upholding my own and others' welfare, long-lived, and free from illness; fortunate, of good complexion, renowned, possessing great strength, famous, and endowed with patience.

28.

28.

Saddho dātaṅgupeto paramasiridharo diṭṭhadhamme viratto,

Lajjī kalyāṇamitto abhiratakusalo pañcasīlādirakkho;

Appiccho appakodho ativujuhadayo iddhimā appameyyo,

Pāsaṃso pemavāco sujanaguṇavidū māmako so bhaveyyaṃ.

Faithful, endowed with the factors of giving, bearing supreme glory, dispassionate towards things seen in this life; conscientious, a good friend, delighting in the wholesome, a guardian of the five precepts and so on; of few wishes, with little anger, with an exceedingly upright heart, possessing spiritual power, immeasurable; praiseworthy, of affectionate speech, a knower of the qualities of good people—may I become such a one.

27. Evaṃ buddho buddhoti ghosotyādigāthāya buddhavandane uyyojanaṃ katvā idāni sugatantyādīhi gāthāhi buddhaṃ vanditvā paṇidhiṃ karonto āha puññenetena sohantyādi gāthādvayaṃ. Ayaṃ pana gāthādvayampi saddharāgāthāti daṭṭhabbā. Tattha paṭhamagāthāyaṃ soahaṃ etena puññena samparāye nipuṇamati ca sato ca…pe… khantupeto ca bhaveyyanti sambandho. Sohanti so ahaṃ. Buddhassa namakkāro soahanti attho. Etena puññenāti iminā buddhavandanapuññakammena attano kārakaṃ pavati sodhetīti puññaṃ. Pudhātu sodhane ṇya. Puññanti ca idha pana buddhapaṇāmakriyābhinipphādikā kusalacetanā adhippetā. Sā ca vandaneyyavandakānaṃ khettajjhāsayasampadāhi diṭṭhadhamma vedanīyabhūtā yathāladdhasampattinimittakassa kammassa anubalappadānavasena tannibbattitavipākasantatiyā antarāyakarāni upapīḷakaupacchedakakammāni paṭibāhitvā tannidānānaṃ yathādhippetasiddhivibandhakānaṃ rogādiantarāyānamappavattiṃsādheti cāti attho ca veditabbo. Samparāye cāti ettha [M 0.0203] casaddo aṭṭhānayogo. So ca nipuṇamatityādīsu padesu yojetabbo. Samparāyeti paraloke. So hi samparāyitabbā upagamitabbā ettha sattehīti ca, kammakilesavasena sattehi samparāyitabbā pāpuṇitabbāti vā etthāti ca samparāyoti vuccati. Saṃparipubba ayadhātu hi gatiyaṃ ṇa. Atha vā kammavasena abhimukho sampareti gacchati pavattatīti samparāyoti vuccati. Saṃpubbaparadhātu gatiyaṃ ṇya. Iti kho ānanda kusalāni sīlāni anupubbena aggāya parentītiādīsu viya hi curādi gaṇavasena parasaddaṃ gatiyamicchanti saddavidū. Tasmiṃ samparāye.

27. Thus, having made the dedication in the homage to the Buddha with the verse beginning 'Evaṃ buddho buddhoti ghoso,' now, having paid homage to the Buddha with the verses beginning 'sugataṃ,' etc., while making an aspiration, he recites the two verses beginning 'puññenetena sohaṃ.' These two verses should be understood as verses of faith and devotion. Therein, in the first verse, the construction is: 'By this merit, may I in the future life be of subtle intellect and mindful... and endowed with patience.' 'Sohaṃ' means 'so ahaṃ' (that I). The meaning is 'that I who have paid homage to the Buddha.' 'By this merit' means by this meritorious kamma of venerating the Buddha. 'Merit' (puñña) is so called because it purifies its agent. The root 'pu' is in the sense of purifying, with the suffix '-ṇya'. And here by 'merit' is intended the wholesome volition that accomplishes the act of bowing to the Buddha. And it should be understood that this volition, because of the excellence of the field of merit and the disposition of the venerator and the one venerated, becomes experienceable in this very life. By providing support for the kamma whose sign is the attainment of whatever has been acquired, it wards off obstructive, oppressive, and destructive kammas that would interrupt the continuity of the resultant produced by that good kamma, and it brings about the non-occurrence of obstacles such as disease, which are caused by them and which obstruct the achievement of what is desired. In 'samparāye ca,' the particle 'ca' is for connection and should be connected with the words 'nipuṇamati,' etc. 'Samparāye' means in the future life. It is called 'samparāya' because beings must go towards it or approach it; or because beings must go towards it or attain it on account of kamma and defilements. The root 'i' (to go), preceded by 'saṃ' and 'pari', is in the sense of motion, with the suffix '-a'. Alternatively, it is called 'samparāya' because one proceeds, goes, or moves forward towards it on account of kamma. The root 'par' with the prefix 'saṃ' is in the sense of motion, with the suffix '-ṇya'. For just as in passages like, 'Thus, Ānanda, wholesome moral virtues lead progressively to the highest,' knowers of grammar accept the word 'para' in the sense of motion, according to the Curādi group of roots. In that future life.

Nipuṇamatīti saṇhasukhumapaññavā ca. Saṇhasukhumaṃ atthantaraṃ paṭivijjhanasamatthāya paññāya sampanno ca vā. Ettha ca nipuṇasaddo saṇhasukhumavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko. Hitāhitaṃ manati jānātīti mati, paññā. Manadhātu ñāṇeti. Nipuṇā saṇhā mati paññā yassa meti nipuṇamati. Satoti satimā ca. Saratīti sati, saradhātu cintāyanti. Sā assa me atthīti sato. Tittoti tappano ca. Yathāladdhavatthunā santuṭṭho cāti attho. Tisanaṃ tappanaṃ titto. Tisadhātu tappane tapaccayo. Sakārassa toādeso. Yathālābha santoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasanto so cāti tividhena santosena santuṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Subtle-minded” means endowed with subtle and refined wisdom. Or, endowed with wisdom capable of penetrating a subtle and refined meaning. Here, the word “subtle” is a term for what is subtle and refined; it is an underived stem. “Mati” is that by which one knows what is beneficial and what is harmful; it means wisdom. The root “man” is in the sense of knowing. “Subtle-minded” is one whose “mati,” that is, wisdom, is subtle and refined. “Mindful” means possessing mindfulness. “Mindfulness” is that which remembers; the root “sara” is in the sense of thinking. One who has it is “mindful.” “Content” means being satisfied. The meaning is: being satisfied with whatever one has obtained. “Titto” is from “tisanaṃ,” satisfying. The root “tis” is in the sense of satisfying, with the suffix “-ta.” The “s” is changed to “t.” It is said that he is satisfied by means of the threefold contentment: contentment with whatever one gets, contentment according to one’s strength, and contentment according to what is suitable.

Dakkhoti taṃ taṃ kicce cheko ca kusalo ca vā. So hi kusalakamme aññasmiñca kiccākicce adandhatāya sīghaṃ gacchatīti dakkho. Dakkhadhātu sīghatthe a. Diṭṭhujjupaññoti diṭṭhiujupaññoti padacchedo. Uju diṭṭhipaññāya samannāgatoti attho. Kesuci potthakesu diṭṭhijju paññoti pāṭho. Diṭṭhiujupaññoti padacchedo, soye vattho[M 0.0204]. Ujūti akuṭilabhāvena bhavatīti uju, ajjavo. Ujudhātu ajjave kvi. Atha vā arati akuṭilabhāvena pavattatīti uju, avaṅko. Aradhātu gatiyaṃ jupaccayo. Arissa uādeso. Sammā passatīti diṭṭhi, mati. Disadhātu passane tapaccayo. Tassa raṭṭhādeso. Dhātvantalopo ca ī ca. Uju ajjavā diṭṭhi mati diṭṭhuju visesanaparanipātavasena. Pakārena jānāti aniccādivasena avabujjhatīti paññā. Papubbañādhātu avabodhane a. Ujudiṭṭhi ca ujupaññā ca yassa meti diṭṭhujjupañño, puggalo. Avikalavīriyoti anūnavīriyo ca paripuṇṇavīriyo cāti attho. Vihīnaṃ karotīti vikalo. Vipubbakaradhātu karaṇe a. Rassalo. Vīrānaṃ kammaṃ vīriyaṃ. Avikalaṃ anūnaṃ vīriyaṃ assameti avikalavīriyo. Na sakkā kusīteneva navalokuttaradhammā laddhuṃ, āraddhavīriyeneva sakkā. Tasmā avikalavīriyoti patthetīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Skilled” means clever and proficient in this or that task. For he proceeds quickly, without sluggishness, in wholesome deeds and in other duties and non-duties; thus he is “skilled.” The root “dakkh” is in the sense of swiftness, with the suffix “-a.” “Of upright view and wisdom” is divided into the words “diṭṭhi-uju-pañño.” The meaning is: endowed with upright view and wisdom. In some books the reading is “diṭṭhijju pañño.” The word division is “diṭṭhi-uju-pañño”; this is the meaning. “Upright” (uju) is that which is so in the sense of not being crooked; it means straight. The root “uju” is in the sense of straightness, with the suffix “-kvi.” Or, “uju” is that which proceeds without crookedness; it means unbent. The root “ar” is in the sense of going, with the suffix “-ju.” The “a” of “ar” is changed to “u.” “View” (diṭṭhi) is that by which one sees correctly; it means understanding. The root “dis” is in the sense of seeing, with the suffix “-ti,” which becomes “-ṭṭhi” through phonetic changes. “Upright” (uju) means straight (ajjavā); “view” (diṭṭhi) means understanding (mati). The compound “diṭṭhuju” is formed by the irregular placement of the adjective. “Wisdom” (paññā) is that by which one knows in detail, that is, understands things in terms of impermanence, etc. The root “ñā” with the prefix “pa-” is in the sense of understanding, with the suffix “-a.” “Of upright view and wisdom” is a person whose view is upright and whose wisdom is upright. “Of unimpaired energy” means one whose energy is not deficient but is complete. “Impaired” is that which makes something deficient. The root “kar” with the prefix “vi-” is in the sense of making, with the suffix “-a,” and with shortening of the vowel. “Energy” is the action of heroes. “Of unimpaired energy” is one who has unimpaired, not deficient, energy. It is not possible to attain the nine supramundane states through laziness; it is possible only through aroused energy. Therefore, it is said that one should aspire to be “of unimpaired energy.”

Bhogavāti bhuñjitabbasampattisukhena sampanno ca. Bhuñjitabboti bhogo, sampatti. Bhujadhātu pālanabyavaharaṇesu ṇa. Bhogo assa me atthīti bhogavā. Saṃvibhāgīti saṃvibhajanasīlo ca saṃvibhajanasampanno ca vā, saṃvibhajati sīlenāti saṃvibhāgī. Saṃvibhajanasīloti vā saṃvibhāgī, saṃvibhajituṃ sīlamassāti vā saṃvibhāgī. Saṃvibhāge sīlamassāti saṃvibhāgī. Ayaṃ tassīlattho. Saṃvibhajati dhammenāti saṃvibhajanadhammoti vā. Saṃvibhajituṃ dhammo assāti vā, saṃvibhajane dhammo assāti vā saṃvibhāgī. Ayaṃ taddhammattho. Saṃvibhajanaṃ sādhukāro assa atthi. Sādhukārinā saṃvibhajatīti vā, saṃvibhajituṃ sādhukārīti vā, saṃvibhajane sādhukārīti vā saṃvibhāgī. Ayaṃ tassā dhukārattho. Saṃvipubba bhajadhātu vibhāge ṇa. Jassa go. Atha vā saṃvibhajanaṃ saṃvibhāgo. So me assa atthīti saṃvibhāgī[M 0.0205]. Assathyatthe ī. Paresaṃ yācakānaṃ annādidānavatthuṃ niccaṃ pariccajanakārīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Wealthy” means endowed with the happiness of possessions to be enjoyed. “Possessions” are what is to be enjoyed; it means wealth. The root “bhuj” is in the sense of protecting and using, with the suffix “-ṇa.” “He has possessions,” therefore he is “wealthy.” “A sharer” means one who is habitually a sharer, or one endowed with the habit of sharing. He shares by habit, thus he is a sharer. Or, sharing is his habit, thus he is a sharer. Or, he has the habit of sharing, thus he is a sharer. This is the meaning in the sense of habit. Or, he shares in accordance with the Dhamma, thus he has the nature of sharing. Or, sharing is his nature, thus he is a sharer. Or, he has the nature for sharing, thus he is a sharer. This is the meaning in the sense of nature. He has the good practice of sharing. Or, he shares as a good practice. Or, he is one who does well in sharing. Or, he does well in sharing, thus he is a sharer. This is the meaning in the sense of good practice. The root “bhaj” with the prefix “saṃvi-” is in the sense of dividing, with the suffix “-ṇa.” The “j” is changed to “g.” Or, “sharing” is “saṃvibhāgo.” “He has this,” therefore he is “a sharer.” The suffix “-ī” is in the sense of “he has.” It is said that he is one who constantly gives away items for giving, such as food, to others, to beggars.

Tikkhoti tikkhappaññavā ca nisānapaññavā vā. Tijanaṃ nisanaṃ tikkhā, paññā. Tijadhātu nisāne kha. Jassa ko. Tikkhā paññā me assa atthīti tikkho. Assathyatthe ṇo. Tikkha paññāya sampanno cāti attho. Paññāya ca sabba kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ seṭṭhattā mūlakāraṇattā ca tikkhoti patthanaṃ karoti. Vuttañhi milindapañhe –

“Sharp” means one with sharp wisdom or with whetted wisdom. “Tikkhā” (sharp) is from “tijanaṃ,” sharpening; it means wisdom. The root “tij” is in the sense of sharpening, with the suffix “-kha.” The “j” is changed to “k.” “He has sharp wisdom,” therefore he is “sharp.” The suffix “-ṇa” is in the sense of “he has.” The meaning is: endowed with sharp wisdom. And because wisdom is the best of all wholesome states and their root cause, one makes the aspiration to be “sharp.” For it is said in the Questions of Milinda:

“Paññā pasaṭṭhā lokasmiṃ, katā saddhammaṭṭhitiyā;

Paññāya vimatiṃ hantvā, santiṃ pappoti paṇḍito”ti.

“Wisdom is praised in the world, made for the stability of the good Dhamma; having dispelled doubt with wisdom, the wise person attains peace.”

Sūroti catūsu parisāsu aṭṭhasu parisāsu ca vīro ca. Sattivanto nibbhayoti attho. Sūrayate virayate sūro. Bhāvasādhanoyaṃ. Sūradhātu vikkantiyaṃ vīre vā a. Atha vā abhiruachambhianutrāsabhāvena sūrati gacchati pavattatīti sūro. Sūradhātu gatiyaṃ a. Sīho viya parisamajjhe sūravīrasampanno cāti attho. Sāsani kehi pana saddhammavidūhi sūrasaddassa nibbacanaṃ na dassitaṃ. Kevalaṃ pana sūroti visiṭṭhasūroti atthavivaraṇamattameva dassitaṃ. Dhitattoti ettha dhita attoti padacchedo. Dhitoti samādhi. Attanti cittaṃ. Ekaggacittasampanno cāti attho. Dhāti tiṭṭhati ekārammaṇehi dhito, ekārammaṇe sampayuttadhamme dhāretīti vā dhito, samādhi. Dhādhātu dhāraṇe ta. Ārammaṇaṃ arati jānātīti attaṃ, cittaṃ. Aradhātu gatiyaṃ ta. Rassa to. Dhito samādhi attaṃ cittaṃ assa meti dhitatto.

“Heroic” means a hero in the four assemblies and in the eight assemblies. The meaning is: powerful and fearless. He acts heroically, he is valiant, thus he is a “hero.” This is a derivative denoting a state. The root “sūr” is in the sense of prowess or heroism, with the suffix “-a.” Or, he proceeds, goes, moves on with a state of no fear, no trembling, and no terror, thus he is a “hero.” The root “sūr” is in the sense of going, with the suffix “-a.” The meaning is: like a lion in the midst of an assembly, he is endowed with heroism and valor. However, by those who know the good Dhamma in the teaching, no derivation of the word “sūra” has been shown. Only an explanation of the meaning has been shown, namely, that “sūro” means a distinguished hero. In “of steadfast mind,” the word division is “dhita-atto.” “Dhita” means concentration. “Atta” means mind. The meaning is: endowed with a one-pointed mind. “Dhito” is that which stands on a single object; or, it is that which holds associated states on a single object; it means concentration. The root “dhā” is in the sense of holding, with the suffix “-ta.” “Attaṃ” is that which goes to or knows an object; it is the mind. The root “ar” is in the sense of going, with the suffix “-ta.” The “r” is changed to “t.” “He has ‘dhita,’ concentration, as his ‘atta,’ mind,” therefore he is “of steadfast mind.”

Saparahitacaroti attahitaparahitacaro, attano ca parassa ca atthaṃ paṭipannako cāti attho. Attano ca parassa ca hitaṃ atthaṃ payojanaṃ carati paṭipajjatīti saparahitacaro[M 0.0206]. Saparahitasaddūpapada caradhātu caraṇe a. Dīghajīvīti dīghāyuko ca. Dīghena jīvitindriyena sampanno vā. Dīgho jīvo jīvitaṃ assa meti dīghajīvi. Āyukappampi dīghajīvitasampanno cāti attho. Arogoti rogaviraho ca ārogyaṃ vā. Rujjati bhañjati aṅgapaccaṅgānīti rogo, byādhi. Rujadhātu bhaṅge ṇa. Atha vā rujjati hiṃsatīti rogo. Rujadhātu hiṃsāyaṃ ṇa. Natthi rogo tassa meti arogo, channavutirogānaṃ abhāvo bhaveyyanti attho. Dhaññoti sirīpuññapaññālakkhaṇasampanno ca. Dhaññasaddo hi sirīpuññapaññālakkhaṇavācakoti daṭṭhabbo. Vuttañhi vessantarajātake “dhaññaṃ maṅgala sammata”nti ca. Temiyajātake “dhaññapuññalakkhaṇasampannaṃ puttaṃ vijāyī”ti ca. Idaṃ pana nibbacanaṃ. Dhananaṃ sampajjanaṃ dhaññaṃ, sirīpaññāpuññalakkhaṇānaṃ sampannanti attho. Dhanadhātu sampanne. Dhātūnaṃ anekatthattā ṇyapaccayo. Ṇakārānubandhe lope kate yapaccayena saddhiṃ nakārassa ñakāraṃ katvā dhaññanti rūpasiddhi veditabbā. Atha vā dhanaṃ sirīpaññā puññalakkhaṇasampadaṃ assa me atthīti dhañño. Assathyatthe ṇyo.

“Practicing for his own and others’ welfare” means one who practices for his own welfare and for the welfare of others; the meaning is one who is engaged in what is for the good of both himself and others. He practices, he is engaged in, the welfare, good, and benefit of both himself and others, thus he is “one who practices for his own and others’ welfare.” The root “car” is in the sense of practicing, with the suffix “-a,” and with the pre-posed word “saparahita.” “Long-lived” means having a long life-span, or endowed with a long life-faculty. “He has a long life, a long lifespan,” thus he is “long-lived.” The meaning is: endowed with a long lifespan, even for a full age-limit. “Healthy” means free from disease, or health. “Disease” is that which breaks, which shatters, the limbs and members; it means affliction. The root “ruj” is in the sense of breaking, with the suffix “-ṇa.” Or, “disease” is that which harms. The root “ruj” is in the sense of harming, with the suffix “-ṇa.” “He has no disease,” thus he is “healthy”; the meaning is: “May there be an absence of the ninety-six diseases.” “Fortunate” means endowed with the characteristics of glory, merit, and wisdom. The word “dhañña” should be seen as a term for the characteristics of glory, merit, and wisdom. For it is said in the Vessantara Jātaka: “Fortunate is considered auspicious,” and in the Temiya Jātaka: “She gave birth to a son endowed with the characteristics of fortune and merit.” This is the derivation: “Dhaññaṃ” is the accomplishment of wealth; the meaning is being endowed with the characteristics of glory, wisdom, and merit. The root “dhan” is in the sense of accomplishing. Because roots have many meanings, the suffix is “-ṇya.” When the indicatory “ṇ” is elided, the “n” together with the suffix “-ya” becomes “ññ,” and thus the form “dhañña” is to be understood as established. Or, “he has wealth, the fortune of the characteristics of glory, wisdom, and merit,” thus he is “fortunate.” The suffix “-ṇyo” is in the sense of “he has.”

Vaṇṇoti vaṇṇasampanno ca. Ettha ca vaṇṇo duvidho hoti sarīravaṇṇaguṇavaṇṇavasena. Tattha sarīra vaṇṇo nāma rūpakāyassa pāsādikarūpasampannatā. Guṇa vaṇṇo nāma sīlasamādhipaññādiguṇena ca dhutaṅgādipaṭipadāguṇena ca sampannatā. Idaṃ pana nibbacanaṃ. Vaṇṇeti vikāramāpannānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti vaṇṇo, sarīrarūpaṃ. Vaṇṇeti attano dabbaṃ pakāsetīti vaṇṇo, guṇo. Vaṇṇadhātu pakāsane a. Idha pana tadubhayampi yujjati. Vaṇṇaṃ assa me atthīti vaṇṇo. Assathyatthe a. Yasassīti parivārasampanno kittivanto vā. Ettha ca [M 0.0207] duvidho hoti yaso parivārakittiyasavasena. Tattha yajiyati pūjiyati etena parivārenāti yaso, parivāro. Yajadhātu pūjāyaṃ a. Jassa so. Atha vā yāti gacchati pāpuṇāti sāmikassa parivāranti yaso, parivāro. Yādhātu gatiyaṃ sopaccayo. Yajiyati pūjiyati etenāti yaso, kittisaddo. Yajadhātu devapūjāsaṅgahakaraṇadānadhammesu a. Jassa so. Atha vā yāti gacchati pāpuṇāti sabbattha byāpananti yaso, kittighoso thutisaddo vā. Yādhātu gatiyaṃ sopaccayo. Yaso ca yaso ca yaso ekasesanayena. So assa me atthīti yasassī, assathyatthe sīpaccayo.

“Of good appearance” means endowed with a good appearance. Here, appearance is of two kinds: physical appearance and the appearance of virtue. Among these, physical appearance is the pleasing quality of the physical body’s form. The appearance of virtue is being endowed with the virtues of morality, concentration, and wisdom, and with the virtues of the ascetic practices. This is the derivation. “Appearance” is that which describes, which makes known the state of having gone to the heart of those who are affected; it is the physical form. “Appearance” is that which describes, which makes known one’s own substance; it is virtue. The root “vaṇṇ” is in the sense of making known, with the suffix “-a.” Here, both are suitable. “He has appearance,” thus he is “of good appearance.” The suffix “-a” is in the sense of “he has.” “Famous” means endowed with a retinue or possessing renown. Here, fame is of two kinds: the fame of a retinue and the fame of renown. Among these, “fame” is that by which one is worshipped, is honored, by this retinue; it means the retinue. The root “yaj” is in the sense of worship, with the suffix “-a.” The “j” is changed to “s.” Or, “fame” is that which goes, proceeds, reaches the master as a retinue; it means the retinue. The root “yā” is in the sense of going, with the suffix “-sa.” “Fame” is that by which one is worshipped, is honored; it is the word “renown.” The root “yaj” is in the senses of worshipping gods, gathering, doing, and giving, with the suffix “-a.” The “j” is changed to “s.” Or, “fame” is that which goes, proceeds, reaches, pervading everywhere; it is the sound of renown or the word of praise. The root “yā” is in the sense of going, with the suffix “-sa.” “Fame” and “fame” become “fame” by the principle of leaving a single remainder. “He has this,” therefore he is “famous.” The suffix “-sī” is in the sense of “he has.”

Atibalavadharoti atibalavantadhārako ca ativiya kāyabalañāṇabalavantaṃ dhāretīti atibalavadharo. Ajātasatturājādayo viya pañcahatthi dasahatthibalassa dhāraṇasamattho ca, sāriputtattherādayo viya ñāṇabalassa dhāraṇasamattho ca bhaveyyanti attho. Kittimāti kittighosavanto ca. Kittiyate kathiyate guṇanti kitti, thutighoso. Kittadhātu sadde i. Kittighoso assa me atthīti kittimā. Assathyatthe mantupaccayo. Khantupetoti khantiyā upeto samupeto samannāgato ca. Khamanaṃ sahanaṃ khanti. Khamudhātu sahane tapaccayo. Tassanti tāya upeto samupeto samannāgatoti khantupeto. Khantivādatāpaso viya khantupeto ca bhaveyyanti attho. Khantiyā hi dukkarattā sabbakusala dhammānaṃ padhānattā seṭṭhatapattā ca khantupetoti patthanaṃ karoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā”ti ca. “Khantyā bhiyyo na vijjatī”ti ca. “Khantībalaṃ balānīka”nti ca.

“Bearer of great strength” means one who bears extreme physical strength and strength of wisdom. The meaning is that one should be capable of bearing the strength of five or ten elephants, like King Ajātasattu and others, and capable of bearing the strength of wisdom, like the Elder Sāriputta and others. “Renowned” means possessing the sound of renown. Because virtue is proclaimed or spoken of, it is “kitti,” the sound of praise. The root “kitt” is in the sense of sound, with the suffix “-i.” “He has the sound of renown,” thus he is “kittimā.” The suffix “-mant” is in the sense of “he has.” “Endowed with patience” means endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of patience. Patience is forbearance, endurance. The root “kham” is in the sense of endurance, with the suffix “-ti.” “Endowed with patience” means one who is endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of that patience. The meaning is that one should be endowed with patience like the ascetic Khantivādin. Because patience is difficult to practice, is the chief of all wholesome qualities, and has attained excellence, one makes the aspiration to be “endowed with patience.” For this was said by the Blessed One: “Patience, forbearance, is the highest austerity.” And: “There is nothing higher than patience.” And: “The strength of patience is the army of strengths.”

“Sīlasamādhipaññānaṃ[M 0.0208], khantippadhānakāraṇaṃ;

Sabbepi kusalā dhammā, khantyāyattāva vaḍḍhare”ti ca.

“Patience is the chief cause of morality, concentration, and wisdom; all wholesome qualities increase, being dependent on patience.”

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. Sohaṃ so ahaṃ, etena puññena iminā buddhavandanapuññakammena samparāye paraloke, nipuṇamati ca saṇhasukhumapaññavā ca, sato satimā ca titto tappano yathāladdhavatthunā santuṭṭho ca, dakkho taṃtaṃkicce cheko ca, diṭṭhujjupañño ujudiṭṭhi paññāya sampanno ca avīkalavīriyo anūnavīriyo ca paripuṇṇavīriyo vā, bhogavābhuñjitabbasampattisukhena sampanno ca saṃvibhāgī saṃvibhajanasīlo ca tikkho tikkhapaññavā ca, sūroti sattivanto nibbhayo ca, dhitatto samāhita citto ca ekaggacitto vā, saparahitacaro attahita parahitapaṭipannako ca dīghajīvī dīghāyuko ca arogo rogaviraho ca dhañño sirīpuññapaññālakkhaṇasampanno ca vaṇṇo vaṇṇasampanno ca yasassī parivārasampanno ca atibalavadharo atibalavantadhārako ca kittimā kitti ghosavanto ca khantupeto khantiyā upeto samupeto samannāgato ca bhaveyyanti.

This is the summary of the construction here. By this merit, by this meritorious act of venerating the Buddha, may I, in the future and in the next world, be one with keen intelligence and gentle and subtle wisdom; mindful and attentive; content, satisfied with whatever has been obtained; skilled and proficient in every task; endowed with straightforward wisdom and right view; with unwavering and unflagging energy, or with complete energy; endowed with the happiness of possessions and enjoyable prosperity; generous and inclined to share; sharp and of keen wisdom; courageous, powerful, and fearless; with a steadfast and composed mind, or with a single-pointed mind; practicing for the welfare of self and others; long-lived; healthy and free from illness; fortunate, endowed with glory, merit, wisdom, and auspicious marks; of good appearance; famous and endowed with a retinue; a bearer of great strength; renowned and possessing the sound of renown; and endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of patience.

Sattavīsatimagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-seventh verse is complete.

28. Evaṃ puññenetenatyādigāthāya samparāye paṇidhiṃ katvā idāni diṭṭhadhamme patthanaṃ kattukāmo saddho dātaṅgupeto tyādigāthamāha. Tattha saddhoti kammādi saddahanalakkhaṇāya saddhāya sampanno ca. Saddahanaṃ saddhā, saddahatīti vā saddhā. Saddahanti sampayuttadhammā etāyāti saddhā. Saṃpubbadhādhātu dhāraṇe ta. Sā pana kammādīsu saddahanalakkhaṇā. Okappanalakkhaṇā vā. Pasādarasā. Udakappasādakamaṇi viya. Pakkhandanarasā vā. Oghuttaraṇo viya[M 0.0209]. Akālussiyapaccupaṭṭhānā adhimuttipaccupaṭṭhānā vā, saddheyyavatthupadaṭṭhānā sotāpattiyaṅgapadaṭṭhānā vā. Sā hatthavittabījāni viya daṭṭhabbā. Bhagavatā hi sā saddhā “saddhāhattho mahānāgo”ti ca. “Saddhīdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭha”nti ca. “Saddhābījaṃ tapo vuṭṭhī”ti ca “saddhāya tarati ogha”nti ca “saddhā bandhati pātheyyaṃ, saddhā dutiyā purisassa hotī”ti ca, “saddhesiko bhikkhave ariyasāvako”ti ca, “saddhādhana”nti ca.

28. Having thus made an aspiration for future lives with the verse beginning “By this merit,” now, desiring to make an aspiration for the present life, he speaks the verse beginning “Faithful, endowed with the factors of giving.” Here, “faithful” means endowed with faith characterized by trust in actions and so forth. “Saddahanaṃ” is faith, or that which trusts is faith, or because associated states trust through it, it is faith. The root “dhā” with the prefix “saṃ” is in the sense of holding, with the suffix “-ta.” That faith is characterized by trust in actions and so forth, or by conviction. Its essence is clarity, like a water-purifying gem. Or its essence is eagerness, like one crossing a flood. It manifests as an unmuddied state or as resolution. Its proximate cause is an object worthy of faith, or the factors of stream-entry. It should be seen as a hand, as wealth, and as a seed. For the Blessed One has said: “Faith is the great elephant’s hand,” and “Faith is the best wealth of a person here,” and “Faith is the seed, austerity the rain,” and “By faith one crosses the flood,” and “Faith binds provisions for the journey, faith is a person’s companion,” and “A noble disciple, monks, is led by faith,” and “the wealth of faith.”

“Yesaṃ atthi saddhā buddhe, dhamme ca saṅgharatane;

Te maṃ ativirocanti, āyunā yasasā siriyā”ti.

“Those who have faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha jewel—they outshine me in life, fame, and glory.”

Ca. “Saddhaṃ upanissāya dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ samādiyati, uposathakammaṃ karoti, jhānaṃ uppādeti, vipassanaṃ uppādeti, maggaṃ uppādeti, abhiññaṃ uppādeti, samāpattiṃ uppādetī”ti ca. “Dullabhā saddhāsampattī”ti ca vuttā. Tasmā saddho ca bhaveyyanti patthanaṃ karoti.

And: “Based on faith, one gives gifts, undertakes virtue, observes the Uposatha, develops jhāna, develops insight, develops the path, develops higher knowledge, and develops meditative absorption.” And it is said, “Attainment of faith is rare.” Therefore, one makes the aspiration, “May I be faithful.”

Sā ca pana catubbidhā hoti āgamasaddhā, adhigamasaddhā, okappanasaddhā, pasādasaddhā cāti. Tattha sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ abhinīhārato āgatattā āgamasaddhā nāma. Ariyasāvakānaṃ saccapaṭivedhena adhigatattā adhigamasaddhā nāma. Buddho dhammo saṅghoti vutte acalabhāvena okappanaṃ okappanasaddhā nāma. Buddhādīsu pasāduppattimattā pasādasaddhā nāma. Idha pana paṇidhānaṭṭhānattā sabbasaddhā adhippetā. Saddhā assa me atthīti saddho. Assathyatthe ṇa.

That faith is of four kinds: faith based on tradition, faith based on realization, faith based on conviction, and faith based on serene joy. Herein, the faith of Bodhisattvas, because it comes from their resolve, is called faith based on tradition. The faith of noble disciples, because it is attained through penetration of the truth, is called faith based on realization. The unwavering conviction when it is said “Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha” is called faith based on conviction. Merely the arising of serene joy regarding the Buddha and others is called faith based on serene joy. Here, however, all kinds of faith are intended because it is the basis of aspiration. “He has faith,” thus he is “saddho” (faithful). The suffix “-ṇa” is used in the sense of “having.”

Dātaṅgupetoti dātassa aṅgāya kāraṇabhūtāya dhanasampattiyā upeto samupeto samannāgato ca. Dātabbavatthu ca, tappaṭiggāhakapuggalo ca, saddhā cāti tīhi aṅgehi upeto samupeto samannāgato ca vā. Diyate dātaṃ. Bhāvasādhanoyaṃ. Dādhātu dāne a. Aṅgīyati [M 0.0210] ñāyati etenāti aṅgo, dhanasampatti. Dātassa aṅgo dātaṅgo, tena upeto samupeto samannāgatoti dātaṅgupeto, atha vā diyatīti dātaṃ, dānavatthu. Dātassa aṅgo dātaṅgo, tena upeto samupeto samannāgatoti dātaṅgupeto, dātabbavatthu ca, tappaṭiggāhaka puggalo ca, saddhā cāti tīhi aṅgehi sampajjāmīti patthanaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuttañhi itivuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saddhā deyyadhammo paṭiggāhako cāti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samukhībhūtakāleyeva hi dānaṃ sambhavatī”ti.

"Endowed with the means to give" means endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of wealth, which is the cause for giving. Or, it means endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of three factors: the object to be given, the person who receives it, and faith. 'Dātaṃ' is what is given. This is a formation in the sense of state. The root is "dā" (to give), with the suffix "a". "Aṅga" means that by which something is recognized—here, wealth. "Dātaṅga" is the means of giving, and being endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of it is "dātaṅgupeta." Alternatively, "dātaṃ" means what is given—the object of giving. "Dātaṅga" is the means of giving, and being endowed, fully endowed, and possessed of it is "dātaṅgupeta"—possessing the object to be given, the recipient, and faith. Thus, it is said that one makes the aspiration: "May I be accomplished in these three factors." For it was said in the Itivuttaka commentary: "Faith, the gift, and the recipient—it is only when these three are present together that giving occurs."

Paramasiridharoti uttamasirīdhārako ca. Uttamasiriṃ dhāraṇasamattho ca vā. Ettha ca sirīti paññāpuññasarīrasobhaggasampattīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Katapuññehi seviyatīti sirī, katapuññe puggale sevati nissayatīti vā sirī, paññāpuññasarīrasobhaggasampatti labbhati. Sidhātu sevāyaṃ iro ī ca.
