Paramā uttamā sirī paramasirī, taṃ dhāretīti paramasirīdharo, paramasiriyā dhāraṇasamatthoti attho.

"Bearer of supreme glory" means one who holds the highest glory, or is capable of bearing supreme glory. Here, "sirī" is a term for the attainments of wisdom, merit, bodily beauty, and good fortune. "Sirī" is what is resorted to by those who have made merit, or it is what resorts to and relies on meritorious individuals—whereby the attainments of wisdom, merit, bodily beauty, and good fortune are obtained. The root is `si` (to serve), with the suffixes `ira` and `ī`. "Paramā sirī" is the supreme glory. "Paramasirīdhara" is the bearer of supreme glory, meaning one capable of bearing supreme glory.

Diṭṭhadhammeti paccakkhabhūte attabhāve. Ettha ca diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkhabhūto attabhāvo. So hi passitabboti diṭṭho, attabhāvo. Diṭṭho passitabbo dhammo sabhāvo assāti diṭṭhadhammoti vuccati. Tasmiṃ diṭṭhadhamme. Virattoti kāmaguṇesu vigataratto ca, rajjanaṃ ratto. Ranjadhātu rāge. Vigato ratto assa meti viratto. Lajjīti pāpahirivanto ca, pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāya lajjāya sampanno ca vā. Atha vā lajjīti hirottappasampanno ca. Lajjīsaddena hi lakkhaṇāhāranayena ottappampi gahetabbaṃ. Kasmā, kusala lakkhaṇasabhāvena samānattā. Vuttañhetaṃ nettipāḷiyaṃ –

"In the present existence" means in the directly perceived individual existence. Here, 'diṭṭhadhamma' is called the directly perceived individual existence. For it is to be seen (passitabbo), thus it is 'seen' (diṭṭho), the individual existence. The individual existence whose nature is a thing to be seen is thus called 'diṭṭhadhamma'. In that present existence. 'Dispassionate' means without passion for sensual qualities; passion is attachment; the root `rañj` is in the sense of passion. One whose passion has departed is 'dispassionate'. 'Conscientious' means one who has shame about evil, or one who is endowed with shame which has the characteristic of disgust for evil. Or, 'conscientious' means endowed with moral shame and dread. For by the term 'conscientious', moral dread should also be included by way of the guideline of characteristics. Why? Because they share the same nature as wholesome characteristics. As it is stated in the Nettipāḷi:

“Vuttamhi ekadhamme, ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā keci;

Vuttā bhavanti sabbo, sohāro lakkhaṇo nāmā”ti.

"When one thing is stated, whatever things share a single characteristic, all are stated. This is called the guideline of characteristics."

Lajjatīti [M 0.0211] lajjā, hiri. Lajjadhātu hiriyaṃ. Lajjā assa me atthīti lajjā, kāyaduccaritādito hirottappasamannāgato cāti attho. Kalyāṇamittoti sundaramitta sampanno ca. Kalyāṇasaddo hi sundaravācako anipphanna pāṭipadiko. Atha vā kalyaṃ hitaṃ aṇayati pāpayatīti kalyāṇo, sumitto. Kalyasaddūpapadaaṇadhātu gatiyaṃ ṇa. Mijjati sinehatīti mitto, mijjiyati sinehiyatīti vā mitto, midadhātu sinehe ta. Kalyāṇo mitto assa meti kalyāṇamitto. Hitadharasumittasampanno ca bhaveyyanti attho. Idha pana saddhāsīlasutacāgavīriyasati samādhipaññāguṇehi samannāgato kalyāṇamitto adhippeto. Taṃ pana sandhāya bhagavatā siṅgālasutte –

One is ashamed (lajjati), hence 'lajjā' (shame), which is 'hiri' (moral shame). The root `lajj` is in the sense of moral shame. One who possesses shame is thus called conscientious, meaning endowed with moral shame and dread regarding bodily misconduct and so forth. 'One with a good friend' means one endowed with an excellent friend. For the term 'kalyāṇa' (good) conveys excellence and is an underived nominal stem. Or, because it brings what is beneficial and leads to welfare, it is 'kalyāṇa', a good friend. The word is derived from the root 'aṇ' meaning 'to go', with the prefix 'kalya'. One who is affectionate is a friend, or one to whom affection is shown is a friend, from the root 'mid' meaning affection, with the suffix 'ta'. One who has a good friend is a `kalyāṇamitto`. The meaning is that one should be endowed with a beneficial and excellent friend. Here, however, a good friend is specifically intended as one endowed with the qualities of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the Siṅgāla Sutta:

“Upakāro ca yo mitto, sukhadukkhe ca yo sakhā;

Atthakkhāyī ca yo mitto, yo ca mittānukampako;

Etepi mitte cattāro, iti viññāya paṇḍito; Sakkaccaṃ

Payirupāseyya, mātā puttaṃva orasa”nti vutto.

A friend who is a help, a friend in happiness and sorrow, a friend who points out what is beneficial, and a friend who is sympathetic—these four kinds of friends the wise should understand and respectfully attend to, as a mother her own child.

Visuddhimagge ca –

And in the Visuddhimagga:

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo. Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no cāṭṭhāne niyojaye”ti vutto. Iti evarūpassa ca kalyāṇamittassa dullabhattā kalyāṇamittena sampajjāmīti patthanaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Dear, respected, worthy of emulation, a speaker and patient with speech, one who speaks on profound matters, and does not engage one in what is unsuitable”—thus it is said. Therefore, because such a good friend is rare, the wish is made: “May I be endowed with a good friend,” it is said.

Abhiratakusaloti dānādipuññakusaladhammesu abhiramaṇo ca. Kucchitaṃ apāyadvāraṃ salanti saṃvaranti pidahanti sādhavo etenāti kusalaṃ, dānādipuññadhammā. Kupubba saladhātu saṃvaraṇe a. Tesu abhiatirekaṃ ramatīti abhiratakusalo[M 0.0212], kitantasamāsoyaṃ. Kusalābhiratoti vattabbe chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ padavipariyāyena evaṃ vuttanti. Atha vā abhiatirekaṃ ramanaṃ abhirato, kusalesu abhirato yassa meti abhiratakusalo, niccaṃ kusalapuññassa karaṇe abhiratacittasampanno cāti attho.

“Delighting in the wholesome” means one who delights in meritorious wholesome qualities such as giving and so forth. “Kusala” (wholesome) is so called because the good prevent, restrain, and close the contemptible door to the states of misery by means of it; these are meritorious qualities such as giving and so forth. This is from the root “sal” with the prefix “ku” in the sense of restraining, plus the suffix “a.” “Abhiratakusalo” means one who delights exceedingly in these; this is a verbal-adjective compound. When “kusalābhirato” should be said, the word order is reversed to preserve the meter. Or alternatively, “abhirato” means excessive delight; “abhiratakusalo” means one in whom there is delight in wholesome qualities. The meaning is, one who is constantly endowed with a mind that delights in performing wholesome and meritorious acts.

Pañcasīlādirakkhoti pañcasīlādīnaṃ rakkhituṃ samattho ca. Ettha ca ādisaddena gihīnaṃ aṭṭhaṅguposathasīlaṃ, sāmaṇerānaṃ dasaṅgasīlañca, bhikkhūnaṃ catupārisuddhisīlañca saṅgaṇhāti. Pañcasīlaṃ ādi yesaṃ teti pañcasīlādi, taṃ rakkhati rakkhituṃ samatthetīti pañcasīlādirakkho. Gahaṭṭhānaṃ niccasīlavasena pañcasīlaṃ sati ussāhasamatthe uposathaṅgavasena aṭṭhaṅgasīlaṃ dasaṅgasīlañca akhaṇḍaṃ acchiddaṃ asabalaṃ akammāsaṃ katvā rakkhituṃ sāmaṇerasīlavasena dasasīlañca, bhikkhusīlavasena catupārisuddhisīlañca rakkhituṃ samattho cāti attho. Bhagavatā hi “sīlavipattihetu vā bhikkhave sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjantī”ti ca. “Sīlasampadāhetu vā bhikkhave sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjantī”ti ca. “Sīlasampanno mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ adhigacchati kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchati. Catuparisaṃ visārado upasaṅkamati amaṅkubhūto. Asammūḷho kālaṃ karoti, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjatī”ti ca vuttattā ca. Aṭṭhakathāyañca “sīlālaṅkārasadiso alaṅkāro natthi, sīlasadisaṃ pupphaṃ natthi, sīlagandhasadiso gandho natthī”ti ca. “Sīla sampattiñhi nissāya tisso vijjā pāpuṇātī”ti ca. “Ādimhi sīlaṃ visodheyyā”ti ca. “Sattā sīlena visujjhantī”ti ca. “Sīlaṃ sāsanassa ādī”ti ca. “Sattasu visuddhīsu [M 0.0213] sīlavisuddhi sarīraṃ nāmā”ti ca. “Sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ avassayo patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyana”nti ca vuttattā pañcasīlādirakkhoti patthanaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Protector of the five precepts and so forth” means one who is capable of guarding the five precepts and so on. Here, the word “and so on” includes the eight-precept Uposatha observance for laypeople, the ten precepts for novices, and the fourfold purity of conduct for monks. “Pañcasīlādi” means that which has the five precepts as its beginning; “pañcasīlādirakkho” means one who guards them, who is capable of guarding them. The meaning is being capable of guarding: for householders, the five precepts as their constant moral practice, and when they have the energy and ability, the eight Uposatha precepts or the ten precepts, keeping them unbroken, unpierced, unspotted, and unblemished; for novices, the ten precepts; and for monks, the fourfold purity of conduct. For the Blessed One has said: “Monks, due to failure in virtue, beings, at the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in the planes of misery, in an evil destiny, in the lower realm, in hell.” And: “Monks, due to accomplishment in virtue, beings, at the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destiny, in the heavenly world.” And: “One accomplished in virtue attains a great mass of wealth; a good reputation arises; one approaches the fourfold assembly confidently, without being timid. One dies unconfused, and at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destiny, in the heavenly world.” Moreover, the commentaries state: “There is no adornment like the adornment of virtue, no flower like virtue, no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue.” And: “Relying on the accomplishment of virtue, one attains the three knowledges.” And: “At the beginning, one should purify virtue.” And: “Beings are purified by virtue.” And: “Virtue is the beginning of the Dispensation.” And: “Among the seven purifications, purification of virtue is called the body.” And: “Virtue is indeed the support, the foundation, the object, the protection, the refuge, the destination, the final resort.” Because it is said thus, the wish is made: “May I be a protector of the five precepts and so forth.” Thus it is said.

Appicchoti aniccho ca, rūpādikāmaguṇesu anicchantoti attho. Abhāvatthohettha appasaddo. Appaḍaṃsamakasavā tātapātiādīsu viya icchanaṃ icchā, rūpādikāmaguṇaṃ icchatīti vā icchā, kāmataṇhā. Isudhātu icchākantīsu a. Dhātvantassaccho. Natthi icchā yassa meti appiccho, rūpādīsu kāmesu anicchanto cāti attho. Appiccho pana catubbidho hoti paccayaappiccho, pariyattiappiccho, dhutaṅgaappiccho, paṭivedhaappiccho cāti. Tattha catūsu paccayesu appiccho paccayaappiccho. Yo pana paccaye bahuṃ dente appaṃ gaṇhati, appaṃ dente appataraṃ vā gaṇhati na vā gaṇhati. Na anavasesagāhī hoti. Ayaṃ paccayaappiccho nāma. Yo pana tepiṭakopi samāno na bahussutabhāvaṃ jānāpetukāmo hoti, ayaṃ pariyattiappiccho nāma. Dhutaṅgasamādānassa pana dhutaṅgapariharaṇabhāvaṃ aññesaṃ jānituṃ na deti, ayaṃ dhutaṅgaappiccho nāma. Yo pana sotāpannādīsu aññataro hutvā sotāpannādibhāvaṃ jānāpetuṃ na icchati, ayaṃ adhigamaappiccho nāma. Imehi appicchaguṇehi sampanno ca ahaṃ bhaveyyanti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Appiccho” (one with few desires) means one who is without desire, that is, one who does not desire forms and other sensual qualities. Here, the word “appa” conveys absence, as in “appaḍaṃsamakasavā” (free from gadflies and mosquitoes). “Icchā” (desire) is the act of desiring, or it is the desire for forms and other sensual qualities, which is sensual craving. The root “is” (from “isu”) is in the sense of desiring and liking, with the suffix “a”; the end of the root becomes “cch”. “Appiccho” means one who has no desire, who does not crave forms and other sensual pleasures. One with few desires is of four kinds: one with few desires regarding requisites (paccayaappiccho), one with few desires regarding learning (pariyattiappiccho), one with few desires regarding ascetic practices (dhutaṅgaappiccho), and one with few desires regarding realization (paṭivedhaappiccho). Among these, one who has few desires regarding the four requisites is a “paccayaappiccho.” This refers to someone who, when given many requisites, takes little; when given little, takes even less or nothing at all—never taking everything available. One who, despite mastering the Tipiṭaka, does not wish to make known their extensive learning is a “pariyattiappiccho.” One who, having undertaken ascetic practices, does not allow others to know of their observance is a “dhutaṅgaappiccho.” One who, having become any one from a stream-enterer upwards, does not wish to reveal their state of attainment is an “adhigamaappiccho.” Thus, it is said, “May I be endowed with these virtues of having few desires.”

Appakodhoti dussanalakkhaṇadosato virahito ca. So hi kujjhatīti kodhoti vuccati. Dosassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Natthi kodho assa meti appakodho.

“Appakodho” (one of little anger) means one who is free from the fault characterized by ill will. For that aversion is called 'anger' (kodha), as it is that by which one becomes angry (kujjhati). This is a designation for aversion (dosa). One who has no anger is “appakodho”.

Kuddho atthaṃ na jānāti, kuddho dhammaṃ na passati;

Andhatamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ kodho sahate naranti.

The angry one does not know the meaning, the angry one does not see the Dhamma; blinding darkness then prevails when anger overpowers a person.

Vuttadesanaṃ manasikaritvā appakodhoti patthanaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Having reflected on the teaching that has been stated, one makes the aspiration: “May I be of little anger”—thus it is said.

Ativujuhadayoti [M 0.0214] atieva ujucittasamannāgato ca. Arati gacchati pavattati akuṭilabhāvenāti uju, ajjavaṃ. Aradhātu gatiyaṃ ju. Arissa u. Ārammaṇaṃ haratīti hadayaṃ, cittaṃ. Haradhātu haraṇe aya. Rassa do. Atha vā ārammaṇaṃ harantaṃ ayati gacchati pavattatīti hadayaṃ, cittaṃ. Harasaddūpapada ayadhātu gatiyaṃ a. Uju ca taṃ hadayañcāti ujuhadayaṃ. Atieva uju hadayaṃ assa meti ativujuhadayo. Gomuttavaṅko ca candalekhāvaṅko ca naṅgalakoṭi vaṅko cāti tīhi vaṅkehi vigato hutvā ativiya ujucittasamannāgato ca bhaveyyanti attho. Tattha ca yo pāpaṃ katvāva na karomīti bhāsati. So gantvā paccosakkanatāya gomuttavaṅko nāma. Yo pāpaṃ karontova bhāyāmahaṃ pāpassāti bhāsati. So yebhuyyena kuṭilatāya candalekhā vaṅko nāma. Yo pāpaṃ karontova ko pāpassa na bhāyeyyāti bhāsati, so nātikuṭilatāya naṅgalakoṭivaṅko nāma hoti. Yassa vā tīṇi kammadvārāni asuddhāni. So gomuttavaṅko nāma hoti. Yassa yāni kānici dve. So candalekhā vaṅko nāma. Yassa yaṃkiñci ekaṃ. So naṅgalakoṭivaṅko nāmāti veditabbo.

“Ativujuhadayo” (one of exceedingly straightforward heart) means one who is endowed with an exceedingly upright mind. “Uju” (straight) means moving or proceeding without crookedness; this is honesty. “Hadaya” (heart, mind) is so called because it carries (harati) the object (ārammaṇa). Alternatively, it is called “hadaya” because it moves (ayati), goes, and proceeds while carrying the object. “Ujuhadaya” is a straightforward heart. “Ativujuhadayo” means one whose heart is exceedingly straightforward. The meaning is that one should be free from the three types of crookedness—the “gomuttavaṅka” (cow-urine crookedness), the “candalekhāvaṅka” (crescent-moon crookedness), and the “naṅgalakoṭivaṅka” (plowshare-tip crookedness)—and thus be endowed with a very upright mind. Here, one who, after doing evil, says, “I did not do it,” is called “gomuttavaṅka” because of turning back and retreating. One who, while doing evil, says, “I fear evil,” is generally called “candalekhāvaṅka” due to his crookedness. One who, while doing evil, says, “Who would not fear evil?” is called “naṅgalakoṭivaṅka” because he is not excessively crooked. Alternatively, one whose three doors of action are impure is called “gomuttavaṅka.” One whose two are impure is called “candalekhāvaṅka.” One whose one is impure is to be understood as “naṅgalakoṭivaṅka.”

Iddhimāti iddhiyā samannāgato ca, iddhisaddassa vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Iddhi assa me atthīti iddhimā. Assathyatthe mantupaccayo. Mānussikāle manussiddhiyā devuppattikāle deviddhiyā samaṇuppattikāle samaṇiddhiyā ca sampuṇṇeyyanti attho.

“Iddhimā” (endowed with psychic power) means one who is endowed with psychic power; the meaning of the word “iddhi” has already been stated above. “Iddhimā” means “he possesses iddhi.” The suffix “-mantu” is in the sense of possession. The meaning is that in the human stage, one should be fully endowed with human psychic power; in the divine stage, with divine psychic power; and in the ascetic stage, with the ascetic's psychic power.

Appameyyoti appametabbehi sīlādiguṇehi sampanno ca. Pametabboti pameyyo. Papubbamādhātu pamāṇe ṇya. Na pameyyo appameyyo, appameyyo sīlādiguṇo me assa atthīti appameyyo. Assathyatthe ṇa. Appameyyehi [M 0.0215] sīlādiguṇehi ca bhogasampattīhi ca sampajjāmīti patthanaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Appameyyo” (immeasurable) means one who is endowed with immeasurable virtues such as morality. “Pameyyo” means measurable. The root “mā” with the prefix “pa” is in the sense of measuring; with the suffix “ṇya” it forms “pameyyo.” Not measurable is “appameyyo.” “Appameyyo” means one who possesses immeasurable virtues such as morality. The suffix “ṇa” is in the sense of possession. Thus it is said that one makes the aspiration: “May I be accomplished with immeasurable virtues such as morality and with wealth and prosperity.”

Pāsaṃsoti sīlādiguṇehi buddhādisappurisānaṃ pasaṃsāraho ca, pasaṃsiyate thaviyate pasaṃso. Bhāva sādhanoyaṃ. Papubbasaṃsadhātu thutiyaṃ, taṃ arahatīti pāsaṃso. Arahatitaddhite ṇa. Buddhādisappurisehi pasaṃsi tabbehi dānasīlādiguṇehi sampanno ca bhaveyyanti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Pāsaṃso” (praiseworthy) means one who is worthy of praise by noble persons such as the Buddha, due to virtues like morality. “Pasaṃso” is praise, that which is praised or extolled; this is a verbal noun. The root “saṃs” with the prefix “pa” is in the sense of praising. One who is worthy of it is called “pāsaṃso”; the suffix “ṇa” is in the sense of deserving. Thus it is said: “May I be endowed with qualities such as generosity and virtue that are to be praised by the Buddha and other noble individuals.”

Pemavācoti atthabyañjanamadhuratāya buddhādisappurisehi pemitabbavācāya sampanno ca. Piyateti pemā, vācā. Pīdhātu tappanakantīsu imo. Vacitabbāti vācā. Vacadhātu viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ ṇa. Pemā vācā assa meti pema vāco. Buddhādisappurisehi pemiyā caturaṅgasamannāgata vācāya sampanno cāti attho. Sappurisānaṃ pana vācā caturaṅgasamannāgatā hoti. Subhāsitavācā ca dhammavācā piyavācā saccavācāti. Tathāhetaṃ vuttaṃ sagāthāvagga saṃyutte –

“Pemavāco” (one with loving speech) means one who is endowed with speech that is beloved by noble beings such as the Buddha, due to its sweetness in meaning and expression. “Pema” (love) is that which is loved. The root “pī” is in the sense of delighting and liking. “Vācā” (speech) is that which is to be spoken. The root “vac” is in the sense of articulate speech. “Pemavāco” means one who possesses loving speech. The meaning is, one who is endowed with speech beloved by noble beings like the Buddha, possessing four qualities. Indeed, the speech of noble beings is endowed with four qualities: well-spoken speech, Dhamma-based speech, affectionate speech, and truthful speech. As it is said in the Sagāthāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya:

Subhāsitaṃ uttamamāhu santo,

Dhammaṃ bhaṇe nādhammaṃ taṃ dutiyaṃ;

Piyaṃ bhaṇe nāppiyaṃ taṃ tatiyaṃ,

Saccaṃ bhaṇe nālikaṃ taṃ catutthanti.

The good say the well-spoken is supreme; second, one should speak Dhamma, not non-Dhamma; third, one should speak what is pleasing, not unpleasing; fourth, one should speak truth, not falsehood.

Ayaṃ panettha yojanā. Santo sappurisā uttamaṃ subhāsitaṃ suṭṭhu bhāsitaṃ vācaṃ āhu, dhammaṃ bhaṇe bhaṇeyya adhammaṃ na bhaṇe na bhaṇeyya, dutiyaṃ taṃ vācaṃ āhu, piyaṃ bhaṇe bhaṇeyya, appiyaṃ na bhaṇe na bhaṇeyya, tatiyaṃ taṃ vācaṃ āhu, saccaṃ bhaṇe bhaṇeyya alikaṃ na bhaṇe na bhaṇeyya, catutthaṃ taṃ vācaṃ āhūti.

Herein is the explanation. Good persons declare supreme, well-spoken speech—that which is rightly spoken—to be so. They declare as the second kind of speech: 'One should speak the Dhamma, not what is contrary to the Dhamma.' They declare as the third kind of speech: 'One should speak what is pleasing, not what is unpleasing.' They declare as the fourth kind of speech: 'One should speak the truth, not falsehood.'

Sujanaguṇavidūti [M 0.0216] buddhādisappurisānaṃ sīlādiguṇaṃ vijānako ca. Sundaro jano sujano. Guṇati pakāseti sīlādiguṇasamaṅgitaṃ puggalanti guṇaṃ, sīlādiguṇaṃ. Guṇadhātu pakāsane a. Sujanānaṃ buddhādisappurisānaṃ guṇo sujanaguṇo, taṃ vidati jānātīti sujanaguṇavidū. Sujana guṇasaddūpapadavidadhātu ñāṇe ū. Buddhādisappurisānaṃ sīlasamādhipaññādiguṇaṃ jānituṃ samattho ca bhaveyyanti attho.

“Sujanaguṇavidū” means one who knows the virtues, such as morality, of the Buddhas and other good persons. A good person (sujano) is a beautiful person (sundaro jano). It is called a virtue (guṇa) because it reveals (guṇati pakāseti) a person endowed with virtues such as morality. The root 'guṇ' is in the sense of revealing. The virtue of good persons, such as the Buddhas, is sujanaguṇa; one who knows or understands that is sujanaguṇavidū. The word is formed from the prefixes 'sujana' and 'guṇa' with the root 'vid' in the sense of knowing. The meaning is: “May I be capable of knowing the virtues of the Buddhas and other good persons, such as morality, concentration, and wisdom.”

Māmakoti buddhādisajjanānaṃ māmako ca. Mamāyatīti māmako. Mamadhātu mānane peme vā ṇvu. Tassa ako. Buddhādiratanattayañca saddhammañca mānanto ca bhaveyyanti attho. Soti so ahaṃ. Bhaveyyanti bhavāmīti.

“Māmako” means one who is devoted to the Buddhas and other virtuous persons. One who regards something as 'mine' (mamāyati) is called māmako. The root 'mam' is in the sense of honoring or affection. The meaning is: “May I be one who honors the Triple Gem beginning with the Buddha, and the true Dhamma.” “So” means 'that I'. “Bhaveyyaṃ” means 'may I be'.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepayojanā. So ahaṃ diṭṭhadhamme paccakkhabhūte attabhāve, saddho saddhāya samannāgato ca, dātaṅgupeto dātassa aṅgāya kāraṇabhūtāya dhana sampattiyā upeto samupeto samannāgato ca, dātabba vatthu ca, tappaṭiggāhakapuggalo ca, saddhā cāti tīhi aṅgehi upeto samupeto samannāgato ca vā, paramasiridharo uttamasirīdhārako ca, uttamasiriṃ dhāraṇasamattho ca vā, viratto kāmaguṇesu vigataratto ca, lajjī pāpahirivanto ca, pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāya lajjāya sampanno ca vā, hirottappasamannāgato ca vā, kalyāṇamitto sundaramitta sampanno ca, abhiratakusalo dānādipuññakusaladhammesu abhiramaṇo ca, pañcasīlādirakkho pañcasīlādīni rakkhituṃ samattho ca, appiccho aniccho ca, rūpādikāmaguṇesu anicchanto ca vā, appakodho dussanalakkhaṇadosato virahito ca, ativujuhadayo atieva ujucittasamannāgato ca, iddhiyā samannāgato ca, appameyyo appameyyehi sīlādiguṇehi sampanno ca, pāsaṃso sīlādiguṇehi buddhādisappurisānaṃ pasaṃsāraho ca, pemavāco atthabyañjanamadhuratāya [M 0.0217] buddhādisappurisehi pemitabbavācāya sampanno ca, sujanaguṇavidū buddhādisappurisānaṃ sīlādiguṇaṃ vijānako ca, māmako buddhādisajjanānaṃ māmako ca, buddhādiratanattayañca saddhammañca mānanto ca vā, bhaveyyaṃ bhavāmīti.

Herein is the concise application: May I, in this present existence which is directly experienced, be faithful and endowed with faith; inclined to giving and endowed with the means for giving—wealth and prosperity—or endowed with the three factors of an object to be given, a worthy recipient, and faith; a foremost bearer of glory, a supreme bearer of glory, or capable of bearing the highest glory; dispassionate towards sensual pleasures and free from attachment; conscientious and ashamed of evil, endowed with the shame characterized by loathing evil, or possessing shame and moral dread; endowed with good friends; delighting in the wholesome, rejoicing in meritorious wholesome qualities like generosity; a guardian of the five precepts and so on, capable of maintaining them; having few desires and free from longing, not desiring sensual pleasures like forms and so on; having little anger, free from the fault characterized by malice; with an exceedingly upright heart; endowed with psychic power; immeasurable, endowed with immeasurable virtues like morality; praiseworthy, worthy of praise by the Buddhas and other good persons for virtues like morality; endowed with pleasing speech—sweet in meaning and expression—worthy of being cherished by the Buddhas and other good persons; a knower of the virtues of good people, understanding the virtues of the Buddhas and other good persons; devoted to the Buddhas and other virtuous persons, or honoring the Triple Gem and the true Dhamma. May I be thus.

Aṭṭhavīsatimagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the twenty-eighth verse is completed.

29.

29.

Itthaṃ asaṅkhaye nātha, guṇe lakkhaṇadīpite;

Gāthāsu sūcakāsveka, gāthampi sarate budho.

Thus, O Protector, among the verses that indicate the countless virtues illuminated by their characteristics, a wise person remembers even a single verse.

30.

30.

Caturāpāyamutto so, sādhakatthadvayassa ca;

Hatūpaddavajālo ca, lābhī hitasukhassa ca.

He is freed from the four woeful states, and is an achiever of the two kinds of benefit; he has destroyed the net of troubles, and is a recipient of welfare and happiness.

31.

31.

Adhipo naradevānaṃ, catudīpissaropi vā;

Bhaveyya antime dehe, tamaññaṃ setachattakaṃ.

He would be the lord of human kings, or even the ruler of the four continents; in his final body, he would have the white parasol, and no other.

32.

32.

Bhāvanāyānamāruyha, samamessati subbato;

Imasmiṃ attabhāvepi, arogo dīghajīviko.

Having mounted the vehicle of meditation, the one of good vows will attain peace; even in this very existence, he will be free from disease and long-lived.

33.

33.

Pūjito sabbalokehi, bhāvanābhiratīmano;

Janappiyo manāpo ca, kā kathākhiladhāraṇe.

Worshipped by all worlds, his mind delighting in meditation, beloved and dear to people—what need to speak of his complete retention?

29. Evaṃ puññenetenatyādi gāthādvayena paṇidhiṃ katvā idāni buddhavandanassa phalānisaṃsaṃ dassento itthantyādi gāthāpañcakaṃ āha. Taṃ pana mūlācariyehi na vuttaṃ, pacchā pana hitakāmehi paṇḍitehi pakkhittaṃ gāthāpañcakanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tā pana gāthāyo pathyāvattagāthāti daṭṭhabbā.

29. Thus, having made a resolution with the two verses beginning 'Evaṃ puññenetenāti,' now, showing the fruit and benefits of venerating the Buddha, he spoke the five verses beginning 'Itthaṃ.' It should be understood, however, that this pentad of verses was not spoken by the original teachers, but was later inserted by well-wishing scholars. And these verses should be understood to be pathyāvatta verses.

Tāsu pana paṭhamagāthāyaṃ itthaṃ asaṅkhaye lakkhaṇadīpite nāthaguṇe sūcakāsu gāthāsu ekagāthampi yo budho sarateti sambandho. Itthanti iminā sugatantiādinā vuttappakārena. Asaṅkhayeti ettakā buddhaguṇāti gaṇetuṃ asamatthe. Saṅkhiyate saṅkhayā. Saṅkhiyati gaṇiyatīti vā saṅkhayā[M 0.0218]. Sakhidhātu saṅkhyāyaṃ yapaccayo. Atha vā saṅkhituṃ na sakkontīti asaṅkhayā. Ettakā buddhaguṇā ettakā buddhaguṇāti niravasesato ekabuddhopi anekavassa satasahassakoṭiyāpi gaṇetuṃ asamatthova. Pageva pana aññeti attho. Vuttampi cetaṃ apadāne –

Among these, in the first verse, the connection is as follows: 'Thus, among the verses that indicate the countless virtues of the Protector, illuminated by their characteristics, a wise person remembers even a single verse.' 'Itthaṃ' means: in the manner stated beginning with 'sugataṃ.' 'Asaṅkhaye' means: unable to count so many qualities of the Buddha. 'Saṅkhayā' is that which is counted. Or, 'saṅkhayā' is that which is counted or enumerated. The root 'khyā' with the prefix 'saṃ' is used in the sense of enumeration. Alternatively, because they cannot be counted, they are 'asaṅkhayā' (uncountable). The meaning is that even one Buddha is unable to completely enumerate so many qualities of a Buddha, even over many hundreds of thousands of crores of years, how much less so others. And this has been stated in the Apadāna:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti ca.

“Even a Buddha might speak the praise of a Buddha, speaking of nothing else for an aeon; that aeon, in the long, vast interval, would be exhausted, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”

“Sakkā samudde udakaṃ, pametuṃ āḷhakena vā;

Natveva tava sabbaññu, ñāṇaṃ sakkā pametave”ti ca.

“It might be possible to measure the water in the ocean with a measure, O Omniscient One, but it would never be possible to measure your knowledge.”

Mahāvaggasaṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyañca “appamāṇā hi buddhā tesaṃ buddhāpi anavasesato vaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ asamatthā, pageva itarā pajā”ti ca. Lakkhaṇadīpiteti upalakkhaṇa nayena pakāsitabbe. Ettha ca padhānanayo nidassana nayo ca labbhati. Nāthaguṇeti buddhassa sīlasamādhi paññādiguṇe. Tassa pana padassa vacanattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Sūcakāsvekagāthampīti sūcakāsu ekagāthampīti padacchedo. Sūcakāsūti pakāsakāsu. Gāthāsūti sugatantyādinā vuttāsu chabbīsativandanagāthāsu. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Kavīhi gāyati kathiyatīti gāthā. Pajjaviseso. Gedhātu sadde tha. Gedhātussa gādeso. Atha vā gaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ. Taṃ tiṭṭhati etthāti gāthā. Gaṃsaddūpapadathādhātu gatinivattiyaṃ. Gaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, tena kavīhi bandhitvā thiyati thapiyatīti vā gāthā, tāsu gāthāsu. Ekagāthampīti ekapajjampi. Ettha ca pisaddo garahattho. Tena anekagāthāya buddhaguṇasaraṇe kā kathāvāti sambhāveti. Budhoti yo paṇḍito. So [M 0.0219] hi atthānatthaṃ budhati jānātītibudhoti vuccati. Sarateti sarati. Chandānurakkhaṇatthañhi parassapadativibhattiyā attanopadatevibhattādeso.

And in the commentary on the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya: “Immeasurable, indeed, are the Buddhas; even those Buddhas are unable to speak their praise completely, how much less so other people.” 'Lakkhaṇadīpite' should be explained by the method of illustration. And here, both the primary method and the method of example are found. 'Nāthaguṇe' means: in the virtues of the Buddha, such as morality, concentration, and wisdom. The verbal meaning of that term has already been stated above. 'Sūcakāsvekagāthampi' is the word division 'sūcakāsu ekagāthampi.' 'Sūcakāsu' means: in the indicating ones. 'Gāthāsu' means: in the twenty-six verses of veneration stated beginning with 'sugataṃ.' This is a locative of specification. A 'gāthā' is so called because it is sung or spoken by poets. It is a type of verse. The root 'ge' (to sing), with the suffix 'tha,' is in the sense of sound. The root 'ge' is replaced by 'gā.' Alternatively, 'gaṃ' is said to be knowledge. A 'gāthā' is that in which it stands. The root 'ṭhā' (to stand), with the word 'gaṃ' as a prefix, is in the sense of motion and cessation. Or, 'gaṃ' is said to be knowledge; it is bound and established by poets, thus it is a 'gāthā'; in those verses. 'Ekagāthampi' means: even a single verse. Here, the particle 'pi' has the sense of deprecation. Thus, it implies: “What need is there to speak of remembering the Buddha’s virtues with many verses?” 'Budho' means: one who is wise. For he understands, he knows, what is beneficial and what is not; thus he is called a 'budho.' 'Sarate' means 'sarati' (he remembers). Indeed, to preserve the meter, the active voice ending 'ti' is replaced by the middle voice ending 'te.'

30. Soti so budho bhaveyyāti sambandho. Caturāpāyamuttoti nirayatiracchānapetaasurakāyasaṅkhātehi catūhi apāyehi vimutto ca. Puññasammatā ayāyebhuyyena apagatoti apāyo. Ayato sukhato apagatoti vā apāyo. Abyayībhāvasamāsoyaṃ. Atha vā tisso sampattiyo ayanti gacchanti pavattanti etenāti ayo, puññaṃ. Ayadhātu gatiyaṃ a. Puññato ayati gacchati pavattatīti vā, puññakārīhi ayitabbo pavattetabboti vā ayo, sukhaṃ. Tato apagatoti apāyo. Caturo apāyo caturāpāyo, tehi mutto vimuttoti caturāpāyamutto. Sādhakatthadvayassa cāti sādhako atthadvayassa cāti padacchedo. Atthadvayassāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikasaṅkhātassa atthadvayassa. Ettha casaddo aṭṭhānayogo. So pana sādhako tyādīsu padesu yutto. Sādhakoti nipphādako ca. So hi sādheti nipphādetīti sādhakoti vuccati.

30. The connection is: 'So' (he), the wise one, 'bhaveyya' (would be). 'Caturāpāyamutto' means: freed from the four states of deprivation, namely, the hell realm, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, and the realm of asuras. 'Apāya' is so called because it is mostly devoid of what is considered good fortune, or because it is devoid of prosperity and happiness. This is an adverbial compound. Alternatively, 'aya' is merit, because the three kinds of prosperity proceed, go, and occur through it. The root 'ay' with the suffix 'a' is in the sense of going. Or, 'aya' is happiness, because it proceeds, goes, and occurs from merit, or because it is to be proceeded to and brought about by those who make merit. 'Apāya' is that which is devoid of that. The four 'apāyas' are 'caturāpāya'; 'caturāpāyamutto' is one who is freed and liberated from them. 'Sādhakatthadvayassa ca' is the word division 'sādhako atthadvayassa ca.' 'Atthadvayassa' means: of the two kinds of benefit, namely, that of the present life and that of the future life. Here, the word 'ca' is misplaced. It is, however, correctly placed in phrases such as 'sādhako.' 'Sādhako' means: an accomplisher. For he achieves and accomplishes, thus he is called a 'sādhako.'

Hatūpaddavajālo cāti hato upaddavasaṅkhātajālo ca. Hanayittha apanayitthāti hato. Hanadhātu hiṃsāyaṃ ta. Upagantvā davati hiṃsatīti upaddavo, jātibhayādi soḷasaupaddavo. Upapubbadudhātu hiṃsāyaṃ, upaddavā nāma pana soḷasavidhā honti jātibhayaṃ, jarābhayaṃ, byādhibhayaṃ, maraṇabhayaṃ, rājabhayaṃ, corabhayaṃ, aggibhayaṃ, udakabhayaṃ, ūmibhayaṃ, kumbhilabhayaṃ, āvaṭṭabhayaṃ, susukābhayaṃ, attānuvādabhayaṃ, parānuvādabhayaṃ, daṇḍabhayaṃ, duggatibhayañcāti. Jalati hiṃsati macche etenāti jālaṃ, macchajālaṃ. Jālaṃ [M 0.0220] viyāti jālo, upaddavo. Nitatthena pana jalati hiṃsati satte etenāti jālo. Upaddavo. Jaladhātu hiṃsāyaṃ ṇa. Hato upaddavasaṅkhātajālo yena soti hatūpaddavajālo. Buddhapaṇāmacetanāya pahito upaddavasaṅkhātajālo bhaveyyāti attho. Lābhī hitasukhassa cāti hitassa ca sukhassa ca lābhī ca. Labhanaṃ lābho, taṃ assa atthīti lābhī, hinoti vaḍḍhatīti hitaṃ, atthaṃ. Sukhayatīti sukhaṃ. Yassuppajjati, taṃ sukhitaṃ karotīti attho. Atha vā suṭṭhu dukkhaṃ khanatīti sukhaṃ. Supubba khanudhātu avadhāraṇe kvi. Hitañca sukhañca hitasukhaṃ, tassa lābhī bhaveyyāti attho.

‘And the net of calamities is destroyed’ means the net designated as a calamity is destroyed. ‘Destroyed’ means removed. The root hana is in the sense of harming; ta is the suffix. Upaddava means it approaches and harms, referring to the sixteen calamities such as the fear of birth. The root du preceded by upa is in the sense of harming. The sixteen calamities are: fear of birth, fear of aging, fear of sickness, fear of death, fear of kings, fear of thieves, fear of fire, fear of water, fear of waves, fear of crocodiles, fear of whirlpools, fear of sharks, fear of self-reproach, fear of others’ reproach, fear of punishment, and fear of a bad destination. Jālaṃ (net) is so called because by it one harms fish—thus, a fishing net. A calamity is a net (jālo), like a fishing net (jālaṃ). By its definitive meaning, however, jālo is so called because by it one harms beings—hence, a calamity. The root jala is in the sense of harming; ṇa is the suffix. Hatūpaddavajālo means he by whom the net designated as ‘calamity’ is destroyed. The meaning is: may the net of calamities be destroyed by the intention of paying homage to the Buddha. ‘A gainer of welfare and happiness’ means one who gains both welfare and happiness. Gaining is lābha; one who has it is a lābhī. Hitaṃ is so called because it promotes or increases; it is a benefit. Sukhaṃ is so called because it makes one happy; the meaning is that for whomever it arises, it makes that one happy. Alternatively, sukhaṃ is so called because it thoroughly digs up suffering. It is from the root khanu preceded by su in the sense of determination; kvi is the suffix. Hitasukhaṃ is welfare and happiness; the meaning is: may one be a gainer thereof.

31-32. Naradevānaṃ adhipo ca catudīpissaropi vā bhaveyyāti sambandho. Naradevānanti narā ca devā ca naradevā, tesaṃ. Kammatthe cetaṃ chaṭṭhīvacanaṃ. Adhipoti issaro ca. So hi attādhīnaṃ pāti rakkhati dhammena vā adhiabhibhavitvā pāti rakkhatīti adhipoti vuccati. Adhipubbapādhātu rakkhane a, narānaṃ adhipo issaro manussarājā ca devānaṃ adhipo issaro devarājā ca bhaveyyāti attho. Catudīpissaropi vāti ettha pisaddo sambhāvanatthe nipāto. Tena pageva ekadīpissararājabhāvo ca, pade sissararājabhāvo cāti sambhāveti. Vā saddo padapūraṇa mattoyeva. Catudīpissaroti pubbavideho, aparago yāno, jambudīpo, uttarakuru cāti catunnaṃ dīpānaṃ issaro cakkavattirājāpi bhaveyyāti attho. Tattha pubbavidehoti sineruno pure bhavaṃ pubbaṃ, vedena paññāya īhanti vāyamanti etthāti vedeho, vidasaddūpapada īhadhātu vāyāme ṇa. Soyeva videho. Imaṃ dīpamupādāya sineruno pubbadisabhāgattā pubbo ca so videho cāti pubbavideho, pubbadīpo.

31-32. The connection is that one may become the lord of humans and gods, or even the ruler of the four continents. ‘Of humans and gods’ means of humans and of gods; this is the genitive case in the objective sense. ‘Lord’ means ruler. For he protects those dependent on himself righteously, or having overcome them, he protects them; thus he is called ‘lord’ (adhipo). It is from the root pā preceded by adhi in the sense of protecting, with the suffix a. The meaning is that one may become the lord of humans, a human king, and the lord of gods, a king of gods. In ‘or even the ruler of the four continents,’ the particle pi is used in the sense of possibility. By this, it suggests the possibility of becoming a king of a single continent, and a king of a region. The particle vā is merely a verse-filler. ‘Ruler of the four continents’ means the ruler of the four continents—Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, Jambudīpa, and Uttarakuru; the meaning is that one may become a universal monarch ruling over them. Therein, Pubbavideha: being in the east of Sineru, it is eastern. Vedeho is so called because ‘they strive (īhanti) with wisdom (vedena)’ there. It is from the root īha in the sense of striving, with the word vida as a prefix, and the suffix ṇa. That itself is Videha. With reference to this continent, because it is in the eastern direction from Sineru, it is the eastern (pubbo) Videha, thus Pubbavideha, the eastern continent.

Aparagoyānoti [M 0.0221] sineruno apare pacchime bhavo aparo. Gavena yanti gacchanti etthāti goyāno. Gosaddūpapada yādhātu gamane yu. Sineruno pacchima disabhāgattā aparo ca so goyāno cāti aparagoyāno, pacchimadīpo. Jambudīpoti jāyatīti jambū. Yojanasatubbedho rukkho. Janadhātu janane ū. Nassa mo. Bakārāgamo. Jalamajjhe dippatīti dīpo, dippanti jotanti ettha saddhammāti vā dīpo. Dīpadhātu dittiyaṃ a. Tassa pana dviāpoti padacchedaṃ katvā dvidhā āpo sandati etthāti dīpoti bahubbīhisamāsopi yujjati. Jambuyā lakkhito paññāto vā dīpo jambudīpo, dakkhiṇadīpo. Uttarakurūti sineruno uttare bhavā uttarā. Dhammatāsiddhassa pañcasīlassa ānubhāvena kaṃ sukhaṃ urumahantaṃ etthāti kuru. Bahubbīhisamāsoyaṃ. Kuṃ vuccati pāpaṃ. Taṃ rundhanti etthāti vā kuru. Kupubbarudhidhātu āvaraṇe kvi. Dhātvantassa lopo. Sineruno uttaradisabhāgattā uttaro ca so kuru cāti uttarakuru. Uttaradīpoti catunnaṃ dīpānaṃ issaro catudīpissaro, cakkavattirājā labbhati.

Aparagoyāna: being in the west (apare) of Sineru, it is western (aparo). Goyāno is so called because ‘they go (yanti) with cattle (gavena)’ there. It is from the root yā in the sense of going, with the word go as a prefix and the suffix yu. Since it lies in the western direction of Sineru, it is called Aparagoyāna—the western continent. Jambudīpa is named after the Jambu tree. Jambū is so called because ‘it is born’ (jāyati). It is a tree a hundred yojanas high. It is from the root jan in the sense of being born, with the suffix ū, the transformation of na to ma, and the insertion of ba. Dīpa means ‘it shines (dippati) in the midst of water,’ or ‘where the true Dhamma shines (dippanti)’. It is from the root dīpa in the sense of shining, with the suffix a. Alternatively, by dividing the word as dvi-āpo, the meaning ‘where water (āpo) flows in two ways (dvidhā)’ is also suitable as a bahubbīhi compound. The island marked or known by the Jambu tree is Jambudīpa—the southern continent. Uttarakuru: being in the north (uttare) of Sineru, they are northern (uttarā). Kuru is so called because ‘by the power of the naturally established five precepts, happiness (kaṃ sukhaṃ) is great (uru)’ there. This is a bahubbīhi compound. Alternatively, kuṃ means evil, and kuru is where ‘it is restrained (rundhanti)’. It is from the root rudh in the sense of obstructing, with the prefix ku and the suffix kvi, with the elision of the final consonant of the root. Since it lies in the northern direction of Sineru, it is called Uttarakuru—the northern continent. The ruler of the four continents, a universal monarch, is obtained.

Evaṃ lokiyahitaṃ dassetvā idāni lokuttarahitaṃ dassento āha antime dehe…pe… subbatoti antime dehe subbato bhāvanāyānaṃ āruyha aññaṃ taṃ setachattakaṃ dhārento samaṃ essatīti sambandho. Tattha pana atthakkamena vaṇṇayissāma. Antimeti carime pacchime vā. Ante pariyosāne bhavo antimo, pacchimasarīro. Tasmiṃ. Deheti sarīre. Dihati upaciyati vaḍḍhatīti deho, sarīro. Dihadhātu upacaye ṇa. Atha vā dihati upacayati etena puññāpuññanti deho, pacchimabhavabhūte bhabbakulaputtabhūte vā sarīreti attho. Subbatoti suṭṭhu paṭipannako hutvā[M 0.0222]. Suṭṭhu vataṃ paṭipannaṃ assāti subbato. Vakārassabbo. Bhāvanāyānamāruyhāti bhāvanāyānaṃ āruyhāti padacchedo. Vipassanābhāvanāsaṅkhātayānaṃ āruhitvāti attho. Bhāvetabbā vaḍḍhetabbāti bhāvanā. Tebhūmaka saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ. Atha vā tadārammaṇaṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti bhāvanā, vipassanāpaññā. Bhūdhātu sattāyaṃ vaḍḍhane vā yu. Sā ca samathavipassanā bhāvanāvasena duvidhā hoti. Tattha idha pana aññaṃ setachattakanti saddantarasanniṭṭhānena vipassanābhāvanā adhippetā. Yanti pāpuṇanti etena nibbānanti yānaṃ, aniccādivipassanāñāṇaṃ. Yādhātu gatiyaṃ yu. Bhāvanāsaṅkhātaṃ yānaṃ bhāvanāyānaṃ, bhāvanā ca sā yānañcāti vā bhāvanāyānaṃ.

Having shown the worldly benefit, now, showing the supramundane benefit, it is said: ‘In the last body… well-practiced…’ The connection is: ‘In the last body, being well-practiced, having mounted the vehicle of development, bearing that other white parasol, one will attain peace.’ Here, we shall explain the meaning in due order. ‘Last’ means final or ultimate. That which exists at the end (ante), at the conclusion (pariyosāne), is the last (antimo); it is the final body. In that. ‘Body’: deho (body) is so called because it is accumulated (dihati), grown, or increased. The root dih is in the sense of accumulation; ṇa is the suffix. Alternatively, it is called ‘body’ because merit and demerit are accumulated by it. The meaning is: in the body of the final existence, being that of a worthy clansman. ‘Well-practiced’ means having practiced well. One for whom the practice (vataṃ) is well (suṭṭhu) undertaken is subbato. The va becomes bba. ‘Having mounted the vehicle of development’: the word division is bhāvanāyānaṃ āruyha. It means having ascended the vehicle designated as the development of insight. Bhāvanā (development) means what should be cultivated or increased. Its object is the conditioned things of the three realms. Alternatively, it is called ‘development’ because one cultivates and increases that object—it is the wisdom of insight. The root bhū is in the sense of being or of growth; yu is the suffix. This development is twofold: serenity and insight. Here, however, by the proximity of the other words, ‘that other white parasol,’ the development of insight is intended. Yāna (vehicle) is so called because by it one goes to, one attains Nibbāna—it is the knowledge of insight into impermanence, etc. The root yā is in the sense of movement; yu is the suffix. The vehicle designated as development is bhāvanāyānaṃ; or, development which is a vehicle is bhāvanāyānaṃ.

Āruyhāti ārohitvā. Pakatiyānasadisaṃ anicca dukkhaanattayānaṃ āruhitvāti attho. Aniccādilakkhaṇena hi vinā maggaphalanibbānaṃ patto nāma natthi. Tasmā bhāvanāyānamāruyhāti vuttaṃ. Aññanti arahattaphalaṃ. Tañhi paṭhamamaggena ādiṭṭhamariyādaṃ anatikkamitvā catusaccadhammaṃ avabujjhatīti aññanti vuccati. Āpubbañādhātu avabodhane kvi. Āsaddo mariyādattho. Setachattakanti odātātapattaṃ. Seviyatīti setaṃ, dhavalaṃ. Sidhātu sevāyaṃ ta. Kilesatapaṃ chādetīti chattaṃ. Chadadhātu saṃvaraṇe ta. Taṃyeva chattakaṃ. Setañca taṃ chattakañcāti setachattakaṃ. Arahattaphalaātapattaṃ labbhati. Aññaṃ arahattaphalasaṅkhātaṃ setachattakaṃ dhārento hutvāti sambandho. Samanti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi sabbaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ samati vūpasamati nirujjhati etthāti samanti vuccati. Essatīti pāpuṇissatīti.

‘Having ascended’ means having climbed. The meaning is having ascended the vehicle of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, which is like an ordinary vehicle. For without the characteristics of impermanence and so on, no one has ever attained the path, fruit, and Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said, ‘having mounted the vehicle of development.’ ‘The other’ (aññaṃ) is the fruit of arahantship. For, not transgressing the limit shown by the first path, it understands the doctrine of the four truths; thus it is called aññā (final knowledge). It is from the root ñā preceded by ā, in the sense of awakening, with the suffix kvi. The particle ā is in the sense of a limit. ‘The white parasol’ means a white umbrella. Setaṃ (white) is so called because ‘it is served’ (seviyati); it means pure (dhavalaṃ). It is from the root si in the sense of serving, with the suffix ta. Chattaṃ (parasol) is so called because ‘it covers (chādeti) the heat of the defilements’. It is from the root chad in the sense of covering, with the suffix ta. That very parasol (chattaṃ) is a small parasol (chattakaṃ). White and that small parasol is setachattakaṃ. The umbrella of the fruit of arahantship is obtained. The connection is: ‘…being one who bears the white parasol designated as the fruit of arahantship…’ ‘Peace’ (samaṃ) is Nibbāna. For, all the suffering of the round of rebirths is calmed (samati), subsides (vūpasamati), and ceases (nirujjhati) therein; thus it is called samaṃ. ‘Will come to’ means will attain.

Idāni diṭṭhadhammikatthaṃ dassento imasmiṃ attabhāvepītiādimāha. Tattha imasmiṃ attabhāvepi arogo ca dīghāyuko ca sabbalokehi pūjito ca bhāvanābhi ratimano [M 0.0223] ca janappiyo ca manāpo ca bhaveyyāti yojanā. Attabhāvepīti ettha pisaddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena samparāyikatthaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Attāti bhavati etena abhidhānaṃ buddhi cāti attabhāvo. Khandhapañcakassetamadhivacanaṃ. Arogoti sabbabyādhiviraho ca. So hi natthi rogo assāti arogoti vuccati. Dīghajīvikoti dīghāyuko ca. So hi dīghā jīvi āyu assāti dīghajīvikoti vuccati.

Now, to show the benefit in this very life, he says, 'imasmiṃ attabhāvepi,' and so on. Herein, the connection is: 'In this very life, may one be free from illness, long-lived, honored by all the world, with a mind delighting in meditation, beloved and pleasing to the people.' In the phrase 'attabhāvepi,' the particle 'pi' has the meaning of inclusion. Thus, it includes the benefit in the future life. 'Attabhāvo' (existence) is so called because by it there is designation and understanding. This is a term for the five aggregates. 'Arogo' means freedom from all diseases. For he who has no illness is called 'arogo.' 'Dīghajīviko' means long-lived. For he who has a long life is called 'dīghajīviko.'

33. Sabbalokehīti sabbadevamanussehi. Pūjitoti pūjitabbo ca. Bhāvanābhiratimanoti samathavipassanā saṅkhātāya bhāvanāya abhiramaṇacitto ca. Janappiyoti sabbajanehi piyāyitabbo ca. Manāpoti sabbasattānaṃ cittavaḍḍhanako ca bhaveyyāti sambandho.

33. 'By all the worlds' means by all gods and humans. 'Honored' means worthy of being honored. 'With a mind delighting in meditation' means having a mind that delights in the meditation known as serenity and insight. 'Beloved by the people' means one who should be loved by all people. 'Pleasing' means one who gladdens the minds of all beings—this is the connection.

Evaṃ chabbīsatiyā vandanagāthāsu ekagāthāmattampi buddhaguṇānussaraṇe phalānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā idāni sabbagāthāyo vacasā dhāretvā buddhavandane anekāni phalānisaṃsāni dassetuṃ kā kathākhiladhāraṇeti āha. Tattha kā kathākhiladhāraṇeti kā kathā akhiladhāraṇeti padacchedo. Sabbabuddhavandanagāthāya vacasā dhāraṇe kiṃ vattabbā yevāti attho.

Thus, having shown the fruit and benefit of recollecting the Buddha's virtues in even a single verse among the twenty-six verses of veneration, now, to demonstrate the many fruits and benefits of retaining all the verses by word and venerating the Buddha, he says: 'What need be said of retaining them all?' Herein, 'kā kathākhiladhāraṇeti' is the division of words 'kā kathā akhiladhāraṇe.' The meaning is: What indeed is to be said about retaining all the verses of veneration of the Buddha by word?

Ettha ca akhilasaddo sabbavācako anipphannapāṭipadiko. Atha vā khiyanaṃ khilaṃ. Khidhātu khaye lapaccayo. Khayaṃ lāti gaṇhātīti vā khilaṃ, appakaṃ. Khayasaddūpapadalādhātu gahaṇe a. Na khilaṃ akhilaṃ, sabbagāthāyo. Dhāriyate dhāraṇaṃ, akhilāya sabbāya gāthāya dhāraṇaṃ akhiladhāraṇaṃ, tasmiṃ. Chabbīsatiyā buddhavandanagāthāsu ekaṃ gāthaṃ vacasā dhārayitvā buddhavandane yathāvuttaphalānisaṃsāni labbhanti, pageva pana sabbabuddhavandanagāthāyo vacasā dhārayitvā dine dine buddhavandaneti [M 0.0224] atthoti. Iminā pana gāthāpañcakena yathāvutta phalānisaṃsaṃ ñatvā saddahako sammādiṭṭhiko kulaputto sabbabuddhavandanagāthāyo vacasā dhārayitvā rattindivaṃ pubbaṇhakāle ca sāyanhakāle ca rattiyā paṭhamayāme ca pacchimayāme ca satataṃ samitaṃ nirantaraṃ buddhaṃ vandeyyāti uyyojanaṃ dassetīti.

Herein, the word 'akhila' denotes 'all' and is an underived nominal stem. Alternatively, 'khila' is 'khiyanaṃ' (decay). The root 'khid' is in the sense of decay, with the suffix 'la'. Or, 'khila' means 'it takes (lāti) or grasps (gaṇhāti) decay (khayaṃ),' hence 'little.' The word 'khaya' is a prefix to the root 'lā' in the sense of grasping, with the suffix 'a'. 'Not khila' is 'akhila,' meaning all the verses. 'Dhāraṇaṃ' is 'upholding'; the upholding of all the verses, which are 'akhila,' is 'akhiladhāraṇaṃ,' in that. By retaining even one verse of the twenty-six verses of veneration of the Buddha by word, one obtains the fruits and benefits as stated; how much more so, then, by retaining all the verses of veneration of the Buddha by word and venerating the Buddha day by day—this is the meaning. Furthermore, by these five verses, it is shown that a faithful son of a good family with right view, having known the fruits and benefits as stated, should retain all the verses of veneration of the Buddha by word and venerate the Buddha day and night—in the morning and evening, during the first and last watches of the night—constantly, perpetually, and without interruption. This shows the exhortation.

Pañcakagāthāvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the five verses is complete.

Iti porāṇācariyehi vanditassa namakkārassa saddatthanayehi chandālaṅkāranayehi ca saṇhasukhumasududdasa gambhīrassa buddhassa duppaṭividhaguṇaparidīpakassa sappurisānaṃ cittapasannajanakassa sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye asaṃhira visāradañāṇacārinā sāsanasodhakena bhaddantareva tattheravarena racitā buddhaguṇappadīpikanāmikā vaṇṇanā.

Thus, the explanation named 'The Illuminator of the Buddha's Virtues' was composed by the venerable elder Bhaddantareva—a purifier of the Dispensation who moved with unhesitating and expert knowledge in the Three Piṭakas with their commentaries. This is an explanation of the homage which was venerated by the ancient teachers; which is profound in its methods of grammar, prosody, and rhetoric; which is subtle, fine, very difficult to see, and deep; which illuminates the qualities of the Buddha that are difficult to penetrate; and which generates serenity in the minds of good people.

Nigamana

Conclusion

Idaṃ pana puraṃ nimmitena sirīpavaravijayānantayasapaṇḍita tribhavanādityādhipatimahādhammarājādhirājāti lañchitanāmikena piṭakattayapāḷiṃ silārūḷhaṃ kārayitvā pañcama saṅgītikaraṇena timahādhammarājena ratanāpuñjanti sammate rājadhānībhūte nānākulasaṃkiṇṇe puññadhaññavantānaṃ sādhūnañca sīlasamādhipaññavantānaṃ bhikkhūnañca nivāsabhūte buddhadhammasaṅgharatanākare candimasūriyā viya buddhasāsanujjotane mantale nagare iti parikittite mahārāme dese vasantena upāsaka guṇasampannena nāmikena upāsakena ca tassupaṭṭhākāya nāmikāya upāsikāya ca samakusalacchandaṃ katvā nibbānassa sacchikaraṇatthāya kārite manorame suvaṇṇena limpitattā suvaṇṇavatī nāmike [M 0.0225] dvibhummike mahiṭṭhakavihāre aṭṭhahi disāhi āgatānaṃ sutesanabhikkhūnaṃ sāṭṭhakathaṃ piṭakattayaṃ dine dine satataṃ nirantaraṃ vācentena adhivasantena sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye asaṃhiravisāradañāṇacārinā mantale pure pariyattisāsanahitadhammācariyagaṇassa jeṭṭhukkaṭṭhabhūtena revatābhipaṇḍitadhajasāsanavaṃsamahādhammarājagurūti ca agga mahāpaṇḍitāti ca laddhalañchitena mūladvādasasāsana karamahāgaṇassa jeṭṭhamahānāyakabhūtena sāsanāpruñño ācariyoti vissutena sāsanasodhaka mahānāyakattheravarena porāṇehi tattha tattha pāḷiyaṃ bhagavatā vuttehi buddhaguṇappakāsakehi buddhaguṇapadehi thomitvā vanditassa atthabyañjanena chandālaṅkāranayena ca pathavīsandhārakassa udakakkhandhassa viya gambhīrassa pabbatena paṭicchādetvā ṭhapitassa vatthussa viya atiduddasassa satadhā bhinnassa vālassa aggakoṭiyā viya atisaṇha sukhumassa puthujjanañāṇena buddhassa duppaṭividhaguṇaparidīpakassa namakkārassa līnatthappakāsanā buddhaguṇappadīpikanāmikā saṃvaṇṇanā tāsu tāsu aṭṭhakathāṭīkāsu āgataṃ saṃvaṇṇanānayaṃ nissāya paññāpāṭavatthāya sāsanavuddhiyā ca katā.

This commentary named Buddhaguṇappadīpikā, which clarifies the hidden meaning of the homage, was composed based on the commentarial method found in various commentaries and sub-commentaries, for the development of wisdom and the growth of the Dispensation. This homage was praised and venerated by the ancients with terms that reveal the Buddha's qualities, spoken by the Blessed One here and there in the Pāli canon. It is profound like the earth-supporting mass of water, extremely difficult to see like an object covered and hidden by a mountain, and exceedingly fine and subtle like the tip of a hair split a hundred times, revealing the qualities of the Buddha that are difficult to penetrate by the knowledge of ordinary people. This work was composed by the great elder, the purifier of the Dispensation, renowned as 'Ācariya Sāsanāpruñño,' the chief great leader of the original twelve Sāsana Kara Mahāgaṇas, who received the titles 'Revatābhipaṇḍitadhajasāsanavaṃsamahādhammarājaguru' and 'Aggamahāpaṇḍita.' He was the foremost among the assembly of teachers of the scriptural Dispensation in the city of Mantale and moved with unhesitating and expert knowledge in the Three Piṭakas with their commentaries. He resided in the delightful, two-storied, magnificent monastery named Suvaṇṇavatī because it was gilded with gold, while continually and daily teaching the Three Piṭakas with their commentaries to the monks who came from the eight directions seeking to learn. This monastery was caused to be built for the sake of realizing Nibbāna by a certain layman endowed with virtue and by his attendant, a certain laywoman, who made a shared wholesome aspiration. It is located in the great monastery in the city of Mantale, renowned as Ratanāpuñja. This city was the capital established by the great king of kings, the great king of Dhamma, whose title is Sirīpavaravijayānantayasapaṇḍita Tribhavanādityādhipati, who caused the Pāli of the Three Piṭakas to be inscribed on stone and held the Fifth Council. This city is teeming with various families, a dwelling place for meritorious and wealthy people and for monks endowed with virtue, concentration, and wisdom, a mine of the gems of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, illuminating the Buddha's Dispensation like the moon and sun.

Ettāvatā ca –

And thus far –

Sampatte cakkavasse sā, dvisahasse catūsate;

Navādhikāsitīyā ca, sakkarāje ca sampatte.

When the wheel-year two thousand four hundred and eighty-nine had arrived, and the Saka era had also arrived.

Sattatisatasahassa, vasse phussamāsasseva;

Kālapakkhasattame ca, buddhadine suniṭṭhitā; Sāmañña.

In the year one thousand two hundred and seventy, in the month of Phussa, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight, on a Wednesday, it was well completed. General.

Esā ca saṅkharontena, yaṃ puññaṃ pasutaṃ mayā;

Aññampi tena puññena, patvā sambodhimuttamaṃ.

By whatever merit has been produced by me while composing this, and by other merit as well,

Saṃsārato [M 0.0226] bahū satte, tārayitvā taṇhakkhayaṃ;

Nibbānaṃ sacchikāreyyaṃ, maggañāṇuttarena ca.

having attained supreme enlightenment and having helped many beings cross over from saṃsāra, may I realize Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, through the supreme path-knowledge.

Sadā rakkhantu rājāno, dhammeneva pajaṃ imaṃ;

Sabbe sattā sukhī hontu, jotentu jinasāsanaṃ.

May kings always protect this people with righteousness; may all beings be happy; may the Teaching of the Conqueror shine forth.

Mrammaraṭṭhe manussā ca, sabbadā nirupaddavā;

Niccaṃ kalyāṇasaṅkappā, pappontu amataṃ padanti.

May the people in the land of Myanmar always be free from calamities; may they constantly harbor wholesome intentions and attain the deathless state.

Buddhaguṇappadīpikanāmikā

The Illuminator of the Buddha's Virtues

Namakkāraṭīkā samattā.

The Sub-commentary on the Homage is complete.
